authorString: Tugaeva GK, Upatova AG, Bunin ES, Efremov YM, Kosheleva NV, Timashev PS.
abstractText: The mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC)-derived secretome is emerging as a promising cell-free therapeutic product for tissue repair and regeneration. It contains soluble proteins, growth factors, nucleic acids, and extracellular vesicles (EVs), whose combined activity supports angiogenesis, immunomodulation, cytoprotection, and extracellular matrix remodelling. However, the biological activity of these components can be compromised during processing, storage, scaffold loading, and release. This review examines electrospun scaffolds as delivery platforms for the MSC-derived secretome, with particular attention to EV preservation and analytical evaluation. Selected non-electrospun platforms are discussed as comparators to clarify the advantages and limitations of electrospun delivery systems. We discuss how polymer composition, solvent exposure, crosslinking, fibre architecture, and loading strategy affect cargo retention, release kinetics, and biological activity. Post-fabrication adsorption generally minimises processing-related exposure of labile components but often results in rapid release, whereas matrix incorporation, affinity-based immobilisation, and microsphere-assisted loading can prolong delivery while introducing additional risks to vesicle and protein stability. Preclinical studies across these scaffold platforms report beneficial effects in models of skin, bone, cartilage, nerve, periodontal, and cardiac repair, but comparisons remain limited by inconsistent secretome preparation, dose reporting, and analytical methods. Progress towards translation will require standardised characterisation of both soluble and vesicular fractions, dose normalisation to scaffold mass or area, functional potency assays, and validation in long-term, clinically relevant animal models. Together, these developments will enable more reproducible engineering of electrospun secretome-delivery systems and support their clinical translation.

title: Ethical Decision-Making for TAVR in Very Elderly Patients: Beyond Chronological Age Toward Meaningful Clinical Benefit.
authorString: da Silveira Maia A, Ribeiro BS, Philippart KS, Filho AAM, Rascov L, Cividanes FR, Grinberg M, de Almeida Palma da Fonseca JH, Jatene FB.

journal.title: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions

abstractText: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has emerged as a transformative therapy for severe aortic stenosis, yet its application in very elderly patients raises complex clinical and ethical challenges. Chronological age alone is an inadequate basis for treatment selection. Patients of similar age may differ substantially in frailty, functional reserve, cognitive status, comorbidity burden and projected survival. Available evidence suggests that carefully selected nonagenarians can experience acceptable survival and meaningful improvements in symptoms and quality of life after TAVR, although outcomes remain heterogeneous and are strongly influenced by factors beyond age. This review examines ethical decision-making for TAVR in very elderly patients through a patient-centered framework integrating projected survival, frailty, functional recovery, cognition, quality of life, and individual preferences. Particular attention is given to the concept of procedural futility and to the challenges of applying these principles in resource-constrained healthcare systems. Brazil is presented as an illustrative example of broader challenges shared by many low- and middle-income countries, including disparities in access, limited availability of multidisciplinary and palliative care, family-centered decision-making, and rapidly aging populations. A shift from chronological age toward expected survival with meaningful clinical benefit may provide a more clinically relevant approach to TAVR selection in advanced age.

title: Unusual Flow Preservation Through a Malapposed Stent Inside a Giant Coronary Aneurysm.
authorString: Papoutsakis A, Pagonidis K, Patrianakos A, Hamilos M.

journal.title: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions

abstractText: Our case illustrates a rare adaptive mechanism in an in-stent chronic total occlusion inside a coronary aneurysm: occlusion of the proximally malapposed stent and restored distal flow through the lateral stent wall inside the aneurysm, enabling distal vessel perfusion. This mechanism was documented with multimodality imaging and has not been previously described. These unique angiographic and imaging findings illustrate a novel compensatory phenomenon inside a giant coronary aneurysm functioning as a natural bypass, maintaining distal myocardial perfusion despite complete proximal stent occlusion.

title: BAT Activation and Cardiometabolic Protection: Weighing Realities of Mechanistic Studies From Epidemiological Promises.
authorString: Hashim D, Carpentier AC, Hoeks J, Blondin DP.
abstractText: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) is a thermogenic organ that, per gram, consumes glucose and lipids at high rates and secretes endocrine factors (batokines) that act on liver, muscle, and the vasculature to modulate insulin sensitivity, lipid metabolism, and hemodynamic function. These features provide several plausible routes by which its activation could improve cardiometabolic health. Large retrospective cohorts have consistently found associations between the incidental uptake of the glucose analogue [<sup>18</sup>F]fluorodeoxyglucose in BAT with lower prevalence of type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hepatic steatosis, cardiovascular disease, and impaired vascular function. Cold exposure and β-adrenergic agonism remain the best-established activators of human BAT metabolism and produce measurable improvements in insulin sensitivity and lipid profiles. Nevertheless, skeletal muscle, white adipose tissue, and the cardiovascular system are coactivated by the same stimuli, rendering difficult to isolate the independent contribution of BAT. This review aims to describe the mechanistic basis, the observational and interventional human evidence, and the safety considerations relevant to BAT as a cardiometabolic target and highlight the lack of specificity in directly targeting BAT thermogenesis to decipher its clinically meaningful impact on metabolic health in humans.

title: Carotene Status Is Associated With Biological Aging and a Resident-Like Macrophage State in Cardiovascular Disease.
authorString: Zhang K, Wang Y, Chen P, Zhang M, Zhou M, Ye S, Zhu Z.
abstractText:
Background

Circulating carotene has been implicated in cardiovascular protection, potentially through modulation of biological aging. Yet the epidemiological, genetic, and mechanistic foundations linking carotene to cardiovascular disease (CVD) remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the associations of circulating carotene with biological aging and cardiovascular disease and to characterize the related cellular and molecular features within atherosclerotic tissues.

Methods

We analyzed data from 8114 participants to assess circulating carotene levels, biological aging metrics, and CVD prevalence using multivariable regression, mediation analysis, and Mendelian randomization. Multiomics profiling, including bulk, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomic analyses, was performed on human atherosclerotic plaques to characterize carotenoid-associated cellular programs. β-Carotene supplementation was also evaluated in a murine atherosclerosis model.

Results

Higher circulating α-carotene and β-carotene levels were associated with lower CVD prevalence and lower biological aging indices. Mediation models yielded estimated indirect-effect proportions of 15% to 23% for the carotene-CVD associations. Mendelian randomization provided evidence consistent with a potential causal relationship between carotene and CVD. Human single-cell analyses identified a resident-like/homeostatic macrophage cluster with M2-like transcriptional features (Macro4) and the highest carotenoid-associated signature score. In spatial analyses, higher carotenoid-associated and Macro4 signature scores coincided with lower SenMayo scores. In mice, β-carotene supplementation was accompanied by reduced plaque burden, lower p21 expression, increased Macro4-like macrophage abundance, and a less inflammatory cytokine profile.

Conclusions

Integrating population, genetic, cellular, spatial, and animal evidence, these findings support an association of carotene with lower CVD prevalence and biological aging indices and suggest that macrophage-associated inflammatory and senescence-related programs may accompany this relationship. The specific contribution of Macro4-like macrophages to the vascular response to β-carotene warrants further investigation.

title: Retrograde Approach for Chronic Total Occlusion Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in Young Patients Post-Arterial Switch Operation: A Case Series.
authorString: Bulnes JF, van Beynum I, Diletti R, Wilschut J.

journal.title: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions

abstractText: We report the cases of three young patients presenting with chronic total occlusions (CTO) affecting reimplanted coronary arteries following arterial switch operation (ASO), who were treated with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) using the retrograde approach. Despite the unique procedural challenges posed by reimplanted coronary vessels, retrograde PCI was technically successful in all cases. This series highlights the potential role of PCI in a population traditionally managed with surgical revascularization and underscores the importance of increasing awareness of CTO PCI within pediatric and congenital cardiology teams. Finally, it raises critical considerations regarding the optimal timing of intervention, balancing procedural feasibility, growth-related anatomical challenges, and the potential consequences of long-lasting coronary occlusion.

title: Developing a Pragmatic Framework for Assessing Unexplained Falls in Older Adults: A Multidisciplinary Delphi Study.
authorString: Averlant L, Morel E, Robinet P, Puisieux F, Visade F.

journal.title: Journal of applied gerontology : the official journal of the Southern Gerontological Society

abstractText: BackgroundFalls in older adults are a major public health concern, and their etiology may remain unclear after initial evaluation. Unexplained falls represent a clinical situation in which no clear explanation is identified following the initial assessment and may require a structured diagnostic approach.ObjectiveTo develop a multidisciplinary framework for the initial assessment of unexplained falls in older adults.MethodsA modified Delphi consensus study was conducted with nine experts in geriatrics, cardiology, neurology, ENT, and general practice. An initial list of 28 items derived from a targeted literature review was evaluated using a 5-point Likert scale. Items reaching consensus were retained, while items not reaching consensus were excluded or discussed and reformulated before re-rating.ResultsThe final consensus identified 16 key items across three domains: case history, clinical examination, and targeted investigations. Cardiovascular, neurological, vestibular, and iatrogenic factors were central to the assessment. Experts emphasized clinical reasoning and targeted investigations rather than exhaustive testing. Cardiovascular assessment, specialist referral when indicated, and medication review were considered essential components of care.

title: Tricuspid Valve Chordae Tendineae: Where are They, How Many are There, and What are Their Properties?
authorString: Haese CE, Kostelnik CJ, Dubey VK, Seetharam S, Mathur M, Tondi D, Duda MM, Higa KC, Fong R, Malinowski M, Piekarska M, Buganza Tepole A, Fuhg JN, Moussa ID, Summers MR, Votta E, Hiesinger W, Timek TA, Rausch MK.
abstractText:
Background:

Tricuspid chordae play an important role in valve function. Unfortunately, they are poorly visible in clinical imaging and their mechanical properties cannot be measured noninvasively. This lack of data on chordal structure and properties limits our understanding of the tricuspid valve in general and efforts to model the valve in particular.

Objectives:

Our primary objective was to quantify chordal insertion patterns, structure, and mechanical properties. Our secondary objective was to test whether chordal structure and properties differed between control hearts and hearts with heart failure.

Methods:

We mapped chordal insertions in 25 excised human valves, measured the cross-sectional areas of 281 specimens, and conducted uniaxial tensile tests on 265 specimens from 12 of the 25 valves (eight control and four heart failure). We used mixed-effects models to assess the influence of heart failure and anatomical position. Finally, we used a hierarchical Bayesian model to represent area-dependent Ogden material parameters.

Results:

We found that chordal insertion density was highest at the free edge (p < 0.001), and lowest in the anterior leaflet (p < 0.001). Median cross-sectional area was 0.223 mm2, with anterior chordae the largest (p < 0.001) and septal the smallest (p < 0.001). A 10% increase in cross-sectional area was associated with 5.3% and 3.3% decreases in toe and calf stiffness, respectively. Heart failure was not associated with larger areas or higher stiffness.

Conclusions:

Human chordal geometry and material behavior varied with location and size. These openly shared data support assigning chordal insertions, sizes, and material properties in tricuspid valve models.

title: FIB-4 Index and Isolated Nocturnal Hypertension Despite Normal Daytime Blood Pressure in a Cross-Sectional Study Running Title: FIB-4 and Isolated Nocturnal Hypertension
authorString: Muştu M, Kılıç O, Oner DY, Coskun CA, Isguder HO.
abstractText: Background Evidence relating the fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index to isolated nocturnal hypertension is limited. We evaluated the association between FIB-4 and isolated nocturnal hypertension in adults undergoing ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM). Methods This single-center retrospective cross-sectional study included 239 untreated adults who underwent ABPM and same-day laboratory testing between October 1, 2025, and June 1, 2026. Isolated nocturnal hypertension was defined as nighttime systolic blood pressure ≥ 120 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure ≥ 70 mmHg, with daytime blood pressure < 135/85 mmHg. FIB-4 was compared between 67 patients with isolated nocturnal hypertension and 172 normotensive participants. Sequential logistic regression models included age in the final model; model calibration and variance explanation were assessed using the Hosmer–Lemeshow test and Nagelkerke R² statistics; and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis evaluated the diagnostic performance of FIB-4 alone. Results FIB-4 was higher in patients with isolated nocturnal hypertension (median [interquartile range], 1.390 [1.000–2.670] vs. 0.785 [0.545–1.043]; p < 0.001). After adjustment for age, C-reactive protein (CRP), urea, creatinine, and sex, FIB-4 remained associated with the outcome (adjusted odds ratio [OR] per 1-unit increase, 11.431; 95% confidence interval [CI], 4.827–27.070; p < 0.001). CRP was also associated with the outcome (adjusted OR, 1.084; 95% CI, 1.022–1.149; p = 0.007). Age was positively associated in univariable analysis but inversely associated in the final model (adjusted OR, 0.956; 95% CI, 0.924–0.988; p = 0.008). The unadjusted area under the ROC curve for FIB-4 was 0.791 (95% CI, 0.723–0.859); a sample-derived cutoff of 0.975 yielded 77.6% sensitivity and 70.9% specificity. Conclusions Higher FIB-4 values were associated with isolated nocturnal hypertension after adjustment for age and other included covariates. Incremental predictive value and clinical utility remain to be established and require independent validation.

title: First-line zanubrutinib-rituximab-methotrexate for newly diagnosed PCNSL (Zana): prospective outcomes and exploratory CSF ctDNA profiling
authorString: Zhao W, Wang L, Xia Z, Zhang M, Song Q, Shi Q, Xu Q, Xu P, Cheng S.
abstractText: Primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) remains an aggressive malignancy with suboptimal long-term control using high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX)-based therapy. We prospectively evaluated zanubrutinib, rituximab, and HD-MTX (ZRM) and explored cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) in newly diagnosed, transplantation-ineligible PCNSL. In this investigator-initiated phase II study (NCT05896007), patients received zanubrutinib 160 mg twice daily, rituximab, and HD-MTX for up to six cycles, followed by zanubrutinib maintenance. The primary endpoint was 2-year progression-free survival (PFS); secondary endpoints included response, overall survival (OS), and safety. Exploratory analyses included tumor and CSF genomics and paired profiles. Twenty-nine patients were enrolled (median age 60 years; 72.4% intermediate/high IELSG risk; 58.6% ECOG ≥ 2). The overall response rate was 89.7%, with all responders achieving complete remission. In the per-protocol cohort (n = 25), estimated 2-year PFS and OS were 84.0% and 96.0%, respectively, after median follow-up of 32.5 months. Grade ≥ 3 neutropenia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia each occurred in 17.2%; no atrial fibrillation, major bleeding, or invasive fungal infections occurred. Tumor and CSF profiling identified MYD88 and CD79B alterations; higher baseline CSF ctDNA burden and TP53/CXCR4 mutations suggested potential risk associations warranting validation.

title: Changes in Renal Function Following Emergency Percutaneous Nephrostomy and Factors Influencing Outcomes: A Retrospective Comparative Study
authorString: Li Y, Fan Y, Jiang W.
abstractText: Background Although emergency percutaneous nephrostomy (PCN) is a standard procedure for relieving hydronephrosis, postoperative renal functional changes are poorly characterized. This study was designed to assess renal function before and after PCN and to explore the influencing factors. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on clinical data from 130 patients who underwent emergency PCN for hydronephrosis at the Affiliated Hospital of Qingdao University over the past 5 years. Data collected included preoperative and short-term postoperative parameters. Results Among the 130 patients, 74 cases were classified into the significant short-term renal function recovery group, while the remaining 56 cases were assigned to the non-significant recovery group. Statistically significant differences between the two groups were observed in preoperative age, cystatin C levels, and the prevalence of hypertension, while logistic regression further confirmed age and cystatin C as significant risk factors. Conclusion For emergency PCN, the degree of preoperative renal pelvis anterior-posterior diameter (APD) showed no correlation with short-term postoperative changes in renal function, whereas advanced age and elevated cystatin C levels may be considered risk factors for short-term functional changes.

title: Long-Term Intraocular Pressure Dynamics After Selective Stromal Melanin Modulation: A Testable Mechanistic Framework
authorString: Mete M.
abstractText:
Background:

Conventional aqueous outflow is governed by trabecular meshwork (TM) cells, juxtacanalicular extracellular matrix (ECM), Schlemm’s canal (SC) endothelium, and local immune-cell populations. Iris-directed selective stromal melanin modulation (SSMM), unlike selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT), does not directly irradiate these outflow tissues. Whether iris-derived debris or secondary soluble signals can generate a persistent change in conventional outflow is unknown.

Objective:

To evaluate the proposed iris-to-outflow signaling chain against primary pigment-loading experiments, SLT studies, resident-macrophage biology, SC mechanotransduction, ECM homeostasis, clinical reports of iris laser treatment, and experimental models capable of falsifying the hypothesis.

Methods:

This targeted, non-systematic narrative synthesis critically compares experimental pigment-loading studies, selective laser trabeculoplasty, outflow-tract macrophage biology, Schlemm’s canal mechanotransduction, matrix remodeling, and clinical reports of cosmetic iris laser procedures. Individual experiments are described within their tested models, and cross-model analogies are distinguished from SSMM-specific predictions. A Goldmann-equation sensitivity analysis is illustrative only. No patient-level SSMM cohort or new experiment was analyzed. Synthesis: In experimental models, pigment loading can obstruct aqueous outflow, whereas phagocytic challenges can elicit substrate-dependent matrix-related gene responses. Monocyte-associated facility changes after SLT and a homeostatic role for resident outflow macrophages in mice are demonstrated in distinct settings; they are not interchangeable mechanisms. Pressure-driven FYN–CDH5 regulation has been measured in mouse Schlemm’s canal, while other endothelial models identify phosphorylation-site and stimulus-specific differences. Clinical reports include serious ocular hypertension after some cosmetic iris laser procedures, whereas a published 1,176-eye series reported no statistically significant average IOP change. Neither sustained SSMM-specific facility improvement nor its proposed causal sequence has been established.

Conclusion:

A persistent favorable change in conventional outflow after iris-directed pigment modification is an untested, falsifiable possibility rather than an observed mechanism. The most informative next studies would characterize laser-generated material, discriminate resident from recruited immune-cell effects, measure facility and tissue injury during exposure, and test persistence after washout. Separate controlled, standardized patient-level follow-up is necessary to establish clinical IOP trajectories and safety.

title: Association Between Renal Failure and Non-Prescription Cosmetic/Skin Care and Herbal Product Use: A Case-Control Study at UNTH, Enugu, Nigeria.
authorString: Onyedikachi UP, Treasure C G, Akpan-Brown IO, Onuwa FC, Oge SO, Oyeniyi DT, Id-Zik CP, Akwaeke JC, Mbakwe FK, Haque M, Abdulsalam MO, Benita NC, Egwu CC, Terkimbi SD, Onu SN.
abstractText:
Background:

Renal failure associated with exposure to potentially nephrotoxic substances in non-prescription cosmetic products, skincare preparations, and herbal remedies represents an emerging public health concern, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where regulation and safety monitoring remain limited. This study investigated the association between renal failure and exposure to cosmetic/skincare and herbal products among adults attending the University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital (UNTH), Enugu. Methods A hospital-based unmatched case–control study was conducted among 300 participants comprising 150 renal failure cases and 150 controls between September and December 2025. Cases included adults with confirmed chronic kidney disease stages 3–5, while controls had normal renal function. Bivariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results Renal failure cases were older than controls (54 ± 14 years vs 41 ± 15 years) and demonstrated lower educational attainment and income levels. Secondary cosmetic exposure was independently associated with renal failure (AOR = 3.40; 95% CI: 1.56–7.44; p = 0.002), while primary and secondary herbal exposure were independently associated with higher odds of disease (AOR = 4.00; 95% CI: 1.88–8.53; p < 0.001 and AOR = 7.50; 95% CI: 3.26–17.27; p < 0.001, respectively). Middle-aged and elderly individuals had higher odds of renal failure compared with younger adults (AOR = 4.46; 95% CI: 2.18–9.09; p < 0.001). Diabetes mellitus (AOR = 14.35; p < 0.001) and hypertension (AOR = 9.83; p < 0.001) were the strongest clinical correlates. Conclusion Renal failure among adults attending UNTH was statistically associated with repeated herbal exposure, secondary cosmetic exposure, older age, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. These findings do not establish causation because CKD etiology, chemical exposure, and renal histology were not assessed; prospective and toxicological studies are needed.

title: Self-Reported Uterine Fibroids and Cardiometabolic Risk Among Non-Hispanic Black Women Aged 20–54 Years: A Nationally Representative Cross-Sectional Analysis of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 1999–2006
authorString: Malasevskaia I, Rebellow D, Hasan M, Joshi A, Kilic A.
abstractText: Background Uterine fibroids disproportionately affect non-Hispanic Black women, who also bear a disproportionate burden of cardiometabolic disease. Evidence on the association between fibroids and cardiometabolic risk factors remains inconsistent. We examined the association between self-reported uterine fibroids and prevalent hypertension, diabetes, and obesity among non-Hispanic Black women aged 20–54 years. Methods Cross-sectional analysis of pooled NHANES 1999–2006 data (four cycles). Hysterectomy status was reconstructed using cycle-specific NHANES skip logic to preserve the full eligible sample. Survey-weighted modified Poisson regression estimated prevalence ratios (PR) with 95% CIs, adjusting for age, BMI, smoking, poverty-income ratio, and menopausal status. Missing covariates were handled with multiple imputation (20 datasets). Sensitivity analyses used alternative hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg) and obesity (BMI ≥25 and ≥ 35 kg/m  2 ) definitions, and included women with prior hysterectomy. Results Among 987 women (weighted n = 6,864,326), 16.3% self-reported fibroids. Women with fibroids were older (41.2 vs 33.9 years), had higher BMI (32.6 vs 31.0 kg/m  2 ), and higher prevalence of hypertension (50.4% vs 32.2%) and diabetes (10.7% vs 5.3%). In fully adjusted models, fibroids were not significantly associated with hypertension (PR 1.13; 95% CI 0.95–1.34), diabetes (PR 1.42; 95% CI 0.87–2.30), or obesity (PR 1.08; 95% CI 0.90–1.31). Using the 140/90 mmHg threshold (PR 1.36; 95% CI 1.07–1.73) and in the hysterectomy-inclusive analysis (PR 1.16; 95% CI 1.03–1.31), statistically significant associations with hypertension were observed. Conclusions After age adjustment, self-reported fibroids were not independently associated with hypertension, diabetes, or obesity in this sample. The significant hypertension findings at the 140/90 mmHg threshold and in the hysterectomy-inclusive analysis may reflect prevalence-ratio compression at the 130/80 threshold rather than a genuine absence of association. Renewal of NHANES uterine fibroid data collection in contemporary cycles is warranted.

title: Uric Acid/HDL Cholesterol Ratio and the Non-Dipping Blood Pressure Phenotype in Primary Hypertension.
authorString: Hancıoğlu E, İşleyen HB.

journal.title: Turk Kardiyoloji Dernegi arsivi : Turk Kardiyoloji Derneginin yayin organidir

abstractText:
Objective

We examined whether nocturnal dipping status in primary hypertension varies according to the serum uric acid-to-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (UHR) and evaluated the ratio's ability to distinguish patients classified as non-dippers from those classified as dippers.

Method

This retrospective cross-sectional study included 260 consecutive patients with primary hypertension and a finalized 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) report. Dipping status was obtained from the finalized clinical report. The UHR was calculated as serum uric acid divided by high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C). Its adjusted association with non-dipping was estimated using multivariable logistic regression. Sensitivity analyses in the 182 participants with retrievable detailed ABPM data additionally adjusted for 24-hour or nighttime mean systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was used to quantify apparent in-sample discrimination.

Results

There were 132 dippers (50.8%) and 128 non-dippers (49.2%). Median UHR values were 0.111 [0.104-0.118] and 0.129 [0.123-0.141], respectively (P < 0.001). In the primary model, the odds ratio (OR) for a 0.01 increase in UHR was 2.922 (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.188-3.901; P < 0.001). In the 182 patients with detailed ABPM data, the association persisted after additional adjustment for 24-hour systolic and diastolic blood pressure (OR, 2.685; 95% CI, 1.911-3.773; P < 0.001) and, separately, for nighttime systolic and diastolic blood pressure (OR, 2.622; 95% CI, 1.512-4.548; P < 0.001). The apparent area under the ROC curve (AUC) was 0.855 (95% CI, 0.805-0.900); the exploratory threshold of 0.122 had a sensitivity of 78.9% and a specificity of 84.8%.

Conclusion

A higher UHR was associated with the non-dipping phenotype, including after adjustment for ambulatory blood pressure levels. These cross-sectional findings do not establish incremental clinical utility, and the observed discrimination and threshold require independent validation.

title: Systolic blood pressure, rather than short-term blood pressure variability, is associated with arterial stiffness in the general population.
authorString: Sare S, Popp PS, Bonetti S, Del Giorno R, Külen A, Gabutti L.
abstractText:
Objective

Short-term blood pressure variability (BPV) has been proposed as a marker of vascular damage, but whether it adds information beyond mean SBP is unclear. We evaluated whether BPV is independently associated with arterial stiffness and nocturnal blood pressure dipping.

Methods

We analyzed 1084 adults from the Swiss population-based TEST study, all with valid 24-h ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), in a cross-sectional analysis. BPV was quantified using time-weighted average real variability (TW-ARV) and variation independent of mean (VIM). The primary outcome was carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cf-PWV); secondary outcomes were oscillometric PWV (o-PWV) and nocturnal systolic dipping.

Results

TW-ARV and log-transformed VIM were associated with cf-PWV and o-PWV in unadjusted analyses, but neither was independently associated with cf-PWV after adjustment: the confidence intervals excluded an effect larger than about 0.11 m/s per standard deviation, against a point estimate of 0.33 m/s per standard deviation for mean systolic pressure. Twenty-four-hour VIM was associated with nocturnal systolic dipping (adjusted beta = 9.90) and daytime VIM was not (beta = 0.25); conditioning the 24-h index on the day-night component reduced the coefficient to 3.75.

Conclusion

In this general population sample, the data excluded an independent association between short-term BPV and arterial stiffness larger than 0.11 m/s per standard deviation after adjustment for mean SBP. The association with nocturnal dipping was largely attributable to the day-night shift embedded in the variability measure.

title: Integrin-guided development of defined supramolecular hydrogels for human kidney tubuloid culture.
authorString: Roskothen-Shevchuk AJC, Veenbrink VA, Rijns L, Bakker B, Pou Casellas C, Drost J, Verhaar MC, Dankers PYW, Slaats GG.
abstractText: Tubuloids are epithelial organoids derived from tissue or urine that model tubular nephron segments of the kidney. Their use in preclinical research is limited by dependence on basement membrane extract (BME), a batch-variable animal-derived matrix that reduces reproducibility. Here, we evaluate defined supramolecular ureido-pyrimidinone (UPy) hydrogels as an alternative matrix for tubuloid culture. Re-analysis of a published tubuloid single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset guides selection of two ligands for UPy functionalization to support cell-matrix interactions: the αVβ3-binding cyclic RGD peptide (cRGDfK) and the laminin-derived IKVAV motif. Tubuloids are cultured in UPy gels functionalized with UPy-IKVAV, UPy-cRGDfK, or both, and compared with BME. UPy hydrogels and BME are comparably soft and predominantly elastic. Across experiments, tubuloid lines from six donors are evaluated by confocal imaging, gene expression analysis, and brightfield imaging. UPy-IKVAV hydrogels support cystic tubuloid formation, most closely resemble BME in morphology and lumen formation, and maintain a kidney marker profile comparable to BME after four days, whereas UPy-cRGDfK is associated with more irregular morphologies. Integrin β1 blockade disrupts lumen integrity in BME and UPy-IKVAV hydrogels, supporting a role for β1-mediated cell-matrix interactions in tubuloid organization. UPy-IKVAV hydrogels therefore support viable cystic tubuloids and show promise as a robust matrix for preclinical tubulopathy research.

title: Management of Advanced Uterovaginal Prolapse Under Local Anesthesia in a Patient with Complete Atrioventricular Block
authorString: Dejene WB, Goshu MT.
abstractText: Advanced pelvic organ prolapse can cause significant urinary and bowel dysfunction. Coexisting complete atrioventricular (AV) block with unavailability of temporary and permanent pacing poses significant perioperative anesthetic challenges. Our case involves a 70-year-old para 8 woman who presented with stage 4 uterovaginal prolapse complicated by difficulty defecating and urinary retention. She also had complete atrioventricular block with a ventricular rate of approximately 38 beats per minute, mild valvular regurgitation, and bronchial asthma. Pacemaker insertion was financially unaffordable. Following multidisciplinary assessment and high-risk informed consent, partial LeFort colpocleisis with perineorrhaphy was performed under local anesthesia using lidocaine infiltration with minimal systemic analgesia and continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring. The patient was stable throughout surgery and postoperatively and was discharged without complications. This case highlights the challenges of perioperative decision-making and the potential role of individualized anesthetic planning in resource-limited settings.

title: Electrophysiological Comparison of Mechanosensitive PIEZO1 Channel Currents across Different Human Cell Types
authorString: Muraki K.
abstractText: The detection of mechanical stress is essential for a wide range of physiological functions in humans, including touch sensation, hearing, and the maintenance of vascular myogenic tone. PIEZO1 is a mechanosensitive cation channel that is widely expressed in both neuronal and non-neuronal cells and plays critical physiological roles in multiple organs. However, the electrophysiological properties of endogenous PIEZO1-mediated mechanosensitive currents have not been systematically compared across different human cell types under identical experimental conditions. Here, the author compared the electrophysiological properties of endogenous human PIEZO1 (hPIEZO1) currents in four cultured human cell types: human aortic endothelial cells, human brain capillary endothelial cells, human fibroblast-like synoviocytes, and human osteoblast-like MG63 cells. Under whole-cell patch-clamp conditions, application of the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1 robustly activated hPIEZO1-like currents in all four cell types. In excised outside-out patch recordings, application of positive pressure to membrane patches from these cells also elicited PIEZO1-like channel currents, which were markedly potentiated by Yoda1 and effectively inhibited by gadolinium, a non-selective cation channel blocker. Furthermore, the unitary current amplitudes of single channel events evoked by mechanical stimulation were comparable to those elicited by Yoda1 across all four cell types. Collectively, these findings provide electrophysiological evidence that endogenous PIEZO1 functions as a mechanosensor in diverse human cell types and suggest that PIEZO1 contributes to mechanically regulated physiological processes in multiple human organs.
