Among 906,686 patients, model-adjusted first-year achievement was 60.6% for tobacco-free status, 61.9% for blood pressure control, 39.5% for antiplatelet therapy, and 63.4% for statin therapy; 10.4% achieved all four. Model-adjusted complete achievement was 12.4% in chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), 10.5% in claudication, and 10.2% in unspecified PAD. Model-adjusted rates varied by sex, race/ethnicity, insurance type, rurality, PAD severity, and comorbidities and ranged from 7.6% to 14.7%. Complete achievement in year 1 was associated with lower adjusted odds of amputation (odds ratio (OR), 0.91), vascular procedures (OR, 0.86), stroke (OR, 0.90), and myocardial infarction (OR, 0.94).

Conclusions:

In this large national EHR cohort, individual quality measures improved after PAD diagnosis, but only 10.4% of patients achieved all four assessed components during the first year after diagnosis. Differences across quality domains and patient subgroups highlight variation in longitudinal cardiovascular risk prevention, particularly among patients with less clinically apparent disease.

title: Intraoperative Hemodynamics and Associated Sex Based Outcomes Following Ascending Aortic Aneurysm Repair
authorString: Driggers J, Tarnasky A, Rosario-Rivera B, McIntyre-Smith A, Sultan I, Howard-Quijano K.
abstractText: Background Sex-based differences in thoracic ascending aortic aneurysm outcomes persist despite adjustment for preoperative factors, suggesting intraoperative variables may contribute to this disparity. While prior studies have examined surgical variables like bypass time and transfusions, modifiable intraoperative hemodynamic factors such as hypotension, hypoxia, and vasopressor requirements remain understudied. The objective of this study was to determine whether sex-based differences in intraoperative hemodynamics are associated with mortality differences following thoracic aortic aneurysm repair. Methods This was a retrospective study of 749 patients over 18 years of age who underwent non-emergent ascending aortic aneurysm repair from 2013–2020 at a single university hospital. Intraoperative variables assessed for both females and males included presence and duration of intraoperative hypotension and hypoxemia, surgical duration, Vasoactive-Inotrope Score (VIS), blood product transfusions, crystalloid and colloid infusion volumes, and hemoglobin levels. The primary outcome was 1-year mortality and secondary outcomes included 30-day mortality and days to death after surgery. Results Comparison of sex-based perioperative variables demonstrated that females, as compared to males, preoperatively were significantly older and had lower starting hemoglobin values. Intraoperatively, females had less hypotension, shorter operative duration, and less blood loss. Postoperatively, females experienced greater 1-year mortality, and less days to death than males. Multivariable regression analysis controlling for significant covariates found no significant association between hemodynamic variables or female sex and postoperative 1-year mortality. Instead, lower intraoperative hemoglobin levels and increased surgical duration were found to be independent predictors of increased 1-year mortality in both males and females undergoing ascending aortic surgical repair. Conclusions The results of this study suggest that differences in intraoperative modifiable hemodynamic variables are likely not associated with the sex-based differences seen in mortality after ascending aortic aneurysm repair. Further studies are needed to determine the underlying cause of sex-based differences in mortality and improve outcomes in this patient population.

title: Peripheral Arterial Disease and Outcomes in Patients Undergoing Renal Transplantation
authorString: De Lima JJG, Gowdak LHW, Pio-Abreu A, Reusing JO, David-Neto E, Ferreira SdAT, Bortolotto LA.
abstractText: Aims Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is prevalent in renal transplant patients but assessment is seldom considered a routine in pre-transplant workup. We examined the consequences of PAD assessment and evaluated if PAD detection may contribute to identify patients at higher risk of events. Methods A retrospective study in 903 renal transplant patients prospectively assessed for PAD by palpation and followed up until death. The endpoint was the composite incidence of death by any cause and/or major cardiovascular events. Results The median follow-up was 62 months. PAD occurred in 162/903 patients (18%). The end-point occurred in 71% in patients with PAD and in 57% of those without PAD (log-rank < 0.0001, HR 1.633, 95% CI 1.327–2.010) and was predicted by diabetes (HR 1.782, 95% CI 1.084–2.930) and coronary artery disease (HR 1.799, 95% CI 1.072–3.071). Patients with PAD had more occlusive arterial events (log-rank < 0.0001, HR 1.921, 95% CI 1.320–2.796) independently associated with diabetes and arteriopathy. Occlusive events occurred in only 31 subjects (3.4% of all subjects at risk). Amputation was performed in 18 patients, 2 subjects underwent percutaneous intervention and 11, were managed medically. Conclusion PAD is frequent in renal transplant patients, correlates with an increased incidence of major cardiovascular events but the probability of events directly attributed to limb ischemia is modest. PAD must be routinely evaluated because it allows the identification of individuals at higher risk of future cardiovascular events but patients with PAD should not be barred from the wait list. The decision to intervene in asymptomatic patients should be made individually.

title: Optical Coherence Tomography-Guided or Intravascular Ultrasound-Guided PCI for In-Stent Restenosis Lesions: Insights From the OCTIVUS Trial.
authorString: Seo KW, Kang DY, Ahn JM, Lee JS, Kim JH, Park HS, An SY, Wee SB, Lee S, Hur SH, Cho YK, Lee CH, Hong SJ, Lim S, Kim SW, Won H, Hong YJ, Yoon YH, Yoon YW, Bae JH, Park SJ, Park DW, OCTIVUS Investigators.
abstractText:
Background

In-stent restenosis (ISR) remains a significant challenge despite advances in percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) technology. Although intravascular imaging improves procedural optimization, direct comparative data between optical coherence tomography (OCT) and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) for ISR treatment remain limited.

Methods

This study was a prespecified analysis of ISR lesions from the OCTIVUS trial (Optical Coherence Tomography-Guided Versus Intravascular Ultrasound-Guided Percutaneous Coronary Intervention). The primary outcome was target-vessel failure, defined as a composite of cardiac death, target-vessel-related myocardial infarction, or ischemia-driven target-vessel revascularization. Crude and adjusted analyses using inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting and overlap propensity score weighting were performed.

Results

Among the 2008 patients enrolled in the OCTIVUS trial, 164 (8.2%) underwent intravascular imaging-guided PCI for ISR lesions; 86 (52.4%) underwent OCT-guided PCI and 78 (47.6%) underwent IVUS-guided PCI. At a median follow-up of 1.8 years, the incidence of target-vessel failure was significantly lower in the OCT-guided group than in the IVUS-guided group (10.5% versus 29.5%; hazard ratio, 0.34 [95% CI, 0.16-0.74]; P=0.007). The lower incidence of target-vessel failure with OCT was consistent in adjusted analyses using inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting (hazard ratio, 0.31 [95% CI, 0.14-0.69]; P=0.004) and overlap propensity score weighting (hazard ratio, 0.31 [95% CI, 0.14-0.70]; P=0.005).

Conclusions

For the treatment of ISR lesions, OCT-guided PCI was associated with a lower risk of target-vessel failure than IVUS-guided PCI. However, given the exploratory nature of this analysis, these findings should not be considered clinically directive and warrant further investigation.

Registration

URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT03394079.

title: Correction to: Cardiovascular Disease Risk with Integrase Inhibitor-based Antiretroviral Therapy: A Causal Inference Analysis in RESPOND.
abstractText: [This corrects the article DOI: 10.1093/ofid/ofag490.].

title: Local Regression of Secondary Cutaneous Mucormycosis Following Intralesional Amphotericin B in a Child With Rhino-Orbito-Cerebral Mucormycosis: A Case Report.
authorString: Abtahi-Naeini B, Ghahfarokhi AB, Pourmoghaddas Z, Pourazizi M, Pourmahdi-Boroujeni M.
abstractText:
Introduction

Mucormycosis is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening fungal infection that predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals, with rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis (ROCM) being the most common form in the head and neck. It might be associated with secondary cutaneous extension, which can make management challenging.

Case presentation

This report describes a 9-year-old girl with uncontrolled insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and COVID-19-related multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) who consequently was diagnosed with ROCM. Despite systemic amphotericin B (AMB) therapy, surgical debridement, and transcutaneous retrobulbar AMB injections, the disease progressed, and she developed cutaneous mucormycosis secondary to ROCM. Intralesional AMB injections were administered as adjunctive therapy, leading to rapid and marked regression of the cutaneous lesions. However, her systemic disease continued to progress, and she subsequently developed septic shock and died.

Conclusions

Based on our experience, intralesional AMB may be considered a potential adjunctive therapeutic option in the management of cutaneous mucormycosis. Further studies are needed to clarify its efficacy and potential role in the treatment of cutaneous mucormycosis.

title: Changes in Body Composition During the Menopausal Transition and Cardiovascular Health Implications: A Contemporary Review.
authorString: Reyes H, Aggarwal B.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

The menopausal transition (MT) coincides with changes in body composition that may contribute to cardiovascular risk. This review synthesizes studies published from 2021 to 2026 on muscle, adiposity, and bone during midlife and menopause, evaluates the extent to which any observed changes can be distinguished from chronological aging, and considers their implications for cardiovascular health (CVH).

Recent findings

Sixteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Evidence of a menopause-specific change was strongest for regional adiposity: longitudinal data using the final menstrual period classification showed accelerated accumulation of visceral and android fat during the MT, followed by slower gain after menopause. Postmenopausal groups often had lower lean or skeletal muscle mass, but much of this evidence came from cross-sectional or baseline-defined comparisons. Bone mineral density declined around the typical age of menopause, although aging and menopause effects were difficult to separate. Resistance training improved muscle and abdominal adiposity outcomes in several trials, whereas findings for hormone therapy, sleep, and diet varied by outcome.

Summary

The strength of evidence for adverse changes in body composition during midlife varies by compartment. Central and visceral adiposity have the clearest longitudinal support, whereas changes in muscle and bone remain more difficult to distinguish from aging. Increases in visceral fat provide the strongest body composition link to adverse CVH. However, most studies assessed cardiovascular risk factors rather than clinical cardiovascular events. Larger, more diverse longitudinal studies that use standardized menopause staging and direct measures of regional adiposity, muscle quality, and cardiovascular outcomes during the MT are needed.

title: Proteomic Investigation of Serum Biomarkers for Early Neurological Prognosis in Patients Undergoing Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Prospective Multi-Center Pilot Study.
authorString: Han AR, Kim SW, Kim YJ, Shin Y, Kim JE, Kwon H, Shin YH, Choi B, Jeong YH, Jang HJ, Cho Y, Lee S, Kim SH, Yang JH, Cho YH, Kim HJ, Jung JS, Son HS, Cho SM, Park HM, Lee JH.
abstractText:
Background

Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has emerged as a promising intervention for refractory cardiac arrest; however, predicting neurological outcomes remains challenging. This study aimed to identify early prognostic biomarkers for neurological outcomes in ECPR patients using comprehensive proteomic profiling.

Methods

In this multi-center prospective cohort study, serum samples were collected at 0, 24, 48, and 72 hours after ECPR and analyzed by high-resolution liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Among 1,135 quantified proteins, differential expression was defined by |log₂ fold-change| ≥ 1 and P < 0.05. Twenty-two patients were enrolled and stratified by 90-day Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) scores: good neurological outcome (CPC score 1-2, n = 15) and poor neurological outcome (CPC score 3-5, n = 7).

Results

Proteomic analysis suggested distinct temporal expression patterns and potential differences in key proteins between neurological outcome groups. Four proteins associated with neuronal function or neuroinflammation, including GRN (24 hours), S100A6 (0 hours), PRDX6 (48 hours), and PTPRF (24 hours, 48 hours), showed numerically greater discriminative performance than neuron-specific enolase (NSE). Their areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve were 0.857, 0.833, 0.821, and 0.821, respectively, compared with 0.800 for NSE at 48 hours.

Conclusion

In this preliminary study, GRN, S100A6, PRDX6, and PTPRF exhibited improved discriminative performance compared with NSE, suggesting their potential as promising serum proteomic biomarkers for early neuroprognostication after ECPR. While these exploratory findings warrant validation in larger cohorts, they establish a compelling foundation for the development of next-generation, biomarker-based models to guide clinical management in ECPR patients.

title: Injectable Self-Healing Microspheres Enable In Situ Assembly of Dynamic Porous Scaffolds for Tissue Repair.
authorString: Cao S, Guo X, Huang H, Ni Y, Shen A, Xuan H, Wang Y, Tao Y, Hua Y, Cai Z, Guan Q, Gao Y, You Z.
abstractText: Tissue engineering scaffolds are indispensable for repairing complex tissue defects; however, conventional prefabricated scaffolds are limited by invasive implantation, poor anatomical conformity, and insufficient adaptability to irregular defect geometries. Here, we report an injectable, self-assembling scaffold strategy that transforms polymer microspheres from isolated functional carriers into dynamic modular building blocks for in situ scaffold construction. Following injection, the self-healing microspheres fill irregular defects, fuse with adjacent microspheres, and form a mechanically stable three-dimensional scaffold with an interconnected porous architecture. This design combines the minimally invasive delivery and functional versatility of microspheres with the structural integrity and mechanical support of macroscopic scaffolds, thereby addressing a key challenge in precise and conformal tissue repair. The platform also enables disease-specific functionalization through metal-ion coordination. Silver-ion-loaded microspheres provide conformal coverage of complex wounds while exhibiting antibacterial activity and supporting skin regeneration. Zinc-ion-functionalized microspheres assemble into defect-matched porous scaffolds and promote osteogenic repair. Copper-ion-integrated microspheres remain localized at tumor sites and provide sustained release of therapeutic agents, thereby reducing systemic toxicity. Collectively, this work establishes a minimally invasive, shape-adaptive, and customizable scaffold platform for complex tissue repair and localized therapy. More broadly, it provides a versatile design framework for the development of next-generation intelligent biomaterials.

title: Sleep, stasis, and thromboprotection: what hibernating mammals can teach us about cardiovascular risk.
authorString: Zauli E, Caruso L, Zauli G, Vaccarezza M.
abstractText: Prolonged immobility is one of the best-known triggers for venous blood clots, yet hibernating brown bears spend months lying still without ever developing them - and something similar seems to hold for many people with chronic paralysis. Thienel and colleagues recently offered a compelling explanation: platelets in hibernating bears sharply downregulate a protein called HSP47, dropping to roughly 55-fold below normal levels. HSP47 turns out to drive clot formation on two fronts at once, by boosting platelet activation and by prompting neutrophils to release the web-like structures that help clots take hold. Suppress it, and both arms of the process weaken together. That this pattern shows up across bears, immobilized patients, bed-rest volunteers, and other animal models suggests it isn't a quirk of bear physiology but something closer to an ancient survival mechanism. Here we consider why immobility's clotting risk seems to shift over time, look at an HSP47-blocking compound called Col003 that is already showing promise, and ask whether HSP47 might eventually double as a marker of clotting and inflammatory risk more broadly.

title: Estimated Glucose Disposal Rate, Genetic Susceptibility and Risks of Incident and Recurrent Coronary Artery Disease: Evidence From the UK Biobank Study.
authorString: Zeng Q, Guo RY, Ding Y, Tao T, Gu A, Wang Z, Zhou D, Zhang N, Zhu Y, He D.
abstractText:
Aims

Insulin resistance (IR) and genetic susceptibility are risk factors for coronary artery disease (CAD). The estimated glucose disposal rate (eGDR) is a surrogate marker of IR. This study aimed to examine their joint effects, interaction and predictive ability for CAD incidence and recurrence.

Materials and methods

460 859 participants were included from the UK Biobank study: 445 281 without CAD for incident CAD analyses and 15 578 with CAD for recurrent CAD analyses. eGDR was derived from waist circumference, hypertension status and glycosylated haemoglobin A1c (HbA1c). Genetic susceptibility was assessed by the polygenic risk score (PRS) for CAD. Multivariable Cox models estimated the hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence interval (CI). Predictive ability was assessed by the C-index.

Results

The median follow-up period was 13.8 years. Compared with the lowest eGDR quartile and medium/high PRS, the highest eGDR quartile with low PRS had the lowest risks of incident CAD (HR = 0.25, 95% CI: 0.23-0.27) and recurrent CAD (HR = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.62-0.73). Interactions between eGDR and PRS were significant for incident CAD (p < 0.001) but not significant for recurrent CAD (p = 0.052). The addition of eGDR and PRS into conventional risk factors significantly improved the predictive ability for incident CAD (△C index = 0.017, 95% CI: 0.016-0.019) and recurrent CAD (△C index = 0.005, 95% CI: 0.003-0.007).

Conclusions

Both eGDR and CAD-PRS are needed to predict incident and recurrent CAD. High levels of eGDR with low CAD-PRS are associated with lower incident and recurrent CAD risk. eGDR and CAD-PRS improve the predictive ability for incident and recurrent CAD.

title: NR6A1 Drives Cardiac Remodeling by Transcriptionally Activating the Mineralocorticoid Receptor.
authorString: Zhang Z, Zhuang H, Chang X, Chen T, Zhao X, Wang Y, Zhang Z, Wang M, Chen J, Li C, Tang X, Wang J.
abstractText:
Background

Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and mineralocorticoid receptor (MR/NR3C2) signaling is a central driver of pathologic cardiac remodeling and heart failure (HF). The transcriptional regulation of NR3C2 and the amplification of RAAS-driven cardiac remodeling remain poorly understood.

Methods

Transcriptome and single-cell RNA sequencing data, along with HF samples from humans and mice, were used for gene expression analysis. Cardiomyocyte-specific Nr6a1 transgenic (Nr6a1-cTG) and knockout (Nr6a1-cKO) mice were subjected to transverse aortic constriction to evaluate cardiac remodeling and dysfunction. Adeno-associated virus 9-shNr3c2 was used to test whether Nr3c2 contributes to remodeling driven by Nr6a1 overexpression. Primary mouse cardiomyocytes were used for in vitro analysis. RNA sequencing, Western blot, chromatin immunoprecipitation, and luciferase assays were performed for the mechanism analysis.

Results

NR6A1 (nuclear receptor subfamily 6, group A, member 1) expression was increased in the heart tissue from human and mouse failing hearts. Activation of NR6A1 contributed to the hypertrophic growth of cardiomyocytes in vitro. In mice, a cardiomyocyte-specific Nr6a1 transgene aggravated left ventricular dysfunction, hypertrophy, and fibrosis after transverse aortic constriction, whereas a cardiomyocyte-specific Nr6a1 knockout protected the heart from failure and remodeling. Transcriptome analysis of NR6A1 downstream transcriptional targets revealed that Nr3c2 is a prominent RAAS-related downstream target in both hearts and cardiomyocytes. The transcription cofactor NR6A1 directly bound the Nr3c2 promoter, increased promoter activity, and enhanced Nr3c2 transcription in cardiomyocytes. Nr3c2 silencing attenuated NR6A1-associated cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in vitro and reduced cardiac dysfunction and hypertrophy in Nr6a1-cTG mice after transverse aortic constriction. Analysis of the upstream regulation of NR6A1 in HF stress revealed that HF-related angiotensin II/AT1R signaling promoted NR6A1 expression and its downstream transcriptional and functional events in a STAT1 (signal transducer and activator of transcription 1)-dependent manner.

Conclusions

RAAS (angiotensin II) increases the orphan receptor NR6A1, which transcriptionally activates MR/NR3C2 signaling and aggravates RAAS-associated pathologic remodeling under HF stress. This regulatory network represents an undefined feed-forward amplification mechanism linking angiotensin II signaling to MR/NR3C2 activation and may be a therapeutic target for HF with persistent MR activation.

title: VAD Wean Recovery Network: Long-Term Outcomes of LVAD Weaning for Myocardial Recovery.
authorString: Patel SR, Potapov E, Kanwar M, Sun B, Selzman CH, Bernhardt A, Ton VK, Schueler S, Yuzefpolskaya M, Díez-López C, Najjar E, Wever-Pinzon O, Agarwal R, Dranow E, Kyriakoulis I, Jorde U, Goldstein DJ, Riesgo-Gil F, Ravichandran A, Schmitto J, Hanff TC, Tseliou E, Stehlik J, Zimpfer D, Rojas SV, Ruiz Cano M, Lundgren SW, Nair A, Diakos NA, Bowles C, Jakstaite AM, Shah P, Birks E, Drakos SG.
abstractText:
Background

Myocardial recovery facilitated by the combination of a left ventricular assist device (LVAD) and guideline-directed medical therapy can lead to sufficient myocardial improvement. This in turn may allow LVAD weaning in appropriately selected patients with chronic advanced heart failure. However, sufficient data on the long-term outcomes of this therapeutic strategy are lacking, thereby hindering widespread adoption of LVAD weaning. We present the primary results from the VAD Wean Myocardial Recovery International Network examining long-term outcomes after LVAD weaning for myocardial recovery.

Methods

We studied 603 patients with chronic advanced heart failure from 60 international centers who underwent LVAD weaning. Preimplantation, LVAD cardiac recovery assessment, and postweaning patient characteristics and outcomes were analyzed. The primary outcome was event-free survival (free of heart transplantation or re-LVAD) in the weaned-for-recovery cohort.

Results

The LVAD-weaned cohort had a mean age of 42±15 years; 33% were female; and 9.4% had ischemic cardiomyopathy. At LVAD implantation, 88% had Intermacs (Interagency Registry for Mechanically Assisted Circulatory Support) profiles 1 to 3, and 41.6% required temporary mechanical circulatory support. Median LVAD support duration was 440 days (interquartile range, 261-770) before weaning. At the time of weaning, median left ventricular ejection fraction was 50% (interquartile range, 45%-57.5%), and left ventricular internal diastolic diameter was 48 mm (interquartile range, 43-53 mm). One-year survival after weaning was 91%, with 2.3% requiring re-LVAD and 3.7% requiring heart transplantation. In a secondary exploratory matched analysis against LVAD bridge-to-transplantation recipients from the International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation registry, long-term survival was similar between groups.

Conclusions

This international, multicenter analysis suggests that in patients with chronic advanced heart failure achieving myocardial recovery with LVAD support, device weaning yields excellent long-term outcomes. These findings may help address the underuse of LVADs as a bridge-to-recovery strategy in select patients.

title: Rare Case of Cushing's Syndrome in Infants With Reversible Myocardial Hypertrophy.
authorString: Ye Q, Zhou H, Feng X.
abstractText: The occurrence of isolated Cushing's syndrome in early infant adrenal cortical tumors is very rare. Cushing's syndrome with left ventricular hypertrophy is considered a risk factor for the development of myocardial ischemia and heart failure. We report a 5-month-old boy with Cushing's syndrome caused by adrenal cortical tumor, who presented with reversible myocardial hypertrophy and subclinical systolic dysfunction detected by left ventricular global longitudinal strain.

title: Psoriasis and Coronary Artery Disease: A Narrative Review of Mechanisms, Risk Estimation and Shared Care.
authorString: Krones C, Lankaputhra M, Stub D, Scardamaglia L.
abstractText: Psoriasis is a systemic immune-mediated inflammatory disease associated with increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, including coronary artery disease. This review summarizes epidemiological and genetic evidence linking psoriasis, severe psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis to coronary outcomes, and distinguishes disease phenotype, current severity, disease duration and cumulative inflammatory burden as related but separate contributors to cardiovascular risk. We outline shared immune, lipid and metabolic pathways that promote endothelial dysfunction, plaque inflammation and atherothrombosis, and review vascular imaging approaches that characterize non-calcified plaque, total plaque burden, adverse plaque features, pericoronary inflammation and coronary microvascular dysfunction. Evidence relevant to cardiovascular risk modification is reviewed, including systemic psoriasis therapies, lipid lowering, incretin-based and other cardiometabolic agents, and anti-inflammatory strategies established in coronary disease. We propose a graded risk framework in which phenotype, severity, duration, adequacy of disease control, conventional cardiovascular risk factors and evidence of subclinical atherosclerosis inform interpretation of calculated risk. We also set out an operational shared-care pathway that assigns responsibility for screening, risk assessment, preventive therapy, monitoring and referral across dermatology, primary care and cardiology. Practical statements are labeled according to the strength of supporting evidence. Until definitive cardiovascular outcome trials in psoriatic disease are available, aggressive management of conventional risk factors alongside optimal inflammatory control remains the most defensible approach to reducing cardiovascular burden.

title: Predicting coronary artery aneurysm regression in Kawasaki disease using CST3 mRNA and explainable machine learning.
authorString: Liang K, Pang Y, Su D.
abstractText:
Objectives

To develop a prognostic model for long-term regression of coronary artery aneurysm (CAA) in Kawasaki disease (KD).

Methods

Five hundred KD patients with CAAs were retrospectively analyzed in a derivation cohort and 159 patients in a temporal validation cohort. Ten clinically relevant variables, including age, fever duration, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) response, CAA classification, white blood cell count (WBC), haemoglobin, platelet count (PLT), C-reactive protein (CRP), prealbumin and CST3 mRNA expression, were included for model development. Eight machine learning (ML) algorithms underwent performance assessment using 10-fold cross-validation. Model explainability was explored through SHAP analysis, and final algorithm was implemented as a Streamlit-based online prediction tool.

Results

The random forest model demonstrated the best overall performance in both cohorts (derivation cohort: AUC = 0.9305; temporal validation cohort: AUC = 0.9338) and was selected for further SHAP-based interpretation. Lower CST3 mRNA expression, smaller aneurysm size, younger age at diagnosis, lower inflammatory burden (WBC, CRP and PLT), lower prealbumin, higher haemoglobin levels, shorter fever duration and responsiveness to IVIG were associated with a higher probability of CAA regression.

Conclusions

We developed an interpretable ML model incorporating CST3 mRNA to predict long-term CAA regression in KD. Its web-based implementation may facilitate individualised risk stratification and clinical decision-making.

Impact

An explainable machine learning model accurately predicts long-term coronary artery aneurysm regression in Kawasaki disease. CST3 mRNA emerged as an exploratory molecular predictor and ranked second only to aneurysm size in SHAP-based feature importance. Integration of molecular and clinical variables improved individualized risk prediction beyond conventional clinical models. The web-based prediction tool may support precision follow-up and clinical decision-making in children with Kawasaki disease.

title: Real-Time Prediction of Cardiac Parameters Using Livestream Transthoracic Echocardiography Images: A Feasibility Study.
authorString: Nainamalai V, Brun H, Sebergsen C, Gromholt Homlong E, Liodden KV, Kupcikevicius I, Elle OJ.
abstractText: The aim of this study is to develop a workflow for acquiring and analyzing livestream echocardiography images from a GE HealthCare Vivid E95 system, a real-time artificial intelligence (AI)-based automatic left ventricle segmentation, and cardiac parameter prediction. The system provides automated echocardiography image analysis independent of electrocardiogram signals. A software pipeline was developed to acquire and analyze livestream echocardiography images from the ultrasound system. A UNet neural network model was trained using publicly available datasets (CAMUS, EchoNet-Dynamic) and an in-house dataset (Physical Activity and Fitness in Childhood Cancer Survivors). AI models were trained using these three datasets and three loss functions, with each model evaluated independently on all three test datasets. The model with the highest Dice score on the test datasets was selected and used to process livestream echocardiography images throughout the entire cardiac cycle. The resulting segmentation masks were used to compute the cardiac parameters. The offline-trained UNet models achieved an average Dice score of 0.9509. The livestream echocardiography image prediction showed average ejection fractions of 48%, 48% and 56%, corresponding to the Simpson's single-plane, area-length and Bullet methods, respectively. In contrast, EchoPAC (the GE HealthCare software tool to compute cardiac parameters) showed an average ejection fraction of 55% in nine volunteers with no known cardiac diseases. This study shows the feasibility of AI-assisted echocardiographic image analysis based on livestream echocardiography. However, the accuracy of the obtained cardiac parameters needs improvement to align with clinical standards.

title: How epigenetic ageing routes cardiovascular cells towards calcification.
authorString: Qian X, Xu L, Li F.
abstractText: Cardiovascular calcification is strongly age-dependent yet pharmacologically intractable. Blood methylation clocks capture systemic ageing but miss vascular and valvular lineage-specific programmes. We propose that age- and stress-associated epigenetic remodelling destabilises cell identity, creating permissive pre-calcific states. Single-nucleus and spatial epigenomics may resolve these states for earlier risk stratification and intervention.

title: The Depression and Heart Development study: design and protocol for assessing maternal depression and its treatment on offspring cardiac development.
authorString: Bowers B, Thukral S, Mat HD, Coulter B, Bischoff AR, Santillan D, Stuart S, McNamara PJ, Colaizy TT, Reinking BE, Haskell SE.

journal.title: The journal of maternal-fetal & neonatal medicine : the official journal of the European Association of Perinatal Medicine, the Federation of Asia and Oceania Perinatal Societies, the International Society of Perinatal Obstetricians

abstractText: Depression is common among women of reproductive age, yet little is known regarding the cardiovascular outcomes of infants born to depressed mothers. Furthermore, treatment of depression during pregnancy with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) is rapidly increasing, contributing to the difficulty differentiating the effects of fetal exposure to SSRIs from effects of underlying maternal depression on newborn health. Few studies have compared cardiovascular development in infants of pharmacologically and non-pharmacologically treated mothers with depression. Our study, the Depression and Heart Development Study, addresses this critical knowledge gap. It is a prospective observational study that uses maternal mental health assessments, maternal and child data, and hemodynamic echocardiographic measurements to investigate the impact of maternal depression and its treatment on ventricular size and function in offspring, with the primary outcomes of interest being left ventricular length in diastole and systole. Participants (n = 165; 55 non-depressed women, 55 depressed women treated with psychotherapy alone, 55 depressed women treated with SSRIs) were recruited from the University of Iowa during pregnancy. A Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 Axis I Disorders was conducted to confirm group placement, and maternal assessments continued through 1 year post-delivery. Infant echocardiograms were conducted at 24-48 h, 1 week, and 1 year of age. Our study will provide important prospective evidence to better inform care decisions regarding depression during pregnancy and its treatment and guide future research in this area.

title: Targeting estrogen receptor signalling for the management of insulin resistance: From hormones to herbal modulators.
authorString: Zang Y, Zhang F, Wu L, Tan Z, Wang Y, Lu H.
abstractText: Estrogen exerts a critical influence on metabolic health by modulating insulin signalling pathways via its receptors (ERα, ERβ and the G protein-coupled oestrogen receptor [GPER]). Estrogen decline, as seen postmenopausally or in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), is strongly associated with insulin resistance and the pathogenesis of Type 2 diabetes. The beneficial metabolic actions of estrogen, including enhanced insulin sensitivity, are mediated through mechanisms such as AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activation, promotion of GLUT4 translocation, and suppression of inflammatory pathways. Conversely, decreased estrogen levels contribute to adipose tissue accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction and exacerbated insulin resistance. Current pharmacological interventions, including hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs), can ameliorate insulin resistance but are accompanied by ongoing debate concerning their cardiovascular safety and oncological risk. These risks highlights the need for more targeted therapeutic strategies. Emerging agents, such as ERβ-selective agonists and GPER activators, alongside the refined application of herbal phytoestrogens, offer promising avenues to develop tissue- and receptor-specific modulators. Consequently, future pharmacological development needs to focus on harnessing these selective estrogenic pathways to achieve optimal metabolic benefits, whilst minimising off-target effects, so paving the way for precision medicine in the management of metabolic disease.

title: Ventricular Septal Pulsed Field Ablation: Noninvasive, Longitudinal Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Assessment of Lesion Structure and Function in a Preclinical Model.
authorString: Chen C, Qian X, Fang G, Ling Y, Zhou N, Li Q, Cheng K, Pang Y, Xu Y, Cheng Z, Yu T, Li Q, Wang S, Huang Y, Yuan H, Shen Y, Chen Q, Gomez T, Sharma T, McCormac A, Nie Z, Zhu W, Chen Q, Ge J.
abstractText:
Background

Ventricular pulsed field ablation (PFA) is an emerging myocardial ablation strategy, but lesion evolution and noninvasive assessment in ventricular myocardium remain incompletely characterized.

Objective

To evaluate interventricular septal (IVS) PFA in a preclinical swine model and assess the feasibility of serial cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) for lesion characterization.

Methods

Eight swine were allocated to acute and chronic cohorts. PFA was delivered to the IVS using a variable-loop circular catheter (VLCC). Multimodality assessments included electroanatomic mapping, serial CMR, echocardiography and pathology. Pathological lesion-depth measurements were obtained at terminal timepoints, whereas serial CMR enabled within-animal longitudinal assessment. CMR-pathology correspondence was evaluated using anatomically matched slices.

Results

Serial CMR showed reductions in late gadolinium enhancement (LGE)-derived lesion mass and volume by Day 21, with stabilization thereafter. Among 37 matched CMR-pathology slices from five animals, CMR-LGE-derived lesion-depth measurements showed positive association with pathology-derived measurements (Pearson's r = 0.77), moderate reliability (ICC = 0.74), and a mean difference of 0.03 mm, with 95% limits of agreement from -1.15 to 1.21 mm. Both methods showed decreased chronic lesion depths, consistent with lesion maturation and fibrotic remodeling. Transient reductions in left ventricular ejection fraction and regional septal mechanics were observed after PFA, followed by partial recovery.

Conclusion

Ventricular septal PFA produced well-demarcated lesions that evolved into chronic fibrotic scars. Serial CMR enabled noninvasive assessment of lesion localization, depth, and temporal evolution, with lesion-depth measurements showing correspondence with anatomically matched pathological measurements, supporting the feasibility of CMR for longitudinal assessment after ventricular PFA.

title: Implantable Cardiac Monitor for Diagnosis and Continuous Monitoring of Type 1 Brugada Electrocardiographic Pattern.
authorString: Notarangelo F, Crocamo A, Bassini M, De Simoni I, Gonzi G, Bearzot L, Barocelli F, Ritacco ML, Del Maestro M, Giacopelli D, Niccoli G.
abstractText:
Background

The spontaneous type 1 Brugada electrocardiographic pattern (BrECG) is a recognized marker of increased arrhythmic risk in Brugada syndrome (BrS), but its dynamic nature may limit detection with conventional electrocardiographic monitoring.

Objective

To evaluate the feasibility of implantable cardiac monitors (ICMs) with remote monitoring for detecting spontaneous BrECG in asymptomatic patients.

Methods

Consecutive patients showing ajmaline-induced BrECG were prospectively enrolled. During drug challenge, surface potential mapping was performed to identify the optimal implantation position, after which a long-sensing vector ICM was inserted subcutaneously. The primary endpoint was the time to first documentation of spontaneous BrECG based on recordings remotely transmitted by the implanted ICM during follow-up.

Results

Fifty-nine patients (46±15 years, 69% male) underwent ICM implantation without complications. The left upper thoracic region with negative inclination was identified as the optimal position for BrECG detection. During a median follow-up of 21.6 months, BrECG was documented in 29 patients (49%); 72% were diagnosed within one month and 86% within two months after implantation. Family history of BrS (p=0.050) and longer QRS duration (p=0.032) were independently associated with diagnosis, whereas higher ajmaline dose was inversely associated (p=0.006). Among 50,666 transmitted recordings, 3.4% showed a positive BrECG, increasing to 7.4% during nighttime, and with a trend toward a higher probability of detection at lower mean daily heart rates.

Conclusion

Continuous ICM monitoring using a long-sensing vector in the left upper thoracic region with negative inclination enables detection of spontaneous BrECG and reveals substantial temporal variability of the ECG phenotype in patients with drug-induced BrECG.

title: Cardioneuroablation for Vasovagal Syncope: A Systematic Computed Tomography-Guided Anatomical Approach.
authorString: Kneizeh K, Plant A, Krisai P, Escande W, Benabou L, Bouteiller X, Behnam S, Moussouni K, Kollias G, Block S, Benali K, Monaco C, Fitzgerald J, Ditac G, Notaristefano F, Verhaeghe L, Kowalewski C, Bouyer B, Charton J, Sacristan B, Tixier R, Pambrun T, Derval N, Pürerfellner H, Sacher F, Jaïs P, Haïssaguerre M, Hocini M, Duchateau J.
abstractText:
Background

Cardioneuroablation (CNA) targeting parasympathetic ganglionated plexi (GP) is a emerging therapy for vasovagal syncope (VVS). Various methods have been proposed to identify GPs and optimize acute denervation.

Objectives

To describe the results of an anatomy-guided, reproducible approach for CNA in patients with implantable loop recorder (ILR) and Holter based indication for ablation.

Methods

Consecutive patients with VVS who underwent anatomy-guided CNA using segmented Computed Tomography (CT) imaging for ILR-guided indication were retrospectively included. The primary outcome included clinical recurrence of ILR-documented bradyarrhythmia.

Results

Fifty-four patients (mean age 39.9±12.7, 50% female) from four centers were included. All patients had spontaneous cardioinhibitory syncope documented, predominantly by ILR (89%), with a mean pause duration of 17.5±12.6 seconds. Contrast-enhanced CT with epicardial fat segmentation identified GP locations and guided ablation in all patients. Extra-cardiac vagal stimulation (ECVS) was used as a procedural endpoint in 61.1% of patients. The superior paraseptal GP and the inferior paraseptal GP were the primary GPs targeted (90.7% and 96.3% respectively). Additional GPs were targeted when ECVS continued to induce sinus arrest or atrioventricular block after initial denervation. Mean procedural time was 127.5 ± 32 minutes. During a follow-up of 17.4±11.9 months, all patients were monitored with ILR; 9 patients (18%) experienced the primary outcome, including atrioventricular block in 33.3%.

Conclusion

An anatomically guided CNA strategy based on fat-pad segmented CT, combined with patient selection using documented spontaneous VVS events and follow-up with ILR, appears to be a practical approach for the management of VVS.

title: Impact of lifetime vascular complication history on cardiorespiratory fitness in older adults with type 1 diabetes: the epidemiology of diabetes interventions and complications (EDIC) study.
authorString: Shah R, Karanchi H, Ghormli LE, Lorenzi GM, Gatcomb P, Bebu I, Braffett BH, Pop-Busui R, Shade DS, Hirsch IB, McGinnis S, Moreno F, Ikoma T, Karger AB, Averkiou X, Nathan DM, Lewis GD, Gubitosi-Klug RA, DCCT/EDIC Research Group.
abstractText: To identify multi-system determinants of cardiorespiratory fitness in adults with long-standing type 1 diabetes (T1D) and assess associations with physical function and quality of life. We performed symptom-limited cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) in 664 participants in the Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (EDIC) study (age 64 ± 6 years; T1D duration 43 ± 5 years; 45 % women) in 2023-2025. We assessed associations of fitness and exercise responses with antecedent and concurrent phenotypes and diabetes complications over ≈40 years. Average VO2peak was 20.1 ± 6.0 ml/kg/min, with approximately one-third of participants having a VO2peak below thresholds for functional independence (<18 ml/kg/min). Beyond glycemia and CVD, renal dysfunction was strongly associated with lower VO2peak, anaerobic threshold, and delayed VO2 recovery. Associations of nephropathy measures with VO2peak were comparable to those of cardiovascular complications. VO2peak declined progressively with increasing complication burden, from 22.7 ± 6.5 ml/kg/min among participants without complications to 17.5 ± 4.7 ml/kg/min among those with complications in every system. Physical function and quality of life were also strongly associated with VO2peak. Cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular complications, particularly renal dysfunction, are associated with reduced cardiorespiratory fitness in long-standing T1D. Addressing multi-system complications may help preserve functional capacity with aging.

title: Trimethylamine N-oxide aggravates lung injury in neonatal rats exposed to hyperoxia via NF-κB/NOX2 signaling.
authorString: Wang L, Geng H, Wang L, Zhang H, Zhang Z, Dong C, Wang L, Wang X, Wang H, Li B.

journal.title: Biochimica et biophysica acta. General subjects

abstractText: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is a common and severe respiratory complication in preterm infants. Previous research has highlighted the importance of the airway microbiota in normal lung function and disease processes. The role of the airway microbiota in BPD among preterm infants and its potential metabolic associations remain unclear. The sputum microbiome was characterized using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and serum metabolites were profiled using untargeted metabolomics. In vitro, lung epithelial cells were treated with trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), with or without the NF-κB pathway inhibitor BAY 11-7082. A hyperoxia-induced BPD model was established in neonatal rats, which were treated with Serratia or TMAO. Histological examination, immunofluorescence staining, and RT-qPCR were performed to assess lung injury. The airway microbiota and serum metabolomic profiles differed between preterm infants with BPD and those with normal lung development. Serratia was enriched in the BPD group and showed a significant positive correlation with serum TMAO levels. Experimental studies further indicated that TMAO exposure was associated with inflammatory responses and lung injury, together with changes in NF-κB/NOX2 signaling. These findings suggest a potential association among airway microbial alterations, TMAO, and BPD-related lung injury. Airway Serratia enrichment was associated with elevated serum TMAO levels in preterm infants with BPD. Experimental findings suggest that TMAO-associated lung injury may involve NF-κB/NOX2 signaling.

title: High Prevalence of Retinal Ischemic Perivascular Lesions in Central Serous Chorioretinopathy Patients.
authorString: Maltsev DS, Kulikov AN, Kalinicheva YA, Amoroso F, Chhablani J.
abstractText:
Purpose

To evaluate the prevalence of retinal ischemic perivascular lesions (RIPLs) in patients with central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR) and to identify factors associated with their presence.

Design

Observational cross-sectional study.

Methods

Two hundred forty-five patients aged 18-60 years with active CSCR and 63 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were included. RIPLs were identified using high-resolution structural optical coherence tomography (OCT) and corresponding en face OCT projections. A RIPL was defined by focal inner nuclear layer thinning with corresponding outer plexiform layer elevation and topographic perivascular correspondence on en face OCT. The presence of at least one lesion in either eye classified a participant as RIPL-positive. Demographic, systemic, clinical, and imaging characteristics were analyzed using univariable and multivariable logistic regression.

Results

RIPLs were identified in 85 of 245 patients with CSCR (34.7%) compared with 7 of 63 healthy controls (11.1%, P < 0.001). Bilateral RIPLs were present in 35 CSCR patients (14.3%) and 2 controls (3.2%, P = 0.028). CSCR patients with RIPLs were older, had a higher prevalence of hypertension, and had lower central retinal and subfoveal choroidal thicknesses than those without RIPLs (P < 0.05). Hypertension showed the strongest association with RIPLs presence in univariable analysis (OR 3.37, 95% CI, 1.74-6.54, P < 0.001) and remained the only independent factor in multivariable analysis (OR 2.66, 95% CI, 1.20-5.87, P = 0.016). Notably, among patients without diagnosed hypertension, RIPLs prevalence remained significantly higher than in controls (24.1% vs. 11.1%, P = 0.035).

Conclusion

RIPLs are highly prevalent in patients with CSCR, potentially reflecting an increased burden of cardiovascular risk factors in this cohort. This finding warrants further investigation.

title: 2-Methylbutyrylcarnitine Promotes Post-AMI Cardiac Injury Through NF-κB-Associated Inflammation and Apoptosis.
authorString: Yu L, Lian J, Ma L, Zhang H.
abstractText: This study aimed to investigate the role of 2-methylbutyrylcarnitine (2MBC) in regulating cardiomyocyte apoptosis and post-infarction cardiac injury. A mouse AMI model was established by ligating the left anterior descending coronary artery. For the in vitro study, primary mice cardiomyocytes were isolated, purified by differential adhesion, and characterized by cardiac troponin I (cTnI) immunofluorescence and flow cytometry (purity > 95%). Cells were subjected to hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) injury and treated with 2MBC in the presence or absence of an inhibitor of nuclear factor-κB α (IκBα) inhibitor. Apoptosis was evaluated by Annexin V/propidium iodide (PI) flow cytometry, TUNEL staining, and Western blot detection of apoptosis-related proteins. To assess inflammatory responses, cytokine levels were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and reverse transcription quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR). Nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB) pathway activation was determined by Western blot, and the expression levels of downstream target genes were quantified by RT-qPCR. Computational analysis revealed a significant association between elevated plasma 2MBC and AMI, accompanied by enrichment of the NF-κB signaling pathway. In mice, 2MBC treatment exacerbated MI, as evidenced by increased serum levels of myoglobin, creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB), cardiac troponin I (cTnI), and cardiac troponin T (cTnT), and increased systemic inflammation. Increased Bax/Bcl-2 ratio and Caspase-3 activation indicated that 2MBC promoted cardiomyocyte apoptosis. These findings suggest the potential of 2MBC may serve as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target to improve post-AMI outcomes. However, in vivo rescue experiments are not performed to further verify this signaling axis.

title: NDUFA7 targeting by Tanshinone IIA mitigates ischemic injury in cardiomyocytes: A mechanism of restoring mitochondrial complex I activity in myocardial ischemia.
authorString: Al-Maamari A, Zhong C, Lin Q, Chen R, Zhang J, Ke L, Han S, Ye S, Hu Y, Wu Q, Yao H.
abstractText: Tanshinone IIA (Tan IIA) is an active component of Salvia miltiorrhiza Bunge (Danshen). Although Tan IIA exerts cardioprotective effects in cardiovascular diseases and its formulation, sodium tanshinone IIA sulfonate, treats ischemic heart disease, its direct molecular targets and mechanisms against myocardial ischemia (MI) remain unknown. This study aimed to identify mechanisms of Tan IIA against MI, focusing on NDUFA7 as a direct target, using in vitro and in vivo models. An ISO-induced MI mouse model was established to evaluate cardioprotective effects using electrocardiogram, histopathological changes, biochemical markers, oxidative stress, immunofluorescence, and western blot. Potential targets were identified by isothermal shift assay (iTSA) and validated using molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), drug affinity-responsive target stability (DARTS), and bio-layer interferometry (BLI). In vitro, a tert-butyl hydroperoxide-induced AC16 cardiomyocyte injury model assessed cell viability, mitochondrial ROS, and complex I activity, with shRNA-mediated knockdown for validation. In MI mice, Tan IIA pretreatment (5/10 mg/kg) ameliorated ECG abnormalities, improved histopathological injury, attenuated myocardial fibrosis, decreased serum cardiac injury biomarkers, and enhanced antioxidant enzyme activities. iTSA identified NDUFA7, a critical subunit of mitochondrial respiratory complex I, as a potential Tan IIA target, confirmed by docking, MD simulations, CETSA, DARTS, and BLI. In vitro, Tan IIA improved cell viability, suppressed mitochondrial ROS, restored complex I activity, and enhanced NDUFA7-MCM3 interaction. NDUFA7 knockdown abolished these protective effects. This study identifies NDUFA7 as a target of Tan IIA that restores mitochondrial complex I activity against MI, highlighting it as anti-MI drug screening.

title: Pulmonary Function Estimation from Opportunistic Chest CT Using a Hybrid Image-plus-Quantitative-Feature Deep Learning Model.
authorString: Carvalho ARS, Guimarães AR, Kee SL, Martins da Fonseca J, Zhang JMF, Pickhardt PJ, Braithwaite D, Perchiazzi G, Sartori AP, Rodrigues RS, Manjarres D, Benos PV, Hochhegger B.
abstractText: Spirometry is underused and most airflow obstruction remains undiagnosed. Chest CT acquired for lung cancer screening contains anatomical and densitometric information that may proxy lung function. Can a deep learning model combining volumetric CT with CT-derived quantitative features estimate spirometric parameters and detect abnormal spirometry in independent external cohorts without retraining? A three-dimensional convolutional neural network trained on 10,371 low-dose CT reconstructions from 5,975 National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) participants was fused with 20 lung densitometry and tracheal geometry features to predict FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC. The frozen model was applied to an External Lung Cancer Screening Cohort (ELCSC, n = 268) and COPDGene (n = 10,302 scans). Ablation, two spirometric-pattern subgroups and prevalence-conditional predictive values were also evaluated. Reference spirometry was pre-bronchodilator in NLST and post-bronchodilator in COPDGene. Abnormal spirometry (FEV1/FVC < 0.70, FEV1 < 80% or FVC < 80% predicted) was assessed with sensitivity, specificity and AUROC, and agreement with the concordance correlation coefficient (CCC). The model detected abnormal spirometry with AUROC 0.898 (sensitivity 89.9%, specificity 66.1%) in the ELCSC and AUROC 0.913 (sensitivity 66.9%, specificity 96.3%) in COPDGene, with CCCs of 0.80-0.88 for FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC. In held-out development data, CCCs were 0.86/0.85/0.71 (full model) versus 0.83/0.82/0.50 image-only and 0.55/0.65/0.35 feature-only. Agreement was lower, with systematic overestimation, in a COPD subgroup (FEV1/FVC < 0.70; CCC 0.62) and in a low-FVC, preserved-ratio pattern (CCC 0.70-0.78). The model estimates spirometric parameters and detects abnormal spirometry across independent cohorts without retraining, with different sensitivity-specificity profiles at the same decision rule. It shows promise for opportunistic assessment of existing CT scans, but referral performance varies by population and prospective utility is unproven. COPDGene, ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT00608764.

title: Acute physical effort enhances interoceptive accuracy without improving error awareness: evidence from the Heart Rate Discrimination Task.
authorString: Culot C, Engelschenschilt J, Garfinkel S, Gevers W, Notebaert W.
abstractText: According to Fechner's law, perceived sensations increase logarithmically with stimulus intensity. During exercise, rising physical effort is therefore accompanied by increasingly salient bodily signals such as heart rate. Interoception, the sensing of internal bodily states, supports adaptive responses to these changing demands, for instance, by guiding the regulation of exertion. Beyond physical regulation, interoceptive signals have also been proposed to inform higher-order monitoring processes, such as error detection. Yet it remains unclear whether acute exercise sharpens cardiac interoception and whether this would translate into greater awareness of errors. In a within-participant design, 36 healthy adults completed two tasks while cycling at low versus moderate intensity: a Heart Rate Discrimination Task assessing cardiac interoception and a Go/No-Go task measuring error awareness through post-error reports. Moderate effort reduced interoceptive bias, bringing participants' perceived heart rate closer to their actual heart rate, while discrimination precision remained unchanged. Confidence in interoceptive judgments increased under moderate effort, but this was not accompanied by improved metacognitive insight. In the Go/No-Go task, commission errors were more frequent at moderate intensity, whereas the proportion of detected errors was unchanged. Interoceptive performance did not reliably predict error awareness. These findings suggest that acute exercise recalibrates cardiac judgment bias rather than improving perceptual sensitivity or metacognitive monitoring. This recalibration did not extend to error awareness; however, given the temporal and reporting constraints of the task, the null effect cannot determine whether cardiac signals contribute causally to conscious error detection.

title: CEBPD promotes smooth muscle cell phenotypic transition and aortic wall degeneration in aortic dissection.
authorString: Li X, Zhong X, Chen H, Liu Z, Luo L, Sang H, Jiang W, Zhang H, Wang M, Liu Y.
abstractText:
Aims

Smooth muscle cell (SMC) phenotypic transition and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling contribute to aortic wall degeneration in aortic dissection (AD). We aimed to identify transcriptional regulators associated with ECM-remodeling SMC states and investigate their contribution to AD.

Materials and methods

Human and mouse transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility datasets were integrated to identify candidate regulators. Validation included human aortic tissue analysis and gain- and loss-of-function studies in human aortic SMCs and a β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN)-induced mouse model. Functional assays, histological assessment, chromatin immunoprecipitation-qPCR, and dual-luciferase reporter assays were performed.

Key findings

Synthetic-like SMC populations expanded in AD and displayed reduced contractile signatures and enhanced ECM-remodeling features. CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein delta (CEBPD) was upregulated and showed increased inferred regulatory activity across human and mouse datasets. Tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) induced CEBPD expression in SMCs. CEBPD overexpression reduced contractile marker expression and impaired contractility, whereas knockdown partially attenuated TNF-α-induced phenotypic changes. Chromatin accessibility analysis identified candidate targets enriched in processes related to SMC proliferation and differentiation, inflammation, and tissue remodeling. Matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP2) was validated as a direct transcriptional target. In vivo, CEBPD overexpression aggravated BAPN-induced aortic dilation, medial degeneration, elastin fragmentation, and SMC phenotypic changes, whereas knockdown attenuated these effects.

Significance

CEBPD promotes SMC phenotypic transition and contributes to aortic wall degeneration. These findings support its involvement in ECM remodeling, with MMP2 representing one validated target within a broader candidate gene set.

title: Evaluation of the frontal QRS-T angle in patients with migraine.
authorString: Kiliçaslan F, Savcilioğlu MD, Akçali AH.
abstractText:
Background

Autonomic nervous system (ANS) dysregulation is related to the pathophysiology of migraine. Disturbed ANS may affect ventricular repolarization, leading to some ECG changes. Frontal QRS-T angle is a novel marker of ventricular repolarization. To the best of our knowledge no study assessed the frontal QRS-T angle in migraine patients. In this study, we aimed to evaluate frontal QRS-T angle and other ECG variables in patients with migraine during pain free period.

Methods

A total of 144 migraine patients between age of 18-50 who were admitted to Patnos State hospital and 45 age-matched healthy subjects without any known cardiac disease were retrospectively included in this study. Frontal QRS-T angle was obtained from the automatic report of the 12‑lead electrocardiography and calculated as the absolute difference between QRS axis and T axis.

Results

Age, height, weight and body mass index were similar between groups, whereas the proportion of women was higher in the migraine group (92.4% vs 68.9%, P < 0.001). In analyses adjusted for age, sex and heart rate, QT, QTc and QRS duration and the P, QRS and T axes did not differ between groups. The frontal QRS-T angle was slightly wider in migraine patients (adjusted difference 10.166°, 95% CI 1.644-18.689; P = 0.020), but this difference was confined to the small male subgroup (11 patients vs 14 controls; group × sex interaction P = 0.006), was absent in women (P = 0.318) and was not significant in a rank-based analysis (P = 0.118). P axis (P = 0.440) and QTc interval (P = 0.133) were similar between the patient and control group. Similarly, no significant difference was found between patients and control subject regarding frontal QRS-T angle (20 [9-37] vs 22 [7-34], P = 0.465).

Conclusion

In this study, no consistent differences were observed in conventional ECG repolarization parameters or the frontal QRS-T angle between migraine patients during the headache-free period and healthy controls. The modest widening of the frontal QRS-T angle observed in adjusted analyses was confined to the male subgroup and requires confirmation in larger studies. Although these findings suggest that interictal ventricular repolarization does not consistently differ between young migraine patients without cardiovascular comorbidities and healthy controls, they should not be generalized to the ictal phase or to older migraine patients or those with cardiovascular risk factors.

title: Health literacy as a determinant of cardiovascular health and outcomes.
authorString: Ricci F, Khanji MY.
abstractText: Despite remarkable advances in cardiovascular prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, substantial gaps persist between evidence-based recommendations and real-world clinical outcomes. Health literacy is an important, yet frequently overlooked and potentially modifiable, determinant of cardiovascular health. Limited health literacy contributes to suboptimal risk-factor control, reduced treatment adherence, delayed recognition of cardiovascular symptoms, and adverse clinical outcomes. There is a need to move beyond the traditional view of health literacy as an individual patient characteristic. Healthcare professionals and healthcare systems need to make cardiovascular information easily accessible, understandable, and actionable. Health literacy has the potential to reduce cardiovascular inequalities and can help address the challenges posed by digital healthcare and misinformation. Practical strategies are highlighted for integrating health-literacy principles into routine cardiovascular care. Health literacy should be regarded not merely as a patient education initiative, but as an actionable component of cardiovascular care quality, with the potential to improve treatment adherence, risk-factor control, and ultimately cardiovascular outcomes.

title: Comparing NfL, GFAP and total tau in tear fluid and plasma from participants with Huntington's disease.
authorString: van der Vleuten J, Schmeetz J, Pirlet E, van Deurse W, van de Sande N, van de Waarenburg M, Linden DEJ, Ramakers IHGB, Oosterloo M, Gijs M.
abstractText: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder for which reliable biomarkers are increasingly important to monitor disease progression and treatment response. Although biomarkers can be measured in cerebrospinal fluid and blood, tear fluid may provide an additional non-invasive matrix suitable for repeated sampling. This study investigated the feasibility of measuring neurofilament light chain (NfL), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and total tau (t-tau) in tear fluid and explored their relationship with corresponding plasma concentrations and HD disease progression. Tear fluid and plasma samples were obtained from 73 participants, including manifest HD participants (n = 18), premanifest HD participants (n = 23), and controls (n = 32). Tear fluid was collected using Schirmer's strips. NfL,GFAP and t-tau concentrations were quantified using the S-PLEX Neurology Panel 1 Human electrochemiluminescence immunoassay. Detectability of all biomarkers in tear fluid was high, with GFAP and t-tau detectable in all samples (100%) and NfL in most samples (range 87% in premanifest to 100% in manifest participants). Tear fluid biomarker concentrations did not differ significantly between groups and showed generally limited discriminatory performance. Plasma NfL was significantly elevated in manifest HD compared with premanifest HD and controls and showed good-to-excellent discriminatory performance (AUC = 0.895 and 0.923, respectively). Across groups, plasma NfL and GFAP concentrations were higher than in tear fluid, whereas t-tau concentrations were substantially higher in tear fluid. These differences were confirmed in participants with paired tear fluid and plasma samples (n = 53; all p < 0.001). NfL, GFAP, and t-tau were highly detectable in tear fluid, but showed limited ability to distinguish between HD disease groups. Further research is required to determine the clinical utility of tear fluid biomarkers in HD monitoring.

title: Development and preliminary analytical evaluation of a magnetic particle-based chemiluminescent sandwich immunoassay for copeptin.
authorString: Li G, Guan Z, Li S, Liu M, Li L, Dong F, Guo Y, Zhang W, Tian X, Zhao Q.
abstractText: This study aimed to independently develop domestic monoclonal antibodies against copeptin (CPP) and establish a magnetic particle-based chemiluminescence immunoassay to improve the accuracy and clinical applicability of early diagnosis of myocardial diseases. CPP amino-terminal and carboxyl-terminal peptides were synthesized by solid-phase peptide synthesis and conjugated to keyhole limpet hemocyanin (KLH) as immunogens. Mice were immunized subcutaneously, and mouse monoclonal antibodies against the amino-terminal region of CPP were generated using hybridoma technology; rabbits were immunized subcutaneously, and rabbit monoclonal antibodies against the carboxyl-terminal region of CPP were generated using phage display technology. The optimal antibody pair was selected by checkerboard titration, and a double-antibody sandwich assay system was established. Antibody affinity was characterized by bio-layer interferometry (BLI). The detection sensitivity of the assay and its consistency with liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) for clinical sample measurement were evaluated using the sandwich chemiluminescence method. A total of 25 mouse monoclonal antibodies and 4 rabbit monoclonal antibodies were obtained. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay identified the optimal pair as rabbit anti-CPP 1148# as the capture antibody and mouse anti-CPP 2# as the detection antibody, with equilibrium dissociation constants in the 10-10 M range. The limit of detection (LOD) of the assay was 0.03 ng/mL, and the coefficient of variation (CV) was below 5%. The results for clinical samples correlated well with those obtained by LC-MS/MS (R2 = 0.95). Bland-Altman analysis showed an estimated 95% limit of agreement ranging from -20.15 to -0.61 pg/mL, with consistency significantly superior to that of a commercially available kit. These monoclonal antibodies provide reliable core reagents for establishing a domestic CPP detection system and lay a foundation for the development of more reliable CPP diagnostic reagents.

title: Evaluating the Feasibility of Cultural Dance as an Integrative Therapeutic Movement Intervention for Parkinson's Disease.
authorString: Shuman R, Tolentino K, Krening E, Look MA, Takata J, Thai K, Faouzi M, Seto TB, Mehta A, Bruno MK.
abstractText:
Objective

To assess the feasibility of hula, Hawai'i's indigenous dance, as a dance-based therapeutic intervention for people with Parkinson's disease (PD).

Background

Therapeutic dance programs have demonstrated physical and psychosocial benefits for individuals with PD. Hula has been studied as an intervention for chronic conditions such as hypertension and cardiovascular disease, however, its feasibility for PD has not been explored. This study evaluated hula as a therapeutic dance intervention for people with PD.

Methods

A three-month hula program was developed using patient and public involvement, with guidance from Hawaiian cultural experts, in collaboration with Dance for PD®. A kumu hula (hula educator) translated this feedback into a curriculum and led weekly one-hour classes. People with PD were recruited through clinical and community outreach. Primary outcomes assessed feasibility through practicality, safety, and qualitative feedback. Secondary outcomes included pre-and post-intervention measures of the 39-item Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire (PDQ-39) and Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale-Part III (UPDRS-III).

Results

Eighteen participants enrolled, and 11 completed the intervention. Mean attendance was 77.6%. One adverse event occurred, unrelated to class activities and without significant complication. PDQ-39 scores showed minimal change, while average UPDRS-III scores decreased by 4.18 points. Qualitative interviews suggested improvements in mood, motivation, social connectedness, and self-confidence. Participants described hula as cognitively engaging, as it integrates choreography with storytelling, illustrating historical and poetic references in traditional Hawaiian songs and chants.

Conclusion

Hula was feasible, safe, and well-received as a culturally grounded therapeutic dance intervention for individuals with PD, supporting further investigation in larger controlled studies.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06543810.

title: Endothelial glycocalyx injury during cardiopulmonary bypass: mechanisms and clinical implications.
authorString: Asopa S, Ali-Ghosh H, Leventis F, Modi A, Ohri SK.
abstractText: PurposeThe endothelial glycocalyx (EG) is a carbohydrate-rich layer lining the luminal surface of the vascular endothelium. During cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), the EG sustains significant damage from ischaemia-reperfusion injury, non-physiological shear stress, systemic inflammation and haemodilution, among other insults. This review integrates current evidence on the biological mechanisms of EG degradation during CPB, the biomarkers used to quantify this injury, the downstream clinical consequences and emerging protective strategies.MethodsThis is a narrative review. A structured literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus combined controlled-vocabulary and free-text terms for the endothelial glycocalyx and cardiopulmonary bypass; English-language original studies and relevant reviews were identified and synthesised narratively.ResultsInitiation of CPB produces rapid, measurable shedding of glycocalyx constituents-notably syndecan-1, heparan sulfate and hyaluronan-driven by reactive oxygen species, matrix metalloproteinases, heparanase, atrial natriuretic peptide release, complement activation and non-pulsatile shear forces. Shedding correlates with microcirculatory perfusion disturbances, capillary leak, oedema, coagulopathy and organ dysfunction, and its magnitude is associated with CPB duration. Several interventions-including volatile anaesthetics, hydrocortisone, albumin, goal-directed fluids, pulsatile perfusion and antithrombin III-attenuate shedding in small studies, but the evidence remains predominantly mechanistic and biomarker-based, and none has shown a reproducible improvement in major clinical outcomes.ConclusionsEG injury is a central, under-recognised mechanism contributing to the systemic inflammatory response and organ dysfunction of CPB. The field is biologically compelling but clinically unproven; glycocalyx-directed monitoring and protective strategies remain research priorities rather than established practice.

title: Autoantibody origins in lupus and upon recurrence post CAR-T therapy.
authorString: Grenov A, Yoon J, Samelis VA, Snell DM, Mikolajczak A, Wang H, Gürel E, Rodriguez-Ronchel A, Yegen G, D'Antuono R, Emmerich M, Turajlić S, Lee L, Esen BA, Rahman A, Maciocia P, Vinuesa CG.
abstractText: Anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T therapy induces profound remissions in lupus by depleting B cells, challenging the view that disease is sustained by long-lived plasma cells. Using molecular antibody tagging in mouse models of monogenic childhood-onset lupus, we show that autoantibody-producing plasma cells are short-lived and require continuous replenishment from T-bet-dependent precursors derived from long-lived B cell cohorts. The spleen is a major plasma cell reservoir, with perivascular enrichment observed in patients with lupus. Both anti-CD19 and anti-B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) CAR-T therapies eliminate anti-DNA antibodies. Recurrent autoantibodies after anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy derive exclusively from newly generated B cells, whereas those following anti-BCMA CAR-T therapy also arise from treatment-resistant clones. Thus, ongoing B cell-to-plasma cell differentiation, rather than plasma cell longevity, can sustain pathogenic antibody responses in lupus and provides a mechanistic framework for optimizing CAR-T therapies.

title: Filling the gap: An overview of approaches for developing a framework for culturally inclusive communication responses during public health emergencies.
authorString: Uribe Guajardo MG, Cunich M, Wilson A, Ravi S, Faraj A, Serhan Z, Gupta L, Milat A, Huckel Schneider C, Greene D.
abstractText: This article proposes the first stage of a theoretical approach aimed at improving communication and supporting a framework for creating community engaged sustainable, and culturally appropriate public health emergency communication and response strategies. This article presents a theoretical overview. Using research and practice-informed approaches, we suggest 5 theoretical steps to gathering the information necessary to inform sustainable framework for developing a culturally aware migrant-focused communication and rapid response panel for public health emergencies. Steps include: (i) a document review; (ii) interviews with key interest-holders; (iii) focus groups exploring needs across sectors from a migrant perspective; (iv) Delphi consensus processes; and (v) development of culturally safe communication strategies. This theoretical approach can provide researchers and practitioners with the capacity to fill evidence gaps in the knowledge and practice of co-creating culturally appropriate rapid response panels for public health emergencies within local contexts.

title: PRISM-MP: Psychology-guided and reliability-aware multimodal learning for cross-musician emotion recognition during musical performance.
authorString: Tong T.
abstractText: Emotion classification during active musical performance is challenging because neural activity, cardiac dynamics, and acoustic expression provide complementary but non-equivalent evidence of intended emotional communication and self-reported affect. This study presents PRISM-MP, a psychology-guided and reliability-aware multimodal framework for cross-musician emotion recognition. We analyzed a publicly available dataset comprising synchronized electroencephalography, electrocardiography, and musical audio recordings from 11 experienced musicians who performed excerpts intended to communicate happiness, sadness, anger, or relaxation. PRISM-MP integrates dynamic frequency-specific electroencephalographic functional graphs with affine-invariant tangent-space covariance representations, models multiscale physiological dynamics, and applies class-conditional source-domain alignment to reduce musician-specific distributional differences. The physiological and acoustic pathways receive auxiliary supervision from felt and communicated valence-arousal ratings, respectively. Their contributions are dynamically adjusted according to signal quality, predictive uncertainty, and cross-modal disagreement. Under nested source-only leave-one-musician-out evaluation, PRISM-MP achieved a musician-macro-averaged performance-level accuracy of 92.14%, balanced accuracy of 91.82%, macro-F1 of 0.910, Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.892, and expected calibration error of 0.041. Against the strongest recent source-only EEG baseline evaluated under the same protocol, the corresponding gains were 3.91 percentage points in balanced accuracy and 0.037 in macro-F1. The framework remained robust when electrocardiography or audio was unavailable and under partial electroencephalographic channel loss. A systematic leave-one-channel-out analysis across 29 EEG electrodes revealed nonuniform channel sensitivity. Removing C3, Cz, C4, and F3 produced the largest balanced-accuracy reductions of 2.22, 2.05, 2.02, and 1.90 percentage points, respectively, while removal of several other channels produced minimal changes. Computational profiling indicated 3.46 million trainable parameters and processing times of 74 ms with GPU-supported audio embedding and 312 ms on a desktop CPU, while physiological encoding and fusion required 18.7 ms after feature preparation. These timings exclude the 30-s observation period and do not represent end-to-end interactive latency. A secondary post hoc within-recording calibration analysis increased macro-F1 to 0.946 using a lightweight residual adapter. These findings support reliability-aware physiological-acoustic modeling as a computational foundation for future musician-centered affective interfaces.

title: Time-dependent alterations of the heart-brain axis in rats following a single microwave exposure.
authorString: Wang H, Zhang C, Deng W, Zhang J, Cao J.
abstractText: This study aimed to investigate the time-dependent changes and possible mechanisms of the heart-brain axis in rats following S-band microwave exposure. A single microwave exposure model was established using 8-week-old male Wistar rats (2.856 GHz, 50 mW/cm², 30 min). At Days 1, 3, and 7 post-exposure, we evaluated electrocardiogram, heart rate variability, and electroencephalogram activities, alongside serum biochemical and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay indicators. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of the hippocampus and myocardium, combined with real-time quantitative PCR, were utilized to validate key molecular changes. The results showed that following a single exposure, the function of the rat heart-brain axis changed in a time-dependent but outcome-specific manner: neuroendocrine, autonomic, and electroencephalographic alterations were most evident on Day 1, most circulating cardiac and brain injury markers were highest on Day 3, and lactate dehydrogenase increased only on Day 7. These changes were primarily characterized by imbalanced autonomic nervous function and heart rate variability, abnormal electrocardiogram and electroencephalogram activities, and elevated injury-related markers. Integrated multi-omics analysis revealed significant molecular remodeling in both tissues on Day 3.
