title: Patent Foramen Ovale Closure Outcomes in Patients of Advanced Age (PFO-COPA): Protocol for a Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Study.
authorString: Jazayeri SB, Phan C, Eghbalnejadmofrad A, Meyer BC, Meyer DM, Yaghi S, Bavarsad Shahripour R.
abstractText: Patent foramen ovale (PFO) is a common cardiac abnormality associated with paradoxical embolism and ischemic stroke. Randomized trials have demonstrated the benefit of percutaneous PFO closure in patients aged <60 years with cryptogenic stroke, but nearly all trials have excluded individuals aged ≥60 years, leaving a critical evidence gap in older populations, in whom competing stroke mechanisms are prevalent. There is currently no dedicated, validated framework to guide closure decisions in this age group. Consequently, clinical practice remains highly variable, and closure decisions are made based on extrapolation from younger cohorts rather than robust evidence. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of PFO closure compared with medical therapy in patients aged ≥60 years with cryptogenic stroke and a confirmed PFO. This multicenter international retrospective cohort study will include consecutive patients aged ≥60 years with imaging-confirmed ischemic stroke, a confirmed PFO, and no alternative definite etiology of stroke after standard diagnostic evaluation, who underwent either percutaneous PFO closure or medical therapy between 2015 and 2025. Outcomes will be collected through standardized chart review and entered into a centralized REDCap database. The primary outcome will be the risk of recurrent ischemic stroke. Secondary outcomes will include major bleeding, new-onset atrial fibrillation, device-related complications, and mortality. Time-to-event analyses, Cox regression, and propensity score methods will be used to adjust for confounding. As of October 2026, 51 centers from 10 countries (Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Greece, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Portugal, Spain, and the United States) have formally agreed to participate in the study. Each site is currently in the process of securing institutional review board (IRB) approval and executing data use agreements. A standardized variable dictionary has been distributed to all centers to ensure consistency in data collection. As of October 2026, 45 centers have applied for local IRB approval, 5 centers have obtained IRB approval, and 3 centers have begun data entry into REDCap. The projected end date of data collection is June 2027. Participating centers are encouraged to propose independent research questions leveraging the pooled dataset. As of October 2026, 23 project titles have been submitted by investigators. These proposals will be evaluated once sufficient data have been accrued. Preliminary pooled analyses are anticipated for release in July 2027. The PFO-COPA (Patent Foramen Ovale Closure Outcomes in Patients of Advanced Age) study will generate the most comprehensive real-world evidence to date on PFO closure in adults aged ≥60 years. By evaluating both effectiveness and safety in this understudied age group, the study will fill a major evidence gap and help guide clinical decision-making. Ultimately, these findings may inform future guideline updates and lay the groundwork for prospective multicenter trials focused specifically on older adults.

title: Clinical and Patient-Centered Outcomes of Catheter Ablation According to Symptom Status in Very Elderly Patients With Atrial Fibrillation: A Subgroup Analysis of the REHEALTH AF Registry.
authorString: Hirata S, Okumura Y, Nagashima K, Watanabe R, Yokoyama K, Matsumoto N, Kato T, Fukaya H, Hayashi H, Nakahara S, Shimizu W, Iwasaki YK, Fujimoto Y, Mukai Y, Ejima K, Otsuka T, Suzuki S, Murakami M, Kimura M, Harada M, Koyama J, Yamane T, Tokuda M, Takami M, Shoda M, Harada T, Nakajima I, Hiroshima K, Tanimoto K, Kumagai K, Okada A, Kobayashi H, Watari Y, Ochiai M, Hayashi T, Tachibana E, Iso K, Sonoda K, Aizawa Y, Fukuoka R, Chikata A, Inoue M, Sakagami S, Minamiguchi H, Makino N, Ichikawa M, Haruta H, Hiro T, Ohkubo K, Arai M, Arima K, Kihara H, Miyanaga S, Fukuda Y, Oiwa K, Koyama Y, Fujiishi T, Akabane M, Ishikawa N, Kusano K, Miyamoto K, Tabuchi H, Shiozawa T, Miyamoto K, Mase H, Murotani K.
abstractText:
Background

Catheter ablation can improve symptoms and functional status in very elderly patients with atrial fibrillation. However, it is uncertain if baseline symptom status can pinpoint those who will benefit the most.

Methods

This exploratory subgroup analysis examined data from the REHEALTH AF registry, which included patients aged 80 and above with non-valvular atrial fibrillation. Patients were categorized by baseline symptom status and compared based on treatment strategy: catheter ablation versus non-ablation management.

Results

Of 703 patients, 238 were asymptomatic, while 465 were symptomatic. Catheter ablation did not significantly reduce the primary composite endpoint in either asymptomatic (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.39; 95% confidence interval, 0.39-4.92; p = 0.61) or symptomatic patients (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.66; 95% confidence interval, 0.36-1.20; p = 0.17), with no significant interaction between treatment and symptoms. Exploratory analyses indicated ablation was associated with more favorable changes in a wider range of 1-year patient-centered measures among symptomatic patients, such as quality of life, self-rated health, Mini-Mental State Examination score, frailty distribution, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide level, and left atrial diameter. In asymptomatic patients, improvements were mainly seen in self-rated health and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide level.

Conclusions

In very elderly patients with atrial fibrillation, baseline symptom status did not identify those with a clear short-term event reduction following catheter ablation. Nevertheless, exploratory analyses revealed more favorable changes across various patient-centered measures in symptomatic patients, although formal evidence of effect modification was limited.

Trial registration

University Hospital Medical Information Network Clinical Trials Registry, UMIN000047023.

title: Health Utility of Thai Patients With Heart Failure Using EQ-5D-5L Instrument.
authorString: Yassen AO, Boonyanuwat W, Sakthong P.
abstractText: To assess health utility in Thai patients with heart failure and to determine the clinical and sociodemographic factors associated with their health status using the EQ-5D-5-Level (EQ-5D-5L) and EuroQol visual analog scale (EQ-VAS) instruments. This cross-sectional secondary analysis of baseline randomized controlled trial data was carried out at Ayutthaya Hospital between November 2022 and May 2023. Patients were interviewed to evaluate their health status. Health utility scores were derived using Thai-specific value sets. Univariate and multivariable Tobit regression models, alongside multivariable logistic regression analyses, were applied to determine independent predictors and dimensional problems. Among 250 patients (mean age 63.5 ± 12.1 years, 54% female, and 59% heart failure with reduced ejection fraction), mean EQ-5D-5L and EQ-VAS scores were 0.82 ± 0.18 and 74.0 ± 14.5. Multivariable logistic regression revealed that age, higher education, medication burden, and diabetes mellitus significantly predicted problems in specific dimensions. In univariate analyses, older age, female sex, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, higher comorbidity, medication burden, diabetes mellitus, and hypertension lowered EQ-5D-5L scores, whereas higher income and higher education increased utility scores; meanwhile, hyperlipidemia, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and higher comorbidity reduced EQ-VAS scores. Multivariable Tobit models showed that older age, female sex, and higher medication burden independently predicted lower utility scores. In this study, health utility was determined more by age, sex, and overall medication burden than by ejection fraction subtypes. These results offer key empirical inputs for national health technology assessment processes and for guiding resource allocation to strengthen medication optimization initiatives and patient-centered strategies focused on older adults and women.

title: Alcohol abstinence and liver stiffness by vibration-controlled transient elastography: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
authorString: Chow W, Wong D, Singh G, Teskey G, Luniewski L, Puglisi L, Spierling Bagsic SR, Deising A, Harris MS, Pockros PJ, Gutierrez JA.
abstractText:
Background

Alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) is a major cause of liver-related morbidity and mortality, and abstinence is fundamental for treatment. Liver stiffness measurement (LSM) using vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE) is commonly used to assess hepatic fibrosis and inflammation. While studies suggest LSM decreases after alcohol cessation, the magnitude and timing of these changes are poorly understood. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated liver stiffness changes after alcohol cessation.

Methods

Medline, EMBASE, and Cochrane databases were searched from 1996 to 2024 for paired VCTE assessments in adults who underwent alcohol cessation and reported abstinence or relapse. Absolute mean kPa changes were back-transformed estimates from pooled effect sizes and standard deviations. ROBINS-I assessed risk of bias.

Results

A total of 6620 articles were reviewed; 75 underwent full-text review, and 11 studies involving 1557 patients were included. In abstinent patients, a mean absolute LSM change was identified to be -1.95 kPa at 7 days, -2.30 kPa at 30 days, and -2.76 kPa after 56 days. The pooled standardized effect size was -0.13 SD units (95% CI -0.20 to -0.07). LSM reduction was significant within 7 days of abstinence (-0.21 SD units; 95% CI -0.38 to -0.05) but not at later follow-up (-0.11 SD units; 95% CI -0.24 to 0.03). In relapse patients, mean absolute LSM change was +0.86 kPa at 30 days and +0.40 kPa after 56 days; pooled standardized effect size was +0.18 SD units (95% CI +0.02 to +0.33).

Conclusions

VCTE detected short-term, directionally opposite LSM changes with alcohol cessation or relapse. These changes are consistent with alcohol-associated inflammatory liver injury, while its correlation with histologic fibrosis is uncertain, necessitating further evaluation with paired VCTE and histology during abstinence.

title: Genome-wide association study identifies a functional myostatin variant increasing lean mass in humans.
authorString: Larusdottir AE, Teitsdottir UD, Tragante V, Palsson F, Kristinsdottir AM, Hjorleifsson Eldjarn G, Stefansdottir L, Oddsson A, Aegisdottir HM, Styrkarsdottir U, Bustamante M, Olafsdottir TA, Snaebjarnarson AS, Olafsdottir T, Einarsson G, Gudjonsson SA, Halldorsson GH, Ferkingstad E, Sigurdarson Sandholt AK, Einarsson E, Vaura F, Pajuste FD, Ripatti S, Palotie A, Laisk T, Mägi R, Ostrowski SR, Pedersen OBV, Sørensen E, Bundgaard JS, Erikstrup C, Mikkelsen C, Topholm Bruun M, Jensen BA, Ullum H, Bundgaard H, Igland J, Andreassen O, Haavik J, Lumbers RT, Shah S, Sunderland N, Jiang JC, Knowlton KU, Nadauld L, DBDS Genomic Consortium, Estonian Genome Research Team, FinnGen, Thorgeirsson G, Sulem P, Thorsteinsdottir U, Bjarnason RG, Ivarsdottir EV, Sveinbjornsson G, Thorolfsdottir RB, Norddahl GL, Ulfarsson MO, Steinthorsdottir V, Thorleifsson G, Holm H, Helgadottir A, Gudbjartsson DF.
abstractText: Muscle mass is central to physical function and metabolic health, but can decrease with disease, aging and weight loss interventions. As weight loss interventions become more widely used, agents that preserve or increase muscle mass are needed. To identify such therapeutic opportunities, we perform genome-wide association meta-analyses of arm, leg, trunk and total lean mass measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, a widely used method to estimate muscle mass. We identify 63 loci, including a rare missense variant in MSTN (p.Ile225Thr, rs143242500), which has the largest effect on leg lean mass (β = 0.28 SD [95% CI: 0.19, 0.37], P = 1.9 × 10<sup>-9</sup>). MSTN encodes myostatin, a negative regulator of skeletal muscle mass and a therapeutic target for muscle wasting disorders. Here, we identify a genome-wide significant association at MSTN in humans and characterize its functional consequences, providing genetic evidence that may inform the long-term systemic effects of myostatin inhibition.

title: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and long-term risk of chronic hypertension and cardiovascular disease: A national claims-based cohort study.
authorString: Ayyash M, Huang Y, Kishkovich T, Bello N, Rosenblum H, Haythe J, Purisch S, Friedman A.
abstractText:
Introduction

Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are increasingly recognized as important predictors of future cardiovascular disease. Although individuals with HDP are known to be at increased risk of subsequent chronic hypertension and cardiovascular morbidity, the association between antihypertensive treatment and long-term outcomes is not well characterized. This study aims to evaluate the association between new-onset HDP and long-term risk of chronic hypertension and cardiovascular disease outcome, and to assess the impact of disease severity and need for antihypertensive treatment on long-term outcomes.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the 2016-2022 Merative™ MarketScan® Commercial Claims and Encounters and Multi-State Medicaid databases. Individuals with a delivery hospitalization and continuous enrollment during the entire pregnancy through 90 days postpartum were included. HDP exposure was defined as gestational hypertension or preeclampsia, excluding those with chronic hypertension during pregnancy. Secondary exposure included antihypertensive medication use from >20 weeks' gestation through 12 weeks postpartum. The primary outcome was incident chronic hypertension beyond 90 days postpartum. Secondary outcomes were cardiovascular conditions including heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, unspecified heart failure, atrial fibrillation, stroke, coronary artery disease, aortic aneurysm, and a composite cardiovascular outcome-defined as the occurrence of any of these cardiac conditions. Cumulative incidence function with Gray's test and Cox proportional hazard models were used.

Results

Among 1,010,658 deliveries, 13.0% had HDP, including 3.0% who received antihypertensive medications. Chronic hypertension occurred in 1.4% of those without HDP, 4.9% with HDP without medications, and 12.6% with HDP receiving medications (p < 0.001). Composite cardiovascular outcome occurred in 0.35%, 0.42%, and 0.54%, respectively (p < 0.001). In adjusted analyses, HDP without medications was associated with increased hazard of chronic hypertension (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 3.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 3.50-3.75) compared to patients without HDP, and HDP with medications was associated with substantially higher risk (aHR, 9.93; 95% CI, 9.53-10.34) compared to patients without HDP. Similar associations were observed for composite cardiovascular outcome (aHR, 1.27 and 1.57, respectively). Time-to-event analyses demonstrated early and persistent divergence in risk, with higher cumulative incidence of both chronic hypertension and cardiovascular outcomes among individuals with HDP, particularly those receiving antihypertensive therapy.

Conclusion

HDP is strongly associated with long-term risk of chronic hypertension and cardiovascular outcomes, with the highest risk observed among individuals requiring antihypertensive therapy. Antihypertensive medication use remained associated with subsequent outcomes after accounting for HDP subtype, suggesting its potential role as a marker of elevated cardiovascular risk. These findings support targeted postpartum cardiovascular surveillance and early risk-reduction strategies.

title: Concordance and validity of federated versus centralized analyses in treatment-resistant depression.
authorString: Saciuk Y, Wang E, Burcu M, Zhang H, Gould L, Hoshen M, Patalon T, Moser S, Joo S, Dibello J, Gazit S.
abstractText: To evaluate whether federated analyses can reproduce centralized results for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) risk prediction using privacy-preserving statistical models. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 7272 adults with incident major depressive disorder initiating antidepressants (2015-2021) in Maccabi Healthcare Services, Israel. Treatment-resistant depression was defined as progression to third-line regimens within 24 months. Data were geographically partitioned into 2 nodes to simulate federation. Federated generalized linear and Cox models were estimated using privacy-preserving iteratively reweighted least squares with cross-validated feature selection. Agreement with centralized analyses was assessed using coefficient differences, statistical-significance concordance, and confidence interval (CI) overlap. Model performance was evaluated using discrimination, calibration, and fairness metrics. Federated and centralized models showed near-perfect concordance. Feature selection produced almost identical predictor sets, and coefficient estimates were strongly aligned, with mean absolute differences <0.01, complete decision agreement among predictors retained by both models, and >95% CI overlap. Predictive performance was modest but consistent across settings (AUC ∼0.65 for logistic; ∼0.62 for Cox), with preserved calibration and similar subgroup patterns. Federated models reproduced major clinical associations observed centrally, including higher TRD risk with prior antidepressant exposure, psychiatric hospitalization, anxiety and personality disorders, and polypharmacy, and lower risk with atrial fibrillation and delayed therapy initiation. Results show that federated implementations of standard epidemiologic models can retain the validity and stability of centralized analyses, even for complex psychiatric outcomes requiring high-dimensional adjustment. Federated analysis can closely replicate centralized statistical model results while preserving privacy, supporting its use for scalable, multi-institutional epidemiologic research.

title: Preoperative depressive symptoms predict long-term mortality and early functional recovery after osteoporotic hip fracture: a 3-year cohort study.
authorString: Gao F, Tu C, Chen Y, Bei M, Chen Y, Li R, Xu S, Chen L, Liu G, Yang M, Wu X.
abstractText:
Depressive symptoms are common in older adults with osteoporotic hip fracture, but their impact on long-term outcomes remains unclear. In this cohort study, preoperative depressive symptoms were associated with increased 3-year mortality and poorer early functional recovery. These findings highlight the importance of psychological assessment in the management of fragility fractures.

Purpose

To investigate the association between preoperative depressive symptoms and postoperative mortality and functional recovery in older adults with hip fracture.

Methods

This secondary analysis was based on a prospective cohort of patients aged ≥65 years undergoing surgical treatment for hip fracture. Depressive symptoms were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) within 24 hours of admission, with a cutoff score of ≥5. Mortality and functional recovery were evaluated at 30-day, 120-day, 1-year, and 3-year follow-up. Cox proportional hazards models and multinomial logistic regression were used after adjustment for potential confounders.

Results

Among 1092 patients, 93 (8.5%) had PHQ-9 ≥ 5. Preoperative depressive symptoms were not associated with short-term mortality but were independently associated with increased 3-year mortality (HR = 1.57, 95% CI: 1.05-2.36). Patients with PHQ-9 ≥ 5 had significantly poorer functional recovery at 30-day, 120-day, and 1-year follow-up, whereas no independent association was observed at 3 years.

Conclusions

Preoperative depressive symptoms were associated with increased long-term mortality and poorer early functional recovery. These findings support the role of early psychological assessment in perioperative risk stratification.

title: A genome-wide cross-trait analysis detects shared genetic architecture between alcohol use disorder and ischemic stroke.
authorString: Fatoba AJ, Fatoba DO, L Simpson C.
abstractText: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a life-threatening mental disorder with high mortality and morbidity due to its various health complications. While observational studies have highlighted the role of alcohol consumption in the risk of ischemic stroke (IS), the contribution of shared genetic factors remains unclear. Our study used cross-trait Multi-trait Analysis of GWAS (MTAG) to investigate the shared genetic architecture underlying AUD and IS using genome-wide association studies (GWAS) summary statistics for alcohol use disorder (N = 500,348) and ischemic stroke (N = 1,296,908) from the FinnGen and GIGASTROKE databases. Local Analysis of Variant Association (LAVA) identified nine loci exhibiting significant positive and negative genetic correlation after Bonferroni correction. We further identified 19 independent genome-wide significant variants (P < 5 × 10<sup>- 8</sup>), among which one variant (rs12979469) mapped to SLC44A2 showed evidence of association with both traits. Gene-based analysis via MAGMA also supports SLC44A2 as a shared gene. Fine-mapping and colocalization further identified additional candidate genes, including CDK6 and RASIP1, which were supported by cross-trait analysis (CPASSOC P < 5 × 10<sup>- 8</sup>) but showed weaker evidence in single-trait GWAS. Summary data-based Mendelian Randomization (SMR) revealed significant associations between the expression of ABO and NBEAL1 and IS in tibial artery tissue (P<sub>SMR</sub> = 4.28 × 10⁻⁶, P<sub>HEIDI</sub> > 0.05), whereas no significant association was observed in brain tissues for AUD. Tissue enrichment analysis by GTEx further supports these findings, showing significant enrichment of AUD in brain tissues but nominal significance of IS in tibial artery tissues. Together, these findings suggest that the genetic overlap between AUD and IS is more consistent with variant-level pleiotropy rather than a shared gene expression or tissue-specific mechanism. Overall, our findings highlight SLC44A2, CDK6, and RASIP1 as candidate genes associated with both IS and AUD, and provide insights into the complex genetic relationship between AUD and IS.

title: Ocular Complications After 1000 Centistoke Silicone Oil Removal in Patients With Previous Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment Repair.
authorString: Madsen R, Wakabayashi T, Mahmoudzadeh R, Salabati M, Mehta S, Cohen MN, Martin J, Spirn MJ.
abstractText: To determine the incidence, types, and outcomes of complications associated with silicone oil (SO) removal in eyes that received 1000 centistoke SO as a tamponade for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD). Patients with RRD who received 1000 centistoke SO tamponade and had at least 3 months of follow-up were reviewed for complications after SO removal, including ocular hypertension, hypotony, cystoid macular edema (CME), epiretinal membrane (ERM), recurrent RD, residual SO, corneal edema, and uveitis. A total of 156 eyes of 156 patients were included. The median follow-up time after SO removal was 2.5 years, with an interquartile range (IQR) of 1.5 to 3.6 years. At the time of SO removal, 144 eyes (92%) had complete retinal attachment. The median time from vitrectomy with SO tamponade to SO removal was 5.6 months (IQR, 4.1-7.7 months). Retinal redetachment occurred in 34 eyes (22%) at a median of 32 days (IQR, 5.5-189 days) after SO removal. Hypotony occurred in 6% of eyes at 7 days (IQR, 1-36 days) and ocular hypertension in 11% at 36 days (IQR, 1-131 days). ERM (28%), CME (15%), and uveitis (10%) also developed with variable times of onset. A large majority of eyes achieved retinal attachment. Despite these favorable anatomic outcomes, a large percentage of eyes had postoperative complications, including redetachment, ocular hypertension, hypotony, ERM, and CME. Due to the wide time range of onset for complications, regular long-term follow-up is recommended for patients after SO removal.

title: Blood Pressure Elevation in Individuals with XY DSD: Clinical Insights from the I-DSD Registry.
authorString: Frixou M, Bryce J, Chen M, Naotunna CR, Sepich M, Tack L, Vermout S, Cools M, Poyrazoglu S, Globa E, Stancampiano M, Claahsen-van der Grinten HL, Güran T, Yavas Abali Z, de Vries L, Hannema S, Güven A, Janus D, Guazzarotti L, Herrmann G, Wabitsch M, Probst-Scheidegger U, Lenherr-Taube N, Konrad D, O'Reilly MW, Steigert M, Uçar A, Wasniewska M, Coco R, Holterhus PM, Schwitzgebel V, Ahmed SF, Lucas-Herald A.
abstractText: XY Differences of Sex Development (DSD) may have an increased risk of high blood pressure (BP) and accelerated vascular ageing. This could be related to reduced exposure to androgens in utero and in later life. Data were obtained from centres using the International DSD (I-DSD) Registry on males with XY DSD. At study initiation, 2,400 individuals with XY DSD were on the I-DSD Registry. Twenty-three centres worldwide participated in the study, with BP readings provided from 282 (32%) (median (range) age 10 (2, 68) years) of 875 eligible cases of boys and men with XY DSD. The most common diagnoses were non-specific XY DSD in (45%); disorders of gonadal development in 64 (23%); and disorders of androgen synthesis in 36 (13%). Of these, 76/282 (27%) had elevated or hypertensive BPs including 42/214 (20%) of boys <16 years old. In multivariable linear regression, systolic blood pressure SDS in boys was significantly associated with age (β 0.8, 95% CI 0.3-1.3, p=0.004) and presence of obesity (β 11.3, 95% CI 1.1-21.5, p=0.03), with no association seen according to presence of co-existing anomaly, type of underlying DSD, gestation at birth, birthweight or family history of hypertension. Nearly 1 in 4 people with XY DSD have an elevated BP at clinic, with 20% of boys with XY DSD being hypertensive at clinic review, and no clear differences between types of DSD seen. These findings highlight the importance of BP assessment as routine for individuals with XY DSD.

title: Association between the stress hyperglycemia ratio and restenosis at 12 months after first percutaneous transluminal angioplasty in patients receiving maintenance hemodialysis.
authorString: Xu T, Wang Y, Jin M, Xu Y.
abstractText: To evaluate whether preoperative stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR) is associated with 12-month target lesion restenosis after first percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) of autologous arteriovenous fistula (AVF) stenosis in patients on maintenance hemodialysis (MHD). We retrospectively included 158 MHD patients undergoing first PTA for autologous AVF stenosis at Shaoxing Second Hospital between January 2023 and December 2024. SHR was calculated from preoperative venous glucose and glycated hemoglobin A1c, and patients were grouped by quartiles. The primary endpoint was target lesion restenosis within 12 months, with all patients retained and follow-up administratively censored at 12 months. Cause-specific Cox models were fitted: Model 0 was unadjusted; Model 1 adjusted for age, sex, BMI, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, statin use and antiplatelet therapy; Model 2 further adjusted for dialysis vintage, access site, dialysis modality, pre-procedure stenosis severity, Ln(C-reactive protein), lesion length and vascular calcification. Kaplan-Meier analysis, restricted cubic splines, subgroup analyses of 13 categorical factors, a Fine-Gray competing-risk model, exploratory mediation analysis and discrimination analysis were also performed. During follow-up, 104 patients (65.8%) developed restenosis, 11 (7.0%) died before restenosis and 43 (27.2%) were censored at 12 months. Restenosis incidence from Q1 to Q4 was 25.6% (10/39), 50.0% (20/40), 94.9% (37/39) and 92.5% (37/40) (log-rank P < 0.001). Compared with Q1, fully adjusted Model 2 HRs for Q2-Q4 were 2.29 (95% CI 1.04-5.04; P = 0.039), 4.30 (2.08-8.87; P < 0.001) and 5.51 (2.52-12.07; P < 0.001). Each 1-SD increase in SHR was associated with an HR of 1.57 (1.25-1.96) in Model 2 (P < 0.001), and restricted cubic splines showed a nonlinear association (P < 0.001). Ln(CRP) was independently associated with restenosis (HR 1.62, 1.06-2.48; P = 0.027). Subgroup and competing-risk analyses were consistent; the exploratory indirect effect through Ln(CRP) was 0.090 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.000-0.199). Preoperative SHR was independently associated with 12-month restenosis after first autologous AVF PTA in MHD patients, showing a nonlinear relationship. As it derives from routine laboratory tests, SHR may aid preoperative risk stratification; causality and clinical utility require prospective multicenter validation.

title: Atypical Presentation of Acute Groin Pain, Two Surgical Pathologies in One, Acute Appendicitis in an Amyand's Hernia.
authorString: Nassar M, Salem W, Devries M.
abstractText: Amyand's hernia (AH), described as the presence of the appendix within an inguinal hernia sac, accounts for ~1% of groin hernias. Appendicitis within an AH is even rarer, posing challenges in diagnosis and management. We report the case of a 65-year-old female with a history of hypertension and prior hysterectomy who presented with 3 days of worsening abdominal pain. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a right inguinal hernia containing an inflamed appendix with surrounding free fluid. The patient underwent open right inguinal hernia repair with laparoscopic appendectomy. Intraoperatively, the appendix was reduced from the hernia sac and found to be necrotic without perforation. The postoperative course was uncomplicated, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day one. She later underwent elective definitive bilateral inguinal hernia repair with mesh. Management of AH depends on the condition of the appendix and degree of contamination. In cases of complicated appendicitis, primary tissue repair is preferred to reduce the risk of mesh infection. This case highlights the feasibility of a staged approach in patients with appendicitis associated with AHs. Although rare, AH with appendicitis should be considered in patients presenting with groin hernias and abdominal pain and subsequently confirmed on CT. Individualized surgical management can lead to favorable outcomes.

title: Cardiometabolic Predictors of Cardiovascular Disease Risk in Veterans with Chronic Spinal Cord Injury.
authorString: Robles JP, Moore ES, Figoni SF, Ewen HH, Hon AJ.

journal.title: Topics in spinal cord injury rehabilitation

abstractText: To develop and evaluate regression models predicting cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk in veterans with chronic spinal cord injury (SCI), incorporating SCI and cardiometabolic syndrome (CMS) covariates, and to explore potential screening thresholds. This was a retrospective cross-sectional study in the Department of Veterans Affairs SCI outpatient rehabilitation and annual evaluation. Of 600 veterans screened with chronic SCI (>1 year), 106 with tetraplegia and 78 with paraplegia were included. Multiple linear regressions and F tests examined age, sex, SCI factors (level, impairment grade, completeness, duration), SCI-related obesity, hypertension, dysglycemia, dyslipidemia, and hypertriglyceridemia as predictors of 10-year Framingham Risk Score (FRS). Full and reduced models were compared using partial F tests. Sensitivity analysis for SCI obesity was performed. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and area under the curve (AUC) against FRS ≥20% were calculated for CMS, age, and SCI duration. Median age and SCI duration were 68 years and 10 years in patients with tetraplegia and 64 years and 15 years in patients with paraplegia, respectively. The most common injuries were incomplete tetraplegia and complete paraplegia. FRS ≥20% (51%), CMS (72%), and diabetes (29%) were prevalent. Full and reduced models were statistically significant (P < .001) in predicting FRS, while retaining parsimony. Individuals with SCI obesity (i.e., BMI ≥ 22 kg/m2) showed a prevalence of CMS, diabetes, and FRS ≥20%. CMS ROC curve showed strong discrimination of diabetes and FRS ≥ 20%. Potential screening thresholds for FRS ≥20% include age ≥62.5 years in individuals with tetraplegia and ≥60.5 years in individuals with paraplegia and SCI duration ≥33.5 years in individuals with paraplegia. Age, sex, and subsets of SCI and CMS covariates predicted CVD risk in this older SCI veteran cohort. Elevated CVD risk underscores cardiometabolic burden in chronic SCI that was driven by distinct risk factors across groups. Data-derived screening thresholds require validation in larger and more diverse SCI cohorts before clinical implementation.

title: Post-ischemic disruptive sequences: Polymicrogyria, porencephaly, hydranencephaly and their accompanying central nervous system pathologies.
authorString: Fisher Y, Shannon P, Parks WT, Shinar S, Miller E, Chitayat D, Das S.
abstractText: Survivors of in utero encephaloclastic injury because of circulatory compromise may develop disruptive sequences in the central nervous system (CNS), including polymicrogyria (PMG), porencephaly, schizencephaly, hydranencephaly, as well as thalamic, cerebellar, brainstem or spinal cord injury (SCI). Although such injuries are associated with circulatory compromise and placental pathology, the associations between the various CNS injuries and the placental pathology, fetal systemic pathology or clinical history have not been systematically studied. In this paper we review 46 consecutive fetal autopsies (gestational age = 17-36 weeks, median = 23 weeks) with well-characterised, non-acute hypoxic-ischemic disruptive sequences of the CNS and reviewed the CNS pathology, autopsy findings, placental examination and clinical history for all cases. We demonstrate two mutually exclusive patterns of in utero CNS injury, the Tegmental pattern, characterised by bilateral symmetrical tegmental injury (BSTI) (N = 20) and the porencephaly (P) pattern, characterised by the presence of porencephaly/schizencephaly (P/S) (N = 12). BSTI was frequently associated with spinal cord and thalamic injury, and occasionally with PMG. P/S was more common in females, associated with cerebellar injury, frequently displayed features of remote intracranial haemorrhage and never demonstrated SCI. Isolated SCI was not observed. Evidence of haemorrhage was prevalent in cerebellar injury, but not in PMG without P/S. A third pattern, hydranencephaly (N = 3) had features overlapping between BSTI and P/S. The remaining cases showed isolated PMG (N = 5), cerebellar injury (N = 2) or an infarct in the distribution of an arterial territory (N = 4). Significant placental disease, systemic pathology or maternal history of disease was the rule (43 of 46 cases) but there was no obvious correlation between placental, maternal or fetal disease or history and the pattern of CNS injury. This comprehensive study of fetal CNS disruptive sequences demonstrates distinct patterns of injury, and raises the question of how these dramatically different morphologies can arise from similar insults.

title: Beyond transfusions: bleeding-related outcomes after repeat TURP.
authorString: Derigs M, Liu E, Lange D, Bhojani N, Wymer K, Forbes CM.
abstractText:
Purpose

We compared perioperative bleeding morbidity after primary transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) versus repeat TURP (re-TURP) to inform counseling and risk stratification.

Methods

We queried the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (2013-2023) for primary TURP (Current Procedural Terminology [CPT] 52601) and re-TURP (CPT 52630). The primary outcome was perioperative transfusion. Secondary outcomes included ICD-10-based hematuria endpoints from postoperative, readmission, and reoperation diagnoses, as well as reoperation CPT categories. Multivariable logistic models adjusted for age, ASA class, bleeding disorder, urinary tract infection, hematocrit, and platelet count; additional models included surgical urgency, operative time, INR, and albumin.

Results

We identified 83,539 procedures: 76,983 primary TURPs and 6,556 re-TURPs. Transfusion occurred in 1.5% after primary TURP versus 1.9% after re-TURP, while hematuria-related postoperative diagnoses accounted for 1.3% versus 3.6%. Re-TURP was associated with hematuria-related postoperative diagnoses after adjustment (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.70, 95% CI 2.27-3.21), whereas its adjusted association with transfusion was nonsignificant (aOR 1.12, 95% CI 0.90-1.39). Older age, bleeding disorder, lower hematocrit, and lower platelet count were associated with both bleeding outcomes. Findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses. Hematuria was the largest recorded readmission and reoperation diagnosis group, and clot evacuation/fulguration/irrigation was the largest reoperation procedure category in both cohorts, without significant between-group differences.

Conclusions

Re-TURP was associated with greater odds of a recorded hematuria-related postoperative diagnosis, while its adjusted association with transfusion was not statistically significant. Because diagnosis codes cannot establish bleeding severity or onset, these findings require confirmation using clinically validated bleeding endpoints.

title: Expert consensus on periodontal management for medically compromised patients.
authorString: Geng F, Lin L, Song Z, Yan F, Xu Y, Liu Y, Sun J, Luan Q, Hu W, Ge S, Chen F, Zhao C, Qiao J, Chen X, Zuo X, Liu X, An L, Wang Z, Zhang D, Li C, Zhao X, Ding Y, Pan Y.
abstractText: Periodontitis is a highly prevalent oral disease that extends beyond local inflammation and tissue destruction to exert a profound influence on systemic health. With the growing burden of multimorbidity, where multiple systemic disorders frequently co-exist, periodontal management has become increasingly complex, yet clear and integrated guidance for this specific patient population remains limited. This manuscript synthesizes current evidence on the bidirectional relationship between periodontitis and systemic conditions, proposes recommendations for dynamic periodontal management, and updates relevant therapeutic strategies. This expert consensus is designed to ensure both the safety and efficacy of periodontal treatment, reduce the risk of complications, and ultimately promote oral and general well-being.

title: Metformin mitigates trophoblast GLUT1 inhibition through HIF-1α/Fibronectin/AMPK pathway in preeclampsia.
authorString: Lee CI, Tsai PY, Tam HL, Su MT.
abstractText: Preeclampsia (PE) is a complex gestational hypertensive disorder associated with dysregulated placental energy metabolism, and fibronectin (FN) plays a critical role in its development. Although metformin has shown potential in reducing the risk of PE, its effects on FN and trophoblast glucose transport regulation remain unclear. In this study, experiments were conducted using FN-pretreated and FN-knockdown HTR-8/SVneo cells, clinical placental specimens, and a preeclampsia mouse model. Aberrant FN and GLUT1 expression was observed in human preeclamptic placentas. Under hypoxic conditions, FN and GLUT1 were upregulated in two trophoblastic cell lines (HTR-8/SVneo and JAR) and in primary placental cells. However, exogenous FN suppressed hypoxia-associated GLUT1 upregulation, reduced extracellular L-lactate levels, and impaired trophoblast invasion and ciliogenesis. These effects were associated with activation of AMPK signaling. Metformin reduced HIF-1α, FN, and phosphorylated AMPK levels in FN-treated trophoblasts under hypoxia, while increasing GLUT1 expression and extracellular L-lactate levels and restoring trophoblast invasion and ciliogenesis. Notably, metformin increased AMPK phosphorylation in FN-silenced cells, suggesting that its effects on AMPK signaling depend, at least partly, on FN status. In the mouse model, increased placental FN was accompanied by altered GLUT1 expression, impaired primary cilia formation, and changes in AMPK-related signaling. Metformin treatment improved maternal blood pressure and fetal growth, reduced placental FN levels, and increased GLUT1 expression and ciliogenesis. In conclusion, FN disrupts trophoblast function under hypoxia and is associated with changes in GLUT1 expression and lactate output, involving AMPK signaling. Metformin alleviates these dysfunctions by suppressing FN and reversing FN-mediated GLUT1 inhibition and AMPK activation. These findings identify the HIF-1α/FN/AMPK axis as a critical mechanism in PE pathophysiology and support the potential repurposing of metformin for PE prevention.

title: The MMRRC as translational infrastructure for biomedical research and the integration of new approach methodologies.
authorString: Magnuson T, Murray SA, Lutz CM, Roiphe L, Amos-Landgraf J, Yokoyama A, Kent Lloyd KC.

journal.title: Mammalian genome : official journal of the International Mammalian Genome Society

abstractText: The central challenge in translational research is aligning each biological question with the model system best suited to answer it. Mouse models are particularly powerful when research questions require mammalian physiology, developmental timing, neuroimmune and cardiometabolic interactions, pharmacology, longitudinal assessment, and other system-wide phenomena. Yet no single mouse model fully recapitulates a human disease, just as no single new approach methodology (NAM) captures the complexity of human pathobiology in vivo. Translational advances therefore depend on integrating complementary experimental systems and comparative cross-species analysis. Within this ecosystem, the NIH-funded Mutant Mouse Resource and Research Center (MMRRC) provides essential infrastructure for translational biomedical research by preserving and providing unique strains, ensuring genetic and microbial quality control, maintaining a reversible cryoarchive, standardizing data and documentation, supporting in vivo phenotyping, and ensuring equal and equitable public access and availability. Recent studies demonstrate how MMRRC-distributed models contribute to mechanistic insights observed from human-based studies, and vice versa. The MMRRC's expanding human pluripotent stem cell collections and informatics capabilities offer further opportunities to integrate human-derived systems with genetically-engineered mouse models. By supporting rigorous, accessible, and increasingly human-informed experimental research, the MMRRC strengthens discovery, improves reproducibility, supports the 3Rs (replacement, reduction, refinement), and enables the integration of complementary models in translational science.

title: Bilateral asymmetric accessory iliopsoas musculature and variant relationships with the femoral nerve: an anatomical case report.
authorString: Wetzel C, Hall B, Templin K, Foster J.
abstractText:
Purpose

Accessory musculature within the interval between the psoas major and iliacus may alter the expected course of the femoral nerve and complicate imaging or surgical exposure. This report describes a rare bilateral but asymmetric configuration of accessory iliopsoas musculature.

Methods

The posterior abdominal wall and iliopsoas regions of an 85-year-old male whole-body donor were dissected bilaterally. Accessory muscle origins, distal fusion patterns, dimensions, and relationships with the femoral nerve were documented.

Results

Two accessory muscular heads were identified on each side. On the left, both arose from the L4 costal process; on the right, the heads arose separately from the L2 and L3 costal processes. One head on each side fused to the native psoas major, and the other to the native iliacus. The femoral nerve passed between the native psoas major and accessory psoas-associated head on the left, but between the two accessory heads on the right. The heads differed in length and caliber between sides.

Conclusion

In this donor, bilateral accessory iliopsoas heads had different origins and femoral nerve relationships. Recognition of unexpected intermuscular nerve intervals may aid anatomical interpretation and operative orientation, particularly in posterior abdominal wall or retroperitoneal exposures. No evidence of femoral neuropathy or altered biomechanical function was available.

title: Comorbidity burden and radiographically significant interval rebleeding after supratentorial intracerebral hematoma evacuation: a single-center cohort study.
authorString: Bánoci J, Magočová VB, Kaťuch V, Knorovský K, Škovranová M.
abstractText: How the association between comorbidity burden and postoperative rebleeding varies with the imaging definition remains incompletely characterized. This single-center cohort included 111 patients undergoing intracerebral hematoma evacuation (2016-2025), with retrospective ascertainment and prospective study-specific data collection after ethics approval. We compared 0-1 versus ≥ 2 documented comorbidity categories. Rebleeding required a visually confirmed new or increased hemorrhagic component between early and second postoperative computed tomography scans, with interval volume increase > 20 mL and > 25% of preoperative volume. Analyses also used alternative volumetric thresholds. Primary rebleeding occurred in 2/78 patients (2.6%) with 0-1 category and 9/33 (27.3%) with ≥ 2 categories: conditional odds ratio (OR) 13.84, exact 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.62-140.31; p < 0.001; absolute risk difference 24.7% points. Associations were weaker under alternative thresholds: OR 2.84 (95% CI 0.89-9.18) for an increase > 25% of preoperative volume and OR 1.54 (95% CI 0.61-4.03) for ≥ 6 mL or ≥ 33% of the early postoperative volume. Excluding five patients with intervening residual-clot revision yielded a similar primary association (n = 106; OR 14.47, exact 95% CI 2.72-147.36). Eight of 11 patients with primary rebleeding underwent revision. Median intensive care stay was 10 versus 6 days. Anticoagulant exposure was associated with rebleeding in crude analysis and overlapped with multimorbidity. Documented multimorbidity was associated with large interval rebleeding under the study definition, but the association depended on the volumetric threshold. The small event count, incomplete neurological assessability, documentation-based exposure ascertainment and residual confounding limit causal and predictive interpretation.

title: Bedside Diagnosis of Biventricular Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy With Isolated Right Ventricular Outflow Tract Obstruction.
authorString: Kawasaki T, Yamano M.
abstractText:
Background

Isolated right ventricular outflow tract obstruction is a rare phenotype of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), usually recognized only on imaging.

Case summary

A 51-year-old man presented with mild exertional dyspnea and an abnormal electrocardiogram; his brother had died suddenly at 31 years of age. Before any imaging, bedside examination revealed a giant jugular a-wave without a y-descent, a fourth heart sound louder at the left sternal border than at the apex, and a systolic ejection murmur that increased on sitting and during expiration (reversed Rivero-Carvallo sign). These findings predicted biventricular HCM with right ventricular outflow tract obstruction but without left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, confirmed by echocardiography, catheterization, and endomyocardial biopsy.

Discussion

Jugular venous waveform analysis, multisite auscultation, and simple postural and respiratory maneuvers can both suggest HCM and localize the site of outflow obstruction.

Take-home message

In HCM, a systolic murmur that intensifies with expiration should prompt consideration of right-sided obstruction.

title: A novel 17-plex multi-pathogen detection for rapid and accurate diagnosis of tick-borne diseases.
authorString: Fu J, Fu L, Chen Q, Su Z, Guan X, Yao X, Xiong J, Qian J, Fang Y, Deng F, Shen S, Wang H, Wu X.
abstractText: In recent years, anthropogenic ecological disruption has escalated tick-borne zoonoses; ticks transmit taxonomically diverse pathogens with overlapping clinical signs, challenging precise diagnosis and increasing risk of simultaneous detection in pooled samples. Despite advancements, current sequencing technologies, such as Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS), Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) assays, and antibody-based detection methods, are hampered by limitations including extended processing times and limited detection throughput. These constraints significantly hinder their effectiveness in high-throughput pathogen screening for animal or patient samples. To address these challenges, we developed an innovative multi-detection method based on the Multi-analyte Suspension Assay (MASA), enabling rapid and accurate diagnosis of a comprehensive panel of 17 vector-borne pathogens. This 17-plex panel comprises Rickettsia spp., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Borrelia recurrentis, Babesia spp., Borrelia burgdorferi, Rickettsia prowazekii, Rickettsia heilongjiangensis, Orientia tsutsugamushi, Coxiella burnetii, Leptospira, Bartonella spp., Candidatus Ehrlichia erytraense, Hantaan Virus (HTNV), Seoul Virus (SEOV), Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus (CCHFV), Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome Virus (SFTSV), and Tick-Borne Encephalitis Virus (TBEV). By combining this novel method with traditional techniques, including nested PCR and Real-Time Quantitative Reverse Transcription PCR (qRT-PCR), we achieved accurate detection of pathogens such as Rickettsia spp., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, and SFTSV in tick samples. Notably, the technique revealed the co-existence of multiple pathogens within the same sample group, highlighting its ability in identifying co-detection of pathogens. Additionally, in suspected cases of tick-borne pathogen infection in febrile patients, the method quickly identified positive results for SFTSV and Rickettsia spp. These preliminary results suggest the potential of this method as a promising screening tool for clinical diagnostics, although larger-scale validation is warranted. This method provides a preliminary technical candidate approach for the development of more sensitive field-deployable detection tools.

title: Lateral muscles to defect ratio as a preoperative predictor to achieve fascial closure in ventral hernia.
authorString: Alayat AA, Soliman NH, Aziz BA, Ali EH, Tobar WL, Elhawary RY.

journal.title: Hernia : the journal of hernias and abdominal wall surgery

abstractText:
Background

Component separation techniques (CST) are utilized to provide tension-free fascial closure (FC) in large hernias. However, in some cases CST are not sufficient and a bridged repair is performed. The use of Botulinum toxin A (BTA) has been proposed to aid in achieving tension-free FC by relaxing the lateral abdominal wall muscles. We conducted a retrospective study to identify preoperative predictors of inability to achieve complete FC after posterior component separation (PCS), utilizing preoperative computed tomography (CT) images to pinpoint patients who might benefit from BTA injections.

Methods

From January 2023 to December 2025, patients who underwent open repair of midline abdominal wall incisional hernias, with PCS were identified. CT images were reviewed to assess the hernia defect width, right and left rectus width, angle of diastasis, and the length of lateral abdominal wall muscles to calculate the Rectus Defect Ratio (RDR), Component Separation Index (CSI). and Lateral Defect Ratio (LDR). CT measurements were compared according to the ability to achieve FC.

Results

A total of 46 patients were included in the study. FC was achieved in 37 (80.4%) of them. LDR demonstrated the highest area under the curve (AUC) with 0.979 and highest accuracy with 95.6% at detecting FC, while CSI had 0.907 AUC and 89.13% accuracy. There was a decrease in the rate of FC with decreasing LDR. It decreased from 100% in patients with LDR > 3 (n = 15), to 95.2% in patients with LDR ranging 2-3 (n = 21), and down to 20% in patients with LDR < 2 (n = 10).

Conclusion

The current study demonstrates that the LDR is a simple preoperative radiological measurement to predict the ability to achieve complete fascial closure of the hernia defect during open PCS. An LDR of > 2 predicts complete fascial closure in 94% of cases and thus can aid in surgical planning, and the potential need for preoperative adjuncts as BTA.

title: Reducing General Anesthesia Use in Pediatric Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
authorString: Bugnitz C, Ralston M, Frey A, VanDorpe M, Williams B.
abstractText:
Introduction

The cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) program at our institution has relied solely on general anesthesia for patients who are unable to lie still or adequately breath-hold. The goal of the project was to decrease the percentage of patients who require general anesthesia for CMR from 34% per month to 20% per month while maintaining high-quality imaging.

Methods

This is an ongoing quality improvement project that began in January 2024 at our free-standing children's hospital. We included all patients scheduled for a CMR, including some adults cared for by our adult congenital cardiology colleagues at a partnering institution. The outcome measure was the percentage of patients who required general anesthesia for CMR.

Results

After 21 months, we shifted our mean from 34% to 6.5% per month and sustained that for 15 months by the time of this article submission.

Conclusions

By implementing a quality improvement project that follows the Institute for Healthcare Improvement model, we significantly decreased the percentage of patients who require general anesthesia to achieve CMR and sustained this reduction. Our experience at a free-standing pediatric children's hospital with a small but growing CMR program can inform improvements in MRI centers of all sizes but could particularly benefit programs of similar size that lack a dedicated cardiac anesthesia program.

title: Human Pregnane X Receptor Modulates Sex-Dependent Hepatic Oxidative Stress and Inflammatory Responses in Alcohol-Induced Liver Injury.
authorString: Ofosu-Boateng M, Twum E, Nnamani DO, Gebreyesus L, Mandal M, Rakib A, Gonzalez FJ, Singh UP, Gyamfi MA.
abstractText: Alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) remains a major global health burden with limited targeted therapies. Although the pregnane X receptor (PXR) has been implicated in ALD pathogenesis, the specific contribution of human PXR signaling to ethanol-induced liver injury remains unclear. Here, we investigated the impact of human PXR on ethanol-induced hepatotoxicity, histopathology, inflammation, oxidative stress, immune-cell composition, and hepatic transcriptional profiles. Male and female wild-type (WT, C57BL/6N) and PXR-humanized (hPXR) mice were subjected to the chronic-plus-binge ethanol regimen, followed by comprehensive hepatic and systemic profiling. Ethanol-fed female hPXR mice developed more severe steatosis and hepatotoxicity than their WT counterparts. This exacerbated liver injury was accompanied by elevated circulating acetaldehyde, increased hepatic hydrogen peroxide levels, oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling, enhanced NF-κB activation, and reduced mitochondrial ALDH2 protein expression and activity, consistent with impaired acetaldehyde detoxification and ROS accumulation. Hepatic transcriptomics identified differential expression of genes associated with xenobiotic metabolism and pathways potentially involved in non-oxidative ethanol metabolism, including members of the Ces2a and Sult2a gene families. Splenic and mesenteric lymph node CD3+ T-cell frequencies and circulating IL-5 concentrations were elevated in females regardless of genotype or ethanol exposure, indicating baseline sex-dependent immune differences rather than broad human PXR-dependent systemic immune activation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that human PXR promotes susceptibility to ethanol-induced liver injury, particularly in females via impaired acetaldehyde clearance, oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling, and altered hepatic gene expression as potential mechanisms. These results establish hPXR mice as a translational model for dissecting human PXR-dependent mechanisms and therapeutic targets in ALD.
