Although left ventricular ejection fraction frequently normalises, persistent abnormalities in myocardial function, tissue characteristics, energetics, symptoms, and exercise capacity are increasingly recognised. TTS should therefore be viewed not simply as a transient and fully reversible disorder, but as a complex clinical syndrome with acute and longer-term consequences that remain incompletely understood.

title: Lung ultrasound in congenital heart disease: from physiology to precision medicine.
authorString: Gregorio-Hernández R, Sánchez-Luna M, Fraga MV.
abstractText:
Congenital heart disease (CHD) affects approximately 8 per 1000 births worldwide. Approximately 25% are classified as critical congenital heart disease (CCHD), requiring early diagnosis and neonatal intervention. Management of these patients is complex, dynamic and multiparametric. Respiratory complications are common during the hospitalization of patients with CHD. Lung ultrasound (LUS) has emerged as a valuable bedside tool to accurately assess lung aeration, particularly in critically ill patients in whom conventional imaging techniques may be difficult to obtain, impractical, or challenging to interpret. Although growing evidence supports the use of LUS throughout the perioperative and postoperative period, its application remains insufficiently characterized. LUS is evolving beyond its traditional role as a diagnostic imaging modality toward a dynamic bedside monitoring tool, with the potential to guide and optimize respiratory management before, during, and after cardiac surgery.

Conclusion

This review aims to summarize the current evidence regarding the use of LUS in this population and to highlight its potential role in the assessment and management of preoperative and postoperative respiratory complications.

What is known

• Lung ultrasound (LUS) is a bedside, radiation-free imaging technique that provides real-time information on pulmonary aeration, interstitial edema, pleural effusion, atelectasis, and pneumothorax in children with congenital heart disease (CHD). • Pulmonary abnormalities in CHD are closely related to the underlying hemodynamic physiology and may change dynamically throughout the preoperative, perioperative, and postoperative periods. However, the clinical application of LUS in this population remains heterogeneous and is not yet routinely integrated into CHD management.

What is new

• This review summarizes the current evidence on LUS in CHD from a pathophysiological perspective, linking ultrasound findings to the underlying cardiac physiology and highlighting potential pitfalls in their interpretation. • LUS may contribute to a precision-medicine approach in children with CHD by integrating bedside pulmonary phenotyping with clinical and echocardiographic assessment, while identifying key areas where prospective studies are needed to establish standardized protocols and determine whether LUS-guided management improves clinically relevant outcomes.

title: Advanced Medical Therapeutic Approaches to Treat Chronic Coronary Syndromes: A Narrative Review.
authorString: Saleem S, Saleem MF, Marryam H, Saleem MF.

journal.title: Turk Kardiyoloji Dernegi arsivi : Turk Kardiyoloji Derneginin yayin organidir

abstractText: Chronic coronary syndromes (CCSs) encompass obstructive and non-obstructive coronary artery disease, including epicardial atherosclerosis, coronary microvascular dysfunction, and coronary vasospasm, which may lead to angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, heart attack, and sudden death. Understanding the pathophysiology of CCS has led to targeted therapeutic approaches aimed at managing dyslipidemia, inflammation, and thrombus formation to reduce cardiovascular burden and mortality risk. This review aimed to explore advanced and emerging therapeutic strategies for the treatment of CCS, including advanced lipid-lowering therapies, Lp(a)-lowering RNA agents, novel anti-inflammatory agents, including interleukin-6 (IL-6)-targeted therapy, Factor XIa-targeted antithrombotic therapy, cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibitors (CETP), angiopoietin-like protein 3 (ANGPTL3) inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), nanoparticle-based targeted therapies, and microbiome-modifying therapies. This review situates each therapeutic agent within the 2024 ESC and 2023 ACC/AHA chronic coronary syndrome guidelines and, because regulatory approval, guideline recommendations, and cardiovascular outcome evidence are distinct concepts, considers each separately: high-intensity statins, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, low-dose colchicine, and semaglutide are approved and guideline-recommended for defined populations with outcome-trial support; inclisiran and bempedoic acid are approved and guideline-endorsed as add-on lipid-lowering therapies, although inclisiran's dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial remains ongoing; and pelacarsen, olpasiran, lepodisiran, zerlasiran, ziltivekimab, and obicetrapib remain investigational, with regulatory approval and guideline recommendations contingent on cardiovascular outcomes trial (CVOT) data. Nanomedicine- and microbiome-based approaches remain preclinical or early-phase and are considered hypothesis-generating. Despite promising advances, long-term safety, optimal patient selection, and cardiovascular outcome benefits remain uncertain. Future research should prioritize outcome-driven trials and personalized therapeutic strategies to address residual cardiovascular risk.

title: The ACROSSS-study. The role of sleep characteristics before and after a cardiovascular event. Rationale and study design.
authorString: Kloetzsch A, Kuehl T, Christ M, Hailer B, Frank B, Koehrmann M, Kleinschnitz C, Bruder O, Stang A.
abstractText: Studies of myocardial infarction and stroke showed a diurnal variation with peaks in the morning and afternoon. So far, night sleep or napping have not been investigated as triggers for cardiovascular events via a case-crossover study. Therefore, the main question of the ACROSSS (Acute CoROnary Syndrome, Stroke and Sleep) study is how much the occurrence of a myocardial infarction/stroke/transient ischemic attack is associated with taking a nap shortly before (topic 1, case-crossover study, 656 patients needed). Moreover, the study aims at assessing the incidence of sleep disturbances three and twelve months after a myocardial infarction/stroke/transient ischemic attack (topic 2, follow-up study, 400 patients needed). Recruitment of patients is carried out in four German hospitals in Essen and Bottrop, North Rhine-Westphalia. The examination program includes the case-crossover questionnaire on potential acute triggers of cardiovascular events, a sleep questionnaire with validated instruments (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, etc.) and a questionnaire on health status and lifestyle habits. Moreover, eligible patients are screened for sleep apnea and during the follow-up sleep is measured by actigraphy. The combination of sleep-related and clinical data offers a deeper understanding of how sleep affects the acute onset of a cardiovascular event and recovery afterwards.

title: Refining Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Risk Assessment Across the Heart Failure Spectrum
authorString: Noh SA, Bae NY, Lim J, Kwak S, Bak M, Park J, Choi H, Park J, Yoon YE, Lee S, Park J, Kim Y, Cho G, Kim H, Hwang I.
abstractText:
Background:

The cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) framework emphasizes risk assessment and prevention of heart failure (HF). However, the prognostic implications and optimal assessment of CKM burden in established HF remain uncertain.

Objectives:

To evaluate the prognostic value of binary and HF-adapted graded CKM burden scores across HF phenotypes.

Methods:

We evaluated 2 independent HF cohorts comprising patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) initiating angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor therapy (HFrEF-ARNI; n=1,450) and patients hospitalized for acute HF (AHF; n = 2,985). AHF patients were stratified by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) into <50% and ≥50% (HFrEF and HF with preserved ejection fraction [HFpEF] groups, respectively). The binary score counted 6 CKM components; the graded score incorporated chronic kidney disease severity and reverse-scored body mass index categories. Associations with the composite outcome of all-cause death or HF hospitalization were assessed using Cox regression. Prognostic discrimination and interactions with HF phenotype were also evaluated.

Results:

Median follow-up was 31.5 months in HFrEF-ARNI and 51.1 months in AHF. Both scores were independently associated with the composite outcome in both cohorts. In HFrEF-ARNI cohort, adjusted HRs per 1-point increase were 1.10 (95% CI 1.02-1.18) for the binary score and 1.11 (95% CI 1.04-1.19) for the graded score. In AHF, both scores were associated with outcomes in HFrEF, whereas only the graded score was significantly associated with the outcome in HFpEF (binary: HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.90-1.02; graded: HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.04-1.15). Significant interactions with HF phenotype were observed for both scores. The graded score showed better discrimination than the binary score in both cohorts (C-index 0.632 vs 0.583 in HFrEF-ARNI; 0.609 vs 0.541 in AHF), particularly in HFpEF (C-index 0.576 vs 0.491). In HFpEF, only the graded score provided significant incremental prognostic information beyond clinical and echocardiographic variables (χ2 = 11.3; P <0.001).

Conclusions:

The HF-adapted graded CKM burden score demonstrated more consistent prognostic associations and better risk discrimination than the binary score, particularly in HFpEF. Incorporating disease severity and HF-relevant prognostic characteristics may refine CKM burden assessment and risk stratification in established HF.

title: The ITE-Transformer: A pre-trained foundation model for predicting individualized treatment effects from electronic health records
authorString: Arceri C, Angelis E, Heesen P, Melnychuk V, Bendszus M, Bauer S, Feuerriegel S.
abstractText: Transformer-based foundation models have shown strong potential for modeling longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), yet existing models focus primarily on risk prediction rather than treatment effect estimation, which limits evidence generation. Here, we introduce the ITE-Transformer, a transformer-based framework that combines self-supervised representation learning from longitudinal patient trajectories with doubly robust causal machine learning for predicting individualized treatment effects (ITEs). As a result, our ITE-Transformer allows to study counterfactual questions of how an individual patient's outcome may differ under alternative treatment strategies. The ITE-Transformer learns temporally contextualized representations of patients' diagnosis and medication histories and subsequently uses these representations to predict treatment assignment, treatment-specific outcome risks, and patient-specific ITEs. The ITE-Transformer is trained using structured EHR data from ~350,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program and evaluated in two clinically different comparative-effectiveness tasks: (i) GLP-1 receptor agonists versus DPP-4 inhibitors among patients with type 2 diabetes, with major adverse cardiovascular events as the outcome, and (ii) immunotherapy versus chemotherapy in a pan-cancer cohort, with all-cause mortality as the outcome. Across both applications, the ITE-Transformer improves the discrimination and calibration of treatment assignment and outcome models compared with existing tabular machine learning approaches and an otherwise identical transformer trained without self-supervised pre-training. The ITE-Transformer further identifies substantial heterogeneity in predicted ITEs and yields interpretable patterns of treatment response associated with patients' diagnoses, medication histories, and comorbidities. Together, our work demonstrates how clinical foundation models can be developed for analyzing heterogeneity in treatment effects and thus support real-world evidence generation.

title: Senescence and Genotoxicity Signatures Across Clinical and Laboratory Outcomes in Patients at High Cardiovascular Risk: An Automated Machine Learning Study
authorString: Kyryk V, Krasnienkov D, Ustymenko A, Tsupykov O, Midlovets K, Skarzhevskyi O, Khomiakov D, Parkhomenko O.
abstractText: Background. Cellular senescence, chromosomal instability, endothelial injury, and altered immune composition may jointly reflect biological aging and cardiometabolic dysfunction. We evaluated whether a fixed 12-biomarker panel provided reproducible feature-level clues for 11 pre-selected clinical and laboratory outcomes in a three-group cohort at high cardiovascular risk. Methods. The dataset included 90 patients suffered from acute coronary syndrome (ACS), divided equally into three groups (n = 30 each): pre-pandemic ACS (Group 1), ACS with concomitant laboratory-confirmed acute COVID-19 during the pandemic (Group 2), and ACS without concomitant acute COVID-19 during the COVID-19 pandemic period (Group 3). Four model families were evaluated separately using 5-fold cross-fitting repeated five times. All imputation, scaling, and model fitting were restricted to training folds. Feature evidence integrated held-out permutation importance, cross-fitted SHAP values, linear coefficient stability, Group+SEX-adjusted partial rank associations, within-group sensitivity analyses, and leave-one-group-out transportability. Results. The largest median improvements over Group+SEX baselines occurred for history of acute myocardial infarction with coronary revascularization procedures (Δ=0.161), glucose level (Δ=0.118), heart rate (Δ=0.096), and glycated hemoglobin percentage (Δ=0.091). Recurrent feature themes included senescence-associated heterochromatin foci and CD34 + progenitor cells for glycemic outcomes, micronuclei for heart rate and prior COVID-19, nucleoplasmic bridges for cardiac-history and inflammatory/immune outcomes, and CD31 hi circulating endothelial cells for leukocyte and granulocyte counts. Absolute performance remained weak for several outcomes despite stable feature rankings. Conclusions. Rather than predicting any single outcome with strong absolute accuracy, the same senescence and genotoxicity markers recurred as leading clues across metabolically, cardiac, and immunologically distinct outcomes, and did so consistently across three pathogenetic different cohorts. This cross-outcome stability suggests these markers may index a shared, stressor-independent dimension of cellular burden in ACS patients rather than outcome-specific biology, a hypothesis that warrants mechanistic follow-up.

title: Low-Dose Aspirin Protects the Neurovascular Unit through Lysine Acetylation of Histone in an Oxygen–Glucose Deprivation Model of Cerebral Ischemia
authorString: Thomas DA, Gangadhar A, Babu M, Rao RM, Gogoi A, Shirin R, Datta A.
abstractText: Low-dose aspirin is widely used as a low-cost prophylactic against atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and for secondary prevention of ischemic stroke due to its anti-platelet action that is mediated by serine acetylation of cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes. However, whether beneficial effects of low-dose aspirin are mediated by direct protective effect on the cells of the neurovascular unit that is platelet-independent, remain unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of chronic low-concentration (10 µM) aspirin pretreatment in cultured brain vascular endothelial cells and neurons subjected to sub-lethal in vitro cerebral ischemia via 4 hoxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD). Chronic aspirin pretreatment abolished the OGD-induced increase in Mcp1/Ccl2 transcript expression suggesting attenuation of inflammatory signalling. This was accompanied by anincreased lysine acetylation on a protein having same molecular weight as histone 3 (H3). Molecular docking calculations showed that aspirin can indeed bind to the lysine residues of H3, with the acetyl group of aspirin being in close contact with side chain lysine residues. Together, these observations indicate low-dose prophylactic aspirin can produce brain cell type-specific anti-inflammatory effect in response to ischemic stress that is associated with lysine acetylation of histone protein.

title: Risk of fragility fractures in individuals with and without HIV infection: a population-based matched case-control study.
authorString: Yang YH, Huang TJ, Tsai SHL, Wu C, Chen MH, Shiao YF, Lee CY, Huang TY, Lin YS, Cheng JS, Kuo TY, Chen YC, Chen PC, Wu MH.

journal.title: Osteoporosis international : a journal established as result of cooperation between the European Foundation for Osteoporosis and the National Osteoporosis Foundation of the USA

abstractText:
HIV infection increases hip fracture risk, but evidence in Asian populations is limited. In this large nationwide matched cohort study, antiretroviral therapy mitigated overall fracture risk and reduced postoperative mortality despite persistent skeletal concerns. These findings highlight the importance of bone health monitoring and prevention in individuals with HIV infection.

Purpose

Patients with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection are at increased risk of comorbidities, including osteoporosis, which predisposes them to fragility fractures (FFs). Evidence from Asian populations is limited. This study investigated the risk of FFs in an Asian population with and without HIV infection.

Methods

We conducted a nationwide retrospective matched cohort study using Taiwan's National Health Insurance Research Database. A total of 3994 individuals with HIV infection and 15,976 matched controls were identified (1:4 ratio). Matching variables included age, sex, monthly income, urbanization, liver cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, renal failure, and hepatitis B and C infection. Fragility fractures were identified using ICD-9-CM codes, and Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Results

The incidence of overall fragility fractures (AFF) was similar between HIV-infected and uninfected individuals (12.9% vs. 11.9%, P = 0.097). However, HIV infection was associated with a significantly higher risk of hip fragility fracture (HFF) (HR 2.22, 95% CI 1.62-3.06, P < 0.001). Risk factors for FFs included age > 50 years, modified Charlson Comorbidity Index ≥ 2, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) mitigated overall fracture risk and was associated with substantially lower postoperative mortality after fracture surgery (9.4% vs. 36.1%).

Conclusion

HIV infection was associated with increased hip fracture risk in this Asian population. ART conferred protective effects on overall fracture risk and survival after fracture, underscoring its net clinical benefit despite skeletal concerns. These findings support targeted bone health monitoring and preventive strategies in individuals with HIV in fection.

title: The effects of size and sex mismatch on kidney functional adaption following living donor kidney transplantation.
authorString: Nankivell BJ, Chicco AFP, Shingde M, Robertson H, Li J, Gruenewald SM.
abstractText:
Introduction

The remarkable functional adaption of transplanted kidneys is poorly understood. Conflicting results for donor-recipient body size and sex mismatches, and concerns for hyperfiltration injury are unresolved.

Methods

This single center, longitudinal cohort study of 194 living kidney transplantations evaluated changes in isotopic 9 9mTc-DTPA measured glomerular filtration rate (mGFR) from side-specific donor function at implantation through 12-months after transplantation against multiple anthropometric parameters, sex mismatch, and pathological hyperfiltration.

Results

Donor kidney mGFR was predicted by younger age, male sex, and heavier body weight using multivariable analysis; and strongly influenced 12-month mGFR. Post-transplant relative and absolute mGFR changes were determined by donor and recipient body sizes (weight, body surface area, and body mass index were statistically interchangeable) and donor and recipient sex using multivariable analysis. mGFR adaption was greatest in smaller female donor kidneys transplanted into large male recipients, but negligible or negative for male kidneys into female recipients. The mGFR ratio significantly correlated with mismatch in donor-recipient body surface area (r=0.285) and body mass index (r=0.248). Absolute mGFR significantly increased with recipient lean body mass (r=0.425) but not total fat content using body composition analysis. Diabetes, fasting blood glucose, hemoglobin A1c, androgenic hormones, and hypertension were unrelated. Evidence of significant maladaptive glomerular hyperfiltration assessed by albuminuria, glomerular pathology, percentage glomerulosclerosis, glomerulomegaly, transcription factor WT1 podocyte immunostaining, chronic interstitial fibrosis, and ultrastructural podocyte effacement at 12-months was absent. Death-censored graft survivals for five-, 10-, and 20-years after transplantation were excellent at 96.9%, 94.3%, and 80.8%, respectively.

Conclusions

mGFR following transplantation depends on input donor quality with adaption driven primarily by larger recipient body size mismatch and male sex. Functional adaption appears as a benign physiological response appropriately calibrated to individual recipient metabolic need without evidence of pathological hyperfiltration injury.

title: Early prediction of noninvasive ventilation failure in acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: Development and internal validation of a clinical risk model.
authorString: Zhu Q, Feng W, Du G.

journal.title: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care

abstractText:
Background

Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) is widely used in acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD), but failure remains common and is associated with poor outcomes. Most existing models rely on severity indicators, limiting early risk identification.

Objectives

To develop and internally validate an early prediction model for NIV failure using non-severity-based clinical variables.

Methods

A retrospective cohort of 180 hospitalized AECOPD patients receiving NIV was analyzed. Candidate predictors included medical history, routine laboratory parameters, and chest radiography findings. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used for variable selection, followed by multivariable logistic regression. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration analysis with 1000-bootstrap resampling, and decision curve analysis (DCA).

Results

NIV failure occurred in 61 patients (33.9%). Independent risk factors included smoking pack-years, mucus plugging/excessive sputum production, acute heart failure/volume overload, pre-admission excessive oxygen therapy, and delayed medical consultation, while serum albumin was protective. The LASSO risk model showed good discrimination (AUC = 0.854) and calibration. Risk stratification demonstrated a clear gradient in NIV failure rates across low-, medium-, and high-risk groups (8.3%, 25.0%, and 68.3%, respectively).

Conclusion

A clinically accessible model based on non-severity variables can effectively predict NIV failure and may support early risk stratification and targeted management.

title: High blood pressure among children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus in Uganda: A multicenter cross-sectional study.
authorString: Mutisya CM, Nduwimana M, Kajoba D, Ndeezi G.
abstractText:
Background

The coexistence of diabetes mellitus (DM) and hypertension (HTN) worsens the clinical outcomes of children with diabetes concerning both microvascular and macrovascular disease. It increases mortality risk by 5 times, with a higher risk of death in developing countries. Therefore, comprehensive care for patients with diabetes, including hypertension screening, must be provided.

Methods

This multicenter health facility-based cross-sectional study included 150 children and adolescents aged from 6 months to 18 years with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) who were treated at Jinja Regional Referral Hospital (JRRH), Mbale Regional Referral Hospital (MRRH) and Lira Regional Referral Hospital (LRRH). Interviewer-administered questionnaires were used to obtain data, which were then analyzed according to the study objectives using STATA® version 18. High blood pressure diagnosis was based on blood pressure (BP) above or equal to the 90th percentile for <13 years and either systolic BP ≥ 120 mmHg or Diastolic BP ≥ 80mmhg for 13 years and older for age, sex and height. The prevalence of high BP was determined as a percentage, whereas associated factors were analyzed at both bivariate and multivariable logistic regression. The significance of associations was set at a p-value <0.05 and a 95% confidence interval.

Results

Of the 150 participants, 115 (76.7%) were above 12 years of age, and the median age was 15 years (IQR 13-17). There were more females [81/150 (54%)] than males. The majority were attending school [130/150 (86.7%)], with a few attending boarding school [26/130 (20%)]. Sixty-one participants (40.7%, 95% C.I 33%-49%) had high BP, and 53 (86.9%) of these patients had poor glycemic control. The factors associated with high BP among T1DM participants included having diabetes for 4-8 years (aOR= 2.23 [95% CI: 1.05-4.75]; p = 0.037), and 9-12 years (aOR= 4.545 [95% CI: 1.075-19.221]; p = 0.040) respectively compared to those less than 4 years. Additionally, having Poor glycemic control (HBA1C ≥ 7%) increased odds for high BP by 2.905 [95% CI: 1.149-7.342]; p = 0.024) times compared to their counterparts with good glycemic control.

Conclusion

There was a high prevalence of high blood pressure among children with type 1 diabetes. Factors associated with high blood pressure included disease duration of more than 4 years and poor glycemic control.

title: An ICD-10-based algorithm for identifying the cause of acute respiratory failure in mechanically ventilated patients
authorString: Kahn JM, Casey CM, Dsouza J, Martinez SJ, Griard TD, Davis BS.
abstractText:
Rationale: Acute respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation is a common reason for admission to an intensive care unit. Epidemiological research is limited by the lack of scalable approaches for identifying the primary cause of acute respiratory failure in these patients.

Objective:

To develop and validate an algorithm for classifying mechanically ventilated patients by the primary cause of acute respiratory failure using International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) diagnosis and procedure codes.

Methods:

We identified adult patients undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation in the electronic health record of a multi-hospital health system in the United States. Using this cohort, we created a preliminary classification schema that assigned patients to one of eight mutually exclusive causes of acute respiratory failure (stroke, chronic lung disease, heart failure, trauma or overdose, pneumonia, non-pneumonia sepsis, post-operative, and other) based on the presence or absence of pre-specified ICD-10 codes. We compared the preliminary classifications to a clinical reference standard ascertained via manual chart review in a stratified random sample of the development cohort, refining the schema to optimize concordance. We then assessed content validity by examining clinical characteristics and outcomes across diagnosis categories, both in the development cohort and in an external all-payer claims dataset.

Results:

Of 8,130 hospitalizations in the development sample, all were successfully categorized into eight mutually exclusive groups. Compared to the reference standard of manual chart review (n=206), overall agreement was moderate (kappa = 0.44, 95% confidence interval: 0.39-0.49). After refinement, overall agreement improved slightly (kappa = 0.46, 95% confidence interval: 0.41-0.52). The final positive predictive values ranged from 78.6% (pneumonia) to 32.3% (stroke). The largest diagnostic category was non-pneumonia sepsis (26.1%), and the smallest diagnostic category was heart failure (6.2%). Clinical characteristics and outcomes approximated those expected from prior literature and were similar in the external dataset.

Conclusions:

A novel ICD-10-based algorithm for determining the primary cause of acute respiratory failure in patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation was moderately accurate. This algorithm is potentially useful for facilitating large-scale epidemiological research in this population.

title: Echocardiographic findings suggestive of complex mitral valve abnormalities in an adult with ALCAPA: a case report
authorString: Zhang D, Li Z, Wang H, Hao Y.
abstractText: Background Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA) is a rare congenital coronary anomaly. Previous reports of associated structural mitral abnormalities in adults have predominantly described isolated abnormalities. Case presentation We report a 38-year-old man with adult-type ALCAPA who presented with acute decompensated heart failure. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe mitral regurgitation and complex mitral structural findings, suggesting that ischemia alone might not explain the regurgitation. The patient was initially managed for valvular heart disease. Coronary computed tomography angiography and coronary angiography subsequently confirmed ALCAPA. He declined surgery, and medical treatment relieved his symptoms. At 1-year telephone follow-up, he reported occasional exertional chest tightness and dyspnea but no rehospitalization. Conclusions This case highlights the need to assess both coronary anatomy and mitral valve morphology in adults with ALCAPA and severe mitral regurgitation, as ischemia alone may not fully explain the valve findings. In adults with ALCAPA and complex mitral valve abnormalities, anatomical and functional assessment can clarify the mechanisms of MR and guide concomitant mitral valve surgery. Unexplained heart failure with severe MR and childhood exertional symptoms should raise suspicion of ALCAPA. Preserved LVEF does not exclude reduced forward cardiac output or myocardial injury. Medical therapy may stabilize the patient but cannot replace surgical correction.

title: Stroke risk screening intention among community residents: Psychometric validation and identification of intention profiles
authorString: Qin F, Wu X, luo L, Zhang Q, Tan Y.
abstractText: Objective This study aimed to further evaluate the psychometric properties of the Stroke Risk Screening Intention Scale among community residents, identify latent profiles of screening intention, and examine factors associated with profile membership. Methods A methodological study comprising two community-based cross-sectional surveys was conducted. The first survey (n = 787) was used for item analysis, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, and reliability and validity assessment. The second survey (n = 827) was analysed using latent profile analysis, followed by multinomial logistic regression to examine factors associated with profile membership. Results The final 25-item SRSIS demonstrated satisfactory internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.901) and test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.810). Confirmatory factor analysis supported the four-factor structure (CFI = 0.963; RMSEA = 0.056). Three distinct screening-intention profiles were identified: high-intention (30.83%), moderate-intention (58.28%), and low-intention (10.88%). Age, hypertension, physical activity, stroke-specific health literacy, perceived social support, and trust in community healthcare services were associated with profile membership. Conclusion The SRSIS may help community nurses assess residents’ stroke risk screening intention. Screening intention was heterogeneous among community residents, with most participants showing a moderate level of intention. Understanding the characteristics of different intention profiles may help community nurses tailor screening education and support to residents’ needs.

title: Frozen MIMIC model evaluation and local development for predicting subsequent atrial fibrillation or flutter coded admissions
authorString: Huang N, Zhao Y, Jia Y, Wang Y, Zhao X, She F, Zhang P.
abstractText: Background Prediction models based on electronic health records may perform differently across care systems. We evaluated frozen MIMIC models and local model development for subsequent admissions carrying atrial fibrillation or flutter codes in Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital (BTCH) records. Methods We analysed 7850 adult inpatient records from a BTCH extract supplied on 8 October 2026. Prediction occurred at index discharge D; the outcome was a target-coded admission starting in (D, A + n calendar years], where A was index admission and n was 1 or 3. Frozen models used 15 clinical variables (Clinical15) or age alone. Local three-year logistic regression used patient-level TRAIN/VALID/TEST partitions and TRAIN-only preprocessing. Paired fixed-model bootstrap confidence intervals used 2000 replicates; internal TEST resampling was event-stratified. Results There were 169 one-year and 374 three-year recorded events. Frozen Clinical15 AUROCs were 0.8134 (95% CI 0.7875–0.8385) and 0.8184 (0.7993–0.8354), below age-only models by 0.0282 and 0.0174. Local three-year Clinical15 achieved 0.8747 (0.8384–0.9084) in 1586 TEST records with 80 events. Its paired AUROC difference versus frozen MIMIC on the same TEST was 0.0554 (0.0316–0.0807). One-year local Clinical15 was not fitted because an event-count rule was not met. Death times were entirely missing; last contact preceded the window boundary in 32.27% and 54.08% of record-negative groups. Conclusions The additional clinical variables did not improve frozen-model ranking over age alone in BTCH records, whereas local fitting improved ranking in retrospective internal evaluation. These results concern coded admissions in the supplied sample; they do not establish incident AF prediction, complete clinical follow-up, mortality-adjusted risk or clinical utility. The study was not prospectively registered.

title: Title: Outcomes of metabolic bariatric surgery in obese CKD patients: A MBSAQIP analysis.
authorString: Pena B, John A, Sanicola C, Francisquini D, Lee E, Spaniolas K, Kressel A.
abstractText: Objective: Compare 30-day and 6-month postoperative outcomes after metabolic bariatric surgery in renal insufficiency (RI) and dialysis-dependent (DD) patients. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the 2023 MBSAQIP database, comparing bariatric surgery patients with RI, DD, and controls. Thirty-day and six-month outcomes included weight loss, complications, mortality, and obesity-related comorbidity changes. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated postoperative outcomes. Results Patients with RI and DD were older and had greater comorbidity burden than controls. At six months, > 10% total weight loss was achieved by 74% of RI, 80% of DD, and 85% of controls (p < 0.001), with improvement in diabetes and hypertension. Thirty-day mortality was < 0.2% and didn’t differ significantly between groups. At six months, mortality remained < 1%; however, RI and DD were independently associated with increased odds of mortality (OR 6.36 and 8.52), as well as any complications (OR 1.94 and 1.78), and readmission (OR 2.07 and 3.57, all p < 0.001), respectively, compared with controls. Conclusions Despite greater comorbidity burden, patients with RI and DD experienced low rates of major postoperative complications and mortality after bariatric surgery. Most achieved meaningful weight loss at six months, supporting bariatric surgery as an option for selected patients in advanced kidney disease.

title: Design and analytical validation of a graphene oxide-modified FTO immunosensor for NT-proBNP detection.
authorString: Maya V, Sasi R, Anil A, Prema Vijayan L, Prabhukumar Baby R, Raj G, Sivadasanpillai H, Gopi M.

journal.title: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications

abstractText: Heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, with timely and accurate biomarker quantification being critical for diagnosis, risk stratification, and therapeutic monitoring. N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is the most clinically reliable biomarker for HF; however, current detection platforms, ranging from chemiluminescent immunoassays to lateral flow devices, are limited by high infrastructure requirements, enzymatic labels, complex fabrication workflows, or insufficient sensitivity at physiologically critical concentrations. Here, we report a label-free, reagent minimised electrochemical immunosensor fabricated by depositing carboxyl functionalised graphene oxide (GO) on fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) glass electrodes, followed by covalent antibody immobilization via EDC-NHS-PEG chemistry. The platform exploits the oxygen containing functional groups on GO to enable stable antibody immobilisation without additional signal amplifying nanomaterials. The immunosensor was characterised using UV-vis spectroscopy, Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, zeta potential analysis, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and confocal Raman chemical mapping, collectively confirming the formation of a uniform GO film and successful antibody immobilisation. Electrochemical characterization by cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) demonstrated that a GO coating concentration of 3 mg mL-1 optimally enhanced charge transfer, increasing the electrochemically active surface area by ∼15% relative to bare FTO. Antigen sensing was performed by monitoring the concentration-dependent increase in charge-transfer resistance (RCT) via EIS across a physiologically and clinically relevant NT-proBNP concentration range of 100 pg mL-1 to 500 ng mL-1, yielding a linear regression of Y = 0.0038x + 676.96 (R2 = 0.997) and a limit of quantification (LOQ) of 100 pg mL-1 directly spanning the diagnostic threshold for HF. The key novelty of this work lies in the synergistic use of the GO-FTO interface, which eliminates the need for additional nanoparticle enhancement, enzymatic signal amplification, or complex multi-layer fabrication, while still delivering clinically actionable sensitivity. The platform is scalable, cost-effective, and compatible with portable electrochemical instrumentation, establishing a strong foundation for point-of-care integration. These findings provide a promising foundation for future optimisation of the GO-FTO immunosensor, including clinical sample validation, device integration, and translation towards point-of-care heart failure diagnostics.

title: Impact of Rehabilitation Initiation Timing on Safety and Efficacy in Patients With Acute Stroke and Concurrent Heart Failure.
authorString: Tamura S, Kamo T, Igarashi T, Kubo H, Kobayashi S, Ohtsubo T, Momosaki R.
abstractText:
Background

The optimal timing of rehabilitation initiation in patients with acute stroke and heart failure remains uncertain due to concerns about hemodynamic instability.

Objective

To evaluate the safety and efficacy of rehabilitation timing in patients with acute stroke and comorbid heart failure.

Methods

This retrospective cohort study used a nationwide Japanese inpatient database. This study included 9827 adult patients hospitalized for stroke with heart failure. Patients were categorized into 3 groups: very early rehabilitation (VER; admission day or day 1), early rehabilitation (ER; days 2-3), and delayed rehabilitation (DR; days 4-7). The primary safety outcome was a composite of major in-hospital adverse events (death, mechanical ventilation, or vasopressor use) within 30 days. The primary efficacy outcome was the Barthel Index at discharge. Multinomial propensity scores were estimated, and inverse probability of treatment weighting was used to adjust for confounding variables. Inverse probability of censoring weighting and augmented inverse probability weighting were used for the relevant outcomes. Pairwise comparisons were performed.

Results

No significant differences in major in-hospital adverse events were observed between the groups. The VER group had a lower risk of in-hospital respiratory failure (risk ratio [RR] = 0.58, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.33-0.99) and 90-day stroke readmission (RR = 0.33, 95% CI = 0.12-0.87) and a higher discharge Barthel Index (mean difference = 3.66, 95% CI = 0.23-7.09) than the DR group.

Conclusions

VER was associated with better outcomes in selected measures than DR, without significant differences in major adverse events.

title: The Burden of Traumatic Brain Injury in Ghana's Middle Belt-Part 2: Predictors of Clinical Outcomes.
authorString: Haizel-Cobbina J, Ahorklo IMK, Darko K, Antwi J, Adjei-Gyamfi J, Odonkor MN, Barthélemy EJ, Park KB, Boakye M, Groves ML, Dewan MC, Nketiah-Boakye F, Bandoh D, Abu-Bonsrah N.
abstractText:
Background and objectives

The study aimed to evaluate in-hospital outcomes and determinant factors among adult traumatic brain injury (TBI) patients presenting at Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital in Kumasi Ghana.

Methods

This was a retrospective cross-sectional study. Survival analysis using the Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate the association between independent variables and outcomes. The primary outcomes of interest were poor outcome as defined as Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended score of 1 to 4 at the time of hospital discharge and in-hospital mortality.

Results

Of the 465 cases, 293 (63%) presented with mild TBI (mTBI), 89 (19.2%) with moderate TBI (moTBI), and 83 (17.8%) with severe TBI (sTBI). One hundred and nine patients underwent surgery, and 356 underwent nonoperative management. Seventy (15.1%) patients had poor outcomes, with a 13% in-hospital mortality rate among them. Patients with sTBI had a significantly higher rate of poor outcomes by hospital day 14 than patients with moTBI and mTBI (41.3% vs 20.2% vs 5.7%, P < .001). Older age [hazard ratio (HR) 3.31, 95% CI, 1.12-9.72], moTBI [HR 5.62, 95% CI, 1.91-16.51], and sTBI [HR 9.47, 95% CI, 3.35-26.77] were associated with an increased hazard for poor outcome and in-hospital mortality, whereas surgery [HR 0.22, 95% CI, 0.07-0.64] was associated with a decreased hazard for poor outcome and in-hospital mortality. Patients with moTBI who underwent surgery had a significantly lower in-hospital mortality (P = .012) and poor outcomes (P = .038) than those who underwent nonoperative management.

Conclusion

Consistent with sub-Saharan Africa data, patients with mTBI and moTBI showed favorable survival and functional recovery, with neurosurgical intervention significantly improving in-hospital outcomes for moTBI cases. Neurosurgical intervention significantly improved in-hospital outcomes for patients with moTBI. Optimizing TBI outcomes necessitates a dual approach: developing evidence-based guidelines through research and upgrading surgical infrastructure, triage, and referral systems.

title: Correlation study between pre-stroke sleep characteristics and early neurological prognosis in patients with acute ischemic stroke.
authorString: Wang J, Li J.

journal.title: Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia

abstractText:
Objective

This study aimed to analyze the association between pre-stroke sleep conditions and 3-month functional outcomes in patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS).

Methods

Consecutive AIS patients admitted between March 2022 and August 2024 were enrolled. The Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, and Berlin Questionnaire were administered within 7 days after stroke onset to evaluate pre-stroke sleep characteristics. Poor functional outcome was defined as a 3-month modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score >2. Binary logistic regression was used to identify prognostic factors.

Results

Of 782 patients completing follow-up, 18.0% had poor functional recovery. Compared with the good-prognosis group, patients with poor prognosis had a higher rate of pre-stroke excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) and more frequent in-hospital sedative-hypnotic use (both P < 0.05). Multivariable analysis demonstrated that age >65 years, female sex, prior stroke history, higher admission NIHSS score, and pre-stroke EDS were independent risk factors for poor prognosis. Small-artery occlusion was protective relative to large-artery atherosclerosis (OR = 0.36, P = 0.002).

Conclusion

Pre-stroke EDS appeared to be independently associated with unfavourable three-month functional outcome, apart from established clinical risk factors. Small-artery occlusion predicts better functional recovery compared with large-artery atherosclerosis.

title: Carotid Artery Stenosis is Associated with Restless Legs Syndrome in the Absence of Stroke
authorString: Ogulnick J, Jun Shin WD, Mathew J.
abstractText:
ABSTRACT

Background

Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common neurological disorder with established links to atherosclerotic disease and secondary causes such as ischemic stroke. Hypothesizing that internal carotid artery stenosis (CAS) could induce secondary RLS through chronic hypoperfusion or microemboli to dopaminergic subcortical structures, even without overt stroke, we investigated the association between bilateral CAS and RLS.

Methods

A retrospective propensity score-matched case-control study was conducted using the TriNetX Global Health Research Network. Cases (n=58,382) had bilateral CAS/occlusion (ICD-10-CM I65.23); controls (n=58,382) had atherosclerosis without CAS. Patients were excluded for prior stroke/TIA, iron deficiency, antipsychotic use, and other secondary RLS causes. Cases and controls were 1:1 matched on age, race/ethnicity, chronic kidney disease, peripheral neuropathy, peripheral artery disease, Parkinson’s disease, and SSRI use. The outcome was RLS diagnosis (G25.81), assessed via conditional logistic regression.

Results

RLS was diagnosed in 1,154 (1.977%) patients with bilateral CAS/occlusion versus 1,060 (1.816%) controls, yielding an absolute risk difference of 0.161% (95% CI 0.005–0.317%; p=0.0437). The adjusted odds ratio was 1.09 (95% CI 1.002–1.186), indicating a modest but significant association.

Conclusion

Severe bilateral CAS/occlusion is associated with a small but statistically significant increase in RLS risk, independently of overt cerebrovascular events and known confounders. These findings support a potential vascular contribution to RLS pathogenesis, possibly through subclinical hypoperfusion affecting basal ganglia dopaminergic pathways. Prospective studies are needed to explore causality, dose-dependency, and the impact of carotid revascularization.

title: Ultra-High-Frequency ECG-Derived Local Depolarization Duration as a Potential Digital Biomarker of Myocardial Scar in Dilated Cardiomyopathy
authorString: Papp R, Molnár L, Ruppert M, Tarjányi Z, Vágó H, Levy N, Curila K, Leinveber P, Soukup L, Panovsky R, Merkely B, Czimbalmos C.
abstractText: Myocardial scarring, detected by late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) on cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging, is associated with sudden cardiac death in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). Ultra-high-frequency electrocardiography (UHF-ECG) characterizes local ventricular activation and may reveal electrical disturbances associated with myocardial scarring. We investigated the relationship between UHF-ECG-derived local depolarization duration and LGE presence and extent in a prospective multicentre cohort of 87 patients with DCM. Mean local depolarization duration across leads V1–V6 was compared with CMR findings, with analyses stratified by QRS duration and morphology. In patients with narrow QRS complexes (n = 34) or intraventricular conduction delay (n = 23), longer mean local depolarization duration correlated with greater LGE extent (ρ = 0.559 and 0.473, respectively). In these subgroups, local depolarization duration also discriminated between patients with and without LGE. No significant association with LGE presence was observed in the overall cohort or in patients with left bundle branch block. These findings suggest that the relationship between local depolarization duration and myocardial scarring may depend on QRS characteristics. UHF-ECG-derived local depolarization duration may serve as a digital biomarker of myocardial scarring in selected patients with DCM, although these exploratory findings require independent validation.

title: Historical perspectives, indications, and benchmark results of the Bentall procedure.
authorString: Coselli JS, McGeoghegan PB, Orozco-Sevilla V, Xue AH, Murrieta-Álvarez I, Alomari LL, Glover VA, Green SY, Moon MR.
abstractText: Aortic root replacement has undergone an impressive evolution since the pioneering efforts of Bentall, De Bono, and others with the introduction of the composite valve graft (CVG) and subsequent refinements in coronary artery reimplantation. The commercial development of mechanical CVGs and, later, bioprosthetic CVGs has aided repair, which for most patients is centered on treating aneurysmal disease, the loss of leaflet coaptation related to annular dilatation, and aortic valve regurgitation. Indications for repair are determined by root diameter, the rate of aortic dilatation, symptoms, and underlying pathology. Operative thresholds also vary according to patient-specific factors such as age, heritable thoracic aortic disease, and bicuspid aortic valve. Of the many options for aortic root replacement, CVG is the dominant approach; however, the selection between mechanical and bioprosthetic options remains an area of active debate. Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has significantly influenced surgical decision-making by introducing the possibility of valve-in-root intervention after bioprosthetic CVG repair. Traditional practice generally favors mechanical CVG in younger patients due to superior durability, whereas bioprosthetic CVG is typically used in older patients and those seeking to avoid lifelong anticoagulation despite a higher risk of late valvular dysfunction. We retrospectively examined our experience with 1250 CVG procedures from 1990 to 2026 and found a shift from mechanical to bioprosthetic CVG repair in contemporary practice. Benchmark outcomes after CVG vary substantially according to patient baseline characteristics and operative complexity, with lower operative mortality rates for elective aneurysm repairs and higher rates for patients with acute type A dissection, nonelective repair, redo sternotomy, or concomitant cardiac surgery. This review summarizes the historical evolution, indications, surgical decision-making, technical considerations, and benchmark outcomes surrounding the Bentall operation.

title: Macrophage Polarization as a Therapeutic Nexus in Atherosclerosis: Epigenetic-Metabolic-Signaling Networks, Herbal Interventions, and Toward Clinical Translation.
authorString: Sun Y, Gao X, Meng X, Jin M, Lin M, Gu X, Huang Y, Li Z.
abstractText: Atherosclerosis (AS) remains a leading cause of cardiovascular mortality. Residual inflammatory risk persists despite optimal lipid-lowering therapy, largely because macrophage phenotypes extend beyond the simple M1/M2 classification. TCM can reset macrophage polarization through multiple targets, but existing reviews treat epigenetic, metabolic, and signaling events as separate modules and do not integrate how herbal agents coordinate these layers. We screened literature published from 2010 to 2026 in multiple languages. We summarize three interconnected mechanisms of TCM action: (i) epigenetic remodeling through DNA methylation, non-coding RNAs, and histone modifications; (ii) metabolic reprogramming that shifts macrophages from glycolysis toward fatty acid oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation; and (iii) suppression of pro-inflammatory cascades (NF-κB, JAK/STAT, MAPK, Notch, PI3K/Akt/mTOR, and cGAS-STING) together with activation of PPARγ-mediated reparative signaling. We highlight metabolite-driven histone modifications, particularly acetyl-CoA/NAD<sup>+</sup>-dependent chromatin remodeling and H3K18 lactylation, as key under-appreciated mechanistic links through which herbal formulas exert network-level immunomodulation rather than single-pathway inhibition. Preclinical plaque-stabilizing effects have been reported, but inter-species differences, poorly characterized active metabolites, and the scarcity of non-invasive in vivo validation remain major barriers to translation. We propose a roadmap that combines humanized myeloid models, AI-assisted multi-omics, and smart nano-delivery systems. This review provides a three-dimensional mechanistic framework for multi-target TCM action in AS and supports the development of precision cardio-immunology.

title: David Procedure in Patients With Acute Type A Dissection: from Controversy to Excellent Results
authorString: Hlavicka J, Fila P, Karimian-Tabrizi A, Horvath V, Ilgin Y, Nicovsky J, Nemec P, Holubec T.
abstractText: Background Aortic valve (AV) reimplantation (David procedure) has demonstrated very good long-term results when performed in the elective setting. Limited use of the technique in patients suffering from the acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD) due to its technical complexity is still debated. We present long-term results of 84 patients operated on using David procedure as part of surgical treatment of ATAAD. Methods Between January 1996 and January 2025 a total of 84 patients with ATAAD were operated on at two institutions in Frankfurt, Germany and Brno, Czech Republic using David procedure for aortic root reconstruction. The primary end-point was defined as AV performance: freedom from the AV regurgitation (AR) ≥ moderate and freedom from the aortic valve and/or root related reoperation in the follow-up. The secondary end-points we defined as perioperative outcomes and late survival. The data were evaluated retrospectively, using medical records and a register. Results The mean age was 45 years and male sex was represented in 83%. Operative risk according to the GERAADA Score was 9.5% and moderate AR or more was present in more than a half (52.4%) of patients. The 30-days mortality was 7.1%. Median follow-up time was 6.96 years (IQR 3.3–6.1). Freedom from the AR ≥ moderate at 5, 10 and 20 years was: 90% (95% CI 83.1%-97.3%), 82.4% (95% CI 72.4%-93.7%) and 73.7% (95% CI 60.3%-90.1%), respectively. Freedom from AV and/or aortic root reoperation at 5, 10 and 20 years was: 92.3% (95% CI 86.0%-99.1%), 86.1% (95% CI 77.5%-95.8%) and 86.1% (95% CI 77.5%-95.8%) respectively. The survival after 5, 10 and 20 years was 90.1% (95% CI 83.7%-96.9%), 72.2% (95% CI 61.3%-85.0%) and 51.2% (95% CI 33.0%-79.4%). Conclusions David procedure performed in patients suffering from acute type A dissection can be performed safely, with low short-term mortality and especially with excellent long-term AV performance (low incidence of reccurent AR requiring redo surgery).

title: Long-term outcomes following balloon aortic valvuloplasty for congenital aortic stenosis in children: a 29-year single-centre experience.
authorString: Kuk Ozalp ZG, Riordan G, Alok E, Sawan E, Raja J, Nguyen Khuong J, Roberts P, Nicholson I.
abstractText:
Background

Initial treatment of critical aortic stenosis in children, balloon or surgical aortic valvuloplasty, remains debated. Our centre used the balloon procedure first in almost all patients for over 29 years, a predominantly balloon-first cohort.

Objective

To characterise long-term outcomes of balloon aortic valvuloplasty as first-line treatment for critical aortic stenosis.

Methods

We retrospectively reviewed 201 patients treated between June 1996 and December 2025, grouped as neonates (0-28 days), infants (29-365 days), and children (>365 days). Freedom from surgery and reintervention were analysed with the Kaplan-Meier method; categorical comparisons used chi-square tests.

Results

Median follow-up was 9 years. Aortic valve surgery was required in 78 patients (38.8%), most commonly a Ross or Ross-Konno procedure (49, 62.8%). Neonates required surgery more often than infants and children (36/74, 48.6% versus 42/127, 33.1%; p = 0.042); median time to surgery in neonates was 6 months. One-year Kaplan-Meier freedom from surgery was 63% in neonates, 91% in infants, and 96% in children. Moderate-to-severe post-procedural valve dysfunction was associated with more surgery than mild dysfunction (49.3% versus 33.3%; p = 0.041). Kaplan-Meier freedom from any reintervention was 47% at 10 years and 31% at 15 years. Mortality was 3.5% overall and 8.1% in neonates, mostly in the early era.

Conclusions

Balloon aortic valvuloplasty is an effective first-line treatment for infants and children with critical aortic stenosis. However, many neonates need surgery within the first year, usually a Ross procedure. In centres with experienced cardiac surgeons, surgical aortic valvuloplasty could be considered a reasonable alternative initial approach for neonates.

title: Clinical presentation of Van Praagh Type A4 truncus arteriosus with interrupted aortic arch in an adolescent.
authorString: Faraz M, Zafar K, Abqari S, Ahmad M, Alam M, Rahmani S.
abstractText: We describe a 14-year-old boy (weight 32 kg, height 148 cm), who was brought to a tertiary care facility in North India, with complaints of progressive exertional dyspnoea, palpitations, and chest pain with a recent episode of moderate haemoptysis. Imaging findings include Chest PA-view demonstrated cardiomegaly with abnormal great vessel contour, prominent superior mediastinal shadow, and increased bilateral pulmonary vascular markings, suggestive of a single large arterial outflow tract. Similarly, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) revealed a large outlet ventricular septal defect (VSD) with a dilated single arterial trunk overriding the defect. Cardiac CT angiography confirmed a large outlet VSD and an interrupted aortic arch, with no continuity between the ascending and descending aorta. The right and left pulmonary arteries, descending aorta, and left subclavian artery arose directly from the truncal vessel, while a separate ascending aorta bifurcated into the right brachiocephalic and left common carotid arteries. This particular case brings a remarkably unusual paediatric presentation with Van Praagh Type A4 truncus arteriosus with interrupted aortic arch and emphasises the effects of late diagnosis. Due to the patient's severe pulmonary arterial hypertension, palliative care was the only option for treatment, and definitive surgical repair was not feasible.

title: A reversible neonatal transverse aortic constriction model prolongs cardiomyocyte proliferative activity beyond the early postnatal regenerative window in mice.
authorString: He M, Cheng Y, Shen B, Liang C, Bin J, Liao Y.
abstractText:
Background

The neonatal mammalian heart retains transient regenerative capacity during the first postnatal week, but this ability rapidly declines thereafter. Whether transient mechanical stress can prolong postnatal cardiomyocyte proliferative competence remains unclear. Here, we established a reversible neonatal transverse aortic constriction (TAC) model to investigate whether short-term pressure overload followed by debanding extends the cardiac regenerative window in mice.

Methods

TAC was performed in 3-day-old C57BL/6 mice by ligating the aortic arch between the brachiocephalic trunk and the left common carotid artery using a 32-gauge spacer. Three days later, the ligature was surgically removed to generate debanded TAC mice. Doppler echocardiography was used to verify pressure overload and unloading. Cardiac morphology, left ventricular wall thickness, heart weight-to-body weight ratio, cardiomyocyte size, and cardiomyocyte proliferative activity were assessed by echocardiography, histology, and immunostaining.

Results

TAC markedly increased aortic flow velocity and pressure gradient at postnatal day 6, confirming successful pressure overload. Transient TAC increased left ventricular posterior wall thickness and heart to body weight ratio, indicating structural remodeling. Following debanding, these changes were partially reversed, although aortic flow velocity remained modestly higher than in age-matched sham controls. Notably, TAC increased cardiomyocyte cell-cycle activity, as indicated by Ki67, phospho-histone H3, and Aurora B staining. This pro-proliferative effect persisted after debanding, with increased cardiomyocyte proliferative activity and abundance still detectable at postnatal day 9.

Conclusions

Reversible neonatal pressure overload prolongs cardiomyocyte proliferative activity beyond the early postnatal regenerative window. This neonatal TAC-debanding model provides a useful platform for studying the mechanical regulation of cardiac regeneration.

title: Regulation of HER signalling through combinatorial receptor interactions.
authorString: Torosyan H, Jura N.
abstractText: The human epidermal growth factor receptor (HER) family of receptor tyrosine kinases, which includes EGFR (also referred to as HER1 or ErbB1), HER2 (ErbB2), HER3 (ErbB3) and HER4 (ErbB4), constitutes an essential signalling network that regulates key cellular behaviours and is frequently dysregulated in cancer. Although HER receptor heterodimerization has long been recognized as a central organizing principle of this network, the mechanisms that determine receptor pairing and translate distinct receptor-ligand combinations into specific signalling outputs remain incompletely understood. This Review examines HER receptor dimerization preferences, their modulation by ligand identity and the mechanisms governing these interactions revealed by recent structural studies. We discuss how HER heterodimers engage major downstream pathways and how signalling is shaped by temporal dynamics, ligand-specific and dimer-specific pathway activation, and receptor trafficking and downregulation. Finally, we consider how receptor overexpression, oncogenic mutations and targeted therapies reconfigure HER receptor interactions to generate ligand-independent signalling, enhance oncogenic output and promote therapeutic resistance.

title: Functional atlas of Parkin predicts variant pathogenicity and Parkinson's disease age at onset.
authorString: Aslanzadeh V, Glendinning S, Sari Y, Clarke M, Rodger CJ, Lin X, Lenka DR, Bhuiyan N, Richardson L, Liang JR, Kleinz T, Sproul D, Lohmann K, Klein C, Sammler EM, Alessi DR, Kumar A, Muqit MMK, Kudla G.
abstractText: Autosomal recessive mutations in the Parkin gene (PRKN) cause early-onset Parkinson's disease (PD). Parkin functions as a ubiquitin E3 ligase acting downstream of the PINK1 kinase to promote phosphorylated ubiquitin at sites of mitochondrial damage. Yet the functional effects of most PRKN gene variants remain unknown. Here, we use a pooled cellular assay measuring phosphorylated ubiquitin accumulation to quantify the activity of ~9200 PRKN missense and nonsense variants. Our screen identifies thousands of loss- and gain-of-function variants, including activating variants mainly residing at autoinhibitory interfaces. Functional scores accurately distinguish known PD pathogenic and benign variants, providing evidence of pathogenicity or benignity for 175/182 variants of uncertain significance (VUS). When combined into biallelic genotype scores, these data predict the age at disease onset in patients, revealing a quantitative link between Parkin activity and clinical manifestation. Our results provide a comprehensive functional genetic map of Parkin and demonstrate the power of multiplexed assays of variant effects (MAVEs) for variant interpretation and precision medicine in PD.

title: Benefits and harms of antihypertensive treatment a modelling study in 5.5 million electronic health records.
authorString: Wang A, Koshiaris C, Gould N, Archer L, Banerjee A, Bellows BK, Clark CE, Clegg A, Hobbs FDR, Mant J, McManus RJ, Payne R, Stevens R, Treadwell J, Usher Smith J, Sheppard JP.
abstractText: Antihypertensive prescription is guided by cardiovascular risk prediction models. However, existing models often exclude individuals with prior cardiovascular disease or those prescribed statin treatment. Consequently, there is limited evidence regarding how the benefits and harms of treatment vary according to an individual's baseline risk. This cohort study includes 5,578,002 patients aged≥40years (mean age 59; 52% women) from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink between 1998-2018. A cardiovascular risk prediction model is developed using the Clinical Practice Research Datalink GOLD dataset and externally validated using the Aurum dataset. The model demonstrates excellent calibration and discrimination. Antihypertensive therapy is more likely to prevent serious major cardiovascular events (eight events prevented per 1,000 patients over 10 years, 95% confidence interval = 1 to 14), than to cause serious falls (two events per 1,000 patients, 95% confidence interval = -4 to 10). The risks of other adverse events indicate more nuanced or potentially harmful trade-offs. Here we show that a cardiovascular risk prediction model developed using routinely collected primary care data accurately predicts risk across a broad population of patients eligible for antihypertensive treatment. These findings will enable clinicians to better communicate individualised benefits and risks of antihypertensive therapy.

title: Cardiac counseling in the setting of trisomy 18: a qualitative fetal heart society research collaborative study.
authorString: Harris KW, Porter AS, Wong B, Carey JC, Kosiv KA.

journal.title: Journal of perinatology : official journal of the California Perinatal Association

abstractText:
Objective

To explore fetal cardiologists' prenatal counseling attitudes and practices around congenital heart disease (CHD) in trisomy 18.

Study design

An online survey presented two hypothetical scenarios regarding a fetus with trisomy 21 or 18, both with severe/complex CHD, and queried prenatal surgical counseling. This sub-analysis used inductive content analysis for free text responses on trisomy 18 and CHD prenatal diagnosis counseling.

Result

Of 142 respondents, 80 provided free text responses. Themes included: (1) need for nuance: individualized counseling is essential, (2) surgical criteria: clinical and institutional factors influence surgical candidacy, (3) prognosis: what constitutes a "good" outcome vary significantly, (4) moral valence: physicians' personal values influence counseling and emotional experience, and (5) lack of consensus: professional consensus and standardized guidance are lacking.

Conclusion

When counseling about prenatal trisomy 18 and CHD diagnoses, fetal cardiologists may benefit from palliative care communication practices and consensus-based guidance alongside case-by-case clinical judgment.

title: Comparing 70 kV and 120 kV photon-counting CT protocols for pediatric cardiac imaging in children weighing 10-30 kg: Radiation dose and image quality.
authorString: Dang NH, Zhou W, Arguello Fletes GM, Weinman JP, Malone LJ.
abstractText:
Background

Scanning at 70 kV on photon-counting CT (PCCT) reduces radiation dose by 50% compared to 120 kV in infants under 10 kg without loss of diagnostic quality. Whether scanning at a lower kV is of benefit in larger children, in whom greater attenuation increases image noise, has not been determined.

Methods

We retrospectively compared ultra-high-pitch cardiac PCCT examinations in children weighing 10-30 kg acquired at 70 kV (n = 79) or 120 kV (n = 80), both at a CARE keV IQ level of 25. We measured signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) in the ascending aorta and main pulmonary artery and compared radiation dose. Two pediatric cardiac radiologists rated image quality in five vascular structures on a 5-point Likert scale.

Results

Groups were similar in age and size. Neither CNR nor SNR differed significantly. Median Likert scores were at least 4 for four of five structures in both groups. Median CTDIvol was 0.49 vs 0.63 mGy (P < 0.001), and effective dose 0.65 vs 0.75 mSv (P < 0.001) for 70 vs 120 kV.

Conclusion

In children weighing 10-30 kg, 70 kV ultra-high-pitch cardiac PCCT was associated with lower radiation dose than 120 kV, with no significant difference in CNR and median reader scores in the diagnostic range. A 120 kV protocol remains appropriate when metal-artifact reduction or advanced spectral reconstructions are needed.

title: Consensus document SED-SEEN-SEMERGEN-SEMFyC-SEMG on the use of continuous glucose monitoring in people with type 2 diabetes mellitus on basal insulin therapy.
authorString: Fernández-Rubio E, Ares Blanco J, Guerrero Casanova L, Peral Martínez IM, Granados Pérez M, Sáez Torralba ME, Roldán Ruano MA, González Blanco C, Ampudia-Blasco FJ.
abstractText: In people with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) on basal insulin therapy, with or without other antihyperglycemic agents, suboptimal glycemic control increases the risk of hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia, which can negatively impact patients' clinical outcomes and quality of life. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has been shown to improve glycemic control by reducing HbA1c and increasing time in range, without increasing hypoglycemic events. It also represents a cost-effective intervention in the analyzed models. This document presents the consensus recommendations of the Spanish Diabetes Society (SED), the Spanish Society of Endocrinology and Nutrition (SEEN), the Spanish Society of Primary Care Physicians (SEMERGEN), the Spanish Society of Family and Community Medicine (SEMFyC), and the Spanish Society of General and Family Physicians (SEMG) on the priority indications for the use of CGM in this population, glycemic control targets, follow-up, and discontinuation criteria.

title: Large Language Models and a Recently Revised Radiology Classification: Modified CIRSE Grading With and Without Current Criteria.
authorString: Türksayar O, Özgül H, Dablan A, Arslan MF, Erdim Ç, Cingöz M, Güzelbey T, Kılıçkesmez Ö.
abstractText: Recently revised professional classifications may create a version mismatch for large language models, as plausible responses can reflect a superseded rather than the current schema. The modified Cardiovascular and Interventional Radiological Society of Europe classification, which subdivided Grades 1 and 3, provided a controlled setting to examine this problem. We evaluated four large language models with and without the current criteria supplied in the prompt. Sixty-four purpose-written vignettes, eight per category, were independently graded by two interventional radiologists, with consensus serving as the reference standard. Four models (gpt-5.6-sol, claude-sonnet-5, gemini-3.8-flash, and deepseek-flash) were queried under closed-book and guideline-augmented conditions three times per vignette, yielding 1536 requests. The primary outcome was run-1 exact-grade accuracy, compared within models using Holm-adjusted McNemar tests. Closed-book exact-grade accuracy ranged from 15 of 64 to 31 of 64, whereas all four models achieved 64 of 64 with the criteria supplied. All Holm-adjusted p values were <0.001. In a post hoc descriptive analysis, exact-grade accuracy was 0 of 128 classifications in the newly subdivided grades and 99 of 128 in grades retaining established labels. None of the four new subclass labels appeared in any of the 256 run 1 closed-book responses. Across all three closed-book runs, superseded grades accounted for 36.5% of responses. Exact-grade accuracy was higher in all four models when the current criteria were supplied. In a post hoc descriptive analysis, complete exact-grade failure was confined to newly subdivided grades. Current classification criteria should be supplied explicitly for model-based complication grading.

title: Loss-of-function variants in the NR2F2 promoter confer susceptibility to isolated congenital heart disease: A rare variant disrupts ETS1-mediated regulation.
authorString: Zhou J, Wei C, Cheng Y, Luo Q, Liu J.

journal.medlineAbbreviation: Biochim Biophys Acta Gene Regul Mech
journal.title: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Gene regulatory mechanisms
journal.isoabbreviation: Biochim Biophys Acta Gene Regul Mech

abstractText: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is the most common birth defect, with the genetic defects remaining unknown in many patients. NR2F2 is a transcription factor that regulates cardiac endocardial development in a dosage-sensitive manner; however, the association between non-coding NR2F2 variants and CHD risk remains unclear. In this study, we performed a case-control analysis of the NR2F2 promoter, and identified four rare variants in isolated CHD patients with a frequency over 3% but undetected in controls. Histone modification analysis showed that two of the candidate variants, g.96330105C > T and g.96330128C > T, overlapped with active promoter-associated histone marks. Functionally, these two variants significantly reduced NR2F2 promoter transcriptional activity and protein expression. In addition, the variant g.96330128C > T abrogated ETS1 binding, thereby impairing ETS1-mediated positive transcriptional regulation of NR2F2. These findings highlight that loss-of-function (LOF) variants in the NR2F2 promoter, particularly g.96330128C > T, confer CHD susceptibility by reducing NR2F2 expression.

title: Is GDF-15 the Missing Link Between Intermittent Hypoxia, Carotid Body Plasticity, and Cardiometabolic Disease?
authorString: Chowdhury D, Garai S, Bodakhe SH.
abstractText: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a worldwide epidemic and is strongly associated with cardiometabolic comorbidities such as hypertension, arrhythmias and heart failure. Its principal cardiovascular pathological driver is chronic intermittent hypoxia (CIH). CIH induces maladaptive plasticity in the carotid body (CB), the main peripheral oxygen sensor. Profound nitro-oxidative stress and localized inflammation lead to relentless sympathetic overactivity and autonomic imbalance, causing persistent CB hyperactivity. Although this chemoreflex arc is well-characterized, the molecular messengers linking local hypoxemic stress to systemic cardiovascular decline are poorly defined. We propose that Growth Differentiation Factor-15 (GDF-15) is a very likely candidate for this bridge. GDF-15 is a well-established cardiovascular prognostic biomarker. It is strongly upregulated by hypoxia, oxidative stress and HIF stabilization. Plasma GDF-15 is related to the severity of OSA, nocturnal hypoxemia and arrhythmogenic remodeling, and is progressively reduced in clinical settings after continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy. In addition to being a systemic biomarker, we speculate that local production of GDF-15 in the oxidative CB microenvironment may have autocrine / paracrine effects that maintain glomus cell hyperexcitability but this remains to be proven experimentally. Also, circulating GDF-15 may act on brainstem GFRAL receptors to enhance chemoreflex drive. We emphasize that this peripheral to central axis, localized CB signaling is a theoretical model that should be tested directly in the lab. Ultimately, therapeutic targeting of this GDF-15 axis at the CB-brainstem interface may provide a life-changing strategy to ameliorate complications of sleep-disordered breathing.

title: Updates on management of pretransplant and peritransplant infections: Guidance from the American Society of Transplantation Infectious Diseases Community of Practice.
authorString: Danziger-Isakov L, Angarone M, Beam E, Chesdachai S, Dulek DE, Haidar G, Julian K, Kaul D, Kodiyanplakkal RPL, Malinis M, Minniear TD, Mueller NJ, Natori Y, Steinbrink JM, Stosor V, Wolfe C, Goldman JD.

journal.title: American journal of transplantation : official journal of the American Society of Transplantation and the American Society of Transplant Surgeons

abstractText: An expert panel of the American Society of Transplantation Infectious Diseases Community of Practice reviewed and updated guidance highlighting developments since the prior version published in 2019. A 5-article series provides guidance on screening, diagnosis, and treatment of infections in transplantation. This section focuses on donor and recipient screening and assessment of donor-derived infections, pretransplant ventricular assist device infections, and perioperative prophylaxis. The assessment and management of posttransplant infectious syndromes, including intra-abdominal infection, pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and diarrhea are presented. Recommendations are made based on the modified Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach.

title: Type 1 innate lymphoid cells promote liver regeneration via ISG15 secretion for regulating the cell cycle in hepatocytes.
authorString: Wang W, Shen X, Yu Y, Li F, Chen M, Cao H, Tian L, Qi X, Li B, Fan Q, Yang T, Zhang Y, Li S.

journal.title: Cellular and molecular gastroenterology and hepatology

abstractText: The liver possesses a robust regenerative capacity that enables the full restoration of mass and function after surgical resection. Although type 1 innate lymphoid cells (ILC1s) were originally identified as liver-resident ILCs, the molecular mechanism by which they govern hepatic regeneration remains largely undefined. Using a murine partial hepatectomy (PHx) model, ILC1s frequency and activity were evaluated by flow cytometry. Co-culture and cell transfer were performed to evaluate function of ILC1s in liver regeneration. Single cell RNA sequencing and ISG15-/- mice were used to demonstrate the role of ISG15 in ILC1s. We compared the dynamic changes in ILC1s and conventional natural killer cells (cNK cells). The proportion and absolute number of ILC1s versus cNK cells increased significantly after PHx. Co-culture with AML12 cells in vitro and adoptive transfer into Rag2-/-Il2rg-/- recipients in vivo demonstrated that only ILC1s isolated from post-operative livers (never cNK cells) potently drove hepatocyte proliferation and accelerated liver regeneration upon cell transfer. Mechanistically, single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that surgery-activated ILC1s upregulated interferon-stimulated gene 15 (ISG15) expression. Genetic ablation of ISG15 or blockade of its receptor, LFA-1, blunted the pro-regenerative capacity of ILC1s. ILC1-derived ISG15 signaled through LFA-1 on hepatocytes, inducing the expression of G2/M-phase drivers, thereby driving the cell cycle progression, and promoting liver regeneration. Our study defined a novel ILC1-ISG15-LFA-1 signaling axis that promotes liver regeneration, thereby redefining ILC1s as repair-competent innate lymphocytes and demonstrating a novel mechanism for liver regeneration.

title: The evaluation of the potential application of friedelin as an alternative to estrogen in an ovariectomized rat model.
authorString: Saini R, Sharma SK, Sonkar VK, Mishra AK, Tiwari KN, Singh J.
abstractText: Menopause is a condition where ovaries stop functioning due to a decrease in hormonal levels (estrogen). It leads to loss of fertility, hot flashes, anxiety, and vaginal dryness.
