Multivariate logistic regression analysis showed four factors; frequency of taking Meat (AOR = 2.47; 95% CI = 1.323-4.6), Alcohol intake (AOR = 2.79; 95% CI = 1.146-6.806), total Cholesterol level (AOR = 2.72; 95% CI = 1.023-7.224) and LDL Cholesterol level (AOR = 2.31; 95% CI = (1.029-5.161) were significantly associated with Metabolic syndrome according to this study.

Conclusion:

- In this study the magnitude of Metabolic syndrome was found to be 75.1% and the associated factors were Alcohol intake, Frequency of taking Meat, Total and LDL Cholesterol level.

Recommendation:

- Counseling of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus patients on the need of decreasing Alcohol and Meat consumption and physicians need to improve the habit of prescribing Lipid lowering medication. Key words: Metabolic syndrome, Type II diabetes, Cardiovascular disease, Waist circumference, Alcohol intake, Cholesterol level.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian models of cardiac interoception in schizophrenia-spectrum disorders with the Heart Rate Discrimination task
authorString: Kittleson AR, Hanson C, Ehmsen JF, Zoltowski A, Woodward N, Cascio C, Allen MG, Sheffield J.
abstractText: BackgroundPerception of external (exteroceptive) and internal (interoceptive) sensory information is critical for a coherent sense of self, others, and the world. Perception depends on the accuracy and precision of sensory beliefs. Predictive processing models propose that altered sensory beliefs contribute to schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (SZ). However, exteroception and interoception are commonly assessed with separate paradigmatic and analysis schemes. We use a Heart Rate Discrimination (HRD) paradigm and Bayesian modeling to assess perceptual accuracy and precision during exteroceptive and interoceptive processing in SZ, and test associations with clinical variables. Methods SZ (N=41) and healthy comparison (HC; N=44) participants completed the HRD and the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness; SZ additionally completed the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale. Hierarchical Bayesian models estimated threshold (bias) and slope (precision), with Bayes factors assessing group difference credibility. ResultsParticipants were less biased and more precise during exteroceptive trials, without evidence of credible group differences in bias. SZ participants had less precise perceptual beliefs overall (BF10=6.74) with no credible group-by-condition interaction. Across all participants, higher interoceptive bias was associated with greater Not-Distracting of internal bodily signals (r=.21, 95% CrI [0.005, 0.41]), and lower interoceptive precision was associated with greater self-reported Body Listening (r=.40, 95% CrI [.08, .67]). Among SZ, lower interoceptive bias was associated with greater positive symptom severity (r=−.29, 95% CrI [−.54, −.01]).Conclusions Sensory beliefs are less precise in SZ. Further, biased interoceptive beliefs relate to psychotic symptoms and subjective bodily awareness. Interventions increasing precision and reducing bias of sensory beliefs may improve psychosis.

title: Genetic, metabolic and hippocampal myelin contributions to episodic memory ageing
authorString: Gayer M, Ramponi C, Bussy A, Pascual MG, Vollenweider P, Marques-Vidal P, Vaucher J, Lutti A, Kutalik Z, Kherif F, Draganski B.
abstractText: There is ongoing controversy about the role of the apolipoprotein-E (APOE) genotype in modulating cognitive trajectories in healthy ageing and Alzheimer’s disease. We investigated associations between APOE genotype, cardiometabolic and inflammatory profiles, lifestyle, and hippocampal microstructure with late-life episodic memory trajectories in a community-dwelling, mid-to-old-age cohort. The genotyped sample (n = 5325) with follow-up spanning over 20 years included nested cognitive (n = 1378) and neuroimaging subsamples (n = 301). We first tested whether the APOE ε4 allele was associated with systemic physiological profiles across adulthood, followed by assessment of APOE associations with cognitive ageing trajectories and their relationships with health profiles and MRI markers of hippocampal myelination. APOE ε4 carrier status was associated with an adverse lipid-related metabolic profile across adulthood. In late-life, APOE ε4 was selectively associated with steeper age-related episodic memory decline across cognitive domains examined, with effects emerging in the eighth decade of life and evident already among heterozygous carriers. Individual metabolic, inflammatory, cardiovascular, and lifestyle markers did not account for this APOE ε4-related memory effect. When considered jointly within their respective domains, adverse metabolic burden was associated with poorer episodic memory performance and reduced odds of memory maintenance, whereas a favorable lifestyle profile was associated with better episodic memory function, independently of APOE genotype. The association between hippocampal myelin content and steepness of episodic memory trajectories was stronger in APOE ε4 carriers, while hippocampal volume showed only a trend. These findings indicate that APOE ε4 is primarily linked to episodic memory decline dynamics, with hippocampal myelin marking trajectory differences, whereas peripheral metabolic burden and lifestyle relates to memory performance level.

title: Impact of obesity with metabolic comorbidities on oncologic outcomes in patients with upper tract urothelial carcinoma.
authorString: Chao L, Chen IA, Yu CC, Chen M, Lin WR, Tsai YC, Yu CC, Huang CP, Lee HY.
abstractText:
Background

Metabolic syndrome (MetS) and its components have been reported with worse oncologic outcomes in several malignancies. However, the prognostic impact of obesity with metabolic comorbidities in upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC) was still inconclusive.

Objective

To evaluate the association between obesity with metabolic comorbidities and survival outcomes in patients with UTUC.

Methods

This retrospective cohort study included patients diagnosed with UTUC between 1988 and 2025 comprising 21 hospitals across Taiwan. Obesity with metabolic comorbidities was defined with a modified definition based on available clinical data, including body mass index ≥27 kg/m² combined with at least one metabolic component, such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or related medication use. Overall survival (OS), cancer-specific survival (CSS), disease-free survival (DFS) were analyzed using univariate, multivariate Cox regression analysis, BRFS was analyzed using the Fine-Gray competing-risk regression model, and Kaplan-Meier method after propensity score overlap weighting.

Results

Among 2,863 patients with UTUC, 510 patients (17.8%) were classified as having obesity with metabolic comorbidities. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed no significant differences in OS, CSS, DFS, or BRFS between patients with and without obesity with metabolic comorbidities, and these findings remained consistent after overlap weighting. In multivariable analysis, obesity with metabolic comorbidities was not independently associated with any survival endpoint. The 5-year OS, CSS, DFS, and BRFS rates were approximately 68.7%, 81.3%, 70.3%, and 76.1%, respectively, in patients with obesity with metabolic comorbidities, compared with 66.3%, 82.8%, 72.4%, and 71.4%, respectively, in those without obesity with metabolic comorbidities. Among individual MetS components, hypertension was independently associated with worse OS (HR 1.30, 95% confidence interval 1.13-1.50, P < 0.001), whereas diabetes mellitus was not significantly associated with survival outcomes in the overall cohort.

Conclusion

Obesity with metabolic comorbidities was not independently associated with OS, CSS, DFS, or BRFS in patients with UTUC. Nevertheless, individual metabolic components may have distinct prognostic implications. Further prospective studies with standardized MetS definitions are needed to better clarify the relationship between metabolic abnormalities and UTUC outcomes.

title: Systemic Treatment Trajectories and Comorbidity Burden in Sarcoidosis: A Retrospective Monocentric Real-World Analysis. Treatment and Comorbidity in Sarcoidosis.
authorString: Pianigiani T, Marrucci S, Natalello G, Dilroba A, Meocci M, Peruzzi M, Mazzon F, Farruggia J, Bergantini L, Olivieri C, Cameli P, Bargagli E.
abstractText:
Background and objective

Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease with a variable clinical course. In real-world practice, treatment initiation, tapering strategies, and duration are heterogeneous, and data on the relationship between treatment exposure and comorbidity burden remain limited.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective monocentric observational study including adults with sarcoidosis followed at a tertiary referral centre from January 2010 to November 2025. Demographic, clinical, radiological, therapeutic, and comorbidity data were extracted from a prospectively maintained database. Associations between treatment variables and documented hypertension and bone mineral density (BMD) impairment were evaluated using univariable and multivariable logistic regression.

Results

A total of 835 patients were included. At baseline, 81.8% received pharmacological treatment, most commonly corticosteroids alone. Extrapulmonary involvement was present in 45.4% and was associated with treatment initiation and escalation to immunosuppressive therapy. During follow-up, 664 patients received systemic corticosteroids for a mean treatment duration of 38.4 ± 64.3 months, and 25.9% received immunosuppressive agents, predominantly methotrexate. After multivariable adjustment, longer corticosteroid treatment duration was associated with documented hypertension (OR 1.008 per month, 95% CI 1.0002-1.016; p=0.045) and BMD impairment (OR 1.009 per month, 95% CI 1.0002-1.018; p=0.046), whereas initial corticosteroid dose was not significantly associated with either outcome.

Conclusion

Longer corticosteroid treatment duration was associated with documented hypertension and BMD impairment. However, unavailable comorbidity onset dates, cumulative corticosteroid dose data, and potential confounding by indication preclude causal interpretation. Prospective studies are needed to clarify treatment-related risks.

title: A 96-well dual-sample-preparation LC-MS/MS method for integrated quantification of eight urinary catecholamines and metabolites.
authorString: Wang Z, Liu Y.

journal.title: Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry

abstractText:
Background

Integrated quantification of urinary free catecholamines and their metabolites is important for the biochemical evaluation of pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma (PPGL) and neuroblastoma, but the physicochemical diversity of these analytes complicates LC-MS/MS analysis.

Methods

A 96-well dual-sample-preparation LC-MS/MS method was developed. Six basic amines-norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine, normetanephrine, metanephrine, and 3-methoxytyramine-were extracted by weak cation-exchange solid-phase extraction with HEPES pH stabilization. Two acidic metabolites-homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid-were analyzed after acid dilution. Detection was performed by positive/negative electrospray ionization multiple reaction monitoring.

Results

The method showed good linearity with r2 ≥ 0.996 over clinically relevant ranges. Intra- and inter-assay precision were 1.62%-7.62% and 1.72%-8.53% RSD, respectively, with accuracy of 94.5%-112.8%. Carryover, matrix consistency, spike recovery, stability, and dilution integrity all met acceptance criteria. External quality assessment deviations were all within ±20%. In 15 patients with primary hypertension, urinary norepinephrine, normetanephrine, and metanephrine were significantly higher than in 15 healthy controls (P < 0.05).

Conclusion

The method enables integrated quantification of eight urinary catecholamines and metabolites in a single workflow, providing a validated analytical platform for combined PPGL and neuroblastoma marker profiling; its diagnostic performance requires validation in confirmed disease cohorts.

title: Proliferative Glomerulonephritis with "Monoclonal" Immunoglobulin Deposits: Time for Revising the Name and a New Classification.
authorString: Nasr SH, Sirac C, Javaugue V, Bu L, D'Agati VD, Dispenzieri A, Royal V, Kastritis E, Leung N, behalf of the International Kidney and Monoclonal Gammopathy Research Group.
abstractText: Proliferative glomerulonephritis with "monoclonal" immunoglobulin deposits (PGNMID) is a glomerular-limited disease characterized by glomerulonephritis with non-organized monotypic immunoglobulin deposits. Most cases are derived from IgG3, while the remainder are derived from IgG1, IgG2, IgA, IgM, or immunoglobulin light chain (LC) only. Despite the known low rates of detection of monoclonal gammopathy (MG) and B-cell clonal proliferative disorders in PGNMID (especially PGNMID-IgG3), it has traditionally been considered a monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance (MGRS) lesion. However, the association with MG has been recently challenged by demonstration that clone detection rate is rare in PGNMID-IgG3 despite ultrasensitive sequencing techniques and that the glomerular deposits in clone-negative cases, while monotypic, are in fact polyclonal. In contrast, most cases of PGNMID-LC and elderly PGNMID-IgG1 are associated with MG. Based on recent advances, we propose changing the official name of the disease from "proliferative glomerulonephritis with monoclonal immunoglobulin deposits" to "proliferative glomerulonephritis with monotypic immunoglobulin deposits", and classifying the disease into MGRS PGNMID and non-MGRS PGNMID. Kidney biopsy reporting of PGNMID should include the immunoglobulin class (and subclass for PGNMID-IgG) given the notable differences in hematologic characteristics among these immunofluorescence morphologic variants. The new terminology and classification of PGNMID should improve communication between pathologists, nephrologists, and hematologists and help stratify patients for precision therapy.

title: Effect Modification by Albuminuria on the Association Between Serum Biomarkers of Kidney Failure Risk and Major Kidney Events Among Patients With Type 2 Diabetes.
authorString: Tangiisuran B, Tye SC, Shah H, Galecki A, Lash JP, Greene TH, Krolewski AS, Doria A.

journal.title: American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation

abstractText:
Rationale & objective

Albuminuric and normoalbuminuric diabetic kidney disease (DKD) may represent distinct pathological subtypes of kidney complications. This study assessed the modifying effect of albuminuria on the association between serum biomarkers and risk of major kidney events (MKE) in type 2 diabetes (T2D).

Study design

Nested case-control study.

Setting & participants

Individuals with T2D from the ACCORD/ACCORDION trial were included. Cases (n=383) comprised participants with baseline serum who experienced an MKE within 7 years, defined as kidney failure (KF), serum creatinine >3.3 mg/dL, and/or 50% eGFR decline. Controls (n=554) were a 15% random sample with baseline serum, at least 7 years of follow-up, and no MKE.

Exposure

Baseline serum concentrations of 21 serum proteins (Joslin Kidney Panel [JKP]).

Outcome

MKE within 7 years.

Analytical approach

Associations between individual JKP proteins and MKE were examined using logistic regression, adjusted for age and sex, HbA1c, diabetes duration, baseline eGFR, baseline UACR, and hypertension status. We stratified the analyses by baseline albuminuria status (ACR ≥30 mg/g; normoalbuminuria: ACR <30 mg/g) to assess for effect modification.

Results

At baseline, 309 subjects had albuminuria, whereas 628 were normoalbuminuric. Five JKP proteins (TNF-R3, TNF-R10B, ANGPT2, KIM1, and WFDC2) were associated (p<0.05) with increased MKE risk in both strata, but more strongly among albuminuric participants (p for interaction with albuminuria <0.05 for all proteins but KIM1). Eleven JKP proteins were associated with increased MKE risk only among albuminuric subjects, with TNF-R11A showing the strongest effect (OR=4.23, 95% CI 2.35-7.93). One protein (TNF-L12) was associated with significantly lower MKE risk after adjustment for risk proteins, uniquely among albuminuric subjects.

Limitations

Biomarkers and albuminuria were measured only at baseline.

Conclusions

Serum biomarkers of KF risk are more strongly associated with MKE in albuminuric than in normoalbuminuric T2D patients, suggesting that albuminuria status identifies biologically distinct pathways driving kidney disease progression.

title: Urinary transferrin/creatinine ratio as a biomarker of reduced allograft function and rapid renal function decline in kidney transplant recipients.
authorString: Huh D, Park J, Kee YK, Shin DH, Oh J, Park JY, Kim DH, Ko K, Jeon HJ.
abstractText: Chronic allograft injury and progressive loss of graft function remain major challenges after kidney transplantation. Urinary transferrin has been proposed as an early marker of renal damage in diabetic nephropathy and chronic kidney disease, but its clinical utility in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) is unclear. We conducted an observational study of 50 adult KTRs who provided a spot urine sample. Thirty recipients had reduced allograft function (estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] <60 mL/min/1.73 m2) at sampling, and 20 served as controls. Urinary transferrin was quantified by proteomics and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and normalized to urinary creatinine (urinary transferrin/creatinine ratio, uTf/Cr). Rapid renal function decline was defined as an annualized eGFR decline greater than 3 mL/min/1.73 m2/year or initiation of dialysis. uTf/Cr correlated positively with serum creatinine at sampling (r = 0.29, P = 0.038) and inversely with eGFR at sampling (r = -0.28, P = 0.050). uTf/Cr was higher in recipients with reduced allograft function than controls (9.2 ± 8.0 vs 4.0 ± 3.3, P = 0.003) and discriminated reduced allograft function with an AUC of 0.753 (95% CI 0.615-0.891) in ROC curves. Rapid renal function decline occurred in 19 recipients (38.0%). uTf/Cr was higher in the rapid renal function decline group than in the stable group (11.6 ± 8.8 vs 4.3 ± 3.6, P = 0.002), with an AUC of 0.832 (95% CI 0.722-0.942). In univariable logistic regression, uTf/Cr was associated with rapid renal function decline (odds ratio [OR] 1.30; 95% CI 1.10-1.53; P = 0.002) and remained significant after multivariable adjustment (OR 1.19; 95% CI 1.02-1.47; P = 0.019). Higher uTf/Cr was also associated with faster annualized eGFR decline (r = -0.47, P = 0.001). In conclusion, urinary Tf/Cr is associated with reduced allograft function and rapid renal function decline in KTRs. These findings support further validation of urinary transferrin as a non-invasive biomarker for contemporaneous and longitudinal allograft dysfunction in KTRs.

title: Proteomic characterization of the renoprotective effects of Goreisan in high-fat diet/L-NAME-treated mice.
authorString: Shimizu T, Hiramoto M, Tempaku M, Matsumoto T, Kido T.
abstractText: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is frequently complicated by chronic kidney disease (CKD). A mouse model combining a high-fat diet (HFD) and N-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester (L-NAME) reproduces key features of HFpEF, including renal injury; however, the underlying renal pathophysiology remains poorly understood. This study investigated the mechanisms of renal impairment in HFD/L-NAME-treated mice and evaluated the renoprotective effects and potential mechanisms of Goreisan (GRS), a traditional Japanese Kampo medicine. C57BL/6J mice were treated with HFD/L-NAME with or without GRS. Renal parameters were assessed, and proteomic analyses of kidney and plasma samples were performed using LC-MS/MS and SomaScan<sup>®</sup>, respectively. Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analyses were conducted to explore disease-associated pathways and the pharmacological effects of GRS. GRS ameliorated HFD/L-NAME-induced albuminuria and glomerular hypertrophy. Proteomic analyses suggested enrichment of complement-related pathways in the kidney and blood coagulation-related pathways in the plasma of HFD/L-NAME-treated mice. Renal complement component 9 (C9) expression was significantly correlated with urinary albumin levels, suggesting an association with kidney injury. GO enrichment analyses suggested that GRS treatment was associated with the modulation of oxidative stress-related pathways in the kidney and, in exploratory analyses, plasma. Consistent with these findings, GRS reduced 24-h urinary 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine excretion, supporting an antioxidant effect in this model. Blood coagulation-, complement-, and oxidative stress-related pathways may be associated with renal injury in HFD/L-NAME-treated mice. GRS exerted renoprotective effects, with oxidative stress modulation identified as a candidate contributing mechanism. These proteomic data provide insight into HFpEF-associated kidney injury and a resource for future systems-level studies of GRS.

title: A dynamic craniospinal state-space framework for fluid and compartmental disorders: a conceptual and testable physiological model.
authorString: López-Valdés JC.
abstractText: The classical Monro-Kellie doctrine (MK 1.0) models the cranial vault as a rigid container of invariable volume, relying on mean intracranial pressure (ICP) and volumetric equilibrium. However, contemporary physiology indicates that intracranial homeostasis is fundamentally governed by craniospinal coupling, compliance reserve, vascular-venous dynamics, pulsatile shockwave transmission, and microscopic fluid exchange. Building upon recent dynamic formulations (MK 2.0-4.0), we propose Monro-Kellie 5.0 (MK 5.0) as a unified, testable craniospinal state-space framework. Rather than postulating a single disease mechanism, MK 5.0 models four clinically divergent craniospinal syndromes as distinct configurations within a six-domain dynamic state space: (1) Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) as a compliance-pulsatility mismatch driven by centripetal systolic pulse waves and periventricular shear strain despite conventionally normal mean ICP; (2) Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH) as an outflow-pressure mismatch characterized by venous sinus resistance and transmural reabsorption failure; (3) Chiari I malformation with syringomyelia as a flow-transmission boundary obstruction across the foramen magnum resulting in systolic tonsillar piston impact and transmural intramedullary fluid driving; and (4) Spontaneous Intracranial Hypotension (SIH) as a volume depletion and dural elastance collapse boundary. We mathematically formalize craniospinal coupling through an analog lumped-parameter circuit, derive its frequency-domain transfer function, and operationalize the model into prospective, falsifiable multivariable regression protocols (TOST equivalence) with prespecified power and sample size. By shifting focus from a single static pressure value to composite dynamic signatures, MK 5.0 provides a quantitative bridge between physical hydrodynamics and precision neurosurgery.

title: Evaluation of Semaphorin 3G (SEMA3G) as a biofluid biomarker of cerebral amyloid angiopathy: evidence from neurodegenerative disease and memory clinic cohorts
authorString: Michaelian JC, Shi L, Barnett M, Wang D, Wang C, Naismith SL, Drummond E.
abstractText:
Introduction:

Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is characterised by amyloid-beta (Aβ) deposition in cerebral vessels, and frequently co-occurs with Alzheimer's disease (AD). Diagnosis based on MRI-based Boston criteria is not definitive, and CAA biofluid biomarkers are needed. Semaphorin 3G (SEMA3G) was recently shown to be selectively enriched in CAA-affected vessels, and correlated with CAA severity. We therefore evaluated SEMA3G as a biofluid biomarker of CAA.

Methods:

: SEMA3G profiles were examined across diagnoses in the Global Neurodegeneration Proteomics Consortium dataset (GNPC) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (N=1982) and plasma (N=6917). SEMA3G was then evaluated in the Healthy Brain Ageing (HBA) memory clinic cohort (N=161) with 3T MRI, where lobar cerebral microbleed burden was used as a proxy for CAA likelihood, with participants grouped by microbleed count (0, 1-2, or ≥3).

Results:

: CSF and plasma SEMA3G were significantly lower in AD and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) compared to cognitively unimpaired controls in GNPC, and were associated with hypertension. Longitudinally, plasma SEMA3G declined significantly over time in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD. In the HBA cohort, plasma SEMA3G did not differ by cerebral microbleed burden on MRI, nor correlate with plasma Aβ isoforms and white matter hyperintensities.

Discussion:

: Although CSF and plasma SEMA3G levels were significantly lower in AD and FTD, plasma SEMA3G was not associated with CAA-associated MRI features in individuals at risk of AD. While these findings do not support plasma SEMA3G for identifying individuals with higher CAA-associated burden, its potential utility warrants further evaluation in genetically susceptible or neuropathologically confirmed CAA cohorts.

title: One blood methylation profile stratifies ten-year risk across 21 common diseases
authorString: Seale KB, Hassouneh S, Balagué-Dobón L, Melnikas M, Aparicio A, Guo T, Ivey KL, Lasky-Su JA, Richmond A, Marioni R, Mallin M, Dwaraka VB, Carreras-Gallo N, Smith R.
abstractText: Blood DNA methylation offers a dynamic readout of inherited and acquired influences on health, creating an opportunity for risk prediction beyond polygenic scores, which are fixed at conception and have yet to demonstrate broad clinical utility. As such, we aimed to develop methylation risk scores for 21 common diseases in 12,785 adults from Generation Scotland and the Mass General Brigham Biobank, combining technically reproducible probes, null-calibrated feature selection and ten-year survival models, with evaluation in a single holdout that was not used for feature selection, model fitting or tuning. The methylation risk scores for eight diseases reached a holdout C-index of at least 0.80: chronic kidney disease, peripheral vascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure and type 2 diabetes with at least 50 events each, and interstitial lung disease, dementia and fatty liver disease with fewer. For the five scores with at least 50 events, adjusted hazard ratios per standard deviation ranged from 2.6 to 4.1, with the highest risk tertile containing 73 to 90% of the ten-year events. Panel CpGs were enriched for cytokine signalling, innate immune sensing and sterol metabolism. Against reported values, the eight top-tier methylation risk scores exceed published polygenic and methylation scores alone, and exceed published polygenic and methylation scores that include clinical covariates for seven of the eight diseases (the exception is type 2 diabetes, where our AUC of 0.865 without clinical risk factors is close to a methylation-plus-risk-factor model at 0.872, and our C-index of 0.809 is lower than the C-index for a polygenic-plus-risk-factor at 0.85). These results indicate that a single blood methylation profile can rank ten-year risk for several common diseases at a level that compares favourably with published genetic and methylation scores.

title: Maternal Hypothyroidism and Documented History of Pregnancy Loss: A Registry Based Cross-Sectional Study of 66,279 Pregnancies in North-Eastern Iran
authorString: Norouzi M, Moradi A, Saeidi MR, Farkhani EM, Afzalnia S.
abstractText: Background Maternal hypothyroidism is a frequent endocrine disorder in pregnancy and has been linked to pregnancy loss, but most evidence comes from selected hospital populations with limited control for social and psychological factors. We examined whether a physician recorded diagnosis of hypothyroidism is associated with a documented history of pregnancy loss in a large primary care population. Methods Registry based cross-sectional study using the Sina Electronic Health Record System, which covers prenatal care in the primary health care network of Mashhad University of Medical Sciences (1 March 2017–20 September 2025). All pregnancies with a recorded diagnosis of hypothyroidism were enumerated (n = 33,079) and an approximately equal random sample of pregnancies without such a record was drawn from the same source population (n = 33,200; total N = 66,279). All included pregnancies ended in a delivery; the outcome was a documented history of pregnancy loss recorded in the maternal file. Because sampling was conditional on exposure and independent of the outcome, exposure specific prevalences, prevalence ratios and prevalence odds ratios are unbiased for the source population, whereas the pooled prevalence is not. Covariates were pre-specified on clinical and causal grounds and all were retained in the model. We report adjusted prevalence odds ratios (aPOR) from logistic regression and adjusted prevalence ratios (aPR) from modified Poisson regression with robust standard errors. Results A documented history of pregnancy loss was present in 3,578 of 33,079 women with recorded hypothyroidism (10.8%, 95% CI: 10.5–11.2) and in 2,145 of 33,200 women without (6.5%, 95% CI: 6.2–6.7): a prevalence difference of 4.4 percentage points (95% CI: 3.9–4.8) and a crude prevalence ratio of 1.67 (95% CI: 1.59–1.76). After adjustment, hypothyroidism remained associated with the outcome (aPOR = 1.61, 95% CI: 1.51–1.71; aPR = 1.50, 95% CI: 1.42–1.58). The strongest correlate was pregnancy number (aPOR = 12.22, 95% CI: 10.95–13.64 for a fourth or later pregnancy), followed by Iranian nationality (aPOR = 5.54, 95% CI: 4.29–7.16) and residence outside the metropolitan area (aPOR 1.41–2.23). Maternal age was positively associated with the outcome before adjustment but inversely associated after adjustment for pregnancy number (aPOR = 0.50, 95% CI: 0.41–0.61 for women older than 40 years). Depression (aPOR = 1.18), recorded obesity (aPOR = 1.20) and genitourinary disease (aPOR = 1.37) were also independently associated, whereas a positive domestic-violence screen, anxiety, diabetes, hypertension and a history of cancer were not. Conclusions Recorded maternal hypothyroidism was associated with a roughly 50% higher prevalence of documented pregnancy loss. Because the registry records neither thyroid function values, antibody status and levothyroxine treatment, nor the timing of the diagnosis relative to the loss, the analysis cannot establish temporality, distinguish overt from subclinical disease, or separate a biological effect from more complete documentation in women under closer follow up. The findings support the recording of thyroid function values and treatment in structured prenatal fields so that these questions can be addressed directly, and they should not be used to justify a particular screening or treatment policy.

title: Family ties and late-life well-being: a cross-sectional analysis of the association between number of children and life satisfaction among Iranian older adults: findings from the Neyshabur Longitudinal Study on Aging
authorString: Hadianfar A, Delgosha SS, Gholami M.
abstractText: Background Population aging is a global demographic process that Iran is experiencing at an accelerated pace. Life satisfaction is a key marker of successful aging. Although family support has traditionally been considered an important determinant of well-being in later life, the association between the number of children and life satisfaction remains unclear, particularly in the Iranian context. Methods This cross-sectional study used data collected during the registration phase of the Neyshabur Longitudinal Study on Aging (NeLSA), a population-based cohort study in northeastern Iran. Of 7,462 participants aged ≥ 50 years, 7,167 with available data were included. Life satisfaction was assessed using the Persian version of the Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS). The main exposure variable was the number of children. Data were analyzed using multivariable linear regression, adjusting for age, sex, marital status, education, income, job status, BMI, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, and physical activity. Restricted cubic splines were used to model the functional form of the association. Results In the crude model, having more children was associated with higher life satisfaction. However, after full adjustment, the association reversed: participants with five or more children had significantly lower life satisfaction than those with 0–2 children (β = −0.40, 95% CI: −0.73 to − 0.07, P = 0.017). Each additional child was associated with a 0.08-point decrease in life satisfaction (β = −0.08, P = 0.003). The association was approximately linear, with the steepest decline observed beyond four children. Conclusions After adjusting for potential confounders, life satisfaction was relatively higher among older adults with a moderate number of children (up to four), whereas having five or more children was associated with lower life satisfaction. This finding challenges the traditional assumption that larger families inherently provide greater support in old age. Policies should focus on strengthening formal social support systems and addressing the socioeconomic burdens that may accompany larger families.

title: Emotional Dysregulation and Emotional Eating in Relation to Hypertension and Diabetes Among Adult Outpatients in Sokoto Nigeria
authorString: Bagudu KA, Muhammad M, Maihaja AI, S/pawa AS, Yusuf F, Sambo M.
abstractText: Background Difficulty in regulating emotions may affect eating behaviour and cardiometabolic health, but evidence from hospital patients in Nigeria is limited. Objective To measure emotional dysregulation among adult outpatients in Sokoto, and to examine its association with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, body mass index (BMI), emotional eating and appetite loss. Methods In this hospital-based cross-sectional study, 204 adults attending the General Outpatient Department (n = 100) and the Medical Outpatient Department (n = 104) of Specialist Hospital, Sokoto, completed an adapted 28-item Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS) and a 36-item section on eating behaviour. All 36 items were analysed as scales for emotional eating, loss of control over eating, eating awareness, appetite loss under stress and general emotion-related eating, and as two single adaptive coping items. BMI, blood pressure and fasting glucose were measured. Data were analysed with chi-square tests, correlation, analysis of variance and regression. Results The mean DERS score was 72.8 (SD = 18.8; Cronbach’s alpha = 0.95), and 32.8% had high emotional dysregulation. DERS level was not associated with hypertension (p = 0.458) or diabetes (p = 0.516), and the adjusted odds ratios per 10-point rise were 1.01 and 1.00. DERS score correlated weakly with systolic blood pressure (r = 0.157), diastolic blood pressure (r = 0.154) and fasting glucose (ρ = 0.15). Mean BMI differed across DERS levels (21.5, 23.0 and 23.1 kg/m²; p = 0.002) but not after adjustment for age, sex and physical activity (p = 0.213). DERS was the strongest predictor of emotional eating (ρ = 0.73); each 10-point rise in DERS raised the emotional eating score by 0.35 (p < 0.001), and the model explained 59% of its variation. Emotional eating (2.54 against 2.21; p = 0.011) and general emotion-related eating (2.59 against 2.26; p = 0.003) were higher in participants with hypertension, and emotional eating remained associated with hypertension after adjustment for age, sex and BMI (adjusted OR = 1.50 per point; 95% CI 1.04–2.17). Appetite loss under stress (mean 2.65) was as common as emotional eating (2.43). Conclusion Emotional dysregulation was moderate and closely linked to emotional eating, but it was not independently associated with hypertension, diabetes or BMI. Emotional eating, however, was linked to hypertension independently of age, sex and BMI, an exploratory finding that needs confirmation. Clinics should screen for emotional wellbeing and teach healthy ways of coping with stress, and longitudinal studies with validated tools are needed.

title: Coexistence of BRAF V600E-Mutated Erdheim-Chester Disease with PDGFRβ- Rearranged Hypereosinophilic Syndrome: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Challenges
authorString: Cariou P, Degrave R, Moinet F, Kahn J, Roos-Weil D, Nguyen-Khac F, Chapiro E, Bulifon S, Schmoll A, Hsoumi F, Abermil N, Ova JO, Amoura Z, Hié M, Haroche J, Papo M.
abstractText: Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) is a rare systemic histiocytosis driven by MAPK-pathway mutations, most frequently BRAFV600E. Myeloid neoplasms occur in 10-15% of ECD patients. This is the first report of ECD associated with clonal hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) in the same patient.A 66-year-old woman was diagnosed with ECD harboring a BRAFV600E mutation concomitantly with HES driven by a TNIP1::PDGFRβ fusion identified by optical genome mapping (OGM). She presented with cutaneous lesions, lymphadenopathy, hypereosinophilia and pulmonary hypertension. Interferon-alpha was discontinued because of disease progression and worsening pulmonary hypertension. Imatinib was attempted but poorly tolerated, resulting in acute heart failure. Cobimetinib resulted in clinical and metabolic improvement of ECD, with limited effect on eosinophilia. Pulmonary hypertension improved after adding tadalafil and bosentan.This case illustrates the interplay between histiocytosis and a coexisting myeloproliferative neoplasm, driven by distinct molecular alterations. BRAF inhibition may cause paradoxical MAPK activation and progression in PDGFRβ-rearranged cells, whereas MEK inhibition with cobimetinib provided an effective and well-tolerated alternative for ECD. OGM was essential for identifying PDGFRβ rearrangement and guiding therapy.We report the first reported case BRAFV600E-mutated ECD associated with HES due to PDGFRβ rearrangement, emphasizing the importance of comprehensive molecular profiling and the therapeutic challenges of managing concurrent clonal hematologic disorders.

title: Clinical Reference Values for Left Ventricular Diastolic Indices in Stable Outpatients with Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction Running Title: Diastolic Reference Values in HfrEF
authorString: Eskandari A, Chenaghlou M, Mohammadi K, Karimi M.
abstractText: Background and Aim: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) requires precise assessment of left ventricular filling pressures (LVFP) for optimal management. While guidelines provide thresholds for detecting elevated LVFP, specific reference values for guiding hemodynamic targets in stable outpatients remain undefined. This study aimed to establish clinical reference values for echocardiographic diastolic indices in stable HFrEF patients. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted in 2023 at the Cardiovascular Research Center of Tabriz University of Medical Sciences. A total of 102 outpatient HFrEF patients (ejection fraction ≤ 40%, NYHA functional class I/II) and 100 healthy individuals with normal cardiac function (ejection fraction ≥ 55%) were enrolled. Patients with significant valvular disease, atrial fibrillation, advanced pulmonary disease, or severe renal failure (eGFR < 30 mL/min) were excluded. Diastolic indices, including left atrial volume index (LAVI), tricuspid regurgitation gradient (TRG), E/e′ ratio, and E/A ratio, were measured using transthoracic echocardiography. Data were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney test in SPSS version 22 (significance level P < 0.05). Results Mean diastolic indices in HFrEF patients were LAVI: 32.5 mL/m² (vs. 25 mL/m² in controls), TRG: 21.5 mmHg (vs. 16.5 mmHg), and E/e′: 12 (vs. 7), all significantly higher than the control group (P < 0.0001). The E/A ratio (0.95 in patients vs. 0.8 in controls) showed no significant difference (P = 0.171). Conclusion The diastolic indices LAVI (32.5 mL/m²), TRG (21.5 mmHg), and E/e′ (12) can serve as clinical reference points for optimizing medical treatment in ambulatory HFrEF patients and for guiding clinical decision-making, as these patients may require drug adjustment to prevent pulmonary congestion and hospital readmissions. Further research is needed to validate these findings and assess their impact on long-term outcomes.

title: Risk Prediction of Failure of the First Planned Weaning Attempt After Hepatectomy: A Cohort Study Using Firth-Penalized Logistic Regression
authorString: Zhang J, Zhang Y, Li P, Wang Y.
abstractText: Background To develop and internally validate a parsimonious model for predicting failure of the first planned weaning attempt after hepatectomy. Methods We included consecutive patients who underwent a first planned weaning attempt after hepatectomy. The primary outcome was reintubation within 48 h after planned extubation. Candidate predictors were limited to variables available before or at the time of weaning. Firth-penalized logistic regression was used to address the low event rate. All subsets of candidate predictors were compared, and the final model was selected according to optimism-corrected area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUC) from 500 bootstrap resamples. Discrimination, calibration, and sensitivity analyses were evaluated. Model reporting followed the TRIPOD framework. Results Of 416 patients included in the final cohort, 21 (5.0%) experienced weaning failure. The final model was fitted in 414 patients and included the PaO 2 /FiO 2 (P/F) ratio at weaning, atelectasis, and hypertension. For each 50-mmHg decrease in the P/F ratio, the odds of weaning failure increased by approximately 1.56-fold. Atelectasis was associated with a higher risk of failure. The apparent AUC was 0.824 (bootstrap 95% CI, 0.74 to 0.93), the optimism-corrected AUC was 0.804, and the optimism-corrected calibration slope was 0.949. Conventional logistic regression and multiple-imputation analyses showed consistent directions of association. Conclusions A three-variable model comprising oxygenation status at weaning, atelectasis, and hypertension may provide individualized risk estimates for failure of the first planned weaning attempt after hepatectomy. External validation in independent, multicenter cohorts is required before use in clinical decision support.

title: From operational analysis to implementable emergency department throughput interventions: Integrating Theory of Constraints and Design Science Research
authorString: Sarimo S, Koivistoinen T, Lukkarinen T, Palomäki A, Torkki P.
abstractText: Background Emergency Department (ED) efficiency is often constrained by crowding, which is driven by non-critical patients and exacerbated by delays in patient transfer to inpatient wards. While numerous studies have identified opportunities to improve ED throughput, fewer have addressed how operational evidence can be systematically translated into implementable interventions. Because indiscriminate acceleration of patient throughput may worsen congestion at the ED–ward interface, this study aimed to develop and operationalise a throughput intervention for dischargeable patients using a combined Theory of Constraints (TOC) and Design Science Research (DSR) approach, providing a systematic framework for translating operational research into healthcare practice. Methods Using a mixed-methods design, ED visits at a Finnish secondary hospital in 2022 (n = 26,814) were retrospectively analysed. Cumulative ED length of stay (CEDLOS) was calculated for each acute diagnosis among dischargeable patients, and diagnoses were ranked accordingly. The highest-ranking diagnosis whose demand coincided with peak ED crowding was selected as the theoretical target segment, from which an identifiable operational target segment was derived for intervention design. Constraints within the operational target segment were characterised using process mapping, quantitative analyses, and semi-structured interviews with healthcare professionals (n = 8). TOC was used to identify and address operational constraints, while DSR translated these findings into an implementable throughput intervention. Results Theoretical target segment analysis identified discharged patients with acute atrial fibrillation as the diagnosis contributing the greatest cumulative ED burden during periods of crowding (912 visits, 5,785 hours). An operational target segment suitable for prospective identification was subsequently defined. Key constraints were information flow and laboratory throughput. A fast-track service incorporating rapid assessment, pull-based external electrical cardioversion, point-of-care testing, and patient education was developed. Conclusions The combined TOC–DSR approach provides a systematic framework for translating operational analyses into implementable ED throughput interventions. By targeting dischargeable patients and requiring no additional resources, the proposed intervention offers a practical pathway for reducing crowding while facilitating the translation of operational research into healthcare practice. Further research is needed to evaluate its effectiveness and generalisability.

title: Case Report: Aortic valve Haemophilus parainfluenzae infective endocarditis complicated by a fistulating aortic root abscess and refractory atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response
authorString: Shalan k, Lynch A.
abstractText: This report details the case of a gentleman in his 50s, with a background of previous bicuspid aortic valve infective endocarditis 28 years prior, presenting to hospital with non-specific symptoms, including shivers, headaches and myalgia. Objective clinical findings included pyrexia, hypotension and atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response (AF RVR). He was initially provided with empirical intravenous antibiotics and isotonic fluids to treat an infection of unclear origin. Despite equivocal preliminary imaging findings, blood cultures isolated  Haemophilus parainfluenzae , an organism implicating endocarditis, and his antibiotics were switched to Ceftriaxone. Even with this change in antibiotics, he consistently remained febrile, developed a significant Troponin-I leak, and his AF RVR exceeded 200 bpm – unamenable to pharmacological rate and rhythm control therapy. Transoesophageal echocardiography later confirmed an aortic root abscess fistulating into his left ventricular outlet tract, where the patient thereupon underwent an aortic valve replacement with patch reconstruction. Post-procedure, his AF was now responsive to Amiodarone, successfully restoring sinus rhythm. His inflammatory markers additionally improved before he was discharged home to complete his four-week Ceftriaxone course under the virtual ward – achieving a successful outcome. Especially in patients with overt risk factors, this case reinforces the need to maintain a high index of suspicion for infective endocarditis in patients presenting to the acute medicine with pyrexia of unknown origin. This case was, however, also remarkable for capturing significant AF RVR instead of the anticipated heart blocks with abscess formation and serves to emphasise the heterogeneity of  Haemophilus parainfluenzae endocarditis cases.

title: Revascularization of Renal Artery Stenosis for "Flash Cerebral Edema" (Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome).
authorString: Yanik AJ, Bhatnagar V, Burdick TR, Block CA.
abstractText:
Background

Appropriate patient selection for renal artery stenosis (RAS) revascularization remains controversial. Consensus guidelines suggest certain high-risk groups benefit. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) has rarely been connected to RAS and is not generally included as an indication for revascularization.

Case summary

A 69-year-old woman presented with confusion and seizures. Brain imaging demonstrated PRES. Blood pressure was 230/110 mm Hg and required nicardipine infusion, despite maximal doses of 4 oral medications. Duplex ultrasonography demonstrated RAS; angiography confirmed right renal artery high-grade ostial stenosis. Percutaneous balloon angioplasty and stent insertion were performed, resulting in immediate improvement in hypertension. At follow-up 6 months later, she was normotensive, and all antihypertensive medications had been discontinued.

Discussion

Clinicians must remain observant for appropriate candidates for RAS revascularization, as high-risk groups were excluded from the pivotal trials. Presentation of RAS with "flash" pulmonary edema is a supported indication for revascularization; PRES has pathophysiology akin to "flash" pulmonary edema and can respond to revascularization. PRES should be included in the list of potential indications for revascularization.

Take-home message

PRES warrants consideration of RAS and addition to the list of conditions that may benefit from revascularization of RAS.

title: VEGF-Driven High-Output Heart Failure in POEMS Syndrome: A Multisystem Case.
authorString: Keykhaei M, Morad TT, Rizner JD, Grant B, Man JJ, Peyda P, Shahrvini T, Cummins CM, Sekhon SS, Aksoy O.
abstractText:
Background

POEMS syndrome, defined by polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal plasma-cell disorder, and skin changes, is a rare vascular endothelial growth factor-driven disorder. Although extravascular volume overload is common, sustained high-output heart failure (HOHF) is rarely recognized.

Case summary

A 43-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy presented with progressive dyspnea, anasarca, and polyneuropathy. Serial right-heart catheterizations confirmed high-output physiology (thermodilution cardiac output 10.85 → 12.33 L/min) with low systemic vascular resistance (approximately 490 → 435 dyn・s cm-5) and low filling pressures. Pulmonary artery pressure-guided diuresis and hemodialysis stabilized hemodynamics. Daratumumab/carfilzomib/dexamethasone yielded partial metabolic response with resolution of ascites, edema, and neuropathy.

Discussion

This case illustrates vascular endothelial growth factor-mediated vasodilation and capillary leak as a mechanism of HOHF in POEMS, with sustained response to plasma-cell-directed therapy.

Take-home message

POEMS should be considered in unexplained HOHF with low systemic vascular resistance, and new symptoms in patients with coexisting coronary disease require reassessment beyond the index diagnosis.

title: Left-sided portal hypertension secondary to pancreatic pseudocyst presenting with anaemia: A case report and literature review.
authorString: Karahan F, Dilek HB, Canpolat K, Dilek ON.

journal.title: Anales del sistema sanitario de Navarra

abstractText: Left-sided portal hypertension (LSPH) is a rare clinical condition most commonly associated with splenic vein thrombosis secondary to pancreatitis. Gastric fundal varices may develop as a consequence of impaired venous drainage and can lead to life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding. We present a case of LSPH secondary to acute pancreatitis and subsequent pancreatic pseudocyst formation, resulting in splenic vein thrombosis, variceal bleeding, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and hypersplenism. The patient underwent splenectomy combined with cystogastrostomy through a left subcostal incision. LSPH-related symptoms resolved completely and the patient was discharged on postoperative Day 5. At the 9-month follow-up, contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated complete resolution of the pancreatic pseudocyst and fundal varices. In patients with pancreatic pseudocysts accompanied by anaemia, complications related to splenic vein thrombosis should be carefully evaluated. In selected patients with LSPH, combined splenectomy and cystogastrostomy may be an effective therapeutic option.

title: Kidney effects of inhaled nitric oxide in critically ill patients: from pathophysiological considerations to clinical implications.
authorString: Robert A, Gonze A, Bulpa P, Hauquiert B.
abstractText: Inhaled nitric oxide is widely used as a selective pulmonary vasodilator in critical care, yet its renal effects remain controversial. While existing reviews mostly focus on indications for inhaled nitric oxide and its impact on outcomes, limited data exist on its renal effects, since it was thought to act only locally in the lungs. This review examine the clinical evidence regarding kidney outcomes associated with inhaled nitric oxide across major indications and provide an integrated mechanistic analysis of nitric oxide signaling in renal physiology and pathophysiology. Nitric oxide is produced by nitric oxide synthases using L-arginine as a substrate. It acts as a smooth muscle relaxation factor and ultimately causes vasodilation through its effect on cyclic guanosine monophosphate. Nitric oxide plays a pivotal role in renal hemodynamic regulation, glomerular filtration, tubular function, and microcirculatory homeostasis. The net renal effect of inhaled nitric oxide likely reflects the balance between improved nitric oxide signaling and oxidative stress generation. Available clinical data suggest that the renal impact of inhaled nitric oxide is context-dependent. In acute respiratory distress syndrome, higher-level evidence indicates a potential increase in acute kidney injury, possibly related to oxidative and nitrosative stress. Conversely, in cardiac bypass surgery, inhaled nitric oxide may confer nephroprotection by restoring nitric oxide bioavailability during hemolysis and free hemoglobin-mediated nitric oxide scavenging. In other conditions, including organ transplantation, pulmonary hypertension, sepsis, and hemolytic disorders, evidence remains limited or inconclusive. Overall, current evidence does not support a uniform renal effect of inhaled nitric oxide, indicating the need for prospective studies with predefined renal endpoints to clarify its clinical relevance.

title: Association of postpartum glycemic control with serum MMP-9, ET-1, hypertension, and dyslipidemia in women with gestational diabetes mellitus.
authorString: Lu H, Song R, Dong J, Tang J, Yan C.
abstractText:
Objective

To examine the association between 12-month postpartum glycemic control and serum matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9)/endothelin-1 (ET-1) levels, hypertension, and dyslipidemia in women with prior gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), and to explore statistical indirect effects involving these biomarkers.

Methods

A total of 300 women with prior GDM followed up at 12 months postpartum were included. HbA1c, MMP-9, ET-1, blood pressure, and lipid profiles were assessed at the same follow-up visit. Participants were stratified into good (n = 141) and poor (n = 159) glycemic control groups based on a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) cutoff of 5.7%. General characteristics, vascular biomarker levels, and the prevalence of hypertension and dyslipidemia were compared between the groups. Correlation and logistic regression analyzes were performed, followed by exploratory regression-based indirect-effect analyzes involving MMP-9 and ET-1.

Results

The poor control group had significantly higher levels of MMP-9 and ET-1. HbA1c was positively correlated with both biomarkers. The prevalences of hypertension and dyslipidemia in the poor control group were 28.9% and 37.1%, respectively, and were significantly higher than those in the good control group. Exploratory analyzes showed significant indirect-effect estimates involving MMP-9 and ET-1, with model-derived proportions of approximately 22% to 26%; however, these contemporaneous associations do not establish causal mediation.

Conclusion

Poor glycemic control at 12 months postpartum was associated with higher MMP-9 and ET-1 levels and a greater prevalence of hypertension and dyslipidemia. The observed indirect effects should be interpreted as exploratory statistical associations rather than evidence of temporal or causal mediation.

title: MRI-Derived Atrial Substrate Score Predicts Recurrence After First-Time Cryoballoon Pulmonary Vein Isolation.
authorString: Koektuerk B, Glaenzer L, Yorgun H, Aytemir K, Stöckigt F, Seyfarth M, Horlitz M, Bansmann M.
abstractText:
Background and aims

The conventional classification of atrial fibrillation (AF) as paroxysmal or persistent may not reflect structural atrial remodeling and has limited value for predicting recurrence after pulmonary vein isolation (PVI). We investigated whether an MRI-derived substrate score combining left atrial (LA) fibrosis and size improves recurrence risk stratification after first-time cryoballoon PVI.

Methods

We retrospectively analyzed 69 patients undergoing first cryoballoon PVI; 67 underwent pre-procedural 3-Tesla late gadolinium enhancement MRI. LA fibrosis was graded using the UTAH classification; the maximal horizontal LA diameter in the two-chamber view was measured, and LA volume was calculated with a 3D tool. An exploratory point-based score was constructed from LA diameter categories (< 44 mm, 0 points; 44-< 48 mm, 2 points; ≥ 48 mm, 4 points) and advanced fibrosis (UTAH stage 3-4, 1 point). Discrimination for 12-month arrhythmia recurrence was assessed by ROC analysis.

Results

Advanced fibrosis was present in half of the patients with paroxysmal AF, with a similar UTAH distribution in both phenotypes (p = 0.83). LA diameter and volume were larger in patients with recurrence and discriminated recurrence (AUC 0.95 and 0.92). The substrate score predicted recurrence (AUC 0.96, 95% CI 0.91-0.99), with recurrence rates of 0%, 41% and 96% in low-, intermediate- and high-risk patients. LA size was the main contributor, with fibrosis providing complementary information, whereas AF phenotype did not provide incremental predictive value.

Conclusions

An MRI-derived substrate score, with LA size as the main contributor and fibrosis as a complementary marker, predicted arrhythmia recurrence after cryoballoon PVI better than the conventional AF phenotype. External validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: Dynamic Risk Assessment of Severe Ventricular Arrhythmia in Patients With Implantable Defibrillators and Reduced Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction.
authorString: Diz-Díaz J, Lillo-Castellano JM, La Rosa G, Soto-Pérez M, Martínez-Ferrer J, Ricoy E, Barrera A, Gabriel Martínez J, Rodríguez-Pérez JC, Rodríguez A, Anguera I, Viñolas X, Peñafiel P, Rodríguez-Mañero M, Roca-Luque I, Porta-Sánchez A, Jiménez-Díaz J, Jiménez-Jáimez J, Cabrera E, Tercedor L, Hernández-Betancor I, Castrejón S, Álvarez-Ortega C, Merino JL, Peinado R, Cañadas-Godoy V, González-Ferrer JJ, Salgado M, Calvo-Cuervo D, Salgado-Aranda R, Cruz A, Marina-Breysse M, García-Torrent MJ, García-Escolano A, Ramos-Prada A, Ramos-López N, Ramírez J, Redondo-Rodríguez A, Quintanilla JG, Priori S, Pérez-Villacastín J, Pérez-Castellano N, Filgueiras-Rama D.
abstractText:
Background

Device shocks are associated with an adverse prognosis in patients with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators. This study aimed to develop and validate a predictive model based on dynamic changes in intracardiac electrograms to assess the risk of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation (VF) events in patients with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).

Methods

Experimental studies were conducted in pigs with HFrEF (N=8) to characterize intracardiac electrogram and surface ECG changes during HF decompensation. Sham-operated animals (N=6) were used as controls. In patients, the study used data from 2 independent cohorts of patients with ICDs. The first cohort included 5089 patients from 50 centers (199 218 tracings), leveraging electrical parameters associated with HFrEF decompensation in the experimental model to train and internally validate a dynamic convolutional neural network model for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia/VF prediction. External validation was performed in a second cohort of 2040 patients from 7 centers (369 845 tracings).

Results

In pigs, HFrEF decompensation was associated with QRS prolongation on surface ECG tracings and reduced bipolar R-wave amplitude in intracardiac electrograms. Hemodynamic and electrical alterations of HFrEF decompensation significantly increased the risk of inducible VF episodes compared with sham-operated controls (87.5% versus 0%, respectively; P<0.001). In a clinical setting, a convolutional neural network-derived model predicted first VF or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia events by analyzing temporal patterns of R-wave amplitude, QRS duration, and premature ventricular complex burden. This approach yielded areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.787 (0.753-0.817) for the training cohort and 0.725 (0.709-0.739) for the external validation cohort. Dynamic risk prediction using the convolutional neural network model significantly outperformed static risk assessment based on clinical variables (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.617 [0.602-0.632]).

Conclusions

A convolutional neural network-derived model, grounded in the pathophysiology of HFrEF, provides dynamic risk assessment of VF or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia events in patients with implantable cardioverter-defibrillator devices.

title: Beyond Continuation: Early Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitor Initiation After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation.
authorString: Jurin I, Unić D, Jurin H, Hadžibegović I.

journal.title: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions

abstractText:
Background

Overall sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor use after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) combines continuation and new initiation. We characterized these distinct prescribing processes and the clinical profiles accompanying initiation.

Aims and methods

This retrospective single-center registry included 653 patients undergoing TAVI in 2022-2025. Exposure was assessed within 90 days before and 30 days after TAVI using discharge summaries and electronic medical records. The primary measure was initiation among previously untreated patients. Admission and wait-list N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) measurements were summarized separately.

Results

Early medication status was known in 639 patients; 260 (40.7%) received SGLT2 inhibitors. Among 638 patients with paired records, 184 continued therapy, 76 initiated, eight did not continue, and 370 had no use in either window. Continuation occurred in 184/192 previously treated patients (95.8%), whereas initiation occurred in 76/446 previously untreated patients (17.0%; 95% confidence interval, 13.8-20.8). Initiation was 70/351 (19.9%) in a secondary subgroup with selected clinical risk features, without established trial eligibility. Admission NT-proBNP was available in 590 patients (90.4%); wait-list values were available in 356, including 349 with both assessments. Initiators had lower ejection fraction and higher admission NT-proBNP. Urinary tract infection explained four of eight non-continuations.

Conclusions

High continuation coexisted with limited new initiation. Transition-specific reporting clarifies early prescribing and supports individualized reassessment after TAVI, but does not establish treatment effects or the appropriateness of individual non-prescription decisions.

title: Clinical, histological, and transcriptomic clustering capture distinct clinically relevant aspects of carotid atherosclerosis.
authorString: Wei S, Hoekstra JKR, van der Laan SW, de Kleijn DPV, Kaikkonen MU, den Ruijter HM, Pasterkamp G, Mokry M.
abstractText:
Aims

Patients with carotid atherosclerosis exhibit substantial heterogeneity in clinical presentation, plaque characteristics, and future cardiovascular risk, which do not always align. Clinical variables, plaque morphology, and molecular profiles are all used for patient stratification, yet it remains unclear which aspects of disease these data types capture and how they relate to clinically relevant outcomes. We therefore aimed to determine how clustering based on clinical, histological, and transcriptomic data relates to current cerebrovascular symptoms, plaque biology, and future cardiovascular risk.

Methods and results

We analysed 1075 patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy with matched clinical, histological, and transcriptomic data. Unsupervised clustering was applied separately to each data modality, and resulting clusters were evaluated for overlap and association with current symptom status and 3-year major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Clusters derived from different modalities showed limited overlap, but distinct associations with clinical outcomes. Clinical clusters were most strongly associated with 3-year MACE, whereas histological and transcriptomic clusters were more closely related to current cerebrovascular symptoms. Transcriptomic clusters further delineated molecular pathways and plaque biology. Integration of modalities provided modest improvement in outcome stratification, indicating that these data types capture complementary rather than redundant information.

Conclusion

Clinical, histological, and transcriptomic data capture distinct but complementary aspects of carotid atherosclerosis, reflecting systemic cardiovascular risk, local plaque phenotype, and underlying biology, with differing relevance to current cerebrovascular symptoms and future cardiovascular risk. The choice of data modality should therefore be guided by the intended clinical or biological question, rather than assuming a single approach can capture the full disease spectrum.

title: EPB41L4A‑AS1 promotes endothelial dysfunction in preeclampsia through the miR‑26a‑2‑3p/15‑LOX‑1/p38 MAPK axis.
authorString: He J, Ran H, Xia R, Peng Z, Liu Y, Cheng X, Zhao Y, Ran D, Chen L, Yang J.
abstractText: Preeclampsia (PE) is a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy characterized by systemic endothelial dysfunction. Long non‑coding RNA EPB41L4A‑AS1 has been implicated in pregnancy‑related disorders, but its role in PE remains unclear. Our previous work demonstrated that downregulation of miR‑26a‑2‑3p promotes endothelial injury via activation of the 15‑lipoxygenase‑1 (15‑LOX‑1)/p38 mitogen‑activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK) pathway. In the present study, whether EPB41L4A‑AS1 contributes to PE pathogenesis by regulating this axis was investigated. EPB41L4A‑AS1 expression was significantly upregulated in placental tissues from patients with PE and negatively correlated with miR‑26a‑2‑3p levels. Functional experiments revealed that EPB41L4A‑AS1 overexpression suppressed miR‑26a‑2‑3p, activated the 15‑LOX‑1/p38 MAPK pathway and promoted endothelial dysfunction, effects that were partially reversed by miR‑26a‑2‑3p mimics. In an L‑NAME‑induced PE mouse model, EPB41L4A‑AS1 overexpression exacerbated hypertension, proteinuria, placental apoptosis and oxidative stress, whereas miR‑26a‑2‑3p agomir administration attenuated these effects. Mechanistically, luciferase reporter assays revealed no direct binding between EPB41L4A‑AS1 and miR‑26a‑2‑3p, suggesting an indirect regulatory mechanism. Collectively, these findings identify EPB41L4A‑AS1 as a critical upstream regulator of the miR‑26a‑2‑3p/15‑LOX‑1/p38 MAPK axis in PE and suggest that targeting this pathway may represent a potential therapeutic strategy.

title: Baicalin attenuates high‑altitude pulmonary edema via PI3K/Akt activation and NLRP3 pyroptosis inhibition.
authorString: Chen W, Pang J, Zhang X, He H, Sun Y, Dai N, Zhao L, Lian J, Liang R.
abstractText: High‑altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) is a severe form of non‑cardiogenic acute lung injury triggered by hypobaric hypoxia, classically attributed to dysregulated pulmonary vasoconstriction and barrier failure, with inflammation and oxidative stress acting as amplifiers of this injury. Baicalin (BA), a flavonoid from Scutellaria baicalensis, has recognized antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory activities, but its effects in HAPE are not fully understood. BA in a hypobaric hypoxia‑induced HAPE was assessed in a mouse model and in a CoCl2‑induced hypoxic macrophage model. Lung edema/injury, redox status and inflammation were analyzed using histology and biochemical assays, immunofluorescence, transmission electron microscopy, western blotting and reverse transcription‑quantitative PCR. Pathway candidates were explored by network pharmacology and molecular docking and then verified experimentally. BA pretreatment reduced pulmonary edema and tissue damage, lowered reactive oxygen species and decreased proinflammatory cytokine production. BA treatment was associated with increased PI3K/Akt phosphorylation in vivo and in vitro and concurrently inhibited NOD‑like receptor family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome activation, limiting caspase‑1 activation, gasdermin D cleavage and IL‑1β/IL‑18 maturation and release. Blocking PI3K largely reversed these benefits, supporting a PI3K/Akt‑dependent mechanism. Overall, BA protects against hypobaric hypoxia‑induced lung injury in association with increased PI3K/Akt phosphorylation and suppresses oxidative stress‑linked NLRP3 inflammasome‑associated pyroptotic signaling, highlighting BA as a potential prophylactic agent for the prevention of high‑altitude‑related lung injury.

title: Compartment-specific remodeling of placental and fetal hepatic amino acid metabolism in a rat model of protein restriction-induced fetal growth restriction.
authorString: Simmerl M, Menendez-Castro C, Schuessler S, Conrad ML, Kahhaleh F, Datye S, Cordasic N, Park J, Woelfle J, Rauh M, Hartner A, Fahlbusch FB.

journal.title: Journal of developmental origins of health and disease

abstractText: Maternal protein restriction is a widely used experimental model of fetal growth restriction (FGR), yet fetal metabolic adaptations across placental and hepatic compartments remain incompletely characterized. We investigated placental and fetal hepatic amino acid and related metabolite profiles in a rat model of protein restriction-induced FGR. Pregnant Wistar rats received either a low-protein diet (8.1% protein; LP) or an isocaloric normal-protein diet (17.3% protein; NP). At embryonic day 18.5, placental and fetal liver samples from standardized uterine positions were analyzed using targeted liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Metabolomic data were evaluated using nonparametric Wilcoxon rank-sum testing with false discovery rate reporting, unsupervised hierarchical clustering, partial least-squares discriminant analysis for visualization, and quantitative enrichment analysis. Maternal protein restriction revealed compartment-specific remodeling of fetal amino acid metabolism. LP placentas showed higher concentrations of non-essential and glucogenic amino acids, driven mainly by glutamate and aspartate, together with higher kynurenine-to-tryptophan ratios and lower tryptophan concentrations. In fetal liver, most altered amino acids were lower in LP fetuses, whereas kynurenine, 2-aminoadipic acid, and kynurenine-to-tryptophan and putrescine-to-ornithine ratios were higher. Enrichment analyses supported involvement of tryptophan metabolism, glutamate-aspartate-linked nitrogen handling, malate-aspartate shuttle activity, arginine/proline metabolism, and lysine degradation. Maternal protein restriction during gestation induced compartment-specific remodeling of placental and fetal hepatic amino acid metabolism, characterized by fundamentally different adaptive amino acid signatures despite both tissues originating from the same fetuses. These findings are consistent with altered hepato-placental amino acid cycling and nitrogen handling and provide a descriptive basis for future mechanistic studies of nutritional FGR.

title: Inhibition of platelet adhesion and aggregation with multifunctional peptide nanoparticles for atherosclerosis treatment.
authorString: Wang A, Yang L, Zhong W, Zhang G, Zhang M, Chen Z.
abstractText: Inhibiting collagen-triggered platelet adhesion and aggregation is a promising strategy for treating atherosclerosis. Herein, we developed multifunctional peptide (MP) nanoparticles with affinity for collagen and fibrinogen to sequentially block platelet adhesion and aggregation. The interactions between platelets and fibrinogen and those of MP nanoparticles with platelets and fibrinogen were investigated through molecular dynamics simulations and in vitro experiments. The efficacy of MP nanoparticles in treating atherosclerosis was assessed in vivo. The results indicate that the EKTEAEK sequence of integrin αIIbβ3 is a potential fibrinogen-interacting motif. The constructed MP nanoparticles exhibit 3.4-fold and 3.2-fold higher adhesion forces toward collagen and fibrinogen, respectively, than toward HUVECs. MP nanoparticles produce an 83% reduction in collagen-induced platelet adhesion and aggregation under physiological shear-stress conditions. In ApoE<sup>-/-</sup> mice, 10-weeks of MP treatment was associated with an observed 71.7% reduction in aortic plaque area, reduced inflammation and platelet deposition, and a trend toward improved plaque stability.

title: The molecular interactions of viruses with apolipoproteins: Evidence, Mechanisms, and Therapeutic Implications.
authorString: Jiang Y, Liu W, Luo B.
abstractText: Host lipid metabolism is extensively hijacked by viruses to support their replication cycle. Apolipoproteins, the core protein components of lipoprotein particles, mediate lipid transport, receptor recognition, and immune regulation, making them key host targets for diverse viruses. This review systematically examines the molecular mechanisms underlying virus-apolipoprotein interactions and establishes a classification framework distinguishing direct from indirect modes of action. Direct interactions involve physical binding between viral components and apolipoproteins or their receptors, exemplified by hepatitis C virus (HCV) ApoE-dependent lipoviroparticle assembly, hepatitis B virus (HBV) ApoE-mediated entry, Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) spike protein binding to high-density lipoprotein (HDL)-associated apolipoproteins, and rabies virus ApoD-glycoprotein interaction. Indirect mechanisms include viral regulation of apolipoprotein expression through epigenetic modifications, cytokines, and oxidative stress. We also compare the differential effects of ApoE2, ApoE3, and ApoE4 subtypes on infection susceptibility and disease severity across HCV, human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1), and SARS-CoV-2. The clinical-pathological consequences, including hepatic steatosis, atherosclerosis (AS), dyslipidemia, and thrombotic complications, are discussed, and therapeutic strategies targeting lipid metabolism are critically evaluated. We close by outlining unresolved questions and suggesting future research directions leveraging single-cell multi-omics, spatial biology, and organoid models.

title: HCM-mutation G716R in β-myosin alters contractile function and responsiveness to mavacamten of human ventricular myofibrils
authorString: Brunkhorst A, Holler T, Piep B, Francino A, dos Remedios CG, Kraft T, Iorga B.
abstractText:
ABSTRACT

Effects of the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) associated mutation Gly716Arg in β-myosin at the sarcomeric level are unresolved. To further understand HCM-pathomechanisms in relation to modern treatment, we investigated the effect of this mutation in subcellular myofibrils isolated from HCM-patient’s myocardium compared to myofibrils from healthy donor hearts, and tested how mavacamten influences force-related parameters. Mavacamten is a state-of-the-art myosin inhibitor aimed to treat ventricular hypercontractility of symptomatic HCM patients. Compared with donor myofibrils, patient myofibrils developed similar isometric forces, while kinetics of maximum force generation and particularly of relaxation were slower. Relaxation impairment was exacerbated when patient myofibrils were incompletely relaxed to mimic residual diastolic calcium levels. Inhibitory effects of mavacamten were dependent on force activation level and significantly less efficient in patient myofibrils. While the drug accelerated full relaxation of donor myofibrils, the slowing down effect of the mutation was not reversed by the drug in patient myofibrils. At partial relaxation, impairment was further aggravated by mavacamten in patient myofibrils. This study suggests that HCM-associated mutation G716R in β-myosin does not evoke gain-of-function in human left ventricular myofibrils, and impaired relaxation could not be rescued by mavacamten. Our findings suggest that HCM-associated mutations may modulate myofibrillar sensitivity to mavacamten, providing a potential mechanistic explanation for differences in treatment response. Studies such as the present one highlight the importance of mutation-dependent sarcomeric properties in understanding variability in responses to myosin modulators and potentially informing more individualized treatment strategies.

title: Integrative Bioinformatics and Experimental Validation Identifies Macrophage Toll Like Receptor 1 as a Therapeutic Target in Carotid Atherosclerosis
authorString: Zhang M, Xiao J, Hou K, Xu S.
abstractText: Carotid atherosclerosis remains a major contributor to cerebrovascular events, with macrophage-driven inflammation playing a pivotal role in disease progression. This study employed an integrative multi-omics approach combining bulk RNA sequencing and weighted gene correlation network analysis to identify critical differential expression genes in atherogenesis. Machine learning algorithms (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator, random forest and artificial neural network) prioritized Toll Like Receptor 1 as the most significant risk gene. Single-cell sequencing of carotid plaques demonstrated TLR1 was predominantly distributed in macrophages. Experimental validation in mouse bone marrow primary macrophages confirmed that coriander inhibits TLR1-mediated macrophage inflammatory response in carotid plaques. Immune infiltration analysis showed that TLR1 was closely related to neutrophil and macrophage activation. Our findings establish TLR1 as a macrophage-specific diagnostic biomarker and suggest that ingestion of coriander supplementation inhibits the inflammatory amplification circuit in TLR1-mediated advanced atherosclerosis.

title: Macrophage Gα Chaperone Protein Ric-8B Exacerbates Atherosclerosis.
authorString: Hu Z, Fu J, Gu X, Cao Y, Yao M, Li Y, Liang L, Su W, Melgiri ND, Jiang L, Zhang L, Sun Y, Huang R.
abstractText:
Background

Macrophage stimulatory G-protein (Gαs/olf)-cAMP signaling promotes cholesterol accumulation and inflammasome activation in atherosclerosis. How obesity-associated inflammation amplifies this pathway is unknown.

Methods

We studied human and murine macrophages, genetically modified low-density lipoprotein receptor-deficient (Ldlr-/-) bone marrow chimeras, and human carotid plaques using biochemical assays and a macrophage-targeted resistance to inhibitors of cholinesterase 8B (Ric-8B)-Gα interference peptide.

Results

oxLDL (oxidized low-density lipoprotein) activated Gαolf through OR6A2 (olfactory receptor 6A2) and Gαs through downregulation of phosphorylated Gα-interacting vesicle-associated protein (p-GIV [phosphorylated Gα-interacting vesicle-associated protein]); both required Ric-8B.
