title: Lipoprotein(a), Cardiovascular Events, and Aortic Stenosis in Routine Care and Implications for Lipoprotein(a)-Lowering Trials
authorString: Kumar-M P, Venkatakrishnan A, Montorzi M, Gibson CM, Soundararajan V.
abstractText:
Importance: In the Lp(a)HORIZON trial, pelacarsen lowered lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] by 78% at 12 months without reducing major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). The neutral result raises the question of whether the cardiovascular risk associated with elevated Lp(a) in routine-care is sufficiently large to yield detectable clinical benefit in ongoing clinical trials.

Objective:

To quantify the association of Lp(a) with recurrent MACE and aortic valve outcomes in routine care, and to explore the implications of these associations for treatment-benefit scenarios in completed and ongoing Lp(a)-lowering trials. Design, Setting, and Participants: The study used a federated analysis of deidentified electronic health records across participating US academic medical centers. The primary retrospective cohort study analyzed adults aged 18 to 80 years with at least one Lp(a) measurement in routine care and documentation of a prior myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, or symptomatic peripheral artery disease as of January 1, 2017 or later. Patients were followed for up to 5 years after meeting all inclusion criteria. Exposure: Baseline Lp(a), categorized as high (at least 150 nmol/L or 70 mg/dL) or low (less than 75 nmol/L or 30 mg/dL), and assessed continuously, including analyses stratified by baseline low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) level. Main Outcomes and Measures: Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, or urgent coronary revascularization, and aortic stenosis or valve replacement, with hazard ratios (HRs) derived from adjusted Cox models.

Results:

Among 13,894 eligible patients, 13,865 contributed follow-up to outcome analyses. MACE occurred in 412 of 3,138 patients with high and 972 of 8,200 with low Lp(a) (5-year cumulative incidence, 20.1% vs 18.3%). The adjusted HR was 1.11 (95% CI, 0.98–1.25) after adjustment for age, sex, race, ethnicity, calendar year of entry, prior care, diagnosis frequency, and type and timing of the qualifying event. There was no consistent evidence of effect modification by LDL-C. In contrast, high Lp(a) was associated with aortic stenosis or valve replacement (HR, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.11–2.36). Under the assumption that pharmacological Lp(a) lowering modifies the risk represented by the observational association, a model-based analysis yielded an illustrative HR of 0.95 (95% CI, 0.89–1.02) for the magnitude of Lp(a) reduction achieved in Lp(a)HORIZON. This estimate was compatible with the reported trial HR of 1.02 and represented a smaller benefit than the trial was powered to detect. Using trial-aligned routine-care cohorts, we then projected the treatment effects for ongoing phase 3 trials of olpasiran and lepodisiran, two Lp(a) lowering agents, based on the approximately 95% reduction in Lp(a) reported in their corresponding phase 2 trials. Under three different assumptions about the timing of clinical benefit, the modeled treatment HRs ranged from 0.94 to 0.98 for OCEAN(a)-Outcomes and 0.89 to 0.97 for ACCLAIM-Lp(a). Conclusions and Relevance: In this multicenter routine-care cohort, elevated Lp(a) showed a modest and statistically insignificant association with recurrent MACE, in contrast to a stronger association with aortic stenosis or valve replacement. Modeled projections based on the observed associations suggested that ongoing trials may not be powered to detect the estimated cardiovascular benefits of Lp(a) reduction. However, these projections do not establish the treatment effects of olpasiran or lepodisiran. The findings highlight the importance of trial population, treatment duration, and clinical endpoint selection, while supporting prospective evaluation of Lp(a)-lowering therapies for aortic valve disease.

title: Cost-effectiveness of a modular intervention to support self-management in cardiovascular prevention: a health economic evaluation of the DECADE cluster-randomized trial.
authorString: Kaier K, Schmoor C, Börger M, Kamp M, Hardt H, Rakebrandt A, Kloppe T, Gräfe W, Kutter S, Riemenschneider H, Maun A, Tinsel I.

journal.title: Cost effectiveness and resource allocation : C/E

abstractText:
Background

To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of two modular components of the DECADE intervention, structured patient-centered follow-up consultations ('Consultations') and patient materials for tailored use ('Materials'), for cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevention in German primary care.

Methods

The health economic evaluation was conducted alongside a 2 × 2 factorial cluster-randomized trial in German general practices. Patients aged 30-75 years with at least one lifestyle-related CVD risk factor were included. The cost-effectiveness of 'Consultations' was assessed by comparing groups that received structured follow-up consultations with those that did not. The cost-effectiveness of 'Materials' was assessed by comparing groups that received patient materials with those that did not. Incremental costs were combined with effects on the patient-reported Patient Activation Measure (PAM13) and the calculated 10-year cardiovascular risk (CVR) score. Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratios (ICERs) were calculated, and statistical uncertainty was assessed using non-parametric bootstrapping and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves.

Results

The 'Consultations' intervention showed a slight, significant improvement in the PAM13 score at 6 months of 1.14 points (95% CI 0.09 to 2.19, p = 0.033). The corresponding ICER was €89.48 (95% CI €46.42 to €1,105.30) per one-point PAM13 improvement. The 'Consultations' intervention did not affect the CVR score (p = 0.72). The 'Materials' intervention was associated with a noninformative result regarding the PAM13 score (p = 0.57), but was associated with a difference of - 1.63% points in the 10-year cardiovascular risk score relative to no materials, which was not statistically significant (95% CI - 3.28 to 0.02, p = 0.053). This difference reflects a stable risk score in the arms using materials (IG1 + 0.09, IG3 - 0.17) against a rising score in the arms without them (control group + 1.16, IG2 + 2.01) rather than an absolute reduction in risk. Based on an incremental cost of €15.03, the resulting ratio was €9.23 per percentage point of 10-year cardiovascular risk avoided (not statistically significant).

Conclusions

Structured, patient-centered follow-up consultations slightly increased patient activation at moderate additional cost; as no willingness-to-pay threshold exists for this outcome, cost-effectiveness cannot be established. The low-cost patient materials did not improve patient activation; the calculated 10-year cardiovascular risk remained stable in the arms using them while it rose in the arms without them, but this difference is statistically uncertain. The modular design allows flexible implementation, and further evaluation with long-term and preference-based outcomes is needed.

title: Clinical evaluation of a novel artificial intelligence-based image processing algorithm for two-dimensional angiography.
authorString: Madoff DC, Aguilar HT, Angtuaco MJ, Asnes JD, Barr JD, Frei DF, George JC, Hohenwalter EJ, Kaestner T, Lacey DL, Meraj P, Obuchowski N, Puma JA, Quinn BP, Sahlein DH, Secemsky EA, Setser RM, Tashenov S.
abstractText:
Background

To evaluate the clinical performance of a novel artificial intelligence (AI)-based image processing algorithm for two-dimensional angiographic imaging compared with its predecessor across multiple imaging modes, anatomic regions, and endovascular specialties.

Materials and methods

This retrospective, comparative, randomized, paired, and blinded multicenter reader study included anonymized images acquired during clinically indicated endovascular interventions at 11 institutions in the United States and Europe. A total of 553 image series from 182 patients representing 51 procedure types across interventional radiology, neurointervention, cardiology, and pediatric cardiology were processed using both the AI-based and predecessor image processing algorithms. Thirteen board-certified physicians independently evaluated paired images using five-point Likert scales for overall image quality, contrast of clinically relevant details, noise reduction, and confidence in assessing device and vessel details. The primary endpoint was non-inferiority of overall image quality. Secondary endpoints evaluated superiority across image quality metrics using a predefined hierarchical testing strategy.

Results

The AI-based image processing algorithm demonstrated non-inferior overall image quality in 98.9% of all evaluations (95% confidence interval [CI], 98%-100%), meeting the primary endpoint across all imaging modes, anatomic regions, and predefined subgroups. Superiority of the AI-based algorithm was demonstrated for overall image quality, contrast of clinically relevant details, noise reduction, and confidence in assessing device and vessel details across fluoroscopy, roadmap, overlay reference, and native acquisition imaging. Overall image quality superiority was not demonstrated for digital subtraction angiography, likely reflecting the intrinsically higher signal-to-noise characteristics of these acquisitions. Inter-reader agreement analysis demonstrated identical ratings in 49.3% of evaluations, with 94.7% of paired ratings differing by no more than one Likert category.

Conclusions

In this multicenter blinded reader study, AI-based image processing demonstrated non-inferior overall image quality compared with its predecessor across all evaluated imaging modes and patient subgroups, with superior performance for multiple image quality metrics in fluoroscopy, roadmap, overlay reference, and native acquisition imaging. These findings support the clinical utility of AI-based image processing for endovascular imaging and provide a foundation for future studies evaluating its impact on radiation dose and procedural outcomes.

title: Gitelman syndrome complicated by pregnancy: clinical management and maternal-fetal outcomes - a systematic review.
authorString: Wang Q, Zhang H, Zhao W, Zhang Y, Cai A, Han J, Zhang J.
abstractText:
Background

Gitelman syndrome (GS), an autosomal recessive tubulopathy caused by SLC12A3 mutations, presents with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypocalciuria and hypomagnesemia. Pregnancy can exacerbate these imbalances, increasing maternal-fetal risks, yet standardized management remains lacking. This review summarizes complications, management strategies, and outcomes to guide evidence-based care.

Methods

Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and CNKI were searched from inception to December 31, 2025, using 'Gitelman Syndrome' AND ('pregnancy' OR 'gestation'). Two reviewers independently performed literature screening, data extraction, and quality assessment. Core data were analyzed descriptively, categorical variables as frequencies (%), continuous as mean ± SD or median (range).

Results

Fifty-six studies (96 pregnancies, 81 women) from 19 countries were included. Among pregnancies with available outcome data, reported maternal complications included gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) (11.5%), oligohydramnios (9.4%), and preeclampsia/hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets (HELLP) syndrome (3.1%); fetal/neonatal complications included preterm birth (16.7%), growth restriction (5.2%), and death (4.2%). Preconception diagnosis showed lower GDM (6.3% vs 18.4%) and fetal/neonatal death (0% vs 8.2%); these comparisons were descriptive and exploratory only. Oral potassium and magnesium were the main treatments. Potassium-sparing diuretics were used in 16 pregnancies (18 exposures); no malformations were reported, but safety is unestablished. Vaginal delivery occurred in 51.2% and Cesarean in 48.8%.

Conclusions

Preconception counseling and multidisciplinary care with close electrolyte monitoring and individualized supplementation may benefit GS-complicated pregnancies, but evidence is limited by case-report data, publication bias, and heterogeneity. Larger prospective studies with standardized outcome reporting are needed to clarify risk factors and guide clinical management.

title: Copper dyshomeostasis and cuproptosis in representative vascular and neurovascular diseases: Molecular mechanisms, disease-specific evidence, and unresolved questions: A scoping review.
authorString: Yang R, Ma J, Ma T, Zhang X, Zhang J, Shi R, Zhou Z, Wu Q, Zhao X, Wang L, Chen Y.

journal.title: Journal of trace elements in medicine and biology : organ of the Society for Minerals and Trace Elements (GMS)

abstractText: Copper dyshomeostasis often coexists with mitochondrial dysfunction, redox imbalance, inflammation and disrupted proteostasis, but none of these changes establishes mechanistically defined cuproptosis. This scoping review, reported according to PRISMA-ScR, applies an author-defined, four-category evidence framework (copper dyshomeostasis, general copper-related injury, cuproptosis-compatible findings, mechanistically defined cuproptosis) to cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI), vascular cognitive impairment (VCI)/vascular dementia (VaD), atherosclerosis and hypertension-related vascular remodeling. For each context, it charts how far the evidence extends along the cuproptosis-defining mechanistic chain and appraises methodological quality separately. In CIRI, copper was quantified in bulk tissue, and readouts came from neurons, neuron-like lines or unsorted brain. In VCI/VaD, the most mechanistic study relied on ionophore-delivered copper in umbilical venous rather than cerebral endothelium, and the only endogenous-hypoperfusion study with a chelator arm had no lipoylation-specific readout. In atherosclerosis, extracellular copper-mediated lipoprotein oxidation must be distinguished from intracellular cuproptosis. The only study to state a non-reducing, non-boiled protocol for higher-order DLAT species, however, measured copper as bulk aortic content. The most complete hypertension study documented the lipoylation lesion, with an independent chelator comparator and labile Cu(I) imaging, but measured no cell death. Across all four contexts, no study demonstrated compartment-resolved copper in a dying cell population or attributed death to a defined lineage, and none reached mechanistically defined cuproptosis. The evidence is disease-specific, with different gaps in each context, and does not support a unified etiology. Closing these gaps requires compartment-resolved copper, validated lipoylation and aggregation assays, and death readouts in the same defined cells.

title: Postoperative White Blood Cell Changes in Cardiac Surgery: A Retrospective Cohort Study From Southern Iran.
authorString: Ghazinour M, Bashiri A, Eilami O, Setoodeh M, Hashemi Ardekani M, Dadvar A, Zibaeenezhad MJ, Shojaiefar P, Sayadi M.
abstractText:
Background

Cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) triggers a systemic inflammatory response, typically reflected by a rise in white blood cell (WBC) count. However, it remains unclear whether the magnitude of this rise-especially when adjusted for baseline values-adds prognostic value for postoperative complications and length of stay.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 143 adult patients who underwent on-pump cardiac surgery at a single center (Shahid Faghihi Hospital) in Shiraz, Iran, over six months. WBC was measured preoperatively and up to 13 times after surgery. We used t-tests, linear mixed models, Pearson correlation, and Firth penalized logistic regression to assess the association between WBC parameters (peak and delta from baseline) and postoperative complications, length of stay, and mortality. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis of delta WBC determined an exploratory cutoff for predicting any complication.

Results

The WBC count peaked on postoperative Day 2 (POD 2). The overall trajectory over time differed significantly between isolated valve and isolated CABG patients (p = 0.047), although single-timepoint comparisons did not reach significance (all p > 0.05). Patients with any complication had a significantly higher mean peak WBC (20.52 ± 7.32 vs. 17.41 ± 5.09 × 103/μL, p < 0.001). The highest peaks were observed in patients with bleeding (p = 0.002), shock (p = 0.048), and in-hospital mortality (p < 0.001). Peak WBC showed a modest correlation with ICU stay (r = 0.175, p < 0.05) and a moderate correlation with hospital stay (r = 0.42, p < 0.001). In a Firth penalized multivariable analysis adjusting for baseline WBC and other confounders, each 1 × 103/μL1 × 103/μL increase in delta WBC was associated with a 9.4% higher odds of any complication (OR = 1.094, 95% CI: 1.020-1.181, p = 0.011). Baseline WBC was not an independent predictor (OR = 1.105, 95% CI: 0.980-1.249, p = 0.102). The exploratory ROC-derived cutoff for delta WBC was 13.4 × 103/μL13.4 × 103/μL (sensitivity 72%, specificity 68%; AUC = 0.74).

Conclusion

In this retrospective cohort, greater postoperative increases in WBC (delta WBC) were associated with a higher frequency of postoperative complications. Serial WBC measurements may provide complementary information for postoperative clinical assessment; however, the observed threshold is exploratory and requires prospective external validation before clinical application.

title: High early burden of post-stroke spasticity and persistent treatment gaps in structured follow-up care.
authorString: Stuckart I, Schoene D, Altarsha E, Pfaff N, Helbig U, Winzer S, Frost L, Barlinn J, Siepmann T, Huttner HB, Barlinn K.
abstractText:
Background

Post-stroke spasticity (PSS) is a frequent and disabling complication after stroke. Real-world data on the implementation of guideline-recommended antispastic treatment within structured follow-up programs are limited.

Methods

In this prospective cohort study, patients with persistent motor deficits after stroke were followed within a structured post-stroke care program. Spasticity was assessed using the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) at predefined follow-up intervals (3 and 12 months after stroke onset). Clinically relevant spasticity was defined as MAS ≥ 2 in at least one joint. Antispastic treatments, including botulinum toxin type A (BoNT-A), were recorded. The implementation gap for BoNT-A was defined as the proportion of patients with a treatment recommendation who had not initiated therapy.

Results

Using a cumulative 12-month MAS-based definition among patients with persistent paresis and available follow-up assessments, clinically relevant spasticity was observed in 40/55 patients (72.7%, 95% CI 59-83.9), while 51/55 patients (92.7%, 95% CI 82.4-97.9) showed any increase in muscle tone (MAS > 0). Clinically relevant spasticity was present in 34/53 patients at 3 months (64.2%, 95% CI 49.8-76.9) and in 26/46 patients at 12 months (56.5%, 95% CI 41.1-71.1). Among patients with clinically relevant spasticity, BoNT-A treatment was recommended in 11.8% at 3 months and 26.9% at 12 months, while no patient with a documented recommendation had initiated therapy.

Conclusions

PSS occurs early and affects a substantial proportion of patients with persistent motor deficits after stroke. Despite structured follow-up and systematic screening, implementation of guideline-recommended BoNT-A therapy remained absent in patients with documented treatment recommendations, indicating substantial barriers to evidence-based outpatient spasticity care.

title: Blunt anatomical cardiac injury (BACI) - lessons from a single trauma center cohort.
authorString: Spencer Netto F, Afifi I, ElMenyar A, Alahmad M, Khan N, Kloub A, Abdelrahman H, AlHassani A, AlMadani A, Peralta R, Rizoli S, AlThani H.

journal.title: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society

abstractText:
Introduction

Patients with anatomical damage to the heart after blunt trauma are rarely seen in hospital settings due to their elevated prehospital mortality. The aim of this study is to review our center experience with this entity.

Methods

After institutional research board approval, a local Trauma Databank search (Qatar National Trauma Registry) was performed from 2016 to 2025. Cases presented with blunt trauma and anatomical changes to pericardium or heart, detected in imaging or surgery, in patients above 13 years old were diagnosed as blunt anatomical cardiac injury - BACI and included.

Results

Amongst 17542 blunt trauma cases admitted to our Trauma Center during the study period, 15 patients (0.09% incidence) met the inclusion/exclusion criteria. All patients were males, with average age of 43 years (ranges 26-75), with ISS of 32 (ranges 10-75). The most common mechanism of injury was pedestrian struck (5cases -33%). Hypotension at trauma room assessment was common (8 cases - 53% of patients) and 8 patients (53%) required surgery. FAST, echocardiogram and computed tomography were used as diagnostic tools. The patients presented in 4 anatomical patterns: (a) intracardiac/valve damage; (b) pericardial effusion; (c) pericardial laceration and (d) cardiac rupture. Three patients (20%) died, all during emergent surgery and sustaining cardiac rupture.

Conclusion

BACI is uncommonly seen at Emergency Departments and carries elevated early mortality in cases with cardiac rupture, requiring high index of suspicion for diagnosis. Different clinical presentations of BACI were observed and described in this series. Further studies with larger number of patients are needed to further clarify possible differences in severity, surgical requirement and mortality according to the BACI structural presentation.

title: Bioactive constituents from <i>Iris domestica</i> attenuate OGD/R-induced PC12 cell injury by suppressing oxidative stress and mitochondrial apoptosis.
authorString: Cui L, Liu Y, Sun J, Hu Z, Jin L, Diao S, Jin M, Zong T, Zhou W, Li G.
abstractText:
Context

Ischemic stroke (IS) causes neuronal injury involving oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptosis. Iris domestica (L.) Goldblatt & Mabb (Iridaceae), known as Shegan in traditional Chinese medicine, has potential neuroprotective properties; however, its structurally defined active constituents remain insufficiently characterized.

Objective

This study aimed to isolate secondary metabolites from I. domestica and evaluate their protective effects and potential mechanisms in an OGD/R-induced PC12 cell model.

Materials and methods

Secondary metabolites were isolated from I. domestica by chromatographic techniques and identified by 1D/2D NMR, high-resolution electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (HR-ESI-MS), and optical rotation. Neuroprotective activity was evaluated in oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R)-injured PC12 cells. Intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), mitochondrial membrane potential, and apoptosis-related proteins were further assessed, and network pharmacology and molecular docking were performed.

Results

Four previously undescribed compounds, irisdomeones A-C (1-3) and irisdomeoside F (4), with 21 known compounds (5-25), were isolated. Eleven compounds showed protective effects at 10 μM. Irisdomeone A (1) and belamchinoside D (24) exhibited the strongest activity and were further evaluated at 5 and 10 μM. Both reduced intracellular ROS accumulation, restored mitochondrial membrane potential, increased the Bcl-2/Bax ratio, and decreased cleaved caspase-3 expression. Network pharmacology and molecular docking suggested involvement of HIF-1 signaling and mitochondrial apoptosis-related targets.

Conclusions

Irisdomeone A and belamchinoside D exhibited protective effects against OGD/R-induced PC12 cell injury, associated with reduced oxidative stress, attenuation of mitochondrial dysfunction, and inhibition of apoptosis. These findings identify compounds 1 and 24 as promising cytoprotective constituents in this in vitro model.

title: Preoperative Mortality Risk Prediction and Equity Using Preoperative Score to Predict Postoperative Mortality in a Diverse US Surgical Population: Retrospective Cohort Study.
authorString: Hall J, Warzecha H, Penhallurick C, Bellala V, Asher S.
abstractText:
Background

The Preoperative Score to Predict Postoperative Mortality (POSPOM), a point-based score using only preoperative variables, was developed and validated to predict in-hospital postoperative mortality in European surgical cohorts. Other widely used clinical risk tools perform differently across racial and socioeconomic groups. Although postoperative mortality has been studied in diverse US surgical populations, POSPOM performance across racial and ethnic subgroups remains insufficiently characterized.

Objective

This study aimed to evaluate POSPOM performance for 30-day postoperative mortality in a diverse US cohort and explore its performance for 1-year mortality among high-risk surgical patients and across racial and ethnic subgroups.

Methods

We performed a retrospective cohort study using the All of Us Research Program. Adults aged 18 to 91 years who underwent 1 of 21 POSPOM-eligible surgical procedures were included, and only each participant's most recent eligible procedure was analyzed. POSPOM scores were calculated from age, procedure type, and 15 weighted comorbidities. The primary outcome was 30-day postoperative mortality, as incomplete discharge data precluded reliable assessment of in-hospital mortality; 1-year mortality was examined as an exploratory secondary outcome. Logistic regression estimated odds ratios (ORs) per 1-point increase in the POSPOM score, and discrimination was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). A high-risk subgroup (procedure points ≥14) was analyzed separately, and outcomes across racial and ethnic subgroups were explored descriptively. Given the small subgroup sizes and few events, subgroup analyses were interpreted cautiously.

Results

Among 17,262 patients, 12 (0.1%) died within 30 days and 45 (0.3%) within 1 year. For 30-day mortality, POSPOM yielded an AUC of 0.764, with higher odds of death per point (OR 1.112, 95% CI 1.040-1.190; P=.002). Discrimination was lower for 1-year mortality (AUC 0.638; OR 1.054, 95% CI 1.017-1.092; P=.004). In the high-risk subgroup (n=536; 30-day mortality 1.1%, 1-year mortality 2.1%), the 30-day AUC fell to 0.583, with no significant association (OR 0.942, 95% CI 0.812-1.092; P=.43). For 1-year mortality, the AUC was 0.692, with an inverse association (OR 0.882, 95% CI 0.781-0.998; P=.046). Descriptively, high-risk Black patients had higher 30-day mortality than White patients (2/61, 3.3% vs 4/348, 1.1%); no deaths were recorded among Asian, other-race, or Hispanic high-risk patients.

Conclusions

POSPOM demonstrated an AUC of 0.764 for 30-day mortality overall but provided limited risk stratification among high-risk surgical patients. Higher observed mortality among high-risk Black patients suggests the score may not fully capture baseline risk across racial groups, possibly reflecting structural and social factors outside its scope. As the 1-year and subgroup analyses were exploratory with few events, larger, adequately powered US studies are needed to evaluate POSPOM at its intended in-hospital end point, assess calibration across diverse populations, and inform recalibration before broader clinical use.

title: Retinal Immunometabolism in Systemic Disease: Molecular Mechanisms, Emerging Biomarkers, and Translational Perspectives
authorString: Por CWS, Thomas GN, Koh VTC, Srinivasan DK.
abstractText: The retina is a specialised neurovascular–immune–metabolic tissue whose high metabolic demands make it vulnerable to systemic metabolic and inflammatory disturbances. Retinal immunometabolism provides a framework for understanding how mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming, endothelial injury, and chronic inflammation contribute to retinal pathology. This narrative review critically examines the molecular mechanisms linking retinal immunometabolic dysfunction with cardiometabolic diseases, including diabetes, obesity, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), hypertension, atherosclerosis, and heart failure, alongside ageing and neurodegeneration. We distinguish established retinal manifestations from emerging associations and experimental mechanisms, highlighting challenges in causality and disease specificity. Advances in retinal imaging, artificial intelligence (AI), oculomics, single-cell transcriptomics, spatial metabolomics, and multi-omics integration offer opportunities for biomarker discovery and disease monitoring. Emerging immunometabolic, senotherapeutic, mitochondrial-targeted, and regenerative interventions also present therapeutic potential, although clinical evidence remains limited. Further mechanistic validation, methodological standardisation, and prospective longitudinal studies are essential to establish clinical utility. Integrating molecular insights with retinal imaging may position the retina as a complementary platform for systemic disease assessment and precision medicine.

title: Speckle-tracking echocardiographic strain parameters in cardiac magnetic resonance-confirmed myocarditis: associations with myocardial edema and subsequent left ventricular functional improvement.
authorString: Cham SLS, Cuaresma JRM, Ong RC, Narvasa JR.
abstractText:
Background

Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) is the noninvasive reference standard for diagnosing myocarditis and assessing myocardial inflammation, but its routine use may be limited by availability, cost, and patient-related factors. Speckle-tracking echocardiography may provide an accessible approach to evaluating myocardial dysfunction and outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the associations of global longitudinal strain (GLS), peak atrial longitudinal strain (PALS), and time-to-peak longitudinal strain (TPLS) with CMR-defined myocardial edema, biomarkers, and subsequent left ventricular (LV) functional improvement in patients with CMR-confirmed myocarditis.

Methods

This single-center ambispective observational cohort study included 40 adults with CMR-confirmed myocarditis and baseline echocardiography suitable for strain analysis. Cross-sectional associations between baseline strain parameters, CMR findings, and biomarkers were assessed, with longitudinal evaluation of subsequent LV functional improvement among patients with follow-up echocardiography. Receiver operating characteristic and regression analyses were exploratory; data-derived thresholds were not internally or externally validated.

Results

Among 40 patients with CMR-confirmed myocarditis, TPLS ≥ 447 ms showed 52.4% sensitivity and 86.7% specificity for CMR-defined myocardial edema (area under the curve [AUC], 0.58). The combined GLS-TPLS model showed 81.0% sensitivity, 53.3% specificity, 69.4% accuracy, and an AUC of 0.64. GLS and PALS correlated inversely with peak N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP; r = -0.438, P = 0.006 and r = -0.396, P = 0.017, respectively). Thirty-five patients had evaluable longitudinal LV ejection fraction (LVEF) measurements; 11 (31.4%) met criteria for LV functional improvement. Baseline GLS was associated with subsequent LV functional improvement, although interpretation is limited by its strong relationship with baseline LVEF.

Conclusions

In CMR-confirmed myocarditis, strain parameters provided complementary functional information across imaging, biomarker, and longitudinal domains. TPLS was associated with CMR-defined myocardial edema, while GLS and PALS were associated with NT-proBNP. Baseline GLS was associated with subsequent LV functional improvement. These exploratory findings support prospective evaluation of strain alongside CMR and development of multimodal risk stratification models in larger, controlled cohorts.

title: Dynein-dependent positioning of multiple organelles regulates adaptive gene expression during oxidative stress.
authorString: Albacete-Albacete L, Jin L, Sato N, Shahbazi MN, Bullock SL.
abstractText: Cells respond to environmental insults through well-characterized changes to their transcriptome and proteome. The contribution that reorganization of intracellular architecture makes to the adaptive stress response is much less understood. Here, we reveal a conserved spatial response to oxidative stress in which the microtubule motor dynein enhances perinuclear clustering of multiple membrane-bound organelles. These events are triggered by reactive oxygen species and protein kinase C and occur without increased association of dynein with its activator dynactin, pointing to a noncanonical mechanism for stimulating retrograde transport. Using a chemically inducible system for dispersing individual organelles, we show that perinuclear localization of multiple compartments potentiates oxidative stress-induced gene expression, with distinct genes depending on inputs from either combinations of organelles or individual compartments. Together, these findings implicate positioning of multiple membrane-bound compartments in gene expression regulation and identify coordinated organelle trafficking by dynein as an additional regulatory layer in the cellular stress response.

title: A Fatigue–Exposure–Decompensation Model of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm: Elastin Fatigue, Collagen Compensation and Immune Amplification
authorString: Hu C.
abstractText:
Background:

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is managed by a diameter threshold, yet 61% of ruptures in contemporary cohorts occur below 55 mm and diameter-matched cohorts of ruptured and unruptured aneurysms show no difference in diameter. Existing computational approaches quantify the wall stress at a given instant but not the cumulative mechanical history of the wall. We tested whether AAA can be reproduced as a fatigue-failure process of elastin, with a discrete transition — damage exposure — separating a purely mechanical phase from a biologically amplified one. The resulting framework rests on two load-bearing components with opposed duties, a discrete exposure transition, and a five-stage progression in which compensation itself fails.Methods. We constructed a two-layer model (the Damage-Exposure Model, DEM) comprising four global state variables — elastin, collagen, junction protein and inflammation — and a 720-point circumferential spatial layer carrying wall thickness, local strength and thrombus coverage. Elastin-specific local stress was compared with elastin-specific local strength. Parameters were assigned to three tiers: 23 measured in the literature, 5 derived from literature values, and 15 calibrated to reproduce specified targets. The model was run for 76 patients whose transcriptomic module scores were mapped to individual mechanical parameters, and against seven external comparisons, three pre-specified testable inferences and a 500-run Monte Carlo analysis.Results. The model reproduces a five-stage progression at ages 20.0, 56.7, 58.7, 66.6 and 73.5 years, a rupture diameter of 55.76 mm, and a two-phase expansion pattern (36.7 years before the transition, 16.8 years after). In the 76-patient cohort, 61% of simulated ruptures occurred below 55 mm and the median rupture age was 71.5 years, against 74.0 years in a 3,642-patient national registry. Of seven external comparisons, one is an independent test, four are calibration-consistency checks and two are not valid comparisons. Of the three testable inferences, one is true by construction rather than empirically, one is contradicted by the data, and one has no discriminating power. Only 4.2% of 500 Monte Carlo parameter draws satisfied five or more of the seven comparisons.Conclusions. A fatigue-based model of elastin depletion with a discrete exposure transition reproduces the timing, the rupture diameter and the sub-threshold rupture fraction of AAA, and explains why diameter alone discriminates poorly between ruptured and unruptured aneurysms. The model is not validated: its time scale is dominated by a single calibrated parameter and fifteen parameters are not identifiable. It should be read as a quantitatively specified hypothesis with an explicit falsification path, not as a clinical prediction tool.

title: Teaching the bigger picture - student perceptions on interprofessional teaching on the patient journey in vascular surgery.
authorString: Morath B, Chiriac U, Hoppe-Tichy T, Schoening T, Böckler D, Bischoff MS, Barb A, Schulz M, Meisenbacher K.
abstractText:
Background

Ensuring drug safety is critical in comorbid vascular surgery patients and can be supported by interprofessional collaboration with clinical pharmacists. Thus, this project aimed to create an interprofessional seminar for medical students using real-life vascular surgery cases, highlighting medication risks and the value of interprofessional collaboration during the cross-sectoral medication process.

Methods

A six-step model (Kern cycle) was used to develop a seminar integrating vascular surgery cases with the medication process from admission to discharge. The implementation was guided by a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT)-analysis to identify challenges and opportunities. After piloting the seminar, self-reported evaluation data were used to describe students' perception of acceptance, perceived learning, and practical relevance. A 14-item questionnaire and qualitative content analysis of free-text responses were used to analyze students' perceptions on the course.

Results

Learning objectives included identifying medication risks, applying literature to solve drug-related problems, and developing interprofessional strategies to improve medication safety. The seminar, led by vascular surgeons and clinical pharmacists, employed various didactic methods (e.g., inverted classroom, small group learning). The seminar was evaluated by 142 of 240 students involved in the pilot phase (response rate 59.1%). Respondents rated the practical relevance, interprofessional approach, and interactive learning methods positively and reported perceived learning progress. The seminar is now part of the vascular surgery curriculum.

Conclusions

The seminar provides a practical framework for integrating cross-sectoral medication management into medical education. By linking clinical practice with collaborative patient care, it offers an opportunity for enhancing students' understanding of collaborative patient care and drug safety in the surgical patient journey. The seminar was successfully integrated into the vascular surgery curriculum and was positively perceived by participating students. This model may be adaptable to other medical specialties to promote interprofessional teaching in the medical curriculum.

title: Di/tripeptides in cancer: from mechanisms to therapeutics.
authorString: Pan H, Huang T, Li J, Xiang Y, Wu M, Du A, Qin K, Zhou X, Zhou Z, Ren S, Ding B, Yuan K.
abstractText: Research on tumor metabolic reprogramming has long centered on glucose, lipids and free amino acids. By contrast, di/tripeptides, which lie at the interface between protein breakdown products and functional metabolic signals, have only recently begun to be recognized as a distinct molecular tier in cancer biology. Compared with longer peptides, di/tripeptides display greater metabolic mobility and a clearer dependence on dedicated transport systems. Here we systematically review the sources, transport, metabolic use, biological functions and clinical translational potential of di/tripeptides in cancer. Current evidence indicates that di/tripeptides arise from endogenous protein degradation, dietary digestion and microbial metabolism. Under nutrient limitation, tumor cells can recover amino acids through carnosine dipeptidase 2 (CNDP2)-mediated extracellular cleavage of dipeptides or uptake of intact di/tripeptides followed by intracellular hydrolysis. Beyond their role as nutrient substrates, selected di/tripeptides directly influence tumor cell proliferation, invasion, metastasis and drug resistance, and shape the tumor microenvironment by modulating acid base balance, redox homeostasis, angiogenesis and immune cell function. At the clinical translational level, di/tripeptides have emerged as candidate metabolomic and peptidomic biomarkers, transporter targeted imaging probes, functionally modified therapeutic agents and engineered delivery modules. Di/tripeptides should be viewed as molecular nodes that connect tumor nutrient adaptation, signaling control, microenvironmental remodeling and clinical translation, with significance extending beyond their role as transient intermediates in protein metabolism.

title: Characterization of meningococcal disease outbreaks in the United States, 2014-2019.
authorString: Cooper GA, Brown NE, Rubis AB, Chang HY, Cubenas C, Marasini D, Retchless A, Sharma S, Meyer S, McNamara LA.
abstractText:
Background

Meningococcal disease, caused by the bacterium Neisseria meningitidis, is a serious bacterial infection that can be fatal or leave survivors with permanent sequelae. Despite decades of declining incidence in the United States (U.S.), meningococcal disease outbreaks are still of public health concern.

Methods

Meningococcal disease cases reported through the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System along with additional data provided by jurisdiction health departments were used to identify outbreak-associated cases and public health response measures during 2014-2019. Outbreaks were defined as 2-3 cases within an organization during a 3-month period, an incidence of meningococcal disease above expected in a community during a 3-month period, or ≥2 cases that occurred in the same family or household during a 24-month period.

Results

Twenty-nine meningococcal disease outbreaks were reported in the U.S. during 2014-2019 (18 organization, 8 community, 3 household). Outbreak-associated cases (n = 130), accounted for 5.8% of all meningococcal disease cases (n = 2,228) reported during 2014-2019 and were predominantly serogroups B and C. Community outbreaks had longer median durations (203 days) compared to family/household and organization outbreaks (136 days and 9 days, respectively). Of the 7 family/household outbreak-associated cases, only 2 occurred within 14 days of each other. Based on available information for 23 outbreaks, a response measure was implemented in 21 outbreaks: mass vaccination campaign alone (14), expanded chemoprophylaxis alone (2), and both mass vaccination campaign and expanded chemoprophylaxis (5).

Conclusion

We identified outbreaks of meningococcal disease in a variety of settings and populations; however, this is the first time family/household outbreaks have been systematically characterized in the U.S. Our findings suggest that household contacts of meningococcal disease patients may be at increased disease risk beyond direct secondary transmission. Additional evaluations will be helpful to better assess the potential benefit of vaccination for family members of cases in household settings.

title: A Gαq/11-IP<sub>3</sub>R1-ANO1 pacemaking axis underlies pressure-induced lymphatic chronotropy.
authorString: Davis MJ, Kim HJ, Li M, Castorena-Gonzalez JA, Schulz ME, Pea G, Pal S, Domeier T, Scallan J, Earley S, Zawieja SD.
abstractText: The frequency of spontaneous lymphatic contractions is exquisitely sensitive to changes in intraluminal pressure, enabling lymph transport to be matched to the filling state of the lymphatic capillary network. The mechanistic basis of this mechanosensitive response was investigated using ex vivo contraction assays of mouse popliteal collecting vessels. Based on electrophysiological and transcriptional similarities between lymphatic muscle cells (LMCs) and arterial smooth muscle, we hypothesized that pressure-dependent chronotropy shares a parallel signaling process with pressure-induced arterial depolarization/constriction. Thus, we probed two potential mechanisms: (1) pressure-induced activation of mechanosensitive cation channels and (2) mechano-activation of GNAQ/GNA11-coupled G-protein receptors (GPCRs) that would generate second messengers to activate those channels. Contraction assays were combined with scRNA-seq analysis of the respective targets and use of transgenic mice. Our findings rule out significant roles for the mechanosensitive channels implicated in arterial myogenic constriction, as well as channels implicated in ionic pacemaking of other tissues. In contrast, smooth-muscle specific knock out or inhibition of ANO1, IP<sub>3</sub>R1, or GNAQ/GNA11 significantly abrogated pressure-induced chronotropy. These results support a scheme whereby mechano-activation of one or more GNAQ/GNA11-coupled GPCRs generates IP<sub>3</sub>, inducing sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca<sup>2+</sup> release through IP<sub>3</sub>R1, which drives depolarization through the activation of ANO1 Cl<sup>-</sup> channels. The major GPCRs expressed in LMCs were identified and ranked by scRNAseq analysis, but individual inhibition or knock out of the top 7 candidates failed to significantly impair pressure-induced chronotropy. Our results implicate one or more GNAQ/GNA11-coupled GPCRs in mediating this mechanosensitive process, but the specific GPCRs remain to be identified.

title: Clinical characteristics and diagnostic challenges of Kawasaki disease in infants younger than 3 months: a 21-year single-center retrospective study from China.
authorString: Geng Y, Sun C, Du J, Liu L, Zhang Q, Hou X.
abstractText: Kawasaki disease (KD) in infants younger than 3 months is uncommon but poses substantial diagnostic challenges because classical clinical manifestations are frequently incomplete during the early phase of illness. Delayed diagnosis increases the risk of coronary artery abnormalities (CAA), yet the clinical characteristics and diagnostic evolution of this age group remain insufficiently understood. We retrospectively reviewed all infants younger than 3 months diagnosed with KD at Peking University First Hospital between January 2005 and January 2026. Clinical characteristics, laboratory findings, echocardiographic features, treatment, and follow-up outcomes were analyzed. Particular attention was paid to the temporal evolution of clinical manifestations and coronary artery abnormalities during the diagnostic process. Fifteen infants were included in the study. Incomplete KD accounted for 86.7% (13/15) of cases. Gastrointestinal manifestations (53.3%), bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) scar reactivation (60.0%), and respiratory symptoms (40.0%) were common and frequently resulted in an initial diagnosis of infection. Coronary artery abnormalities developed in ten patients during the disease course. Three infants had normal initial echocardiographic examinations but subsequently developed coronary artery abnormalities on repeat evaluation between fever days 7 and 10. Fourteen patients responded to initial intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) treatment, whereas one patient was IVIG-resistant. Coronary artery abnormalities and other cardiac echocardiographic involvement resolved in all patients during follow-up.Conclusion: KD in infants younger than 3 months is characterized by an evolving clinical presentation in which classical clinical manifestations and echocardiographically detectable coronary artery abnormalities emerge sequentially rather than simultaneously. Recognition of this evolving diagnostic process may facilitate earlier diagnosis. Persistent clinical suspicion, together with longitudinal clinical reassessment and appropriately timed repeat echocardiography, may improve recognition before clinically significant coronary injury develops.

title: Fetal structural and chromosomal anomalies and cesarean delivery for non-reassuring fetal status: A population-based study in Central New York.
authorString: Rojas-Mendez P, Sampson R, Wojtowycz M, Canavan T.
abstractText:
Background

Prior studies suggest higher cesarean delivery (CD) rates among pregnancies complicated by congenital anomalies; however, the contribution of specific indications, particularly CD coded as non-reassuring fetal status (NRFS), remains understudied.

Objective

To evaluate the association between fetal anomalies and the likelihood of CD coded as NRFS, and to characterize this association across joint categories of small-for-gestational-age (SGA) and preterm birth.

Study design

This retrospective cohort study used data from the New York Statewide Perinatal Data System, including 220,368 deliveries ≥20 weeks' gestation from 2011 to 2023. The primary outcome was CD coded as NRFS as the sole indication. The primary exposure was the presence of ≥1 structural or chromosomal fetal anomaly, analyzed as a composite and by anomaly subgroup. Logistic regression estimated adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and absolute risk differences were calculated to aid clinical interpretation. Joint-category analyses were performed to evaluate the association across combinations of SGA and preterm birth. Bivariate analyses compared baseline characteristics by anomaly status.

Results

Among 220,368 deliveries, 904 (0.4%) were classified as having a composite anomaly. The rate of CD coded as NRFS was higher among pregnancies with a composite anomaly (9.8% vs. 3.7%; relative risk, 2.69), corresponding to an absolute risk difference of 6.2 percentage points. After adjustment, composite anomaly status was associated with higher odds of CD coded as NRFS (aOR, 2.72). The magnitude of association varied by anomaly type, with higher odds observed in omphalocele (aOR, 4.66), chromosomal disorders other than trisomy 21 (T21) (aOR, 4.09), and congenital heart disease (aOR, 2.97). In joint-category analyses, the magnitude of association varied across combinations of composite anomaly status, SGA, and preterm birth.

Conclusion

Selected fetal structural and chromosomal anomalies were associated with higher odds of CD coded as NRFS, after adjustment for intrapartum factors. This association varied by anomaly subtype and across joint categories defined by SGA and preterm birth. These associations may reflect both underlying fetal vulnerability and variation in clinical decision-making rather than physiologic intolerance to labor alone.

title: Peripartum infective endocarditis in complex congenital heart disease: Melody valve infection after caesarean delivery.
authorString: Hopkins TM, Wander G, Tari S, Patel R, Johnson MR.
abstractText: We describe the pregnancy and postpartum course of a 26-year-old nulliparous woman with repaired double outlet right ventricle, ventricular septal defect, and severe pulmonary stenosis who was managed by a multidisciplinary pregnancy heart team. She underwent emergency caesarean delivery at 38 weeks. Her postpartum course was complicated by suspected pulmonary embolism and infective endocarditis of a Melody valve, requiring right ventricle-pulmonary artery conduit replacement. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of postpartum cardiopulmonary symptoms in women with complex congenital heart disease and raises important questions regarding infective endocarditis prophylaxis in women with prosthetic cardiac material.

title: Primary Sjögren's Syndrome Presenting With Complete Atrioventricular Block and Myocardial Injury: A Rare Immune-Mediated Cardiac Case Report.
authorString: Liu Y, Chen X, Zheng H, Liu J, Liu Q.
abstractText: Primary Sjögren's syndrome (pSS) is a systemic autoimmune disorder predominantly involving exocrine glands; cardiac complications represent rare extra-glandular manifestations, and complete atrioventricular block (CAVB) is uncommon. We report a 58-year-old female presenting with acute chest tightness and transient loss of consciousness. Her electrocardiogram showed CAVB with ventricular escape rhythm and elevated cardiac troponin-I. Emergency coronary angiography excluded significant obstructive coronary artery disease. Positive anti-SSA, anti-SSB, anti-Ro52, cardiac-specific autoantibodies, together with minor salivary gland biopsy, confirmed pSS. She received methylprednisolone and hydroxychloroquine for immunomodulation, plus dual-chamber permanent pacemaker implantation for persistent symptomatic conduction defects. Symptoms resolved and cardiac biomarkers normalized in short-term follow-up. This case alerts clinicians to pSS-related immune-mediated cardiac injury as a differential diagnosis for unexplained CAVB after excluding coronary artery disease.

title: Neurodevelopment among children under five years with sickle cell disease in Eastern Uganda: A propensity score analysis.
authorString: Maumbe B, Mukunya D, Nambozo B, Oguttu F, Abeso J, Mutonyi S, Okwir J, Musaba MW, Lunyolo S, Nabudere HK, Ssegawa L, Munube D, Kiguli S, Olupot-Olupot P.
abstractText:
Aim

We compared neurodevelopment among children under-five years with and without sickle cell disease in eastern Uganda.

Methods

We conducted a cross-sectional study between March and September 2025 at the pediatric sickle cell clinic of Mbale Regional Referral Hospital. We included 350 children under five years (117 with sickle cell disease and 233 without sickle cell disease). The primary outcome was neurodevelopment assessed using the Malawi Development Assessment Tool. We performed independent sample t-tests to compare development for age z-scores between children with and without sickle cell disease. We used inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses to calculate the effect of sickle cell disease on neurodevelopment.

Results

The median age of the children was 40.9 months (interquartile range 27.8 to 54.3 months). Children with sickle cell disease had 0.89 lower DAZ scores compared to their peers without sickle cell disease. Among the children with sickle cell disease, those not enrolled on hydroxyurea had 0.4 lower DAZ scores in the social and language domains compared to those on hydroxyurea. The average exposure effect, obtained from the inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses, was -0.87, 95% CI [-1.19, -0.55] and the average exposure effect among the exposed was - 0.62 95% CI [- 1.01, - 0.23].

Conclusion

Children with sickle cell disease had lower developmental scores across all domains (social, gross motor, fine motor and language) compared to community controls. These findings highlight the developmental vulnerability associated with sickle cell disease in early childhood. Efforts towards timely screening and management of developmental delays among children are needed to improve their quality of life and long-term development. This may be through integration of neurodevelopmental screening into routine sickle cell disease care.

title: Pregnancy as an important factor in female autoimmunity.
authorString: Pelczar P, Przywara D, Kowalczyk E, Koziej S, Gil-Kulik P.
abstractText: Autoimmune diseases (ADs) affect 5-10% of the population, with 80-85% of diagnosed patients being women. This pronounced sexual dimorphism is influenced by genetic factors (X chromosome), fluctuations in sex hormones, and unique immunological changes occurring during pregnancy and the postpartum period. These factors contribute to women's distinct susceptibility to autoimmune disorders and may influence their clinical course. This narrative review critically evaluates the immunological, hormonal, and pregnancy-related factors contributing to female autoimmunity with particular emphasis on the bidirectional interactions between pregnancy-induced immunomodulation and maternal autoimmunity. By contrasting four distinct diseases systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), multiple sclerosis (MS), and type 1 diabetes (T1D), representing different immune paradigms (type 1 T helper (Th1) vs. type 2 T helper (Th2), systemic vs. organ-specific), we aim to analyze how mechanisms like placental tolerance and fetal microchimerism specifically shape disease trajectories and obstetric outcomes, contextualized within the evolutionary pregnancy compensation hypothesis. A literature review (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science) was conducted to synthesize clinical and molecular evidence. The mechanisms of placental immune tolerance, the phenomenon of fetal microchimerism, and the evolutionary pregnancy compensation hypothesis were analyzed. Selected autoimmune diseases were used to illustrate disease-specific manifestations of these mechanisms. The literature highlights the complex interplay between genetic, hormonal and immunological factors in female autoimmunity. Estrogens, progesterone, androgens and prolactin exert distinct immunomodulatory effects influencing immune cell activity, cytokine production and immune tolerance. Fetal microchimerism (FMc) may have long-term immunological consequences, potentially contributing to either immune regulation or autoimmune pathology. These mechanisms may help explain the variable effects of pregnancy on autoimmune disease activity and obstetric outcomes, as illustrated by SLE, RA, MS, and T1D. The pregnancy compensation hypothesis offers an additional evolutionary perspective. However, it remains speculative and requires further investigation. Pregnancy induces complex, disease-specific immunomodulatory changes. Instead of one-size-fits-all regimens, caring for pregnant women with autoimmune disease requires a highly personalized and multidisciplinary approach based on risk stratification and monitoring of specific biomarkers. Current evidence suggests an intriguing influence of molecular changes on the course of autoimmunity; however, a full understanding of these mechanisms requires further, targeted research.

authorString: Martins-Martinho J, Bandeira M, Raimundo D, Velho I, Naique S, Sopa I, Dourado E, Pestana J, Novais T, Santos M, Carones A, Inês L, Soares CD, Silva S, Águeda A, Teixeira V, Rodrigues P, Khmelinskii N, Ponte C.

title: Echoes of infection: viral persistence, immune activation, and histopathological changes in long COVID: a systematic review.
authorString: Elmahroky A, Aly Y, Farghaly A, Abdelrasoul H, Suliman H, Badawi M, Tanbedawy OW, Helmy AE, Nabeh OA.
abstractText: Long COVID, or post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC), affects an estimated 10-20% of individuals following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Despite its substantial global burden, the pathophysiological mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This systematic review aimed to synthesize available evidence on viral persistence, immune activation, and histopathological changes across multiple organ systems, drawing from studies of individuals with Long COVID as well as broader post-acute cohorts, autopsy investigations, and case-based reports relevant to Long COVID pathophysiology. Following PRISMA guidelines and holding a PROSPERO registration (CRD420261403869), a systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, EMBASE, and Cochrane CENTRAL. Eligible reports were stratified as (A) symptom-defined Long COVID assessed at or after 12 weeks, (B) post-acute or mixed populations without a consistently confirmed Long COVID definition or timing, (C) autopsy studies, and (D) isolated case/fetal reports. Findings were synthesized narratively by specimen, assay target, and unit of analysis. JBI checklists were used for item-level appraisal, not as certainty-of-evidence ratings. Forty-five reports were included: 16 in stratum A, 23 in stratum B, three autopsy studies, and three isolated case/fetal reports. SARS-CoV-2 genomic RNA, viral proteins, and markers compatible with recent viral activity were reported in selected tissue and blood compartments, but detection varied with population selection, timing, specimen, and assay. No included study established replication competence by recovery of infectious virus. Histopathological abnormalities included inflammatory infiltrates, fibrosis, and vascular injury; however, causal attribution to Long COVID was limited by acute disease severity, biopsy indication, comorbidity, and incomplete comparator data. A single participant total was not reported because of overlapping cohorts, repeated sampling, and outcome-specific denominators. The review supports biological heterogeneity after SARS-CoV-2 infection, including residual viral material, immune dysregulation, vascular injury, and maladaptive tissue repair. Organ-specific prevalence, a hierarchy of tissue tropism, replication-competent reservoirs, and superiority of antiviral or immunomodulatory treatment remain undefined. Standardized Long COVID definitions, representative cohorts, validated assays, appropriate comparators, and longitudinal studies linking biological markers to clinical outcomes are required.

title: Cardiorespiratory Limits Exist in HFpEF Independent of Age and BMI
authorString: LaGalbo S, Gowda M, Hess T, Tipnis P, Raza F, Saleh D.
abstractText:
Background

Heart-failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a clinical syndrome marked by exercise intolerance associated with impairments in cardiac and respiratory performance. HFpEF is associated with age and weight; however, it remains unclear whether cardiorespiratory limitations exist independent of these comorbidities.

Hypothesis

Independent of age and BMI, there are cardiorespiratory limitations inherent to the HFpEF syndrome that have yet to be fully elicited.

Methods

A patient cohort with a clinical diagnosis of HFpEF (HFpEF; N = 38) and counterparts without identifiable cardiopulmonary disease (control; N = 21) underwent phenotyping with echocardiography and cardiopulmonary exercise testing with invasive hemodynamic monitoring.

Results

Study cohorts were similar in age, BMI and height (p=NS for all metrics). Body-surface area (BSA) (2.1 m 2 v 1.9 m 2 , p < 0.05), atrial fibrillation prevalence (50 v 14%, p < 0.05), and average E/e’ (11.5 v 9.5, p < 0.05) were elevated within the HFpEF cohort. Peak VO 2 (14.1 v 19.1 mL/Kg/min, p < 0.001) was also diminished among those with HFpEF. Resting (17.1 v 11.4mmHg, p < 0.001) and exercise wedge pressures (29.3 v 16.7mmHg, p < 0.001) were elevated whereas stroke volume (93.3 v 110.4 mL, p < 0.05) and cardiac output (Direct Fick; 8.0 v 9.8, p < 0.05) during exercise were diminished in HFpEF patients. FVC, FVC%, FEV1 and FEV1% were also significantly diminished in the HFpEF cohort.

Conclusions

Cardiorespiratory limitations exist as a feature of the HFpEF syndrome, independent of age and BMI. BSA remained associated with HFpEF in keeping with adiposity as a feature of pathophysiology.

title: Long-term impact of anorexia nervosa on cardiovascular morbidity in men and women: A longitudinal cohort study: Incidence à long terme de l'anorexie mentale sur la morbidité cardiovasculaire chez les hommes et les femmes : étude de cohorte longitudinale.
authorString: Bahous R, Potter BJ, Israël M, Steiger H, Côté-Corriveau G, Brousseau É, Healy-Profitós J, Auger N.

journal.title: Canadian journal of psychiatry. Revue canadienne de psychiatrie

abstractText: BackgroundAnorexia nervosa is associated with cardiovascular morbidity in women, but the relationship is less studied in men. We assessed the association between anorexia nervosa and the long-term risk of cardiovascular disease in men and women.MethodsWe analyzed a cohort of 7332 patients with anorexia nervosa and 73,215 matched controls from Quebec, Canada. The exposure was anorexia nervosa diagnosed between 1989 and 2023. The outcome was cardiovascular hospitalization for heart failure, conduction disorders, cardiac arrest, and other cardiovascular events up to 34 years later. We derived adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the association of anorexia nervosa with cardiovascular morbidity using Cox regression, with men and women analyzed separately.ResultsAmong 7332 patients with anorexia nervosa, 467 (6.4%) were men. Compared with matched controls, anorexia nervosa was associated with 1.43 times the risk of cardiovascular hospitalization in men (95% CI [1.08-1.90]) and 2.23 times the risk in women (95% CI [2.06-2.42]). Risk of cardiovascular hospitalization was highest within one year of diagnosis for anorexia nervosa among both men and women. Anorexia nervosa was particularly associated with conduction disorders (HR 3.24, 95% CI [2.84-3.69]) and heart failure (HR 1.99, 95% CI [1.54-2.56]) in women, but similar associations did not stand out in men.ConclusionBoth men and women with anorexia nervosa have an increased risk of cardiovascular disease later in life, although women appear to be more affected. Men and women with anorexia nervosa may benefit from closer monitoring to prevent adverse cardiovascular events.

title: Chylous Ascites: A Rare Complication After Living-Donor Liver Transplantation.
authorString: Malik MA, Mehfooz H, Ramzi SHT, Hassan SMS, Israr A, Qasim M, Mubashir L, Shahab SH, Habib F.
abstractText: A 60-year-old man underwent living-donor liver transplantation for cryptogenic cirrhosis. On postoperative day 45, he developed chylous ascites with triglycerides of 1819 mg/dL. Low-fat diet and octreotide were initiated, resulting in improvement after 5 months. Chylous ascites is a rare post-transplant complication responsive to conservative management.

title: Failed-repair proximal tubular epithelial cells in the transition from acute kidney injury to chronic kidney disease: mechanisms, identification, and therapeutic implications.
authorString: Liu X, Zhao X, Bao C, Liu Y, Zhang X, Wang Y.
abstractText: Acute kidney injury (AKI) increases the risk of chronic kidney disease, even after apparent recovery of kidney function. Incomplete proximal tubular repair provides a cellular basis for this discrepancy. Failed-repair proximal tubular epithelial cells (FR-PTECs) retain impaired differentiation and inflammatory or profibrotic activity during recovery, forming a persistent epithelial subset within the broader spectrum of maladaptive repair. This review examines their conceptual definition, mechanisms, identification, and therapeutic implications. Single-cell, multiomic, and spatial studies characterize divergent repair trajectories and interactions between abnormal epithelia, immune cells, and stromal cells. Metabolic dysfunction, chromatin remodeling, cell-cycle arrest, and senescence can sustain these responses, but are not universal criteria for identifying FR-PTECs. Experimental studies support functional contributions to fibrosis, whereas human evidence predominantly establishes tissue phenotypes and associations rather than a causal post-AKI trajectory. Tissue assessment provides direct phenotypic evidence; fluid biomarkers offer complementary information about injury, recovery, and prognosis without specifically measuring FR-PTEC burden. Potential interventions are considered according to preservation of adaptive repair, restoration of epithelial function, and selective suppression or clearance of pathological cells. This therapeutic framework remains hypothesis-generating. Translation requires reproducible classification and longitudinal evidence linking epithelial states to kidney outcomes and treatment response.

title: Mapping redox networks in cardiomyocytes reveals non-overlapping response pathways for cytosolic versus mitochondrial H₂O₂ signaling.
authorString: Chen Y, Cárdenas-Arciniegas JC, Vergel Leon AM, Maurer W, Ibrahim AM, Zieseniss A, Kurschat L, Hillemann A, Bauer L, Nanadikar MS, Guo J, Berecic B, Gorshkova A, Cyganek L, Vikram Vamsi P, Mondal S, Brügmann T, Wagdi A, Tiburcy M, Urlaub H, Lenz C, Rehling P, Brandenburg S, Katschinski DM.
abstractText: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are essential redox messengers, yet their effects depend on concentration, localization, and duration. Here, we investigate how compartment-specific hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) production influences cardiomyocyte redox signaling and function. Using human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CM) expressing the H₂O₂ biosensor HyPer fused to D-amino acid oxidase (DAO), we achieve chemogenetic control of H₂O₂ generation in the cytosol, mitochondria, or nucleus. Cytosolic H₂O₂ propagates throughout the cell, whereas mitochondrially generated H₂O₂ remains spatially restricted, reflecting compartmentalized antioxidant buffering. Cytosolic H₂O₂ impairs contractility and relaxation in both 2D and 3D engineered heart tissue models, accompanied by preferential oxidation of Z-disc-associated and actin-binding proteins and by altered sarcomere organization. Antioxidant treatment attenuates these effects. In contrast, mitochondrially produced H₂O₂ is better tolerated and associated with adaptive redox remodeling, with preserved contractile performance that is antagonized by conoidin A-induced inhibition of cytosolic peroxiredoxin activity. These findings demonstrate that the subcellular source of H₂O₂ shapes redox propagation, oxidation patterns, and functional responses, highlighting redox compartmentalization as a determinant of cardiomyocyte performance and stress resilience.

title: Surgical Resection of Extra-Abdominal Metastases of Low-Grade Serous Ovarian Cancer: A Case Series.
authorString: Gaillard T, Mariolo A, Hotton J, Laas E, Lecuru F.
abstractText: Surgical removal of extra-abdominal spread of low-grade serous ovarian cancer has not been largely described in the literature. We report three cases of the association of abdominal and thoracic surgery in patients with metastatic low-grade serous ovarian cancer. It seems to have no deleterious impact on global management. Real impact on survival remains unclear.

title: Viral persistence and post-acute outcomes following high-consequence negative-sense RNA virus infections.
authorString: Davies KA, Welch SR, Lo MK, Spiropoulou CF, Spengler JR.
abstractText: High-consequence viral pathogens, including filoviruses, arenaviruses, bunyaviruses, and henipaviruses, can cause severe acute disease with high case-fatality rates. Although survivors occur in the absence of specific therapies, outcomes may be improved through early diagnosis, supportive care, and, for select pathogens, licensed or investigational countermeasures. The increasing number of survivors has focused attention on post-acute consequences of infection. Viral RNA, viral antigen, and infectious virus have been detected after recovery in selected body fluids and tissues, raising questions regarding transmission risk, reservoirs, and persistence. Survivors may also experience diverse long-term sequelae affecting neurological, ocular, auditory, musculoskeletal, cardiopulmonary, and general health. In some cases, late-onset disease or relapse has been reported months to years after recovery. Here, we review evidence for persistence of high-consequence negative-sense RNA viruses, summarize sequelae, examine late syndromes, and highlight research priorities needed to improve survivor care and preparedness.

title: Mapping the range of tests commercially marketed as screening tests to asymptomatic people in the UK in comparison to those recommended by the NHS: a cross-sectional study.
authorString: McCartney M, Donnelly PD, Khudyk A, Lui T, Imam S, Mohammed A, Watt L, Hong J, Oliver K, Fore L, Ayodele V, Sullivan F.

title: Clinically Relevant Toxic Effects of Over-the-Counter Nutraceuticals and Herbal Pain Products.
authorString: Anwar AI, Apgar TL, Daniel CP, Forte JA, Vo MT, Nelson JR, Coffman GD, Jenkins LG, Schiano Lo Moriello E, Bernhardt FY, Anand T, Lewy HD, Hasoon J, Kaye AD.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

The herbal supplement and nutraceutical industry has grown immensely over the past two decades, with large increases being driven by patients seeking alternative methods for pain management. Unlike pharmaceuticals, supplements face a low barrier to market entry with lax regulations allowing these products to be sold without pre-market testing.

Recent findings

While products like glucosamine and turmeric are commonly used and have demonstrated moderate efficacy for pain conditions such as osteoarthritis, there is a lack of long-term randomized control trials to support widespread use. Additionally, product use is associated with safety concerns stemming from known toxicities, manufacturing contaminants, and herbal-drug product interactions.

Summary

These limitations have prompted calls for better regulatory oversight of herbal supplements to improve manufacturing standards, recognize safety concerns from product use, and establish long-term data for effective use. Clinicians are also encouraged to recognize known benefits and risks of nutraceutical use to better inform patients using these products and to reduce potential morbidity and mortality.

title: The human microbiome in non-communicable diseases: Mechanistic insights into dysbiosis, systemic inflammation, and precision therapeutics.
authorString: Ganguly K, Vanekar MFR, Pal D, Lalhriatrenga R, Roy A, Ramaiah S, Anbarasu A.
abstractText: The human microbiome contributes to immune regulation, metabolic homeostasis, epithelial barrier integrity, and inter-organ communication. This review integrates evidence from gut, oral, skin, and cervicovaginal microbiomes, focusing on epithelial barrier dysfunction, altered microbial metabolite signaling, innate immune activation, inflammatory signaling, immune dysregulation, and host-microbe interactions across non-communicable diseases and microbiome-based therapeutic approaches in these contexts. Collectively, current evidence suggests that dysbiosis may represent not only a disease-associated microbial signature but also a potential mechanistic contributor to disease development and progression, although substantial interindividual and disease-specific variability remains. Microbiome-based diagnostics, fecal microbiota transplantation, personalized nutrition, and microbial therapeutics show considerable translational potential; nevertheless, causal relationships and clinical efficacy remain insufficiently established for several applications. Future research should therefore prioritize rigorously designed interventional and longitudinal studies integrating multi-omics profiling with host genetics and immune phenotyping to establish causal mechanisms, identify reproducible biomarkers, and support the development of precision microbiome-based therapeutic strategies.

title: Reestablishing aortic continuity: transcatheter repair of interrupted aortic arch.
authorString: Kumar D, Nath R, Ansari AH, Akhtar S, Pandit S, Rao S, Ahuja P, Gupta P, Gupta A.

title: Stress-induced alterations in neurodevelopment in iPSC-Derived <i>i</i> <i>n vitro</i> model systems.
authorString: Mukhopadhyay R, Sengupta A, Biswal S, Pal R.
abstractText: Psychological stress is common in women during pregnancy and after childbirth, showing a prevalence of up to 15.6% in pregnant women in developing countries. Clinical and pre-clinical studies have implicated their role in negatively affecting pregnancy outcomes and have been linked to adverse child outcomes. Yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood, specifically the signatures associated with their effect on human fetal development. Thereby, impairing our further understanding of the effects of therapeutics used to treat these disorders in expecting mothers. This study proposes the use of human iPSC-derived embryoid bodies (EBs) and forebrain-specific organoids as complementary human developmental models to investigate the effects of exposure to prenatal stress (mediated by glucocorticoids) across distinct stages, in vitro. Our findings suggested that excessive glucocorticoids altered early lineage specification in an exposure-dependent manner. This was evidenced by a brief increase in pluripotent and neural progenitor populations, with mild alterations in proliferative dynamics without a net change in proliferative capacity. Changes in lineage-associated markers were observed in ectodermal and meso-endodermal layers of EBs. Particularly, focusing on neurogenesis (forebrain-specific organoids) to understand the impact of stress on neurodevelopment, we saw concentration-dependent changes in progenitor maintenance and neuronal- glial differentiation. Furthermore, the activation of inflammatory and oxidative stress responses can be implicated as signalling mechanisms responsible for the differences observed. Together, these results suggest that glucocorticoid signalling linked to prenatal stress can alter developmental trajectories by modifying cellular states rather than directly altering proliferation or survival during early development.

title: Device-detected new-onset atrial fibrillation after dual-chamber pacemaker implantation in patients with sick sinus syndrome under managed ventricular pacing: a risk nomogram from the 3-month landmark.
authorString: Xie JM, Shan CH, Xiao YJ, Ma J, Lu RR, Zheng ZJ.
abstractText:
Background

New-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) is common after dual-chamber pacemaker implantation, but existing prediction models were derived from mixed populations of patients with sick sinus syndrome (SSS) and atrioventricular block and included heterogeneous pacing strategies.

Methods

In this single-centre retrospective cohort study, consecutive patients with SSS who received a first permanent Medtronic dual-chamber pacemaker with managed ventricular pacing (MVP) enabled as the default strategy were screened. Patients with atrial fibrillation or an atrial high-rate episode (AHRE) within 3 months after implantation were excluded, and prediction time started at this 3-month landmark, with atrial pacing percentage (AP%) and ventricular pacing percentage (VP%) measured at that visit. Patients implanted in 2015-2021 formed the development cohort (n = 322), and those implanted in 2022-2025 formed a temporal validation cohort (n = 121) reserved exclusively for validation. Twenty-six candidate predictors were assessed by univariable and multivariable Cox regression with backward Akaike information criterion (AIC) selection. Internal validation repeated the complete model-building procedure within 2,000 bootstrap samples. Temporal performance was assessed using discrimination and calibration at 1, 2 and 3 years after the landmark.

Results

NOAF occurred in 90 of 322 development patients (28.0%) during a median follow-up of 41.6 months [interquartile range (IQR), 13.7-80.1], and in 28 of 121 temporal validation patients (23.1%) during a median follow-up of 30.5 months (IQR, 8.8-45.9). Age (hazard ratio [HR] per year, 1.043; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.019-1.067), maximum P-wave duration (Pmax; HR per 10 ms, 1.200; 95% CI, 1.085-1.326), left atrial volume index (LAVi; HR per 1 mL/m2, 1.051; 95% CI, 1.030-1.073), AP% > 50% (HR, 1.845; 95% CI, 1.198-2.840) and VP% > 40% (HR, 1.898; 95% CI, 1.045-3.446) were independently associated with NOAF. The apparent C-index was 0.735; repeating the complete model-building procedure within 2,000 bootstrap samples gave a mean optimism of 0.036 and an optimism-corrected C-index of 0.6992. In temporal validation the C-index was 0.769 (95% CI, 0.639-0.873) and cumulative/dynamic AUC values were 0.753, 0.881 and 0.916 at 1, 2 and 3 years after the landmark. Calibration-in-the-large was -0.17, 0.24 and 0.35 and calibration slopes were 0.90, 0.99 and 0.98 at 1, 2 and 3 years, respectively.
