Serum ISG15 levels were significantly elevated in HTG patients compared with controls (3.18 ± 0.29 vs. 1.64 ± 0.19, P < 0.001). Multivariate logistic regression identified ISG15 as an independent predictor of HTG (OR: 1.214, 95% CI: 1.015-1.416, P = 0.033). RCS analysis revealed a nonlinear dose-response relationship with an inflection point at approximately 1.52 ng/mL. ROC analysis demonstrated good diagnostic performance (AUC: 0.697, sensitivity: 86.40%, specificity: 45.00% at cut-off 0.873 ng/mL). In HFD-fed mice, serum ISG15 levels were significantly elevated, and immunohistochemistry and western blotting confirmed increased ISG15 expression in liver, subcutaneous white adipose tissue, and epididymal white adipose tissue.

Conclusions

ISG15 is independently associated with HTG and exhibits a nonlinear relationship with diagnostic potential. These findings establish ISG15 as a potential biomarker and suggest its involvement in the immunometabolic crosstalk underlying HTG pathogenesis, warranting further mechanistic investigation.

title: Integrated Transcriptomics, Molecular Dynamics, and In Vivo Validation of Novel Sesquiterpene Lactones from Monosis parishii (Hook.f.) H.Rob. & Skvarla as COX-2 Inhibitors for Rheumatoid Arthritis.
authorString: Ishaq M, Khan H, Li Y, Xinhuan Q, Shahab M, Yongxiang H, Xu W, Zhou H.
abstractText: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease characterized by synovial inflammation and pannus-driven joint destruction. Current NSAIDs and DMARDs therapies control symptoms but carry gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, and hepatic risks with long term use. Monosis parishii (Hook.f.) H.Rob. & Skvarla (syn. Vernonia parishii), traditionally used as a root decoction for rheumatism and bone pain in Yunnan, China, is a promising source of alternative anti-arthritic agents. This study investigates the phytochemical profile of M. parishii leaves and branches and evaluates their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-arthritic potential. A new sesquiterpene lactone, verparishinolide A (1), and eight known compounds (2-9) were isolated and structurally defined by ESI-MS, HRESIMS, 1D/2D NMR and single-crystal X-ray diffraction, which established the absolute configuration of compound 1. Anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and anti-arthritic potential were evaluated using in vitro LPS-stimulated assays, carrageenan and CFA-induced in vivo models, and an integrated transcriptomic/molecular docking approach to identify a druggable target. Compounds 1 and 2 inhibited LPS-induced nitric oxide production and proinflammatory cytokines (IC50 = 6.41 and 7.01 μM) and demonstrated significant in vitro antioxidant activity (DPPH 84.71%, 74.11%; NO 76.66%, 83.33%; Fe2+ chelation 81.82%, 72.72%; OH 81.42%, 80.01%), findings that were subsequently confirmed in vivo through restoration of endogenous antioxidant enzymes (catalase, superoxide dismutase, peroxidase, glutathione) under dexamethasone and saline-controlled conditions. To prioritize a druggable target, rheumatoid-arthritis synovial transcriptomics from three cohorts was integrated with compound-specific target prediction: among 11 proteins at this intersection, PTGS2 (COX-2) combined the highest prediction probability with a 3.37-fold, cross cohort-concordant increase in RA, and was advanced to 200-ns molecular dynamics, where compounds 1 and 2 docked with scores of -5.87 and -5.14 kcal mol-1, with native-pose recovery validated at 0.912 Å RMSD. In carrageenan-induced acute inflammation compound 1 (10 mg/kg) reduced paw swelling by 78.52 ± 2.89%, and compound 2 by 75.57 ± 1.92%. In CFA-induced chronic arthritis, Dexamethasone produced the strongest suppression of paw inflammation, followed by compounds 1 and 2, both of which restored endogenous antioxidant enzymes (catalase, superoxide dismutase, peroxidase, glutathione) and reduced inflammatory markers (nitric oxide, thiobarbiturates, IL-6, COX-2) in paw tissue. Histological and immunohistochemical analysis confirmed these effects, showing reduced inflammatory infiltration and IL-6 expression together with preservation of mature collagen and tissue architecture, approaching the effect of dexamethasone, with compound 1 consistently the more potent. These findings identify verparishinolide A as a structurally novel, mechanistically supported natural COX-2-directed anti-inflammatory lead from M. parishii.

title: Chronic exposure to low-concentration urban PM2.5 promotes maladaptive kidney repair after ischemic injury via mitochondrial dysfunction and lysosomal stress.
authorString: Sun P, Parra AC, Sanches TR, Wikuats CFH, Butter L, Claessen N, Baelde HJ, Schimmel IM, van der Wel N, Berlingerio SP, Janssens GE, Houtkoope RH, Vaz FM, Roelofs JJTH, Boor P, Strauch M, de Fatima Andrade M, Andrade L, Florquin S, Kers J, Romagnolo A, Tammaro A.
abstractText: Chronic exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is increasingly associated with kidney function decline and chronic kidney disease (CKD), particularly in individuals with pre-existing vulnerability, yet the mechanisms by which PM2.5 modifies kidney disease trajectories remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether prolonged exposure to low-level urban PM2.5 during recovery from ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI)-induced acute kidney injury (AKI) promotes maladaptive repair, a risk factor for AKI-to-CKD transition. Mice subjected to IRI or sham surgery were exposed for six months to filtered air or real-world ambient PM2.5. While PM2.5 induced only limited changes in sham kidneys, it markedly altered repair after IRI, promoting inflammation, microvascular rarefaction, mitochondrial injury, and metabolic reprogramming and fibrosis. PM2.5-associated elements accumulated within proximal tubular lysosomes, linking inhaled particle exposure to lysosomal stress, lipid remodeling, and tubular senescence. Transcriptomic drug-repurposing analysis identified nicotinamide as a candidate metabolic intervention, which improved mitochondrial dysfunction in PM2.5-challenged proximal tubular epithelial cells in vitro. Together, these findings show that even low-level urban PM2.5 exposure can act as a disease-modifying environmental stressor in injured kidneys, promoting maladaptive repair. Our findings reveal the post-injury recovery phase as a critical window of heightened susceptibility, during which air pollution can compromise kidney recovery.

title: Failure to Reverse Hypoxic Adaptation in Cardiovascular Aging: HIF-1α-Mitochondrial Decoupling and Intercellular Relay Signaling.
authorString: Feng Y, Li Q, Liang X, Cheng S, Qi Y, Li Y, Liu B, Yu H, Gao K, Yan J, Zhang L.
abstractText: Cardiovascular ageing decreases the body's ability to cope with and recover from ischaemic, metabolic and inflammatory stress before the development of clinical disease. Mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic inflammation and fibrosis are all attributes of cardiovascular ageing, but the reasons why damaged tissues cannot return to a normal state are still unknown. This paper puts forward the idea of "failed recovery from hypoxic adaptation" and studies whether metabolic and functional readjustment can make up for the loss of HIF-1α-mediated protection. Good recovery requires coordination of the suppression of adaptive signals, revival of oxidative metabolism, mitochondrial turnover, resolution of inflammation, microvascular repair, regulation of tissue remodelling, etc. Disruption of the above processes will increase the signal of mitochondrial damage and inflammation, and reduced blood flow and extracellular matrix degradation will also impair metabolic recovery. Interaction among cardiomyocytes, endothelial-pericyte units, macrophages, fibroblasts and vascular smooth muscle cells can worsen these abnormalities and cause all sorts of cardiovascular diseases. Reanalysis of public transcriptomic data shows that age and injury are associated with changes in metabolic, vascular and inflammatory pathways, but it does not prove causality. We will present time-resolved criteria for differentiating between reversible adaptation and persistent pathological signalling, and investigate the combination of clinical indicators and disease-specific molecular signatures for patient stratification. At home and abroad, many therapeutic strategies have been developed and researched to improve the recovery speed and function of patients. Finally, I will extend the observation and study of cell-specific mechanisms over a long period to determine whether the intervention can restore coordinated tissue function and establish a disease-specific therapeutic window.

title: Acute pericarditis after atrial fibrillation ablation in the pulsed-field ablation era: Energy source-specific insights from a large multicenter registry.
authorString: Horie T, Miyazaki S, Nagata Y, Nitta J, Sato Y, Yamashita S, Yamauchi Y, Murata K, Ono Y, Taomoto Y, Inaba O, Hachiya H, Miwa N, Suzuki M, Kato N, Takahashi Y, Tanaka A, Takahashi A, Nakashima E, Handa K, Suzuki A, Hayashi Y, Mizukami A, Sasano T.
abstractText:
Background

Acute pericarditis is a clinically relevant complication of atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation, but its incidence after pulsed-field ablation (PFA) relative to thermal ablation is uncertain.

Objective

To compare clinically diagnosed pericarditis after PFA-based and thermal-based AF ablation procedures and describe events across contemporary PFA platforms.

Methods

Data from consecutive AF ablation procedures at 20 cardiovascular centers between 2022 and 2026 were analyzed. Pericarditis was diagnosed clinically by the treating physicians, and fulfillment of the 2025 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) diagnostic criteria was assessed retrospectively.

Results

Among 19,555 consecutive AF ablation procedures included in the analysis, PFA, radiofrequency (RF), and cryoballoon was involved in 5743, 12768, and 5729 procedures, respectively. Clinically diagnosed acute pericarditis occurred in 5 of 5743 among PFA-based procedures (0.09%) and 38 of 13,812 (0.28%) among thermal-based procedures (P = 0.011). Twenty-nine (67.4%) cases fulfilled definite diagnosis of the ESC 2025 criteria for pericarditis, and the remaining 14 cases (32.6%) met possible diagnosis. In multivariable analysis, mitral isthmus linear ablation was independently associated with a higher risk of pericarditis (odds ratio [OR], 2.457; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.136-5.311; P = 0.022), whereas PFA use was independently associated with a lower risk (OR, 0.382; 95% CI, 0.149-0.980; P = 0.045).

Conclusion

In real-world clinical practice, clinically diagnosed acute pericarditis was rare after both PFA-based and thermal-based AF ablation. In the overall cohort, the observed incidence was significantly lower after PFA-based procedures, but the small number of events limits the certainty of this association and warrants further study.

title: Association of early-life particulate matter exposure with childhood carotid intima-media thickness: identification of sensitive windows and exploratory analysis of vitamin D status.
authorString: Duan Y, Xu H, Li J, Ren Q, Sun X, Zhou Z, Xiong W, Zhang L, Wu C, Liu Y.
abstractText:
Background

Particulate matter (PM) exposure may accelerate atherosclerosis, but mostly in adult populations. Early-life PM effect on childhood carotid intima-media thickness (cIMT), sensitive windows, and whether vitamin D status modifies these associations remain unclear.

Objective

To evaluate associations of early-life (pregnancy and first postnatal year) PM2.5 and PM10 exposure with cIMT in children, identify sensitive windows, and exploratorily examine whether associations differ by vitamin D status.

Methods

From December 2023 to July 2024, 990 children aged 2-14 years in Wuhan, China were enrolled. Generalized linear models assessed PM-cIMT associations; distributed lag nonlinear models identified weekly sensitive windows (95% CI excluding null); potential effect modification by vitamin D was explored using stratified and combined-effect analyses, with interaction terms formally tested.

Results

Early-life PM2.5 and PM10 exposure were positively associated with cIMT [percent change ranged from 2.67% (95% CI: 0.35%, 5.04%) to 9.98% (4.37%, 15.89%)]. Associations were stronger for internal carotid artery (ICA)-cIMT [e.g. 8.49% (3.09%, 14.17%) for PM2.5] than common carotid artery (CCA)-cIMT [2.87% (0.71%, 5.09%)]. Sensitive windows for CCA-cIMT appeared at postnatal weeks 11∼17 and 48∼52; for ICA-cIMT, the window concentrated at postnatal weeks 6∼22. Children with high PM exposure and vitamin D insufficiency showed greater ICA-cIMT; however, no PM × vitamin D interaction was statistically significant.

Conclusion

Early-life PM exposure is associated with increased childhood cIMT, with ICA-cIMT more sensitive than CCA-cIMT; the first postnatal year is a critical vulnerability window. Targeted air pollution control during this window in children could reduce the long-term risk of cardiovascular disease.

title: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection: implications for women's health, clinical care, and future research.
authorString: Bay B, Magnussen C, Adlam D, Al-Nasser LA, Al-Lamee R, Appelman Y, Alfonso F, Jobe M, Kovacic JC, Lam CS, Leopold J, Saw J, Zaman S, Clemmensen P.
abstractText: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is an increasingly recognised cause of acute coronary syndromes, characterised by spontaneous separation of the layers of the coronary arterial wall. It predominantly affects younger women, and recent registry and imaging studies indicate that SCAD is more common than previously appreciated, challenging its historical classification as a rare condition. Clinically, SCAD is associated with a substantial early risk of adverse events, particularly in the first weeks after the index dissection. Given the high frequency of spontaneous healing, conservative management is preferred for most patients, whereas revascularisation is generally reserved for ongoing ischaemia or haemodynamic compromise. However, evidence to guide both pharmacological and interventional management remains scarce. This Review summarises current evidence on SCAD epidemiology, underlying mechanisms including genetic susceptibility, diagnostic approaches, management principles, implications for reproductive and women's health, and research priorities to improve outcomes for affected patients.

title: Therapeutic targeting of circ-ZNF609 attenuates cardiac remodeling by modulating the expression of ZEB1.
authorString: Wang L, Wang J, Wang T, Zhang S, Sun J, Cui X, Cui C, Ding X, Gokulnath P, Vulugundam G, Xu Y, Shao Y, Yang Y, Wan W, Hu Y, Bi S, Li G, Cretoiu D, Li X, Dai Y, Xiao J.
abstractText: Currently, there are no effective therapeutic strategies to reverse heart failure. This study aims to investigate mechanisms underlying cardiac remodeling and identify potential therapeutic targets. Here, we demonstrate that circ-ZNF609 is upregulated in cardiac tissue, isolated adult cardiomyocytes, and cardiac fibroblasts 4 weeks after transverse aortic constriction (TAC) in mice. Small hairpin RNA (shRNA)-mediated silencing of circ-ZNF609 attenuates TAC-induced cardiac remodeling. To further assess its therapeutic potential, we use an RNA-targeting hfCas13x-crRNA system and show that circ-ZNF609 inhibition attenuates established cardiac hypertrophy in mice. In vitro, circ-ZNF609 inhibition reduces cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and fibroblast differentiation into myofibroblasts. Mechanistically, circ-ZNF609 interacts with YTHDF3 in an m<sup>6</sup>A-dependent manner to regulate ZEB1 (zinc finger E-box-binding homeobox 1) expression. circ-ZNF609 inhibition suppresses ZEB1. YTHDF3 knockdown also protects against cardiac remodeling. These findings support circ-ZNF609 inhibition as a potential therapeutic approach for pathological cardiac remodeling and heart failure.

title: Tonlamarsen, a Hepatocyte-Directed Antisense Oligonucleotide Targeting Angiotensinogen: Phase 1 and 2a Clinical Studies.
authorString: Morgan E, Weinland J, Lin T, McMullen G, Ward JH, Saksi J, Geist GE, Del Rio CL, Geary R, Mullick A, Tsimikas S.
abstractText: Tonlamarsen, a hepatocyte-directed antisense oligonucleotide targeting angiotensinogen (AGT), produced rapid, dose-dependent reductions in circulating AGT in healthy participants and patients with uncontrolled hypertension. A single dose reduced AGT by up to 75.2%, while monthly dosing achieved reductions of up to 79.0% after 4 doses. Tonlamarsen was generally well tolerated, with no clinically meaningful effects on platelet count, potassium, renal function, liver enzymes, or hypotension. Exploratory analyses demonstrated lower systolic blood pressure with tonlamarsen than placebo. These findings support further evaluation of hepatic AGT suppression as a novel therapeutic strategy for hypertension. A Study to Assess the Safety, Tolerability, and Efficacy of Monthly Subcutaneous Administration of ION904 in Participants With Uncontrolled Hypertension: NCT05314439).

title: Pulmonary hypertension in rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease: A case with possible contribution of alveolar septal inflammation.
authorString: Adachi M, Watanabe S, Muto A, Akasaki K, Goten C, Yoshida M, Sakai N, Ikeda H, Tanaka T, Yano S.
abstractText: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) associated with connective tissue diseases is heterogeneous, and immunosuppressive therapy has been reported to improve PH in selected patients; however, the pathological basis of such responsiveness remains unclear. We report a 39-year-old never-smoking woman with PH complicated by rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD). PH showed a marked and reproducible response to systemic corticosteroids, paralleling ILD activity. Thoracoscopic lung biopsy demonstrated lymphocytic alveolar septal inflammation with fibrotic and emphysematous changes, without significant pulmonary arterial remodeling. Although initially steroid-responsive, PH became irreversible, with progressive fibrosis and emphysema. This case suggests that inflammation-mediated alveolar-capillary injury may contribute to a transiently reversible component of PH in RA-ILD, highlighting the importance of sustained inflammatory control.

title: MRI-informed computational framework for non-invasive index of microcirculatory resistance in ischemic heart disease.
authorString: Mahmoudi M, Pogosyan A, Teeraratkul C, Ming Z, Han F, Currier JW, Arzani A, Nguyen KL.
abstractText: Coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) is an underdiagnosed driver of ischemic heart disease (IHD). Its diagnosis using the invasive index of microcirculatory resistance (IMR) provides spatially limited characterization of microvascular pathology. We aim to develop an MRI-informed computational framework that reconstructs tissue-specific microvascular networks for estimation of hemodynamics and synthetic IMR (synIMR) across IHD phenotypes. Ferumoxytol-enhanced MRI-derived fractional myocardial blood volume maps from 12 subjects with IHD were used to inform an adaptive, multistage, constrained constructive optimization of microvascular network generation. Five stochastic microvascular networks were generated per coronary artery (165 arterial networks). Hyperemic one-dimensional hemodynamic environments were simulated, and mean transit time (Tmn) was estimated using Lagrangian particle tracking. synIMR was calculated from hyperemic distal pressure and Tmn. Synthetic arterial networks recapitulated FE-MRI depiction of remote, ischemic, and scarred myocardium (r = 0.996, p < 0.001). Mixed-effects testing revealed distinct microvascular remodeling patterns across tissue phenotypes. Relative to remote myocardium, ischemic tissue exhibited increased vascular volume fraction (+0.19%, p < 0.001) and terminal vessel density (+22%, p < 0.001); whereas, scar tissues showed microvascular rarefaction (-28%, p < 0.001). Synthetic Tmn was prolonged in hypertrophic and scar territories (remote: 0.21 ± 0.05s; hypertrophic: 0.34 ± 0.06s; scar: 0.31 ± 0.04s, p ≤ 0.02), with corresponding elevation in synIMR. In subjects with invasive measurements, synIMR and Tmn estimated invasive values with a bias of +12.6% and 4.4% respectively. These findings support the feasibility of our MRI-informed computational framework for noninvasive quantification of IMR and phenotyping of microvascular remodeling in IHD. By noninvasively extending IMR assessment, this platform may support earlier CMD detection, disease monitoring, and therapeutic targeting.

title: Intracameral lidocaine-epinephrine has minimal effect on heart rate and blood pressure and is an effective sole mydriatic during phacoemulsification in dogs.
authorString: Pumphrey SA, Gibson LK, Maggio F, Lindsey J, Wetmore LA.
abstractText: To investigate heart rate (HR) and rhythm, blood pressure (BP), and pupil diameter in dogs that received intracameral (IC) preservative-free lidocaine-epinephrine (ILE) as a sole mydriatic agent during phacoemulsification. Records were retrospectively reviewed for HR and BP data and anesthesia concerns following administration of ILE during cataract surgery (IC group, 130 eyes from 83 dogs). Similar data were obtained for a control group undergoing phacoemulsification that received topical mydriatics (topical treatment [TT] group, 40 eyes from 21 dogs). Pupil diameter was measured prospectively following administration of ILE in an additional 20 eyes from 11 dogs. Average baseline HR was 13 beats/min higher in the TT group than in the IC group for both eyes operated (P ≤ .04). Heart rate increased more from baseline in the IC group than in the TT group at 15 and 20 minutes after administration, but the difference was not clinically significant (average of 4 beats/min). Changes in BP were minimal and did not differ between groups. No significant arrhythmias or other anesthetic complications were noted in either group. Mean pupil diameter was 11.3 mm (95% CI, 11, 11.6) immediately following ILE administration and 11.8 mm (95% CI, 11.5, 12.1) at the conclusion of surgery. ILE produced adequate, durable mydriasis when used as a sole mydriatic in canine eyes undergoing phacoemulsification. Intracameral lidocaine-epinephrine does not appear to affect cardiovascular parameters when administered during phacoemulsification in dogs. ILE is a reasonable mydriatic choice for canine phacoemulsification.

title: Test-retest repeatability of MBSS-T1: a model-based, subject-specific self-supervised motion correction method for robust cardiac T1 mapping.
authorString: Zehavi Lenz A, Hanania E, Volovik I, Link-Sourani D, Freiman M.
abstractText: Reliable myocardial T1 mapping is essential for quantitative cardiac tissue characterization but remains sensitive to respiratory motion, particularly during free-breathing acquisitions. This study evaluated the test-retest repeatability of MBSS-T1, a subject-specific, model-based, self-supervised deep-learning method for motion-robust myocardial T1 mapping.Approach. Seventeen healthy male volunteers aged 20-36 years underwent 3 T cardiac MRI using a 5(3)3 MOLLI acquisition under breath-hold (BH) and free-breathing (FB) conditions. Same-day repeat scans were acquired after a 20 min interval that included removal from and repositioning in the scanner. T1 maps were reconstructed using (1) MBSS-T1, (2) the contrast-agnostic deep-learning registration method SynthMorph, (3) scanner-inline motion correction, and (4) no motion correction. Repeatability was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), relative Bland-Altman analysis, within-subject coefficients of variation (CVw), relative 95% repeatability coefficients (RC95), and variance-based bootstrap inference with Holm correction.Main results. All four methods included 17 complete participant-level test-retest pairs under each breathing condition. Under BH conditions, the global ICC point estimates were 0.77, 0.64, 0.65, and 0.60 for MBSS-T1, SynthMorph, scanner-inline correction, and no correction, respectively. Under FB conditions, the corresponding values were 0.41, 0.32, 0.27, and 0.16. MBSS-T1 also had the lowest descriptive CVw under both conditions. However, none of the paired comparisons of absolute test-retest differences was significant after Holm correction (all adjusted p ≥ 0.623). The smallest Holm-adjusted variance-ratio result was obtained for MBSS-T1 versus no correction under FB conditions (variance ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.30-0.68; adjusted p = 0.058), which did not meet the prespecified significance threshold. Significance. MBSS-T1 yielded favourable descriptive repeatability estimates, particularly under FB conditions, but no pairwise comparison remained statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. These results characterize same-day, same-scanner measurement precision rather than absolute T1 accuracy and require confirmation in larger and more clinically diverse cohorts.

title: The numerical study on cardiac ablation considering dynamic blood flow by high frequency bipolar pulses with determined lethal threshold in vitro.
authorString: Lv Y, Liu L, Tian Y, Lu Y, Liu G.
abstractText: Pulsed Field Ablation (PFA) is a promising non-thermal energy modality for catheter-based cardiac ablation. Treatment planning using numerical simulations of PFA is important for predicting the ablation region. However, owing to the high voltage-to-electrode distance ratio, thermal effects should be considered during treatment planning. This study aims to analyse the ablation region for cardiac treatment planning considering the thermal effect. this study aimed first to determine the lethal electric field threshold (LEFT) of H9C2 myocardial cells exposed to high-frequency bipolar pulses (HFBPs). Then two simplified pulmonary vein (PV) models with a circular electrode array were constructed to investigate electric field and thermal distributions, accounting for dynamic blood flow and conductivity variation. cell experimental results showed that under the condition of equivalent energized time, fewer pulses per burst and prolonged interpulse delay of HFBPs can reduce the LEFT of myocardial cells. The LET reached 720 V/cm when applying 120 HFBPs of 1000 μs duration. Numerical simulations revealed that temperature rises sharply when blood flow is neglected, with a maximum temperature of 67 ℃. However, thermal effects are substantially limited (peak temperature of 38.3 ℃) due to blood flow, even when HFBPs with a high voltage-to-electrode distance (1250 V) are applied. The temperature rise rapidly declines and reaches a plateau at higher blood velocities. HFBPs can produce a full circumferential ablation region, and the ablation width increases linearly with rising applied voltage. this study demonstrates that dynamic blood flow and conductivity effects should be considered for myocardial ablation assessments, which may assist clinicians in precise pulse selection.

title: MRAST-Net: A Lightweight Multi-Receptive-Field Residual Temporal Network for 12-Lead ECG Classification.
authorString: Wang M, Zang M, Liu T, Zhou S, Liu C, Wang Q.
abstractText: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals play an important role in cardiovascular disease screening, clinical monitoring, and remote healthcare. However, existing high-performing ECG classification methods usually rely on complex deep learning architectures, which often involve a large number of parameters, high computational cost, and limited deployability in resource-constrained scenarios. To balance classification performance and lightweight deployment, this paper proposes MRAST-Net, a lightweight multi-receptive-field residual temporal network for 12-lead ECG classification. The proposed model first employs a lead mixing layer to enable cross-lead information interaction. It then uses a lightweight multi-scale residual depthwise convolution module to extract local waveform morphology features under different receptive fields, while an efficient channel attention mechanism is introduced to enhance informative channel responses. On this basis, a temporal convolutional network is further incorporated to model long-range dynamic dependencies, and attentive statistics pooling is used to aggregate global statistical features for final multi-label classification. Experiments on two public 12-lead ECG datasets, PTB-XL and CPSC-2018, show that the proposed model achieves AUC scores of 93.12 $\pm$ 0.16\%, 92.29 $\pm$ 0.80\%, and 92.62 $\pm$ 0.51\%, and ACC scores of 89.17 $\pm$ 0.09\%, 96.40 $\pm$ 0.02\%, and 97.72 $\pm$ 0.07\% on the 5-superclass, 23-subclass, and 44-diagnostic-class tasks of PTB-XL, respectively. On CPSC-2018, MRAST-Net achieves an AUC of 96.57 $\pm$ 0.43\% and an ACC of 96.59 $\pm$ 0.26\% under 5$\times$3 nested cross-validation. These results demonstrate that MRAST-Net achieves competitive classification performance while maintaining a low parameter scale, indicating its potential for deployment in resource-constrained scenarios such as portable monitoring devices, real-time assisted diagnosis, and primary healthcare.

title: Rhythm priors and beat-specific cardiomechanical information in ECG-anchored PCG-envelope estimation.
authorString: Li Y, Zhou Q, Ding W, Liu Z.
abstractText: Electrocardiographic (ECG) R alignment and cardiac rhythm can supply strong priors for phonocardiographic (PCG) envelope estimation, complicating interpretation of accuracy as beat-specific mechanical information.Methods: Frozen participant-held-out accelerometer (ACC) predictions covered 12,000 beats from 40 healthy participants. Experiment A reassigned predictions across 100 same-participant, same-fold wrong-beat mappings approximately matched on neighboring RR intervals (ECG R-to-R intervals). Experiment B used training-only nested-selected continuous RR templates. The three principal outcomes were envelope mean absolute error (MAE), correlation, and corrected second-heart-sound (S2) timing MAE. Corrected S2 evaluation excluded seven references outside the fixed 180-520-ms window (11,993 eligible events), distinct from label correction or multiplicity adjustment. Benjamini-Hochberg correction covered all six original comparisons, with unchanged prespecified stability rules.Results: True correspondence improved MAE by 0.0096 (95% CI 0.0080-0.0111; 40/40 participants; q=7.28×10⁻¹²). ACC improved MAE over continuous RR by 0.0093 (95% CI 0.0036-0.0150; 29/40; q=0.00252). Only MAE met complete stability under both controls. Correlation and corrected S2 showed favorable average effects with lower participant consistency in Experiment B; first-heart-sound (S1) timing remained an unfavorable outcome. Additional descriptive sensitivities retained average MAE benefits under expanded bandwidths (0.0085; 28/40) and balanced dual-RR matching (0.0097; 40/40). The expanded grid reduced the original B advantage by 8.262% without eliminating the average ACC benefit.Conclusions: Complementary rhythm and correspondence controls support an outcome-specific envelope-MAE increment associated with the true mechanical beat. The evidence concerns offline, non-causal, ECG R-anchored normalized-envelope estimation in one healthy cohort; clinical and external validation remain future requirements.

title: State of the Art Off-Pump Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting.
authorString: Lima RC, Salerno TA, Angelini GD, Buffolo E.
abstractText: Off-pump coronary artery bypass grafting (OPCAB) has evolved into a mature and reproducible strategy for myocardial revascularization. Although conventional on-pump coronary artery bypass grafting (ONCAB) became the standard approach with the advent of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), advances in cardiac stabilization, positioning, intracoronary shunting, and anesthetic management have enabled complete multivessel revascularization on the beating heart without CPB. Clinical studies have shown that OPCAB achieves outcomes comparable to ONCAB in appropriately selected patients while reducing perioperative complications, particularly in high-risk populations. Advances in surgical expertise, institutional infrastructure, and techniques including minimally invasive and hybrid approaches continue to expand the role of OPCAB. This review highlights the evolution, evidence, indications, and future perspectives of OPCAB as an important complementary strategy in modern cardiac surgery.

title: The Contemporary Ross Technique: A Stepwise Surgical Guide. Technical Innovations, Patient Selection, and Programme Establishment for Young Surgeons.
authorString: Costa FDAD, Ferreira ADA, Collatusso C, Collatusso DFF, Oliveira CL.
abstractText: The Ross operation has gained significant renewed interest in recent years. This resurgence is particularly notable among young and middle-aged patients requiring aortic valve replacement. The procedure is increasingly viewed as an optimal alternative, driven by its excellent long-term outcomes, low incidence of valve-related events, and the positive impact on patients' quality of life. This has been reflected in a recent reported European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery consensus on the recommendations of when the Ross operation should be considered as an optimal alternative. However, the operation is technically more complex, and the consensus underscores the importance of careful patient selection and specialized surgical expertise to maximize outcomes. This article provides a detailed, stepwise guide to the contemporary Ross technique, including technical innovations that address late complications, and serves as a resource for young surgeons willing to establish a Ross programme.

title: Interfacial Reorganization by Nonionic Surfactants Governs the Stability and Bioactivity of Exosomes.
authorString: Lv JY, Feng W, Wang Y, Zhang TY, Wu SY, Shen JH, Sun YM, Xie HF, An W, Fang WJ.
abstractText: Exosomes are promising nanoscale agents that can serve both as efficient drug delivery carriers and as bioactive therapeutics with intrinsic biological functions. Yet their clinical translation is hindered by formulation-dependent instability and an incomplete understanding of excipient-membrane interactions. Here, we systematically and, to our knowledge, for the first time dissect how nonionic surfactants govern exosome stability, membrane organization, and bioactivity across sub- to supra-critical micelle concentration regimes. Using bovine exosomes as a model, we verify that exosomes in phosphate-buffered saline are intrinsically metastable, undergoing progressive interfacial reorganization and particle loss even at 4 °C. Surfactants exhibit distinct, structure-dependent effects: polysorbates (PS20, PS80) reduce hydrodynamic size but accelerate particle loss, whereas poloxamer 188 (P188) preserves both size and concentration. Membrane analysis shows that polysorbates increase lipid fluidity, potentially through interactions with the lipid bilayer. P188 may act through preferential surface association with limited effects on the measured lipid packing environment. Functionally, PS20 enhances cellular uptake at the expense of structural integrity, whereas P188 maintains vesicle integrity with moderate functional gain. Across multiple exosome sources, these trends are conserved, demonstrating the generality of the underlying mechanisms. Together, our results establish a mechanistic framework linking surfactant structure, concentration, and membrane interaction to both physicochemical stability and biological performance, providing actionable design principles for exosome formulations.

title: Knowledge, Practices, and Training Needs Related to Radiation Protection among Critical Care Staff Exposed to Portable Radiography: A Cross-Sectional Study.
authorString: Juha E, Lahham A.
abstractText: Portable radiography is frequently performed in critical care settings, where healthcare workers may be exposed to scattered ionizing radiation. Adequate knowledge and appropriate protective practices are important components of occupational radiation protection. To assess radiation protection knowledge, practices, and training needs among nurses and physicians working in critical care units during portable radiography in hospitals in Bethlehem and East Jerusalem, Palestine. A descriptive cross-sectional questionnaire-based study was conducted among nurses and physicians working in intensive care units, cardiac care units, and neonatal intensive care units in nine hospitals between November 2022 and March 2023. The questionnaire assessed demographic characteristics, objective radiation protection knowledge, reported radiation protection practices during portable radiography, personal protective equipment use, training history and needs, and self-rated knowledge. A total of 142 critical care staff participated, including 104 nurses and 38 physicians. The mean objective radiation protection knowledge score was 8.30 ± 2.83 out of 14 (59.3%). Although 85.3% of participants rated their radiation protection knowledge as good or very good, objective assessment indicated that 68.3% had poor or fair knowledge. Regarding reported practice behaviors during portable radiography, leaving the unit during image acquisition was the most common response (37.3%), followed by maintaining maximum distance within the unit (23.2%), relocating to a break room (19.0%), remaining at the nursing station (12.0%), and standing behind shielding (8.5%). Use of personal protective equipment was limited, with 48.6% reporting that they never used lead aprons, 62.7% never using thyroid shields, 68.3% never using lead gloves, and 73.9% never using protective eyewear. Most participants (72.5%) had never attended formal radiation protection training, and 85.2% reported a need for additional education. Critical care staff demonstrated a discrepancy between perceived and objectively assessed radiation protection knowledge and reported inconsistent use of protective measures during portable radiography. The findings support structured and continuing radiation protection education and institutional measures to reinforce appropriate occupational protection practices.

title: Mapping Mesoscale Cardiac Architecture With Axially Swept Dithered Light-Sheet Microscopy.
authorString: Almasian M, Saberigarakani A, Zhang X, Brewer ES, Hameed R, Chai J, Lu Y, Ware SA, Zhou S, Wen Y, Lalami H, Hossein Beigi H, Yuan J, Liao J, Dean KM, Hong Y, Wu M, Tong D, Sapkota D, Ding Y.
abstractText: Comprehensive characterization of cardiac microstructure and vascular networks is critical for assessing cardiovascular development, disease progression, and therapeutic interventions. While volumetric imaging combined with tissue clearing enables high-resolution organ-level analysis, the densely organized cardiac microenvironment, characterized by compacted and trabeculated myocardium, remains technically challenging to resolve in its entirety. To address these limitations, we exploit the temporal dynamics of illumination-detection interplay to create a time-averaged beam profile, thereby maximizing system throughput across multi-scale specimens. Our dithered light-sheet (DiLS) approach extends the confocal region by over 40% and improves the space-bandwidth product while largely preserving optical sectioning capability. Building on this, the axially swept dithered light-sheet (AS-DiLS) employs a dual-actuator strategy that combines rapid beam dithering and axial sweeping to further accelerate imaging speed while achieving micrometer-scale resolution across centimeter-scale scanning ranges, enabling detailed cardiovascular morphological and topological assessment from embryonic to adult stages. We anticipate that this scalable imaging scheme will advance in-depth investigations of organ morphogenesis and disease pathogenesis across a broad spectrum of models.

title: Screening for Cardiac Amyloidosis in Men with Angina and Non-Obstructive Coronary Finding: The CHEST-CA study.
authorString: Noory N, Westin O, Damgaard M, Mørup P, Kragelund C, Hove JD, Ripa R, Kristensen T, Mylin AK, Maurer MS, Rossing K, Fosbøl E, Hasbak P, Gustafsson F.
abstractText: Background Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) may cause microvascular dysfunction leading to chest pain, even in the absence of obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD). Whether angina in older men may represent an early clinical manifestation of previously undiagnosed CA remains unknown Methods In this prospective multicenter study, 150 men aged ≥65 years presenting with chest pain were recruited from three outpatient cardiology clinics in the Capital Region of Denmark. All par-ticipants had non-obstructive findings on coronary imaging by either cardiac computed to-mography angiography or myocardial perfusion imaging. A systematic screening protocol in-cluded clinical evaluation, electrocardiography, echocardiography, blood and urine tests for monoclonal proteins, and cardiac scintigraphy. ATTR-CA was defined by Perugini grade ≥2 myocardial uptake in the absence of monoclonal gammopathy. Results The median age was 72.6 years (IQR: 68.8-77.4). Most patients underwent perfusion imaging (63.0%) prior to inclusion. Median high-sensitive troponin T was 12.0 ng/L (IQR, 9.0-18.0), and median NT-proBNP was 173.9 ng/L (IQR 81.9-459.9). Heart failure was present in 24.0% and atrial fibrillation or flutter in 39.7% of patients. In total, two patients (1.3%; 95% CI 0.2- 4.%) were diagnosed with wild-type transthyretin CA with grade 3 cardiac uptake. One patient had manifest cardiomyopathy, and the second CA patient had normal cardiac biomarkers and echocardiography and was surveilled. Conclusions Among elderly men with suspected cardiac angina and non-obstructive coronary findings, the prevalence of undiagnosed ATTR-CA was low (1.3%). Additional enrichment criteria may be necessary to improve diagnostic yield, but this remains hypothesis-generating.

title: Haze and health: a mixed method approach exploring physical and psychological challenges of smog faced by university employees in Pakistan.
authorString: Masood M, Sajjad S, Khalid F.
abstractText: The present study was designed to explore the role of smog on the physical and psychological health of university employees in Lahore, Pakistan, during November 2024. A mixed-methods approach was designed to assess the relationship between perceived air quality, psychological distress (depression, anxiety, stress), and physical symptoms (respiratory, digestive, sleep disturbances, headaches) in university employees. Study 1 was a cross-sectional survey of 350 university employees to assess the relationship between study variables. Results indicate a significant positive relationship between poor air quality, psychological and physical symptoms. In study 2, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 employees, exploring their exposure to smog and its impact on their physical and psychological health and the coping strategies they use to overcome these impacts. Thematic analysis highlighted greater vulnerability among older employees and those with preexisting conditions. Challenges included respiratory and cardiovascular issues, increased stress, cognitive impairments, and reduced productivity. Institutional shortcomings like inflexible policies worsened impacts. Recommended interventions include remote work, improved indoor air quality, and mental health support to alleviate these challenges and enhance well-being.

title: Empagliflozin preserves cardiac function and modulates metabolism in a mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
authorString: Zeidler BJ, Thomas C, Salvas JP, Javier AJS, Richards AM, Bean LA, Earl CC, Agrawal A, Narra N, Kozakiewicz SN, Zeng L, Witczak CA, Huot JR, Kim IM, Madhur MS, Kowala MC, Markham LW, Goergen CJ, Welc SS.
abstractText: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a fatal genetic disorder characterized by skeletal muscle degeneration and cardiomyopathy. Effective cardiac therapies remain limited. This study investigated the therapeutic potential of the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor empagliflozin (EMPA) in the dystrophin-deficient DBA2/J-mdx mouse model of DMD. Male mice received control chow or EMPA-containing chow (~25mg/kg/day), and cardiac function was evaluated longitudinally using four-dimensional ultrasound imaging. EMPA did not alter left ventricular mass or volume but delayed the onset of systolic dysfunction, preserving ejection fraction (EF) for 12 weeks and maintaining significantly higher EF through 24 weeks. EMPA also attenuated progressive impairments in systolic and diastolic myocardial deformation. Functional preservation was accompanied by reduced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and reduced expression of cardiac stress genes. EMPA increased mtDNA copy number, reduced mtDNA damage, preserved the mtDNA-encoded respiratory chain protein MT-CO1, and increased myocardial ATP content, supporting improved mitochondrial integrity and myocardial energetic capacity. In addition, EMPA induced transcriptional changes consistent with enhanced fatty acid and ketone metabolism. Systemically, EMPA improved growth trajectory, preserved relative lean mass, increased skeletal muscle torque, attenuated fiber-type remodeling, and did not adversely affect renal function. Together, these findings support SGLT2 inhibitors as a promising therapeutic strategy for DMD-associated cardiomyopathy.

title: Temporary Diuretic Withdrawal to Restore Responsiveness in Heart Failure.
authorString: Pourafshar N, Madapoosi SS, Karimi A, Testani J, Wilcox CS.
abstractText: Patients with heart failure often experience recurrent episodes of volume overload that respond to loop diuretics. However, this leads over time to neurohormonal activation, worsened sodium avidity, and tubular remodeling that contributes to diuretic resistance. Temporary diuretic withdrawal during volume removal by ultrafiltration, direct sodium removal, or other mechanical or pharmacological means may restore diuretic response at lower doses when therapy is re-introduced. This may persist for months after cessation of therapy. Collectively, these data support temporary periods of loop diuretic withdrawal or down-titration during management of volume loss by alternative means as a promising approach to overcoming diuretic resistance with heart failure.

title: Circadian disruption worsens postseptic pulmonary fibrotic remodeling through a CLOCK/PIEZO1-linked myeloid immunometabolic program.
authorString: Wang X, Sang A, Wang W, Liu Y, Zhao Z, Li H, Xiong X, Cai J, Xu M, Li X.
abstractText: Whether circadian rhythm disruption (CRD) promotes fibrotic remodeling after septic lung injury remains unclear. We tested whether CRD drives this process through macrophage CLOCK-PIEZO1 signaling. Lung specimens from patients with sepsis-associated lung injury and non-injured controls were analyzed alongside public murine lung transcriptomic datasets. Mice underwent cecal ligation and puncture or sham surgery and were maintained under stable or repeatedly shifted light-dark cycles; selected experiments included LysM-lineage Piezo1 deletion. Day-3 lung injury and day-28 fibrosis were assessed, and mechanisms were defined using genetic, biochemical and co-culture approaches. CRD suppressed CLOCK expression in macrophage-lineage cells, leading to increased PIEZO1 expression and aggravated collagen deposition. CLOCK repressed Piezo1 transcription through a promoter E-box. Loss of myeloid Clock reduced Clock mesor and amplitude by 66.3% and 90.3%, respectively, increased Piezo1 mesor by 54.0%, and produced genotype-by-rhythm interactions for both genes (P < 0.0001). PIEZO1 activation impaired lysosomal acid lipase (LAL)-dependent lipophagy and promoted ZDHHC19-mediated peptidylarginine deiminase 4 (PAD4) palmitoylation and extracellular-trap formation. LysM-lineage Piezo1 deletion attenuated fibrosis. PIEZO1 inhibition or DNase I reduced epithelial injury and fibroblast activation induced by extracellular DNA-rich macrophage signals. CRD promotes post-septic fibrosis through a CLOCK-PIEZO1-linked macrophage immunometabolic program, identifying PIEZO1, extracellular DNA-rich traps and impaired lipid clearance as candidate targets.

title: Experiences and Perceptions Around Eating Among Older Adults Living with Serious Mental Illness: A Qualitative Analysis.
authorString: Hubbard E, Leutwyler H.
abstractText: People living with serious mental illness (SMI) have, on average, a life expectancy 10-20 years shorter than those without SMI and are at an increased risk for comorbid conditions such as metabolic syndrome (comprised of abdominal obesity, hypertension, impaired glucose tolerance, and hypertriglyceridemia), contributing to the risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. External circumstances such as precarious living environments and poor socioeconomic status influence access to healthy food, and psychiatric symptoms may further impede healthy eating habits. To better understand facilitators and barriers to healthy eating among community-dwelling older adults living with SMI, we report the results of a qualitative analysis. We interviewed 10 community-dwelling older adults living with SMI (mean age 64.57, SD 6.815, range 53-76). A qualitative analysis using constructivist grounded theory methodology was conducted to assess participants' experiences and perceptions around eating and access to food. Two main themes emerged in our analyses: 1. Formative Life Course Influences and 2. Current Contextual Influences. Participants indicated that the early home environment, work experience, and time spent in mental health programs can influence eating habits. Participants also described how contextual influences guided the types of food they consume. This contextual-based approach to nutrition often determined whether participants ate non-nutrient-dense foods. Among community-dwelling older adults living with SMI, eating behaviors reflected the cumulative influence of lifelong experiences together with current contextual barriers. These findings suggest opportunities for community mental health services to support healthy eating through nutrition education, cooking experiences, and improving access to affordable, healthy foods.

title: Analysis of nighttime heart rate variability during rapid eye movement and non-rapid eye movement in OSA.
authorString: Niu X, Lu C, Ma L, Zhou Y, Zhu S, Su Y, Xie Y, Wang Z, Yuan Y, Hou W, Feng Y, Liu H, Cai F, Ren X, Shi Y.
abstractText: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a heterogeneous condition. However, many inconsistencies remain regarding the analysis of heart rate variability (HRV) and autonomic nervous system (ANS) function differences among patients with rapid eye movement (REM)-related OSA, nonrapid eye movement (NREM)-related OSA during different sleep periods. This retrospective study included 373 patients with OSA who completed polysomnography (PSG) at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University from May 2023 to February 2024. Patients were classified into REM-related OSA (REM-OSA), NREM-related OSA (NREM-OSA), and non-stage-specific OSA groups according to PSG. Clinical demographics, PSG parameters, and HRV indices were compared across the three groups. Multivariable regression models were constructed to examine the independent associations of AHI and OSA phenotype with HRV, adjusting for age, gender, BMI, and segment duration. A total of 373 OSA patients were included (120 REM-OSA, 90 NREM-OSA, and 163 non-stage-specific OSA). In female patients with mild-to-moderate OSA, no significant differences in HRV were observed across the three phenotypes. In male patients with mild-to-moderate OSA, the REM-OSA group exhibited lower LFnu and LF/HF and higher HFnu during N1 and N2 sleep compared with the other phenotypes. During REM sleep, the REM-OSA group showed higher SDNN than the NREM-OSA group. In patients with severe OSA, the non-stage-specific group showed lower SDNN, RMSSD, and pNN50 during REM sleep than the NREM-OSA group. Multivariate regression showed that AHI was significantly associated with frequency-domain HRV indices across all sleep stages. After adjusting for age, gender, BMI, and segment duration, the REM-OSA phenotype was independently associated with lower LFnu and LF/HF and higher HFnu during N1 and N2 sleep, but not during REM sleep (explaining 8.6%-24.7% of variance). The autonomic effects of REM-OSA are sex-dependent and severity-dependent. In male patients with mild-to-moderate OSA, the REM-OSA phenotype was associated with relative parasympathetic dominance during N1 and N2 sleep, but not during REM sleep. ANS function may not be the primary mechanism linking REM-OSA to cardiovascular risk, and the autonomic profile of REM-OSA is more nuanced than previously recognized.

title: Precision gene targeting: comparative roles of siRNA, miRNA, and CRISPR technologies in gene silencing and genome editing: a review.
authorString: Aboelhassan DM, Abozaid H.
abstractText: Precision gene targeting has emerged as a powerful approach for selectively regulating gene expression and modifying disease-associated genetic pathways. Among the principal technologies, small interfering RNA (siRNA), microRNA (miRNA), CRISPR-Cas9, and CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) provide distinct yet complementary strategies for gene regulation and genome manipulation. siRNAs mediate sequence-specific post-transcriptional gene silencing through degradation of complementary messenger RNA, enabling potent and generally transient suppression of target genes. In contrast, miRNAs are endogenous regulatory RNAs that modulate multiple transcripts through translational repression and mRNA destabilization, thereby influencing diverse cellular processes and regulatory networks. CRISPR-Cas9 expands the scope of precision gene targeting by enabling programmable modification of genomic DNA, whereas CRISPRi uses catalytically inactive Cas9 to achieve targeted transcriptional repression without introducing DNA double-strand breaks. This review provides a comparative and critical analysis of these technologies, emphasizing their molecular mechanisms, target recognition, specificity, delivery strategies, therapeutic applications, clinical development, advantages, limitations, and safety considerations. Collectively, these platforms have demonstrated therapeutic potential across a broad range of diseases, including cancer, genetic and metabolic disorders, cardiovascular and neurological diseases, infectious diseases, and ocular disorders. However, important barriers to clinical translation remain, including delivery limitations, molecular stability, target and off-target effects, immunogenicity, toxicity, genomic instability, and the need for precise and durable control of gene modulation. For CRISPR-based approaches, additional considerations include modality-specific genomic alterations, prolonged editor activity, and the ethical and regulatory implications of permanent genome modification. Continued advances in molecular engineering, delivery technologies, target-selection strategies, and platform optimization may improve the specificity, safety, durability, and therapeutic efficacy of these approaches and facilitate their responsible integration into precision medicine.

title: Semantic alignment of phenotype and disease terminologies for mouse and human facilitates the discovery and validation of human disease genes and variants.
authorString: Feng Q, Smith CL, Dickson AL, Xin Y, Wu H, Serley S, Wei-Qi W, Bult CJ.
abstractText: Leveraging the curated, structured knowledge of phenotype-genotype associations available in model organism databases has proven valuable for predicting gene-disease associations in humans. While efforts to improve algorithms for semantic similarity using phenotype and disease ontologies for mouse and human are ongoing, significant gaps remain. Specifically, there are no comprehensive, validated mappings of equivalent terms from the primary phenotype ontology for the laboratory mouse (i.e., the Mammalian Phenotype Ontology [MPO]) and the human clinical phenotype terminologies (e.g., International Classification of Diseases [ICD] codes) used extensively in electronic health records (EHRs) and for genome and phenotype-wide association studies in human genetics research. Using two case studies, we demonstrate the potential to advance disease gene discovery by bridging EHR-based and laboratory mouse phenotype terminologies and outline the challenges that need to be addressed to realize this potential. We then propose using new methods, such as combining ontology-based and AI-driven similarity matching, to address limitations in previous approaches for mapping equivalent terms in mouse phenotype terminologies and human clinical terminologies; applying these methods, we provide results from preliminary mapping focused on cardiovascular phenotypes to demonstrate the feasibility of cross-ontology alignment and one-to-many mapping. We conclude that such methods, combined with expert manual review for validation and refinement, are needed to bridge the gaps currently limiting the translation of gene-phenotype knowledge from model organisms to the discovery and validation of phenotype-disease-gene associations in humans.

title: From Competence to Expertise in Congenital Cardiology: The LENS Model for Learning to See Problems Differently.
authorString: Venter A, Ryan C, McMahon CJ.
abstractText: Competency-based medical education has improved how paediatric and congenital cardiology defines readiness for independent practice. Competencies and entrustable professional activities describe what trainees should be able to do, and the degree of supervision they require. Competence is an essential threshold rather than the endpoint of professional development. The mechanisms through which a competent congenital cardiologist subsequently develops expertise remain incompletely understood. Research in medical education and cognitive psychology suggests that experts do not simply accumulate more knowledge or more clinical experience. Expertise involves changes in knowledge organisation, clinical problem representation, information selection, recognition of discordance, management of uncertainty, decision-making and adaptation when familiar solutions are insufficient. These concepts are particularly relevant to congenital cardiology, where clinicians integrate complex anatomy, physiology, imaging, haemodynamics, previous interventions and longitudinal trajectories while frequently making decisions despite incomplete evidence. We propose that the expert congenital cardiologist may be distinguished not simply by knowing more answers, but by seeing problems differently. We introduce the LENS model as a conceptual framework for this process: Link information into a coherent clinical representation; Extract the discriminating signal from noise; Notice discordance, uncertainty and possible failure of the initial pattern; and Shift reasoning strategy, seek distributed expertise or learn when the existing model is insufficient. The framework integrates literature on medical expertise, deliberate practice, adaptive expertise, uncertainty and congenital cardiac decision-making. It offers a vocabulary for teaching, faculty development and future empirical study while deliberately preserving the distinction between career stage, reputation and demonstrated expertise.

title: Transpulmonary pressure monitoring in neonates and infants.
authorString: Vedrenne-Cloquet M, Baudin F, Clausen J, Kneyber MCJ, Durrmeyer X, Khemani RG.
abstractText:
Transpulmonary pressure (PL) monitoring has been extensively studied in adult critical care, but evidence remains limited in neonates and infants despite their high vulnerability to lung and cardiac injury. This narrative review summarizes the physiological rationale, measurement techniques, and clinical evidence for PL monitoring in neonates and infants. PL is the distending pressure of the lungs. PL monitoring may help characterize lung stress and strain, assess respiratory effort, guide PEEP selection, and better understand cardiopulmonary interactions. Esophageal pressure monitoring remains the reference method for estimating PL, but its invasiveness and technical limitations restrict its use, particularly in extremely preterm neonates. Alternative approaches, including diaphragmatic electrical activity or airway occlusion maneuvers, may provide less invasive estimates, although most remain insufficiently validated in neonates. Current clinical evidence is scarce but suggests that excessive respiratory effort and elevated lung stress may occur in preterm infants, including during non-invasive respiratory support. PL monitoring may also help to optimize lung recruitment and cardiopulmonary interactions in infants with congenital heart disease or right ventricular failure.

Conclusions

PL monitoring offers a promising physiological approach to individualize respiratory support in neonates and young infants. Further studies are needed to validate minimally invasive or non-invasive surrogates of PL and to determine their clinical relevance in this population. Integration of automated occlusion maneuvers and other advanced monitoring tools into neonatal ventilators may facilitate the transition towards physiology-based, individualized respiratory and cardioprotective strategies.

What is known

• Neonates' physiology may increase their vulnerability to ventilator-induced injuries. • Transpulmonary pressure (PL) reflects the true lung distending pressure, but neonatal evidence remains limited and esophageal pressure monitoring is challenging.

What is new

• Emerging alternatives (diaphragmatic electrical activity and airway occlusion maneuvers) could provide emerging approaches to estimate lung stress and respiratory effort. • PL-informed PEEP titration may help optimize lung recruitment to optimize hemodynamics in neonates with our without congenital heart disease.

title: Clinical evaluation of radiation-shielding effects of a head-and-neck X-ray protective device during cardiovascular interventional procedures.
authorString: Sato T, Shinobu A, Hino T, Yamazaki C, Eguchi Y, Saida T, Chida K.
abstractText: This study evaluated the radiation-shielding effects of a novel head-and-neck X-ray protective device, Triple Guard (TG; Maeda Co., Ltd, Tokyo, Japan), on occupational eye lens dose under routine clinical conditions in interventional cardiologists (ICs) performing coronary interventions and cardiac electrophysiologists (EPs) performing electrophysiological procedures. This observational study was conducted during routine clinical practice between December 2021 and March 2023 and included four physicians (two ICs and two EPs). A DOSIRIS eye lens dosimeter was positioned on the outer side of the left lens of the protective eyewear of each operator. The radiation-shielding effects of TG were evaluated in 289 procedures. Monthly DOSIRIS values obtained during the TG and non-TG periods were compared after normalization by the number of procedures, fluoroscopy time, air kerma at the patient entrance reference point (Ka,r), and air kerma-area product (PKA). For the ICs, the mean radiation-shielding effects were 66% per procedure, 74% per minute of fluoroscopy, 66% per unit Ka,r, and 68% per unit PKA. For the EPs, the corresponding values were 93%, 81%, 88%, and 89%, respectively. These findings suggest that TG may be a useful option for reducing occupational eye lens dose among physicians performing cardiovascular interventional procedures under routine clinical conditions. However, because this was a single-center observational study involving only four operators, further validation through multicenter studies and direct comparisons with conventional protective devices is warranted.

title: Synbiotics Reduce Hypercholesterolemia and Aortic Inflammation Via Modulation of Cholesterol Metabolism.
authorString: Palani Kumar MK, Szmigiel D, Motiram Halami P, Serva Peddha M, Geisberger S, Rauch A, Anders W, Karlik A, Bartolomaeus TUP, Löber U, Wilck N, Kempa S, Haghikia A, Forslund SK, Markó L, Przybyl L.
abstractText: Synbiotics have emerged as a potential intervention to alleviate high-fat diet (HFD)-induced metabolic and cardiovascular dysfunction. Here, we evaluated a novel synbiotic formulation in HFD-fed ApoE⁻/⁻ mice for its effects on lipid metabolism, intestinal and systemic T-cell immunity, and gut microbiome composition. ApoE⁻/⁻ mice were fed a HFD and treated with either vehicle or synbiotics for 4 weeks. Serum LDL cholesterol levels and hepatic lipid accumulation and cholesterol content were assessed. Expression of cholesterol metabolism genes was analyzed in the liver and in the small intestine. Flow cytometry was used to examine T-cell populations in mesenteric lymph nodes and spleen. Gut microbiome composition was profiled by shotgun sequencing, and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) levels were quantified in serum and stool as well as aortic inflammation was evaluated. Synbiotic treatment significantly reduced LDL cholesterol and hepatic lipid accumulation without altering body or organ weights. In the intestine, synbiotics attenuated HFD-induced dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism genes and maintained hepatic cholesterol levels comparable to standard chow-fed mice. Immunologically, synbiotic-fed mice showed reduced Th17 cells in mesenteric lymph nodes and increased cytotoxic T cells in the spleen, indicating immune reprogramming. Despite HFD-induced dysbiosis, synbiotic treatment preserved SCFA-producing taxa, including Lactobacillus johnsonii, Bacteroides fragilis, and Eubacterium spp., and significantly increased fecal butyrate levels. Notably, synbiotic-treated mice showed a complete absence of aortic inflammation, in contrast to vehicle-treated HFD controls. In conclusion, synbiotic intervention ameliorates diet-induced cardiometabolic dysfunction in HFD-fed ApoE⁻/⁻ mice by modulating intestinal cholesterol metabolism, restoring microbiota-derived metabolite production, and reshaping T-cell responses. These findings support synbiotics as a promising strategy to counter diet-driven cardiometabolic dysfunction.

title: Discriminatory value of non-contrast CT coronary artery calcium radiomics for major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with coronary artery disease.
authorString: Song X, Wang W, Ma J, Yin M, Yu M, Zhang J, Qian J, Dai N, Zeng M, Lu H, Jin H, Zhang J, Dai Y.

journal.title: The international journal of cardiovascular imaging

abstractText: To evaluate whether radiomic features derived from non-contrast coronary artery calcium (CAC) CT provide incremental discriminatory information beyond conventional CAC measures for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). This study retrospectively analyzed 208 patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) who underwent coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) from 2014 to 2022. Radiomics features were extracted from each coronary artery segment on non-contrast CT images. Six predictive models were constructed using logistic regression with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LR-LASSO): (1) clinical model; (2) conventional CAC measures model; (3) radiomics-only model; (4) radiomics combined with conventional CAC measures model; (5) radiomics combined with clinical model; and (6) comprehensive model integrating radiomic features, clinical features, and conventional CAC measures. Model performance was evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) analysis, and assessed using the DeLong test with false discovery rate (FDR) correction. In this study, a total of 104 patients with MACE and 104 non-MACE patients were included. The radiomics combined with conventional CAC measures model achieved AUC of 0.830 and 0.825 in the training and testing cohorts. Compared with the conventional CAC measures model, its discriminatory performance was significantly improved in both cohorts (p < 0.001 and p = 0.008). However, further incorporating clinical features into this model did not result in a significant additional improvement in predictive performance (p > 0.05). In this cohort, adding radiomic features to conventional CAC measures improved MACE discrimination, whereas adding conventional CAC measures to radiomics did not significantly improve discrimination.

title: Multi-omics profiling reveals sex-dependent cardiac remodeling and SIRT4-associated metabolic patterns during late-life aging.
authorString: Ma YS, Wu QF, Lin CJ, Liu PY, Xu YM, Chen ZY, Lu CN, Tang DY, Yang QX, Cai YF, Liu BH, Yu H, Ye LY, Wang YZ, Fu D, Huang Y, Xu XD, Zhang L.
abstractText: Extreme longevity is accompanied by cardiac molecular remodelling, yet the basis of sex-associated adaptation during late-life aging remains incompletely understood. Here, we performed cardiac proteomic and multi-compartment metabolomic profiling metabolomic profiling of heart tissue, serum, and urine from naturally long-lived male and female mice across late-life aging stages. Multi-omics analyses revealed pronounced sexual dimorphism during extreme cardiac aging. Proteomic and metabolic changes varied between sexes and across aging transitions, particularly in pathways related to mitochondrial metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, lipid metabolism, and redox homeostasis. Trajectory analyses further demonstrated dynamic and non-linear aging patterns, with distinct temporal patterns observed between males and females across molecular compartments. Among the identified molecular features, SIRT4 emerged as a candidate showing a prominent age-associated change in the female cardiac proteome and associations with mitochondrial metabolic processes. In addition, SIRT4-centered metabolic networks in identified associations between SIRT4 abundance and metabolic features across cardiac and systemic compartments, with more associations observed in females than in males. Importantly, representative histological evaluation showed relatively preserved myocardial morphology in naturally long-lived mice, indicating that these molecular changes occurred in the context of relatively preserved cardiac aging. Collectively, our findings provide a systems-level view of age- and sex-associated cardiac molecular trajectories and identify SIRT4 as a candidate associated with metabolic remodelling during late-life cardiac aging.

title: The role of the frailty index in new-onset cardiovascular disease among middle-aged and older adults with prediabetes and diabetes: an exploratory mediation analysis of depression.
authorString: Bian M, Li Y, Peng F, Wang Z, Yan M, Bu L.
abstractText:
Background

The interplay between frailty and depression as interconnected risk factors for cardiovascular disease (CVD) is increasingly recognised in ageing populations, yet it remains poorly understood among individuals with dysglycaemia. This study aims to clarify their interrelationship and the potential role of depression in the association between the frailty index (FI) and CVD.

Methods

A longitudinal study was conducted using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) 2011-2020. After exclusions, 5,389 participants aged ≥ 45 years with prediabetes or diabetes were included. FI was calculated based on 27 health deficits and multiplied by 10, yielding a scale of 0-10. Covariates and mediator were assessed; statistical analyses included Cox proportional hazards regression and exploratory mediation analysis.

Results

Among the 5,389 participants, 1,432 developed new-onset CVD during follow-up. The baseline FI was significantly higher in the new-onset CVD group (1.90 ± 1.39 vs. 1.50 ± 1.19, P < 0.001). Restricted cubic spline analysis revealed a non-linear association between FI and new-onset CVD. In the multiple imputation analysis, each 1-unit increase in FI was associated with a higher risk of new-onset CVD in the one-line model (HR = 1.20, 95% CI 1.15-1.24; P < 0.001). Two-piecewise Cox regression identified an inflection point at FI = 1.85 (95% CI 1.10-2.68). Below this threshold, the HR was 1.47 (95% CI 1.32-1.65), whereas at or above the threshold the HR was 1.11 (95% CI 1.05-1.17; both were P < 0.001). FI was positively associated with new-onset CVD across subgroups, with significant effect modification by sex but no significant interaction among those with hypertension. Depression accounted for 16.96% (95% CI 7.76%-27.55%) of the total association between FI and new-onset CVD.

Conclusions

The FI was independently associated with the risk of new-onset CVD in adults with dysglycaemia, with a non-linear pattern. In exploratory mediation analysis, depression may partly explain this association. These findings support incorporation of FI and depressive symptom assessment into cardiovascular risk stratification and warrant future studies evaluating integrated interventions targeting both physical and psychological vulnerability.

title: The Changing Metastatic Landscape in the Modern Oncologic Era: Emerging Tumor Behaviors, Procedure-Related Dissemination, and Implications for [<sup>18</sup>F]FDG PET/CT Interpretation: A Structured Narrative Review.
authorString: Ibrahim EA, Alper E.
abstractText: Classical metastatic patterns, rooted in Paget's seed-and-soil hypothesis, have guided oncologic imaging interpretation for over a century. The widespread adoption of immune checkpoint inhibitors, targeted therapies, and minimally invasive surgical techniques has introduced new variables that may alter the metastatic geography encountered on positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT). This structured narrative review examines how modern cancer therapies, prolonged survival, and procedure-related factors have reshaped recognizable metastatic patterns and created new interpretive challenges for [18F]FDG PET/CT readers. A structured literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science (January 2020 to March 2026), supplemented by landmark earlier publications. The Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) guided the review. Evidence was synthesized narratively across four domains: therapy-driven clonal evolution and organotropism, emerging atypical metastatic sites, iatrogenic dissemination, and immunotherapy-era mimics and pitfalls. Treatment-induced clonal selection, tracked through circulating tumor DNA, is increasingly reported as a driver of metastatic evolution toward non-classical organ sites. Atypical metastatic locations, including skeletal muscle, thyroid, and cardiac deposits, are increasingly recognized. Iatrogenic dissemination through port-site implantation (incidence 0.16-2.3%) and needle tract seeding represents a distinct, procedure-related pathway of tumor spread. Immunotherapy-related phenomena, including sarcoid-like granulomatous reactions and pseudoprogression, can mimic or obscure metastatic disease on [18F]FDG PET/CT. Fibroblast activation protein inhibitor-based tracers show promise for peritoneal disease detection, where [18F]FDG PET/CT underperforms. The metastatic landscape on contemporary PET/CT is shaped by treatment pressure, survival prolongation, and procedural factors. Nuclear medicine physicians should calibrate their interpretive frameworks to these evolving realities, integrating clinical context, treatment history, and awareness of emerging metastatic patterns into routine reporting practice. Prospective validation through multi-institutional registries is warranted.

title: PIEZO Channels Within the Hair Cell Mechanotransduction Machine.
authorString: Zheng Y, Lee JH, Chiamvimonvat N, Yamoah EN.

journal.title: Journal of the Association for Research in Otolaryngology : JARO

abstractText: Hair cell mechanotransduction converts sound, head motion, and body position relative to gravity into electrical signals with exceptional speed and sensitivity. Although major components of the mechanoelectrical transduction (MET) complex have been identified, the molecular organization of the native complex and the specific structural and functional contributions of individual proteins remain incompletely resolved. Genetic, physiological, and functional evidence supports the designation of TMC1 and TMC2 as putative components of the MET complex. At the same time, growing evidence implicates PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 in several forms of inner ear mechanosensation, including reversed-polarity currents, high-frequency and ultrasonic hearing, vestibular function, and hair cell development and maintenance. Recent studies further affirm that PIEZO channels localize near stereociliary transduction sites, associate with established MET proteins, and contribute to native hair cell currents. Here we summarize the physiological and molecular framework of hair cell MET, assess the evidence for PIEZO function in hair cells, and highlight priorities for future research. These priorities include defining PIEZO channel roles under native conditions, resolving their nanoscale organization relative to canonical MET components, evaluating the genetic evidence for PIEZO as the pore, reconstituting minimal functional mechanotransduction assemblies, and translating molecular insights into suggestive therapeutic strategies to preserve or restore auditory and vestibular functions during disease and aging.

title: Collaborative APRN stress testing protocols enhance remote cardiology services.
authorString: Schwarz MJ, Patel JR.
abstractText: Cardiac stress testing is a noninvasive method of detecting coronary artery disease and other cardiac conditions. In rural settings, continued closures of rural hospitals, limited resources, and distance to specialty services can hinder timely diagnostic evaluation. To address local rural cardiology care gaps and expand access, the objective was to implement a collaborative advanced practice registered nurse-physician cardiology telemedicine stress testing program at a rural critical access hospital. Risk stratification and procedure workflows were developed to formalize supervision and escalation pathways and are described. Data on stress test volumes, coronary artery disease identification, and cardiac rehab enrollment were collected before and after program implementation. The total volume of cardiac stress tests increased by 62.9%, from 140 to 228. Angiographic obstructive coronary artery disease identification rates doubled from 2% to 4%. Functional exercise stress test completion prior to cardiac rehabilitation and subsequent follow-up enrollment were similar, and enrollment in cardiac rehabilitation remained high. 'Likelihood to recommend' score for noninvasive cardiology postimplementation was 92.2%. Findings indicated that a collaborative advanced practice registered nurse-physician telemedicine program can enhance access to noninvasive cardiology services in a rural setting, possibly enabling earlier detection of obstructive coronary artery disease. The program maintained high cardiac rehabilitation enrollment rates and patient satisfaction scores. These outcomes and the proposed care models support the viability and benefits of such programs in enhancing rural health care delivery.

title: Intermittent Hypoxia Induces Epigenetic Changes and p16-Mediated Senescence in Vascular Dysfunction in Male Mice.
authorString: Cortese R, Cataldo K, Badran M, Milciute M, Gordevicius J, Qiao Z, Eusey J, Khalyfa A, Gozal D.
abstractText:
Study objectives
