In multivariable analysis, new and clinically important echocardiographic findings were associated with an elevated troponin (odds ratio [OR], 2.26; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.22-4.19; P < 0.01) and the absence of a prior echocardiogram (OR, 3.19; 95% CI, 1.67-6.01; P < 0.01).

Conclusions

TTE studies completed overnight were nearly always appropriate by AUC, were frequently classified for overnight performance, and demonstrated a high diagnostic yield of new and clinically important findings; this study did not assess whether these findings changed clinical management. Future work should examine the clinical impact of overnight echocardiography and triage algorithms for directing limited resources. This study describes only TTEs that were completed overnight and does not capture the performance of the triage process among all overnight requests, including those deferred, cancelled, or not performed.

title: Combining metabolomics and genomics to describe genetic factors affecting the metabolism in growing Duroc pigs.
authorString: Bovo S, Bolner M, Holl J, Valente B, Lewis C, Schiavo G, Bertolini F, Fontanesi L.
abstractText:
Background

Metabolites are molecular phenotypes that can provide insights into the basic biological mechanisms underlying complex phenotypes. In this study, we combined high-throughput untargeted plasma metabolomics, analysing over 700 metabolites (including lipids, amino acids, nucleotides, peptides, carbohydrates, cofactors and vitamins, partially characterised molecules, energy-related metabolites and uncharacterised metabolites) and genomic data in a population of growing purebred Duroc pigs. Through this approach, we identified genetically influenced metabolites (GIM), metabolite Quantitative Trait Loci (mQTL) and candidate genes that control metabolite levels and key metabolic pathways. mQTL were detected from metabolite genome-wide association studies (mGWAS) for single metabolites and their ratios, as well as by integrating results from conditional mGWAS.

Results

Genomic heritability (h²G) of 354 metabolites (~ 60% of the filtered metabolomic dataset) was ≥ 0.10, with gamma-glutamylglycine having the highest value (h²G = 0.83). In total, 71 mQTL regions were identified, encompassing 162 metabolites (101 from single metabolite GWAS and 61 from metabolite ratio GWAS). Across all associations, individual SNP explained an average of 15.34 ± 8.38% of the phenotypic variance, with values ranging from 8.12% for N-formylmethionine to 43.50% for N6-methyllysine, which also exhibited the strongest association (p-value = 8.98 × 10- 36). After conditional analyses, 92 out of the 101 associated metabolites identified in single-metabolite mGWAS were characterised by a single major mQTL peak, with the majority of these mQTL being for lipids and amino acids. A total of 83 significant metabolite ratios involving 94 metabolites were deemed significant, with most pointed to mQTL regions previously identified in single-metabolite analyses, along with nine novel mQTL regions. Functional interpretation of mQTL regions based on previous findings in humans and known metabolic pathways highlighted plausible candidate genes for approximately 50% of them.

Conclusions

This study has provided an updated and integrated catalogue of genetic factors that influence the pig plasma metabolome, enhancing our understanding of metabolic regulation at the genomic and pathway levels. By linking genetic variation to biologically relevant metabolic pathways, these findings support the use of metabolomic traits to inform enhanced breeding strategies for complex phenotypes such as growth performance, feed efficiency and resilience.

title: Transapical Beating-Heart Septal Myectomy for Obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
authorString: Wei X, Fang J, Wan S.
abstractText: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a prevalent heterogenous genetic cardiac disorder. In the cardiac myosin inhibitor era, the guideline-directed management of HCM remains an emerging frontier worldwide. Septal myectomy has been the gold standard treatment option for obstructive HCM over the past 60 years. However, the complexity of this procedure and required expertise (and lack of qualified training) have limited its success and availability beyond high-volume HCM centers. Transapical beating-heart septal myectomy (TA-BSM), a newly developed innovative technique, simplifies conventional septal myectomy by eliminating the need for sternotomy, cardiopulmonary bypass, and aortotomy. Most important, the inclusion of real-time intraoperative echocardiographic guidance and evaluation makes TA-BSM safer, more precise, cost-effective, and reproducible. The apparent advantages of TA-BSM, including substantial reductions in surgical trauma and operating times and much faster postoperative recovery in patients with obstructive HCM, are encouraging. TA-BSM is particularly feasible in patients with long-segment obstruction, or small aortic valve annulus, or in those who had undergone previous cardiac operations. The frequent resolution of systolic anterior motion and associated mitral regurgitation after TA-BSM, without concomitant mitral valve intervention, highlights the central role of intraoperative echocardiography and close surgeon-echocardiographer collaboration in achieving optimal procedural outcomes. Further multicenter evaluation of TA-BSM will help define its role among septal reduction strategies for patients with obstructive HCM.

title: A morphological reference index of the abdominopelvic vasculature in the domestic sheep (Ovis aries): A quantitative computed tomography angiography study.
authorString: Amin FM, Haugo C, Banyard FP, Hornung ED, Van Slooten S, Potel KN, Carney JP.
abstractText: Detailed morphological characterization of vascular anatomy is critical for optimizing cardiovascular device design and procedural safety. Although the domestic sheep is an industry standard large-animal model for cardiovascular research, high-resolution reference data for its abdominopelvic vasculature are scarce. This study utilized computed tomography angiography (CTA) and multiplanar reconstructions (MPR) to quantitatively map the abdominopelvic arterial and venous architecture of 24 adult sheep. Major external iliac and femoral and inferior vena cava (IVC) vessels were systematically measured to determine diameter, circumference, and cross-sectional area. Results showed that arteries maintained consistent dimensions with low variability, while veins exhibited segment-specific dimensional elevations and greater variability, consistent with high vascular compliance. Modest correlations with age and weight were observed in select vessel segments. While statistically significant breed-related differences were isolated to select left-sided medial and distal femoral arterial dimensions, breed did not systematically alter the broader abdominopelvic architecture. Comparative analysis revealed segment-specific variations, characterized by distinct bilateral asymmetry within the proximal external iliac arteries, whereas true symmetry was maintained across all femoral artery segments and the venous network, alongside an overall but non-linear proximal to distal tapering. Vessel dimensions converted to French sizing demonstrated that ovine pelvic vessels are anatomically comparable to common human endovascular delivery systems, although procedural feasibility requires in vivo confirmation. These findings establish the first comprehensive CTA-based morphological reference index for ovine abdominopelvic vasculature. This architectural framework provides a critical resource for preclinical endovascular research, facilitating precise device evaluation and procedural planning. Ultimately, the consistent vascular geometry of the domestic sheep reinforces its role as a robust translational model for cardiovascular device development.

title: Guideline-directed discharge medication patterns and post-discharge outcomes in older patients with acute coronary syndrome and multivessel coronary disease: A real-world observational study.
authorString: Dang HNN, Nguyen HM, Tran PT, Ho BA, Luong TV, Nguyen TV.
abstractText:
Background

Guideline-directed medical therapy is central to secondary prevention after acute coronary syndrome (ACS), but recommendations are usually framed at the medication-class level. In discharge practice, clinicians must select individual agents, especially in older patients with multivessel coronary disease. This study described discharge prescribing patterns and examined associations between within-class medication choices and short-term major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).

Methods

This prospective, multicenter, real-world observational cohort included 277 patients aged ≥60 years with ACS and multivessel coronary disease. The primary outcome was 3-month MACE. Risk ratios (RRs) were estimated using modified Poisson regression with robust standard errors.

Results

Core secondary prevention therapies were frequently prescribed, including dual antiplatelet therapy in 99.3% and statins in 99.6%. In fully adjusted within-class analyses, ticagrelor versus clopidogrel had an RR of 0.70 for short-term MACE (95% CI, 0.40-1.21; P = 0.203), empagliflozin versus dapagliflozin had an RR of 1.55 (95% CI, 0.93-2.59; P = 0.094), and rosuvastatin versus atorvastatin had an RR of 1.21 (95% CI, 0.79-1.85; P = 0.372). Exploratory subgroup analyses showed nominal signals for ticagrelor versus clopidogrel among patients with frailty (RR, 0.36; 95% CI, 0.15-0.89; P = 0.026), and for empagliflozin versus dapagliflozin among patients with left ventricular ejection fraction <50% (RR, 1.86; 95% CI, 1.07-3.21; P = 0.027) and non-ST-segment elevation acute coronary syndrome (RR, 2.26; 95% CI, 1.05-4.88; P = 0.037). However, none remained statistically significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons.

Conclusions

In older patients with ACS and multivessel disease, secondary prevention was widely implemented. Within-class comparisons showed no clear short-term MACE differences, while subgroup signals require validation.

title: Flavonoid modulation of the NLRP3 inflammasome: molecular mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
authorString: Shaikh T, Ogale S, Dhangar R.
abstractText: The NLRP3 (NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain containing 3) inflammasome is a critical mediator of innate immune signaling and plays an important role in the pathogenesis of several chronic inflammatory diseases, including gout, type 2 diabetes, atherosclerosis, and neurodegenerative disorders. Although NLRP3 represents an attractive therapeutic target, clinically approved agents that directly inhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation remain limited. Flavonoids, a diverse group of plant-derived polyphenolic compounds, have attracted considerable interest because of their ability to modulate multiple molecular events associated with NLRP3 activation. This review critically examines the molecular mechanisms by which six flavonoids- quercetin, fisetin, luteolin, apigenin, kaempferol, and epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG)-modulate the NLRP3 inflammasome. Particular emphasis is placed on their effects on inflammasome priming, NF-κB signaling, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, ASC oligomerization, autophagy, oxidative stress, and related signaling pathways. The available evidence is evaluated according to the strength of mechanistic support and experimental evidence from cellular, animal, and clinical studies. Among the flavonoids reviewed, quercetin and fisetin demonstrate comparatively stronger mechanistic evidence, whereas evidence for luteolin, apigenin, kaempferol, and EGCG is more frequently associated with indirect modulation of NLRP3-related signaling. Despite promising preclinical findings, limitations including poor bioavailability, insufficient NLRP3-specific clinical biomarkers, and limited human evidence remain major barriers to translation. Overall, flavonoids represent promising but clinically unvalidated modulators of the NLRP3 inflammasome, and future studies should prioritize mechanistically specific biomarkers, improved formulations, and well-designed clinical investigations.

title: ECMO-assisted valve-in-valve transcatheter aortic valve replacement following surgical aortic valve replacement failure in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus-associated libman-sacks endocarditis: a case report.
authorString: Ibrahim N, Batri A, Ammari S, Fala H.

journal.title: The Egyptian heart journal : (EHJ) : official bulletin of the Egyptian Society of Cardiology

abstractText:
Background

Libman-Sacks endocarditis (LSE) is a non-infective valvular manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), affecting 15-30% of patients with APS. Characterized by sterile vegetations predisposing to thromboembolism and valvular dysfunction, optimal anticoagulation and intervention strategies remain challenging, particularly with rapid prosthetic failure.

Case presentation

A 63-year-old African American man with a 20-year history of SLE and triple-positive APS presented with cardiogenic shock five months after surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) for LSE. Echocardiography revealed severe bioprosthetic obstruction (mean gradient 79.6 mmHg, valve area 0.30 cm²). Given prohibitive redo surgical risk (STS-PROM 18.2%), he underwent ECMO-assisted valve-in-valve transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with a 26 mm Edwards SAPIEN 3 valve. Left ventricular ejection fraction improved from 25-29% to 55-59% at 4.5 months, sustained at 50-54% at 8-month follow-up. He remained stable on warfarin (INR 2-3), hydroxychloroquine, and rituximab under multidisciplinary care.

Discussion

This case demonstrates diagnostic challenges differentiating LSE from bioprosthetic valve thrombosis (BPVT); a competing diagnosis that could not be excluded without histopathologic confirmation, critical limitations of DOACs in triple-positive APS, and feasibility of ECMO-supported TAVR as an exceptional rescue strategy. Rituximab was administered for refractory APS, though its independent contribution to the favorable outcome cannot be determined.

Conclusion

To our knowledge, this is the first reported ECMO-assisted valve-in-valve TAVR following SAVR failure in APS/SLE-associated LSE. It emphasizes multidisciplinary care, warfarin-based anticoagulation, immunosuppression escalation, and long-term surveillance for complex autoimmune valvular disease.

title: Taurine metabolism: a potential target for neuroprotection in age-related neurodegenerative diseases.
authorString: Daghini E, Tribble JR, Amato R, Brautaset R, Williams PA.

journal.title: Mammalian genome : official journal of the International Mammalian Genome Society

abstractText: Taurine is one of the most abundant free amino acids in mammals and plays essential roles in cellular homeostasis, mitochondrial function, calcium regulation and neuronal survival. Taurine availability varies markedly across tissues, species and sexes, reflecting the balance between endogenous synthesis, dietary intake, transport and efflux. Although reduced taurine levels have been reported in some aging tissues, recent longitudinal studies indicate that circulating taurine does not decline universally with age, and its value as a biomarker of aging remains debated. Alterations in taurine or its transporter SLC6A6 have been described in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, Huntington's disease and retinal degenerations. Preclinical studies indicate that taurine supplementation mitigates excitotoxicity, stabilizes mitochondrial function, reduces neuroinflammation and supports myelination and synaptic balance. Despite this strong mechanistic rationale, clinical evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, underscoring the need for biomarker-guided trials and a clearer definition of optimal therapeutic windows. In this review, we summarize the general properties of taurine and its metabolic regulation. We examine taurine's neuroprotective properties across different neurodegenerative conditions and discuss future perspectives for targeting taurine metabolism as a promising but largely unexplored strategy for intervention in age-related neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Smooth muscle K  <sub>Ca</sub>  3.1 limits plaque progression and alters plaque composition in mice
authorString: Alam P, Tharp D, Bowles H, Bui H, Bender S, Bowles D.
abstractText:
Increased expression of K Ca 3.1 has been found in vascular smooth muscle cells (SMC), macrophages, and T cells in atherosclerotic lesions from humans and mice. While the efficacy of pharmacological inhibition and global silencing of K Ca 3.1 in limiting atherosclerosis has been demonstrated, the relative cell-specific contributions of K Ca 3.1 have not been determined. Therefore, we generated a smooth muscle (SMC) specific inducible K Ca 3.1 -/- mouse with global Apoe -/- knockout (iSMKO) and assessed lesion development in the brachiocephalic artery (BCA) of tamoxifen vs. vehicle injected iSMKO mice on a Western diet (WD) for 15 or 40 weeks. In BCAs of iSMKO mice, lesion size and relative stenosis were increased and lumenal area decreased compared to vehicle injected mice. Additionally, iSMKO mice exhibited a significant reduction in SMC and collagen content at 15 weeks and 40 weeks, while macrophage content increased at 40 weeks. RNAseq analysis of BCA samples from tamoxifen and vehicle injected iSMKO mice prior to WD feeding (baseline) indicated increased mitochondrial function and PPAR-dependent signaling, similar to that found in prior studies of global K Ca 3.1 silencing. However, following 15 weeks of WD and induction of disease, these differences were no longer observed. Overall, this study provides the first cell-specific silencing of K Ca 3.1 to elucidate the contribution of K Ca 3.1 in smooth muscle to prior observations of K Ca 3.1 silencing. Our findings reveal both a beneficial role of SMC K Ca 3.1 in limiting plaque size and macrophage infiltration, and a potentially detrimental effect of reducing plaque SMC and collagen content. Combined with previous studies, this raises caution in the use of pharmacological K Ca 3.1 inhibitors in atherosclerosis and highlights the need for cell-specific targeting of K Ca 3.1 in optimizing potential therapies.

Highlights

Smooth muscle specific genetic knockout of K Ca 3.1 in mice results in larger atherosclerotic plaques with increased macrophage content revealing a beneficial role of smooth muscle K Ca 3.1 in limiting atherosclerotic lesion development. Silencing K Ca 3.1 in smooth muscle leads to a significant reduction in smooth muscle cell and collagen content within the plaques, consistent with a role for K Ca 3.1 in smooth muscle proliferation and medial-to-intimal cell migration during atherosclerosis. Thus, our findings reveal both a beneficial role of SMC K Ca 3.1 in plaque size and macrophage infiltration, and a potentially detrimental effect of reducing plaque SMC and collagen content, resulting in a lesion with characteristics of a more unstable plaque. RNA sequencing predicted similar downstream signaling effects in both SMC-specific and global K Ca 3.1 silencing, including increased mitochondrial function and PPAR signaling, which likely plays a role in inhibiting smooth muscle proliferation and medial-to-intimal migration in atherosclerosis. While global inhibition of K Ca 3.1 has been demonstrated to have beneficial effects on atherosclerosis development, this study highlights the need for cell-specific targeting of K Ca 3.1 to optimize potential therapies.

title: Identification of JMJD1C as a key mediator of fibroblast remodelling in human AF by single-nucleus multi-omics
authorString: Fu Y, Li L, Tubeeckx MRL, Virzì A, Ekhteraei-Tousi S, Troffaes J, Thienpont B, De Keulenaer GW, Heidbuchel H, Segers VFM, Roderick HL.
abstractText: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most prevalent arrhythmia, accounting for up to 15% of arrhythmias in the elderly. Atrial enlargement associated with fibrotic and hypertrophic remodelling, termed atrial myopathy (AM), is considered a precursor to AF development. The mechanisms underlying the development of AM and its progression to AF remain incompletely resolved. To identify the unique and combined contributions of the major cellular mediators of AM and AF, we combine single-nucleus transcriptomics of human left and right atrial appendages (LAA and RAA) with paired RNA and chromatin-accessibility profiling of 20 LAA samples. We validate these findings through histological and functional studies in primary human cardiac fibroblasts (HCFs). Patients were stratified according to the presence of AF and AM (identified by left atrial volume dimensions; LAVI, Hi and Lo), generating Hi-AF, Hi-SR, Lo-AF and Lo-SR groups that separate AF-associated from structural-remodelling-associated alterations. Across 75,654 qualified nuclei, AF was associated with chamber-dependent shifts in cellular composition and gene expression, with extracellular matrix (ECM) and TGF-β programmes prominent in LAA. Multiome analysis identified a stressed atrial cardiomyocyte (aCM4) state expressing natriuretic peptide A (NPPA) and natriuretic peptide B (NPPB), with altered  cis -regulatory connectivity, and an inflammatory fibroblast (PTGDS  + FB) state characterised by  IL-6 expression and matrix- and TGF-β-associated programmes. Enhancer-driven network analysis identified  GLIS3 ,  TWIST2 and  TBX20 as regulators of FB state transitions. The histone demethylase  JMJD1C was enriched in PTGDS  + FB and induced by TGF-β1; its depletion attenuated α-smooth-muscle-actin (α-SMA) accumulation and reprogrammed TGF-β1-responsive transcription. Ligand–receptor analysis further predicted macrophage-to-FB TGF-β signalling, showing the contribution of macrophages to the atrial inflammatory environment. These data define discrete aspects of rhythm-and structure-associated remodelling of human atrial tissue and identify a candidate macrophage–TGF-β–JMJD1C–FB interaction for potential therapeutic development.

title: Age-dependent downregulation of endothelial lamin A/C impairs mechanotransduction and promotes cardiovascular disease
authorString: Ruiz-Polo de Lara I, Bar A, Gonzalo P, del Monte-Monge A, González-Amor M, Barettino A, Pascual S, Torroja C, Alonso J, Andrés-Manzano MJ, Pyka J, de Rivas Hidalgo G, Berkimbayeva Z, Taurón M, Heymans S, Rodríguez C, Martínez-González J, Dorado B, Millán J, Chlopicki S, Benedicto I, Andrés V.
abstractText:
Aims

Aging is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, but the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated age-associated changes in endothelial lamin A/C expression and the contribution of endothelial lamin A/C loss to cardiovascular dysfunction and disease.

Methods and Results

Aging was associated with reduced endothelial lamin A/C expression in human coronary arteries and mouse aorta and heart. We generated an inducible endothelial-specific Lmna knockout mouse model on an atheroprone Ldlr -null background ( Lmna KO iEC ), which exhibited a 14.6% reduction in median survival. Vascular and cardiac phenotypes were evaluated using vascular reactivity assays, magnetic resonance imaging, blood pressure measurements, echocardiography, histology, nitric oxide assays, and biochemical analyses. Lmna KO iEC mice exhibited increased atherosclerotic burden, impaired endothelium-dependent vasodilation, vascular hyperpermeability, arterial stiffening, and hypertension. They also displayed increased cardiac mass, elevated NT-proBNP levels, incipient myocardial fibrosis, and signs of increased cardiac filling pressures despite preserved systolic function, resembling early stages of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Cardiac proteomics revealed inflammatory, profibrotic, and metabolic remodeling, with enrichment of molecular signatures associated with human HFpEF. Mechanistically, aortic single-cell transcriptomics revealed endothelial activation and suppression of the flow-responsive KLF2–NOS3 pathway. Consistently, endothelial lamin A/C deficiency reduced aortic nitric oxide production ex vivo, while siRNA-mediated LMNA knockdown impaired shear stress-induced KLF2 and NOS3 expression in human aortic endothelial cells.

Conclusion

These findings identify age-associated endothelial lamin A/C downregulation as a previously unrecognized contributor to cardiovascular aging and disease, and suggest preservation of endothelial nuclear mechanotransduction as a potential therapeutic strategy.

Translational Relevance

Our findings identify age-associated endothelial lamin A/C downregulation as a previously unrecognized contributor to cardiovascular aging, linking impaired nuclear mechanotransduction to age-related endothelial dysfunction and cardiovascular pathologies, including atherosclerosis, hypertension, and cardiac alterations resembling early HFpEF. These results highlight endothelial lamin A/C and downstream flow-responsive KLF2-NOS3 signaling as potential targets for therapeutic strategies aimed at preserving endothelial function and mitigating age-related cardiovascular disease.

title: Heart rate variability and calcium economy in sarcoidosis: the role of parathyroid hormone.
authorString: Giallafos E, Katsarou O, Oikonomou E, Tryfou E, Kolilekas L, Lama N, Katsanos S, Seitaridi G, Zisimos K, Tomos G, Drakopanagiotakis F, Steiropoulos P, Manali E, Siasos G, Ilias I.
abstractText:
Background

Sarcoidosis (SA) dysregulates calcium metabolism, causing relatively suppressed/low normal parathyroid hormone (PTH). Autonomic dysfunction, assessed by heart rate variability (HRV), occurs in SA-related cardiac/neurological involvement. Their relationship in SA remains uncharacterized.

Methods

Cross-sectional analysis of 373 SA patients, having 24-h HRV and calcium measurements. Spearman correlations were computed for 11 HRV indices against 5 calcium parameters (PTH, serum calcium, urinary calcium, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25(OH)2D), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D)). Multivariable linear regression models were constructed, adjusting for age, sex, body mass index (BMI), cardiac involvement, corticosteroid use, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus.

Results

The short-term fractal scaling exponent of detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA1) (r = -0.202, p = 0.0001, q = 0.005, n = 370), low-frequency (LF) power (r = -0.165, q = 0.027) and the LF-to-high-frequency ratio (LF/HF) (r = -0.140, q = 0.042) were inversely correlated with PTH. DFA2, the long-term fractal scaling exponent, was positively correlated with PTH (r = +0.147, q = 0.032). Urinary calcium was positively correlated with LF power, LF/HF, DFA1, and mean heart rate (HR) (r ≈ 0.23-0.24, all q < 0.05). SD2, a Poincaré-plot index of longer-term HRV, was positively associated with 25(OH)D (r = 0.166, q = 0.027). In multivariable analysis, DFA1 was independently predicted by age, sex, cardiac involvement, and diabetes mellitus. The PTH-DFA1 correlation was numerically larger without than with cardiac involvement (r = -0.228 vs -0.078), but formal tests did not establish a difference (interaction p = 0.608; Fisher's z p = 0.224). Between corticosteroid users and non-users (r = -0.407 vs -0.155), the interaction was nominally significant (p = 0.035), but Fisher's z test was not (p = 0.062). Subgroup analyses are exploratory.

Conclusions

PTH/urinary calcium associate with fractal and sympathovagal HRV indices in SA. These exploratory findings suggest modest calcium-autonomic associations warranting prospective study.

title: Endocardial TIE1 synergizes with TIE2 to regulate the atrial internal muscular network assembly.
authorString: Ding K, Xu B, Yu X, Jia X, Li T, Shen X, Li J, Cao X, Liu Y, Zhang Z, He Y.
abstractText: Atrial cardiomyopathy is characterized by altered atrial structures, yet its underlying genetic basis remains inadequately explored. TIE1 mutations are reported in lymphedema patients, but whether they exhibit cardiac defects alongside lymphatic abnormalities remains unknown. Here, single-cell RNA sequencing showed high Tie1 and Tek expression in atrial endocardial cells. TIE1 deficiency severely disrupted atrial morphogenesis, with only minor ventricular defects. Bulk RNA-seq showed reduced transcripts for endothelial development and cardiac trabeculation in Tie1 mutants. Separate RNA-seq analysis of the atria and ventricles further confirmed these findings, revealing a more pronounced downregulation of trabecular genes, including Tek, in the atria upon Tie1 loss. Endothelial deletion of Tek impaired trabeculation, particularly in atria. Consistently, Tie1 loss combined with a single null Tek allele disrupted both atrial and ventricular trabeculation. Strikingly, atrial morphogenesis defects appeared within 48 hr of induced endothelial Tie1 loss coupled with Tek heterozygous deletion, implying a critical endocardial role in organizing the atrial muscular network. The synergy of TIE1 and TIE2 in remodeling atrial trabeculae was confirmed postnatally, whereas TIE1 insufficiency alone had no obvious effect. Together, TIE1 is differentially required for atrial versus ventricular development, acting synergistically with TIE2 to regulate endocardial cell-coordinated assembly of atrial internal muscular network.

title: Synergistic modulation of cardiac lipid metabolism by Hedan Pill and Shexiang Baoxin Pill through the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α-carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A axis in experimental heart failure.
authorString: Wang F, Wang L, Zhang Q, Niu G, Li P, Wang Y, Cao C, Ding X, Yan X, Xie L, Yu Y, Li Y.
abstractText: Congestive heart failure (CHF) is associated with profound cardiac metabolic remodelling, particularly in lipid utilization. While Hedan Pill and Shexiang Baoxin Pill are traditional Chinese medicines with cardiovascular benefits, their synergistic mechanisms in CHF remain unclear. Network pharmacology and molecular docking were combined with in vivo validation using ApoE<sup>-/-</sup> mice fed a high-fat diet and subjected to isoproterenol (ISO) treatment. Animals were allocated to seven groups: control, model, Entresto, Hedan Pill, Shexiang Baoxin Pill, Entresto + Hedan Pill, and Entresto + Shexiang Baoxin Pill. Cardiac function, serum lipids, myocardial histopathology, and protein expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α (PPARα), carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) and sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1c (SREBP-1c) were assessed. Network analysis indicated convergence on the PPARα-lipid metabolism pathway, with strong binding affinities between several active compounds and PPARα (≤ -7.0 kcal mol<sup>-1</sup>). In vivo, Hedan Pill or ShexiangBaoxin Pill alone improved ejection fraction, reduced triglycerides, and alleviated fibrosis and lipid deposition. Compared with Entresto alone, both combination regimens further reduced serum triglycerides and LDL-C, whereas ejection fraction did not differ significantly. Mechanistically, both agents upregulated myocardial PPARα and CPT1A while suppressing SREBP-1c. Hedan Pill and Shexiang Baoxin Pill synergistically improve cardiac lipid metabolic homeostasis through the PPARα-CPT1A axis, thereby protecting against CHF-induced myocardial injury. These findings provide physiological and mechanistic evidence supporting their translational potential as complementary interventions in CHF.

title: Analysis of a recent human parvovirus B19 outbreak using a new genomic surveillance system.
authorString: Cordsmeier A, Steininger P, Albrecht JC, Korn K, Ensser A.
abstractText: Human parvovirus B19 is the causative agent of various clinical diseases like erythema infectiosum, transient aplastic crisis, fetal hydrops, reactive arthritis, and rarely potentially fatal organ diseases. The worldwide seroprevalence of parvovirus B19 has been assessed to be about 40-60%. It has been shown that parvoviruses can also infect new host species, adapt, and co-evolve. A comprehensive genomic surveillance is essential to gain a better insight in the adaptation, evolution, and also epidemics of parvoviruses. In the scope of the large parvovirus B19 epidemic 2023/24 following the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, we developed a rapid and convenient system to analyze parvovirus B19 genomes directly from patient samples by next-generation sequencing. We utilized this system to study the part of the unusual outbreak in Southern Germany (Central Franconia), comprising the counties Nuremberg, Fuerth, and Erlangen. This detected a certain genetic diversity within the analyzed samples and identified shared mutations in comparison to reference sequences. Here, two phylogenetically distinct groups were observed, compatible with the co-circulation of at least two B19V lineages in the region and a putative new genotype of human parvovirus B19, possibly induced by immunosuppression was identified. We established a new, quick, and convenient surveillance system for human parvovirus B19 that enables the analysis of outbreaks and monitoring of viral genetic changes.

title: Genetic variants in recurrent euploid pregnancy loss.
authorString: Aminbeidokhti M, Halstead M, Rodriguez-Escriba M, Tise CG, Bernstein JA, Cakmak H, Pollard E, Giudice LC, Merrion K, Shaw GM, Edelman A, Baldwin M, Stevenson DK, Stephenson M, Snyder MP, Sirota M, Lathi RB, Yatsenko SA, Rajkovic A.
abstractText:
Background

Recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL) affects ~ 5% of couples. Known causes of RPL include aneuploidies and unbalanced chromosome rearrangements, however the genetic basis of losses with normal karyotype and chromosomal microarray analysis remains unclear. We hypothesized that deleterious variants in genes essential for early development, including genes previously associated only with neonatal lethal disorders, contribute to RPL.

Methods

Genome sequencing was performed on 118 families with unexplained, euploid RPL; 95% lacked major fetal structural anomalies on ultrasound. A tiered variant prioritization pipeline integrated model organism, human population databases, essential developmental pathways, and fetal transcriptomic profiles. Rare variants (allele frequency ≤ 0.1%) were assessed and confirmed by orthogonal methods. Parental samples were analyzed for mosaicism.

Results

Pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants were identified in 18 families (15.3%) across 17 genes. These include six families with DHCR7, PIEZO1, PIGV, PRF1, SLC12A3, and SMN1 biallelic variants; two cases with ALAS2 and IKBKG hemizygous variants; and four pregnancies with heterozygous alterations inherited from affected parents with MYH3 and TNNI3 variants, and from asymptomatic parents with SCN5A and FLT4 variants. Additionally, four families had presumed de novo heterozygous variants in the EFTUD2, HNRNPK, FGFR2, and KAT6A genes (associated with autosomal dominant conditions), while two exhibited parental germline mosaicism in the FGFR2 and PORCN genes. Variants of uncertain significance were detected in 12 families (10.2%) across the ABCB7, CLPB, CRB2, FBN1, FLT4, GJA1, LYST, MAGED2, PTPN14, RNF213, TLR8, and VPS35L genes. Of 28 genes with plausible variants, 13 genes were previously implicated in perinatal lethality, whereas 15 were novel candidates. Overall, variants in candidate genes were inherited in 80% of families. Four additional families (3.4%) had biallelic ultra-rare variants in genes, which are involved in fundamental developmental pathways but not yet linked to human disease, pointing to a possible role in prenatal lethality. Transcriptomic analyses supported novel gene involvement in hematopoiesis, cardiovascular development, inflammation, and fluid homeostasis processes.

Conclusions

Genome sequencing revealed plausible monogenic etiologies for unexplained euploid pregnancy loss, providing new insights into the biology of early human lethality, phenotypic spectra, recurrence risks, and inheritance patterns. These findings support expanding RPL diagnostics beyond karyotyping and chromosomal microarray analysis.

title: Two-dimensional speckle-tracking imaging for assessing cardiac dysfunction in liver cirrhosis: correlation with Child-Pugh score.
authorString: Ma J, Ding Y, Shao H, Zhang B, Jiang C.
abstractText:
Background

Although two-dimensional speckle tracking imaging (2D-STI) enables sensitive and quantitative assessment of myocardial deformation, its application in patients with liver cirrhosis (LC) has largely been limited to ventricular function. This study applied 2D-STI to evaluate both ventricular and atrial function in order to identify early myocardial dysfunction in this population.

Methods

A total of 82 patients with LC were enrolled and stratified according to the Child-Pugh classification into Class A (n = 30), Class B (n = 29), and Class C (n = 23). Thirty healthy individuals served as controls. All 112 participants underwent conventional echocardiography and 2D-STI assessment.

Results

Compared with controls, all LC groups showed reduced left ventricular global longitudinal strain (LVGLS) and right ventricular free wall longitudinal strain (RVFWLS) (both P < 0.05), with a progressive decline from Class A to Class C. In contrast, right ventricular global longitudinal strain (RVGLS) was significantly decreased only in Classes B and C (P < 0.05). Left atrial conduit strain (LAScd) was significantly reduced across all LC groups (P < 0.05), whereas left atrial reservoir strain (LASr) and contractile strain (LASct) demonstrated a biphasic pattern -initially increased, then decreased- compared with controls. Overall, 2D-STI detected cardiac dysfunction earlier than conventional echocardiography. Significant negative correlations were observed between Child-Pugh score and LVGLS, RVFWLS, and RVGLS.

Conclusion

Cardiac function is impaired in patients with LC and deteriorates with increasing disease severity. Compared with conventional echocardiography, 2D-STI detects cardiac dysfunction at an earlier stage, providing valuable support for early clinical intervention.

title: Drug delivery systems: current applications and future directions.
authorString: Noh K, Jung E, Kim JY, Kim E, Kim S, Yoo W.
abstractText: Drug delivery systems (DDS) have become central determinants of therapeutic feasibility with modern medicines increasingly expanding beyond small molecules to biologics, nucleic acid therapeutics, and living medicines. As therapeutic modalities have continually diversified, delivery technologies, ranging from synthetic nanomaterials and molecular conjugates to biological carriers and hybrid systems have rapidly expanded. The increasing complexity of delivery strategies has thus necessitated conceptual frameworks enabling systematic comparison across platforms while accounting for engineering principles, biological barriers, and disease-specific therapeutic requirements. Accordingly, major delivery modalities now encompass lipid nanoparticles, polymeric and inorganic nanoparticles, targeted molecular conjugates, viral and non-viral vectors, cell- and bacteria-mediated delivery systems, extracellular vesicles, hydrogels, and device-assisted technologies. Although the mechanisms, clinical maturity, and therapeutic applications of these platforms differ substantially, they share common challenges associated with biological complexity, safety, manufacturability, and clinical translation. This review proposes a unified systems-level framework for contemporary drug delivery systems by organizing diverse delivery platforms according to carrier identity, payload class, and targeting mechanism. Engineering principles are integrated with a multiscale biological barrier framework encompassing systemic, tissue-level, cellular, and intracellular processes, thus providing a common mechanistic basis for comparing delivery performance across platforms. Clinical applications are further reorganized as per disease-specific biological barriers and delivery challenges spanning oncology, neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, metabolic, and autoimmune disorders, shifting the focus from platform-centered descriptions toward context-dependent therapeutic deployment. Emerging directions, including AI-enabled design, integrated delivery architectures, manufacturing scalability, and precision deployment, are discussed along with the shared translational bottlenecks that continue to limit broader clinical implementation. By synthesizing the engineering, biological, and clinical perspectives within a common conceptual framework, this review provides an integrated view of contemporary drug delivery systems and highlights the common engineering and translational principles facilitating the rational design, evaluation, and clinical implementation of future drug delivery systems.

title: <i>In situ</i> gelling polymeric hemostatic powders: molecular design, interfacial mechanics and translational outlook of dry-to-wet functional interfaces.
authorString: Wang H, Li Y, Yang S, Xu J, Ma J, Song S, Liu D, Dang Y.
abstractText: Rapid control of hemorrhage in complex, deep-seated, and non-compressible scenarios remains a critical challenge in both surgical and battlefield settings. Conventional hemostats face an intrinsic physicochemical dilemma. Powders offer superior conformability but lack resistance to washout under high-flow conditions, whereas pre-formed hydrogels achieve robust tissue sealing yet cannot be precisely delivered to irregular wound beds. Against this backdrop, in situ gelling polymeric hemostatic powders have emerged as a transformative strategy. By leveraging blood-triggered, ultrafast powder-to-gel phase transition kinetics, these materials realize on-demand switching from a dry, flowable state for delivery to a wet, cohesive state for sealing, reconciling the two sets of mutually exclusive functional demands. This review establishes a comprehensive research framework covering molecular design, interfacial mechanics, and organ-specific material optimization. We first systematically dissect core crosslinking mechanisms and multicomponent synergistic principles that underpin rapid in situ gelation. Subsequently, we analyze tailored material engineering strategies for harsh physiological microenvironments, including acidic gastrointestinal lesions, high-pressure arterial hemorrhage, and deep traumatic cavities. Finally, we identify the remaining cross-cutting challenges and outline future directions, including stimulus-responsive precision crosslinking, artificial-intelligence-assisted molecular design, and multifunctional integration, toward an active hemostatic system that senses the bleeding microenvironment and degrades with programmed kinetics.

title: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation in the Presence of Aortic Coarctation: Current Evidence and Practical Approaches.
authorString: Bajoras V, Širvys A, Petraitytė G, Kundelis R, Usoris L, Davidavičius G, Čėsna S.

journal.title: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions

abstractText:
Background

Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become an established treatment for severe aortic stenosis across a wide spectrum of surgical risk. As TAVI is increasingly used in younger patients and in those with congenital valve disease, the coexistence of aortic stenosis and untreated coarctation of the aorta (CoA) is being encountered more frequently. However, evidence guiding the procedural strategy in this complex anatomical setting remains limited.

Aims

To systematically review the published literature on TAVI in adult patients with untreated or residual coarctation of the aorta, focusing on patient characteristics, procedural strategies, vascular access selection, management of coexisting CoA, and clinical outcomes.

Methods

A systematic literature search was performed in PubMed, Wiley Online Library, ScienceDirect, and the Cochrane Library to identify published reports describing TAVI in adult patients with angiographically confirmed native or residual severe CoA. Case reports and case series published between January 2013 and September 2025 were included. Studies involving repaired CoA without restenosis or surgical aortic valve replacement were excluded. Clinical characteristics, access routes, procedural strategies, and outcomes were analyzed.

Results

Nine patients from published reports met the inclusion criteria. Hemodynamically significant CoA was present in five patients (55.6%). Bicuspid aortic valve anatomy was reported in six cases. Transcatheter access routes included transcarotid (44.4%), transfemoral (33.3%), transsubclavian (11.1%), and transaxillary (11.1%) approaches. A staged strategy with initial CoA stenting followed by TAVI was performed in two patients (22.2%), whereas seven patients (77.8%) underwent single-procedure management, including concomitant treatment of both lesions in two cases. Procedural success was achieved in all cases, although technical challenges related to valve delivery and stent expansion were occasionally encountered.

Conclusions

TAVI in patients with untreated or residual CoA is feasible and can be performed with high procedural success when individualized strategies are applied. Access selection and the timing of CoA intervention should be guided by anatomical characteristics and hemodynamic severity. Given the limited evidence base, careful preprocedural planning and a multidisciplinary approach are essential to optimize outcomes in this complex patient population.

title: Distinct circulating proteomic patterns associated with thoracic aortic diameter and stiffness: A proteome-wide study in the UK Biobank
authorString: Choi A, Hobbs AJ, Tsui J, Hingorani AD, Paliwal N.
abstractText:
Background:

Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is characterized by abnormal dilation and functional remodelling of the thoracic aorta. Current detection and surveillance rely largely on imaging, limiting population-wide risk stratification. Circulating proteins may provide biological insight into aortic remodelling and support future biomarker development. We aimed to identify circulating proteomic patterns associated with imaging-derived thoracic aortic diameter and aortic stiffness in a large population-based cohort.

Methods:

A proteome-wide association study was conducted in 6773 UK Biobank participants with available plasma proteomic and cardiac imaging data. A combined thoracic aortic diameter was derived from taking the maximum of standardized ascending and descending measurements, while stiffness was derived using a pressure-free index of aortic wall properties. Associations with 2920 circulating proteins were evaluated using multivariable linear regression with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Functional enrichment analysis was performed using the complete ranked protein list across Hallmark, curated, and Gene Ontology Biological Process collections. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed as a secondary analysis to explore shared and divergent variation between the two phenotypes.

Results:

In age- and sex-adjusted analyses, 358 proteins were associated with aortic diameter and 60 with stiffness after FDR correction. Sequential adjustment materially altered these associations; in the primary fully adjusted models, 417 proteins were associated with diameter and six with stiffness. Functional enrichment analyses highlighted complement/coagulation, extracellular matrix organization, and contractile pathways associated with aortic diameter. In contrast, although only a few individual proteins were associated with stiffness, rank-based pathway analysis across the full proteome identified a distinct enrichment pattern involving cytokine signalling, protein processing, and intracellular transport. Aortic diameter and stiffness were only modestly correlated (r = 0.21). Secondary PCA showed that the first principal component (PC1) largely overlapped with the diameter-associated profile, with 310 of 370 PC1-associated proteins also associated with diameter. Four proteins (REN, BCAN, GGH and THY1) were associated with both diameter and stiffness in addition to being associated with PC1.

Conclusion:

Circulating proteomic profiling identified markedly different and minimally overlapping molecular patterns associated with thoracic aortic diameter and stiffness. Structural dilation was primarily linked to complement/coagulation, extracellular matrix, and contractile pathways, whereas stiffness reflected a smaller, more distinct aspect of aortic remodelling involving cytokine signalling and cellular transport processes. The four shared proteins across both phenotypes (REN, BCAN, GGH and THY1) represent candidates for further biomarker and causal investigation.

title: Impact of Implantation Site and Bioprosthetic Valve Type on Valve Failure: Analysis of Explanted Valves from Chinese Patients.
authorString: Tang X, Feng W, Zhang H, Li L, Fan G, Wang H, Duan X, Zhai W, Zuo H, Fan Y.
abstractText:
Purpose

Analysis of explanted bioprosthetic heart valves reveals causes of valve failure. While explant studies are common, factors driving rapid valve deterioration remain unclear. Moreover, long-term valve durability is biomechanically influenced. Understanding how implantation site and bioprosthetic valve type biomechanically affect failure modes is crucial to optimizing valve design and longevity.

Methods

121 failed bioprostheses were explanted from Chinese patients aged 5 to 78 years. Patient and valve data were collected. Failure characteristics and rapid-deterioration characteristics were examined and analyzed. Influences of implantation site (aortic vs. mitral) and bioprosthetic valve type (porcine aortic valve vs. bovine pericardial valve) on failure were statistically assessed.

Results

Younger patients exhibited comparable or exceeding implantation durations versus older patients (age ≤ 40 at implant: 121 ± 60 months vs. age > 40: 95 ± 46 months, p = 0.019). Compared to the group with bioprosthetic in-vivo durability > 5 years, vegetation significantly contributed to rapid failure (>5 years: 9% vs. ≤ 5 years: 45%, p < 0.001). Porcine aortic valves and valves in mitral sites (higher diastolic pressure) showed susceptibility to commissural dehiscence or tears. Calcification distribution correlated positively with high-stress regions. Pannus overgrowth, influenced by hemodynamics, was more prevalent on inflow surfaces (higher flow velocity) than outflow surfaces (98% vs. 67%, p < 0.001).

Conclusions

Biomechanical differences in implantation site and bioprosthetic valve type significantly impact valve failure characteristics, which should be considered in future valve improvements and clinical selection strategies. Moreover, we found that rapidly and gradually failed bioprostheses exhibited distinct failure characteristics; valve durability was not reduced in younger patients.

title: Incidence of Aortic Vascular Graft and Endograft Infection in Patients with Bloodstream Infection - A Population-Based Study.
authorString: Cewers A, Sunnerhagen T, Tverring J, Sörelius K, Ljungquist O.
abstractText:
Objective

To assess incidence and predictors of vascular graft and endograft infection in patients with prior aorto-iliac graft surgery and concurrent blood stream infection.

Methods

A population-based observational study was conducted in Skåne, Sweden, between 2010-2022. Patients with prior aorto-iliac graft or endograft surgery were identified in the Swedish Vascular Registry and linked to local blood culture data. Electronic medical records were reviewed according to a predefined protocol and vascular graft and endograft infection was assessed using MAGIC-criteria. Fine-Gray models were used to evaluate predictors of vascular graft and endograft infection diagnosis within three months of a bloodstream infection episode.

Results

A total of 418 patients were identified with 569 bloodstream infection episodes. Of 569 bloodstream infection episodes, 83% (n=473) occurred in men and mean age was 74.9 ± 9 years. The 3-month incidence of vascular graft and endograft infection diagnosis was 7.5%. Elevated C-reactive protein at bloodstream infection onset (sHR; 1.004, 95% CI 1.002-1.007, p<.001) and prior urgent aorto-iliac index surgery (sHR 2.77, 95% CI 1.31-5.87, p=.007) were positively associated with vascular graft and endograft infection. C. albicans (sHR 3.97, 95% CI 1.3-12.1, p=.02), Actinomycetales (sHR 8.29, 95% CI 2.3-29.84, p=0.001), L. monocytogenes (sHR 18.22, 95% CI 11.21-29.63, p <.001) or S. aureus (sHR 1.98, 95% CI 1.05-3.72, p=.03) bloodstream infections were positively associated with vascular graft and endograft infection.

Conclusion

The 3-month incidence of vascular graft and endograft infection diagnosis after bloodstream infection was 7.5%. Clinical suspicion of vascular graft and endograft infection should be higher in patients with prior urgent aorto-iliac surgery, markedly elevated levels of C-reactive protein at index culture, or bloodstream infection with S. aureus, Actinomycetales, L. monocytogenes or C. albicans.

title: First detailed reconstruction of the remipede circulatory system indicates the circumoesophageal vessel ring as a labiocaridan apomorphy.
authorString: Rillich B, Baender A, Iliffe TM, Wirkner CS.
abstractText: Remipedia is a taxon of crustaceans, discovered only in 1981, that inhabit anchialine caves. Their phylogenetic position has long been debated, but recent studies increasingly support a placement as the sister group to Hexapoda, positioning Remipedia as a phylogenetic link that facilitates the interpretation of character transformations between 'Crustacea' to Hexapoda. In this context, the cardiovascular system of Remipedia-so far only scarcely described-is examined here. For this purpose, the cardiovascular and nervous systems of Xibalbanus tulumensis were reconstructed based on µCT scans and semi-thin section series and visualized in 3D. Additionally, section series of various remipede species were examined. A dense network of arteries supplying the superior oesophageal ganglion was identified. Furthermore, a structure described as the circumoesophageal vessel ring (COR) was found. The COR is a broad, triangular vascular ring located posteriorly to the brain, encircling the oesophagus. Based on an ancestral-state reconstruction analysis, this structure is hypothesized here as an apomorphy of Labiocarida, the clade comprising Remipedia and Hexapoda. These findings provide a morphological framework for evaluating cardiovascular character evolution within Tetraconata.

title: GLP-1(9-37) Improves Left Ventricular Function in a Murine Model of Cardiac Pressure Overload by Promoting Mitochondrial Biogenesis.
authorString: Moellmann J, Stöhr R, Maas SL, Winz O, Mottaghy FM, van der Vorst EPC, Lebherz C, Lehrke M, Marx N.
abstractText:
Aim

Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is an incretin hormone that is released in response to nutrient intake and inflammation. Its active form, GLP-1(7-37), binds to the GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R), but GLP-1 is rapidly degraded by dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) into GLP-1(9-37), which does not bind to the classical GLP-1R. Both peptides exhibit cardioprotective effects, although the underlying mechanisms are unclear and the role of GLP-1(9-37) remains poorly understood.

Methods and results

In this study, we investigated cardiac and metabolic effects of GLP-1(9-37) in a mouse model of cardiac pressure overload. LacZ and GLP-1(9-37) were overexpressed using an AAV vector system. While GLP-1(9-37) does not affect glucose metabolism, it mechanistically activates key metabolic regulators, as evidenced by increased AMPK and PGC1α signalling. This shift suggests an improvement in cellular energy balance and mitochondrial function under hypertrophic stress conditions. GLP-1(9-37) was also found to mitigate adverse cardiac remodelling. Treatment is associated with reduced septal thickness and decreased cardiac fibrosis, indicating attenuation of structural hypertrophy.

Conclusions

In summary, our data suggest a protective role of GLP-1(9-37) in pressure-overload-induced cardiac remodelling, which is associated with AMPK/PGC1α-signalling.

title: p66shc N6-methyladenosine methylation induces micronuclear rupture and promotes cardiac fibrosis.
authorString: Liu ZY, Mao S, Liu P, Lin LC, Dong L, Luo H, Tao XM, Yang JJ, Zhao JY, Tao H.
abstractText:
Aims

Dynamic interactions between micronuclear and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species influence micronuclear homeostasis and associated heart diseases. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying micronuclear rupture during cardiac fibrosis remain largely unknown.

Methods and results

Cardiac fibroblast-specific YTHDF1-deficient and wild-type mice were treated with isoproterenol/transverse aortic constriction to induce cardiac fibrosis. To investigate the roles of YTHDF1, p66shc, and m6A modification in cardiac fibrosis, AAV9 vectors carrying a cardiac fibroblast-specific periostin promoter were used to induce p66shc overexpression or deliver small hairpin RNA targeting YTHDF1, along with the m6A inhibitor 3-deoxyadenosine. Histological and molecular biology analyses were conducted to examine how YTHDF1 regulates p66shc mRNA stability during cardiac fibrosis. Additionally, p66shc reconstitution in YTHDF1-deficient cardiac fibroblasts and mouse hearts was performed to assess its effects on micronuclear rupture and fibrosis. Human atrial fibrillation heart tissue was used to validate these findings.During cardiac fibrosis, the increased micronuclear rupture was accompanied by p66shc upregulation and excessive mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production. Fibroblast-specific p66shc depletion inhibited micronuclear rupture, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and fibroblast pyroptosis, and alleviated cardiac fibrosis. Notably, p66shc upregulation was correlated with elevated m6A modification of mRNA. Mechanistically, YTHDF1 recognized the m6A-modified site on p66shc mRNA, enhancing its stability and translation. Conversely, YTHDF1 knockdown inhibits the stability and expression of p66shc, leading to opposing effects. In human atrial fibrillation heart tissues, increased YTHDF1 and p66shc levels were associated with enhanced micronuclear rupture, excessive mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production, fibroblast pyroptosis, and cardiac fibrosis.

Conclusions

This study revealed a novel epigenetic mechanism in which m6A methylation of p66shc drives micronuclear rupture and exacerbates cardiac fibrosis. These findings provide new insights into potential measures for preventing cardiac fibrosis.

Translational perspectives

These findings reveal a clinically significant role of the YTHDF1/p66shc axis in mitigating cardiac fibrosis. Targeting m6A methylation of p66shc to suppress mitochondrial ROS generation, micronucleus rupture, and cardiac fibroblast pyroptosis may offer a promising therapeutic strategy for cardiac fibrosis.

title: Introducing the Open Educational Resource PAVIN: a blended-learning, interprofessional multiplayer virtual reality training in paediatric emergencies.
authorString: Müller PA, Widder A, Flayyih O, Straub C, Heinzmann A, Stiller B, Köpper H.
abstractText:
Background

The inherent dynamics of paediatric emergencies create substantial challenges for interprofessional teams and limit the availability of an optimal learning environment for developing emergency‑care competencies. Consequently, there is an increasing demand for educational approaches that replicate the dynamics of paediatric emergencies while offering a safe learning environment. Virtual reality (VR) scenarios deliver realistic, repeatable training experiences that allow novice interprofessional teams to acquire their first exposure in challenging situations. To encounter the demand paediatric-emergency trainings, we aimed to implement a blended-learning course that couples e-learning modules with VR scenarios and incorporates objective feedback systems.

Methods

We developed the Paediatric virtual reality emergency training (PAVIN), an interprofessional blended-learning course that integrates three complementary components: (1) preparatory e‑learning modules, (2) on-site sessions and (3) multiplayer VR scenarios. The case‑based e‑learning modules supply the theoretical basic medical knowledge and introduce essential non‑technical skills in communication and interprofessional collaboration. Interprofessional tandems - comprising medical, nursing and midwifery students and nursing apprentices - subsequently train in multiplayer VR simulations, offering a safe, reproducible learning environment.

Results

The pilot phase demonstrated that PAVIN could be implemented successfully. Of the ten participants, nine (90% response rate) completed the evaluation questionnaire and awarded the course an overall "very good" rating. They gave positive scores across several self-reported domains: they judged the course highly relevant to their future work, reported heightened interest in interprofessional learning and found the blended-learning framework appropriate. Moreover, participants reported that the immersive VR scenarios helped them internalise paediatric-emergency procedures and that communication and collaboration with their tandem partner improved. We integrated multiple feedback mechanisms throughout the course, encompassing both the e-learning modules and the multiplayer VR scenarios, which participants found useful. They are supplemented with team-performance instruments, such as the virtual Team Performance Observation Tool (vTPOT) and pre- and post-intervention self-assessments.

Conclusion

PAVIN is a blended-learning course that offers a safe environment for participants to gain experience in paediatric-emergency care and communication while training in interprofessional teams. Multiple feedback systems are embedded to enable data-driven debriefings. Available as an Open Educational Resource (OER), PAVIN may represent a promising approach for interprofessional medical education, could help meet the ongoing demand for paediatric-emergency training and might has the potential to support medical education in patient safety.

title: Retrograde Approach Through Arteriovenous Loop Creation for Difficult Balloon Pulmonary Valvuloplasty.
authorString: Egala A, Chawla R, Agarwal A, Swain A, Kumar B.
abstractText:
Objective

Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty (BPV) is traditionally performed using antegrade femoral venous approach. However, in severe pulmonary stenosis with challenging anatomy where conventional strategy fails, an arteriovenous loop approach through the patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) can be successful. We describe successful BPV in a 4-year-old child using this approach.

Key steps

1) Traverse the pulmonary valve retrogradely from the aorta through the PDA. 2) Externalize the guidewire using a snare. 3) Perform stiff-wire exchange. 4) Introduce a valvuloplasty balloon over the arteriovenous loop for serial dilatation.

Potential pitfalls

1) Arterial access site complications in young children: ensure appropriate sheath size, adequate anticoagulation, patent hemostasis. 2) Tricuspid subvalvular apparatus injury and balloon entrapment. Meticulous echocardiographic and fluoroscopic guidance is needed during retrograde crossing. Track a balloon-wedge or standard diagnostic catheter over the arteriovenous loop before rigid hardware.

Take-home message

Retrograde arteriovenous loop creation via the PDA is an effective and safe bailout strategy for BPV in severe pulmonary stenosis when the pulmonary valve is not crossed antegradely.

title: Evidence-Aware Missense Variant Interpretation with a Typed-Decision Language Model
authorString: Lomoio U, Veltri P, Guzzi PH.
abstractText: The interpretation of missense variants requires the integration of sequence, structural and evolutionary evidence, yet most computational predictors operate on specialised representations rather than curator-readable descriptions. We investigate whether a typed-decision language model can use this evidence directly. Using GLiDE-9B, we construct four increasingly informative text representations and evaluate them on a gene-disjoint ClinVar benchmark derived from 199,243 germline missense variants. On 33,478 commonly scored test variants, zero-shot ROC-AUC rises from 0.817 with variant-level information alone to 0.933 with conservation. Low-rank adaptation on 20,000 gene-disjoint ClinVar training variants yields ROC-AUC 0.976 and average precision 0.944, compared with 0.973 and 0.941 for REVEL; the difference in ROC-AUC is significant (DeLong p = 4.5 × 10−5), whereas the average-precision difference is not (p = 0.14). A second adapter trained using population- and primate-derived proxy labels, without ClinVar labels as optimisation targets, achieves ROC-AUC 0.940 and average precision 0.862; however, ClinVar validation labels are still used for checkpoint selection and calibration. The ClinVar- trained model achieves a calibrated Brier score of 0.054 and validation-derived thresholds corresponding to PP3/BP4 evidence strengths up to Strong. These results are qualified by lower performance than leading comparators when ranking variants within individual genes, more modest associations with functional assays, and near-chance performance in autism and congenital heart disease case–control comparisons. The findings support evidence-aware decision modelling as a complementary approach to missense variant prioritisation, while emphasising the need for prospective, independently curated validation before clinical use

title: Consensus Statements on the Clinical Practice for Patients With Fontan-Associated Liver Disease.
authorString: Kanto T, Akagi T, Yamagishi H, Ohfuji S, Tokuhara D, Kusano H, Sakamori R, Tateishi R, Kogiso T, Yoshizumi T, Muneuchi J, Toh N, Inuzuka R, Ohuchi H.

journal.title: Hepatology research : the official journal of the Japan Society of Hepatology

abstractText: The Fontan procedure has been transformative for patients with univentricular physiology. By using a single ventricle as the systemic pump and relying on passive venous return to drive pulmonary circulation, Fontan circulation alleviates cyanosis and heart failure, allowing children to engage in normal activities during school and adolescence. Nevertheless, Fontan circulation is characterized by chronically elevated systemic venous pressure, which leads to systemic venous congestion and long-term multiorgan effects. Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD) is now recognized as a major long-term complication. Approximately 50% of patients develop hepatic abnormalities within 10-20 years after surgery, and some progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Despite this risk, strategies to identify individuals at high risk for early HCC and to provide better prognostic information remain limited. This article compiles knowledge from congenital heart disease specialists and hepatologists on FALD, including areas where evidence is limited. By facilitating early diagnosis, structured follow-up, and multidisciplinary management of FALD, this initiative aims to improve outcomes, build a nationwide clinical experience, and ultimately support the development of formal, evidence-based guidelines for FALD management.

title: Markers of Cardiovascular Risk Associated With Pregnancy.
authorString: Crooks T, Kondapalli L.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

We sought to provide a brief review of available scores and factors to consider when assessing cardiovascular risk of pregnancy. We also discuss maternal cardiovascular risk stratification of survivors of childhood and adolescent cancer and congenital heart disease and identify gaps in knowledge.

Recent findings

The modified WHO 2.0 I-IV in conjunction with the CARPREG II provides the most robust risk score to date but still has shortcomings. No score specifically addresses cardiovascular risk of pregnancy in survivors of cancer. While several tools for assessing risk exist, consideration of patient-specific factors also play an important role. Moderate and high-risk patients may be best cared for by multidisciplinary teams.

title: Birth and long-term health outcomes of intrauterine offspring after local methotrexate treatment for heterotopic pregnancy: A retrospective study and focused literature review.
authorString: Chen Q, Wan S, Li Q, Liu S, Yang Y, Xing L, Sun S, Bai L, Tang M, Zhu Y.

journal.title: International journal of gynaecology and obstetrics: the official organ of the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics

abstractText:
Objective

To report birth outcomes and long-term intellectual and physical development follow-up data of intrauterine offspring after local methotrexate (MTX) injection for heterotopic pregnancy (HP), and to summarize relevant published cases.

Methods

We included 29 patients with HP involving uncommon ectopic implantation sites who underwent transvaginal ultrasound-guided local MTX injection to treat the ectopic gestation (2006-2023). We evaluated birth outcomes and the intellectual and physical development in offspring aged 4-17 years, and conducted a focused review of published cases from 1990 to 2025 via PubMed.

Results

Pregnancy outcomes were available for 27 of 29 patients. Twenty-four women delivered 26 live-born offspring, including 23 without and three with congenital anomalies (congenital heart disease, hypospadias, and multiple craniofacial and limb abnormalities, respectively). Matched comparative analyses included 11 preschool-aged, eight school-aged, and seven adolescent offspring. Across the cognitive, anthropometric, blood pressure, and laboratory outcomes assessed, three between-group differences showed nominal P-values of below 0.05, involving preschool uric acid, school-age systolic blood pressure, and adolescent blood urea nitrogen. Among these, the systolic blood pressure difference was accompanied by high-normal blood pressure or hypertension in some offspring in the MTX group. None of the three differences remained statistically significant after Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. After the exclusion of overlapping observations, the focused literature review identified 14 independent live-born offspring from previously reported cases, of whom two had congenital anomalies.

Conclusion

Most live-born offspring following local MTX treatment for HP had no congenital anomalies, and no long-term offspring outcome comparison remained statistically significant after FDR correction. However, congenital anomalies were reported in both our cohort and the published literature, and the small sample size and limited evidence preclude firm conclusions regarding long-term safety.

title: Adult Care in a Pediatric Hospital: Patterns and Implications of an Internal Medicine Consult Service at a Children's Hospital.
authorString: Goodman A, Herbst B, Kinnear B, Caldwell A, Kelleher M, Damari N, Weber D, Janiczek J, Knopp MI, Schoenberger A, Peterson RJ.
abstractText:
Objective

Adults with childhood-onset conditions are increasingly admitted to children's hospitals, yet many pediatric systems lack the infrastructure and expertise to manage adult-related medical needs. One approach to bridge this gap is the use of an adult medicine consult service. We aim to describe the demographics, clinical complexity, and consultation patterns of patients admitted to a freestanding children's hospital and evaluated by an adult medicine consult service, which is a current gap in the literature.

Patients and methods

A retrospective descriptive cohort study was performed of admitted patients with a Hospital Medicine Adult Care (HMAC) service consult from July 2014 through June 2023.

Results

Annual adult admissions increased over the study period, from 7.4% to 10.2% of all admissions. HMAC consulted on 1666 admissions for 1008 unique patients (median age, 27 years [range, 14-71 years]). The most frequent reasons for consult were venous thromboembolism prophylaxis (33.7%), age older than 25 years (21.2%), transition of care (7.6%), and hypertension (7.6%). HMAC physicians addressed a mean of 5.5 diagnoses per encounter. Patients averaged 3.6 admissions (range, 1-22) and 4.9 comorbidities (range, 0-21) each. The most common comorbidities were technology dependence (47%), solid tumor malignancy (22.5%), genetic conditions (20.2%), epilepsy (19.7%), congenital heart disease (17.4%), and cerebral palsy (15.7%).

Conclusions

Adult consult services in children's hospitals support a medically complex population with diverse childhood-onset and adult conditions and function as longitudinal clinical partners. These findings support the role of adult medicine expertise in children's hospitals to help recognize and manage adult-specific care needs and transitions.

title: Coronary Embolism Followed by Concurrent Superior Mesenteric Artery and Infrarenal Aortic Embolism in Atrial Fibrillation Despite Full Anticoagulation and Dual Antiplatelet Therapy: A Fatal Case of Acute Mesenteric Ischemia.
authorString: Rizon M, Da Silva Eli G, Damasceno TK, Celezinsky M.
abstractText: We describe a patient with atrial fibrillation (AF) in whom embolic events involved the coronary, mesenteric, renal, and aortic territories within four days, the last of them during full-dose anticoagulation and dual antiplatelet therapy. A 52-year-old woman presented in AF with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction caused by thrombi in the proximal and distal apical segments of the left anterior descending artery, without atherosclerotic disease; revascularization was planned for a later stage. Echocardiography showed an apical left ventricular (LV) thrombus, and therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin was started. On the fourth day after admission, despite full-dose anticoagulation and dual antiplatelet therapy, she developed abdominal pain and distension with hemodynamic instability. Computed tomography angiography showed an extensive filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery from its origin, a concurrent filling defect in the infrarenal abdominal aorta, left renal infarction, pneumatosis intestinalis, and portal venous gas. Emergency laparotomy revealed necrosis of the entire small bowel and colon with microperforations. Given the non-salvageable extent of necrosis, the abdomen was closed, and comfort care was provided. The patient died 12 hours later. In this patient, a second embolic event occurred within days of an embolic myocardial infarction despite therapeutic anticoagulation, and the CT findings at diagnosis already indicated non-salvageable bowel. The case illustrates why new abdominal symptoms in an anticoagulated patient with a recent cardioembolic event warrant immediate imaging and surgical assessment.

title: Emergency Mastectomy for Necrotizing Fasciitis of the Breast During Lactation: Case Report.
authorString: Dereje WM, Bogale AD, Tassew MT, Abera SA, Kefale GG, Amare AG.
abstractText: Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly progressive infection of the skin, soft tissues, and fascia, most commonly affecting the groin, abdomen, or lower limbs, while breast involvement is particularly uncommon. Patients often present with redness, swelling, and fever following trauma, and delayed presentation can lead to tissue necrosis and septic shock. Despite advances in diagnosis, mortality remains high, especially when the condition occurs in unusual sites like the breast, where diagnosis may be delayed or missed. A 46-year-old para 7 woman presented with a one-week history of right breast swelling that began as a small ulcer in the upper outer quadrant and rapidly progressed to involve the entire breast, right axilla, and chest wall, with severe pain, purulent discharge, fever, and malaise. She delayed seeking care, assuming it would resolve spontaneously. Although necrotizing fasciitis carries high morbidity and mortality, early recognition, initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotics, and prompt surgical excision of necrotic tissue before the onset of septic shock are crucial for successful outcomes. In this case, despite late presentation, timely surgical and antimicrobial management resulted in complete recovery and wound healing at 6 weeks.

title: Feasibility of AI-Guided Handheld Echocardiography for Rheumatic Heart Disease Screening by Non-Cardiologists in Rural Nepal: A Mixed-Methods Diagnostic Accuracy Study
authorString: Alattar H, Magesh D, Pal A, Mureau-Haines R, Young T, Ronen K, Zhang D, Pal JD.
abstractText:
Background

Rheumatic heart disease remains a major cause of preventable morbidity and mortality in rural Nepal, where access to cardiovascular specialists and echocardiography is limited. We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and feasibility of AI-guided echocardiography performed by nurse practitioners for community-based RHD screening.

Methods

We conducted a triangulation mixed-methods study (QUAN > qual) combining a paired cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study with semi-structured interviews during community screening camps in Damak, Nepal, in November 2025. Nurse practitioners performed AI-guided handheld echocardiography using EchoNous Kosmos Plus devices, with cardiologist overread serving as the comparator. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, and kappa. Interviews were analyzed thematically.

Results

Of 90 participants enrolled, 76 were included in the final analysis. Mean age was 50.8 years, 57.8% were male, and 42.2% had undergone prior cardiac evaluation. Detection of any valvular lesion demonstrated 95.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity, with near-perfect agreement with cardiologist interpretation (κ=0.97). Lesion-specific performance included mitral regurgitation sensitivity 66.7% and specificity 97.3% (κ=0.55), mitral stenosis sensitivity 100% and specificity 97.2% (κ=0.81), aortic regurgitation sensitivity 90.9% and specificity 96.9% (κ=0.84), and tricuspid regurgitation sensitivity and specificity of 100% (κ=1.00). Mean scan duration was 5.8 minutes. Portability, AI-assisted acquisition, and remote review facilitated implementation, while training needs, workflow constraints, and technical issues were barriers.

Conclusions

AI-guided handheld echocardiography performed by nurses demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy and feasibility for rural RHD screening. AI-assisted task-shifting may expand access to early RHD detection in underserved settings.

title: High-fat diet-altered expression profile of mitochondrial functional molecules contributes to myocardial remodeling in type 1 diabetes mellitus.
authorString: Lv H, Zan S, Ma J, Qiu X, Lei Y, Chen W, Guan F, Dong W, Lu D.
abstractText:
Background

The most frequent underlying cause of death for type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is cardiovascular damage. Extreme fat consumption causes deterioration in lipid metabolism in DM; however, how a high-fat diet (HFD) affects the progression of pathological process of diabetic myocardial dysfunction, especially the identification of candidate intervention targets, has become an urgent need.

Methods

The T1DM Syrian golden hamster model was induced by streptozotocin (STZ) injection, and a 6-week HFD intervention (42.0% calories from fat) was given in the early stage of T1DM. Changes in body weight and biochemical indicators of glucose and lipid were tracked weekly.
