Aortic cross-clamp time was not associated with 30-day mortality when analyzed as a continuous variable; however, an exploratory cutoff of ≥ 63 minutes was associated with increased mortality (HR 3.20, 95% CI 1.34–7.65, p = 0.009). In univariable Cox regression, MELD-XI ≥ 12.5 (HR 2.87, 95% CI 1.13–7.32) and lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L at 18 hours (HR 4.47, 95% CI 1.48–13.52) were associated with 30-day mortality, but neither remained independently associated in multivariable analysis. Conclusions Biological markers, including MELD-XI and lactate, could provide complementary prognostic information before and after ECMELLA implantation, whereas the prognostic value of a prolonged aortic cross-clamp time, observed only in an exploratory threshold analysis, remains uncertain.

title: In-hospital inclisiran for early LDL-C lowering after atherosclerotic ischemic stroke: an observational pilot study.
authorString: Merlino G, Sperotto R, Toraldo F, Marinig R, Janes F, Lorenzut S, Kuris F, Nesi L, Tereshko Y, Bax F, Gentile C, Gigli GL, Valente M.

journal.title: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology

abstractText:
Background

Guidelines recommend low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) below 55 mg/dL and a ≥ 50% reduction in very-high-risk patients, including after atherosclerotic stroke. Recurrence risk peaks in the acute phase, yet oral therapy reaches target slowly. Early in-hospital use of inclisiran after stroke is largely unexplored.

Objective

To assess the feasibility of in-hospital inclisiran after high-risk ischemic stroke and describe the early LDL-C trajectory.

Methods

Single-arm observational pilot study from a prospective single-center registry. Fifteen consecutive adults with ischemic stroke due to large-artery atherosclerosis or branch atheromatous disease meeting Italian fast-track reimbursement criteria received inclisiran 284 mg during admission on top of intensified oral therapy. LDL-C was measured at baseline, days 3, 7, 10, 14, and three months.

Results

Fifteen of 18 eligible patients (83.3%) were treated, a median of 3 days after the LDL-C result. Baseline LDL-C was 138 mg/dL and fell to 75 and 31 mg/dL at days 3 and 14 after the dose (median reductions 45% and 77%). The composite goal (≥ 50% reduction from the acute-phase baseline and LDL-C < 55 mg/dL) was met by 33.3% at day 7, 80.0% at day 14, and 86.7% at a median of 87 days. Oral therapy was modified in 13 patients, so inclisiran's contribution cannot be isolated. No recurrent stroke or inclisiran-related adverse event occurred.

Conclusions

In-hospital inclisiran was feasible, and most patients reached the goal within two weeks of the combined regimen. These hypothesis-generating findings warrant a controlled study measuring proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9, with clinical outcomes and longer follow-up.

title: Beyond the target vessel: CT pitfalls in acute chest pain.
authorString: Ko SM.
abstractText: Acute chest pain computed tomography can succeed technically yet fail clinically when interpretation stops at the requested vascular territory, enhancement is inadequate, or disease evolves after a negative examination. This pictorial essay illustrates target-vessel tunnel vision, partial diagnostic success mistaken for complete exclusion, and false reassurance after an initial study. The cases emphasize review of all acquired structures, scanner-specific protocol selection, and recognition of limitations imposed by coverage, contrast timing, and cardiac phase. Wider cardiac acquisition windows and delayed myocardial imaging should be selected to answer a specific unresolved question while limiting radiation and avoiding treatment delay. Reports should identify the likely cause of symptoms, distinguish diagnostic from nondiagnostic territories, and link unresolved findings to an appropriate next step.

title: Resuscitation strategies incorporating peripheral perfusion targets in septic shock: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
authorString: Bispo EJS, de Melo Baptista L, da Cunha CBC, Monteiro VS.
abstractText: Resuscitation strategies incorporating peripheral perfusion targets (RSIPPT) have emerged as promising tools in septic shock. However, whether they improve clinically relevant outcomes remains uncertain. We aimed to evaluate whether these strategies reduce 28/30-day mortality and improve other clinical outcomes compared with usual care. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) using a random-effects model was conducted. Electronic searches of PubMed, EMBASE, and CENTRAL were performed through May 27, 2026 (PROSPERO CRD420261400115). The RoB 2 and GRADE tools were used for assessment of risk of bias and certainty of evidence (CoE), respectively. Five RCTs involving 2180 patients with septic shock were included. Compared with conventional strategies, RSIPPT were not associated with significant differences in 28/30-day mortality (four RCTs; RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.78-1.09; I2 = 10%; moderate CoE) or 90-day mortality (three RCTs; RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.83-1.05; I2 = 0%; low CoE). However, RSIPPT were associated with fluid reduction during the first 6-8 h of resuscitation (three RCTs; MD -264.53 mL, 95% CI -425.28 to -103.77; I2 = 1%; low CoE). No significant differences were observed in intensive care unit or hospital length of stay, organ dysfunction, vasopressor-free days, ventilator-free days, or renal replacement therapy-free days. In early septic shock, RSIPPT were associated with a modest reduction in resuscitation fluid during the first 6-8 h. A mortality reduction was not demonstrated, although clinically important benefit or harm cannot be excluded. Differences in intervention algorithms and comparators limit attribution of these findings to peripheral perfusion monitoring itself.

title: SGLT2 Inhibitors in Stage 5 Chronic Kidney Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Cardiovascular and Kidney Outcomes
authorString: Ahmed HM, Rehman Uu, Owais M.
abstractText: **Background:** Evidence supporting sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor use in stage 5 chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains limited because major randomized trials have largely excluded this population. We evaluated associations between SGLT2 inhibitor use and cardiovascular and kidney outcomes in patients with stage 5 CKD.  **Methods:** We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Google Scholar through April 10, 2026. Studies comparing SGLT2 inhibitors with nonuse or other glucose-lowering therapies were eligible. Hazard ratios (HRs) were pooled using random-effects models, and risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I. Certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE.  **Results:** Five observational cohorts met inclusion criteria, of which three contributed to the meta-analysis, comprising 57,156 participants, including 28,559 SGLT2 inhibitor users. SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with fewer heart failure hospitalizations (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.72-0.85) and acute myocardial infarctions (HR 0.64; 95% CI 0.56-0.72). Associations with all-cause mortality (HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.58-1.21) and dialysis initiation (HR 0.63; 95% CI 0.30-1.33) were not statistically significant. In analyses restricted to treatment-initiation cohorts, the association with fewer heart failure hospitalizations persisted, whereas the myocardial infarction association was no longer significant. Certainty of evidence was low or very low across outcomes.  **Conclusions:** Observational evidence suggests potential cardiovascular benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors in stage 5 CKD, particularly fewer heart failure hospitalizations. Effects on mortality, dialysis initiation, and myocardial infarction remain uncertain. Dedicated randomized trials are needed to establish efficacy and safety in this population.

title: Limb Salvage and Clinical Outcomes of Percutaneous Versus Surgical Deep Venous Arterialization for No-option Chronic Limb-threatening Ischaemia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
authorString: Balomenos V, Moschovaki-Zeiger O, Giannaki K, Filippiadis D, Lechareas S.
abstractText: To compare percutaneous with surgical deep venous arterialization for no-option chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and to examine whether percutaneous outcomes differ by device type. MEDLINE was searched via PubMed on 8 August 2026. Eligible cohorts reported at least 10 limbs with Rutherford class 5 or 6 chronic limb-threatening ischaemia. Hybrid procedures were classified as surgical; superficial venous arterialization was excluded. The primary endpoint was 12-month limb salvage. Proportions were pooled on the logit scale using random-effects models with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman confidence intervals. Device type was a pre-specified secondary analysis. Eleven cohorts comprising 470 limbs were included-eight percutaneous (382 limbs) and three surgical or hybrid (88 limbs). Pooled 12-month limb salvage was 71.0% (95% confidence interval [CI] 66.0-75.5%; I2 = 0.5%), with no significant difference between modalities (71.8% vs. 72.6%; p = 0.81). Technical success was 95.9% (91.7-98.0%) and did not differ between modalities (p = 0.69), but within the percutaneous arm was higher with a dedicated system than with off-the-shelf technique (97.9% vs. 94.3%; p = 0.03). Amputation-free survival was 59.5% (50.1-68.2%), and reintervention occurred in 43.5%; neither was reported by any surgical cohort. Egger test indicated small-study effects (p = 0.009). Deep venous arterialization achieved limb salvage in approximately 71% of patients with no-option chronic limb-threatening ischaemia. Limb salvage did not differ between percutaneous and surgical approaches, whereas technical success was higher with a dedicated device. These indirect comparisons from single-arm cohorts do not establish superiority of either technique. Level 3 a-Systematic review of non-randomized observational studies.

title: Biofilms in drug-coated medical devices: Mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance and perspectives on new approaches.
authorString: Patwekar M, Patil A, Patwekar F, Kari ZA, Ahmad Mohd Zain MR, Mohammed A, Parratte S.
abstractText:
Background

Bacterial biofilms are a major cause of treatment failure in orthopedic implant surgery, contributing to a large proportion of chronic, device-associated infections. Biofilms contain bacteria that are able to survive antimicrobial concentrations 10-1,000-fold higher than the planktonic equivalent, and antimicrobial-coated implants, which are designed to limit this risk, can still be colonized after depletion of the antimicrobial reservoir on the implant. This systematic review aims to address how biofilm-associated antimicrobial resistance occurs on drug-coated orthopedic devices and what current and future strategies can be employed to prevent it.

Methods

During the preparation of this manuscript, a literature base of 72 references was identified and screened for direct or translatable relevance to orthopedic implants and musculoskeletal device-associated infection, using explicit criteria. Eligible studies focused on mechanisms of biofilm formation or antimicrobial resistance or on the efficacy of device technology designed to inhibit fouling or disrupt biofilms or incorporate drugs. Non-orthopedic devices (urinary, cardiovascular, dental) were included only where they provided an example of a mechanism or coating that had a reasonable chance for translation to orthopedics and are marked as such throughout.

Results

The formation of a biofilm on orthopedic implant surfaces occurs in five broadly accepted stages: reversible attachment, irreversible adhesion, formation of microcolonies, maturation, and dispersal, with most of the orchestration of these stages being regulated by quorum-sensing signaling. The resistance of mature biofilm is due to multiple overlapping mechanisms, including the limitation of matrix diffusion, oxygen and metabolic gradients that stimulate the growth of persister cells, upregulation of efflux pumps, enzymatic degradation of drugs, and increased horizontal gene transfer. In a pooled analysis of seven comparative studies, current drug-coated orthopedic devices (e.g., gentamicin- or silver-coated tibial nails and arthroplasty components) have been found to have a lower periprosthetic infection rate than uncoated devices (2.93, 95% CI 1.72-4.99, p < 0.001). Antifouling (PEG-based) surface modifications, enzymatic matrix-disrupting agents, bacteriophage-based therapies and biosensor-triggered smart implants are consistently effective in vitro and in pre-clinical models, although only limited clinical-trial evidence has been generated for most of these approaches related to orthopedic implants.

Conclusions

The scientific basis for biofilm-related resistance mechanisms is solid and heterogeneous: the quantitative efficacy claims of next-generation coatings have been supported by in vitro or preclinical studies, but not by orthopedic clinical studies. Future clinical trials in the field would focus on novel clinical evaluation of antifouling and enzymatic methods for preventing prosthetic joint infections, standardized reporting of biofilm results, and the risk-stratified use of antimicrobial coatings to reduce unnecessary antimicrobial exposure.

title: A Fine-Tuned Large Language Model Workflow to Support Risk of Bias Assessment: Development, External Validation, and Reviewer Verification Study.
authorString: Li Y, Chen J, Liang L, Geng X, Wang G, Geng J.
abstractText:
Background

Given that randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard for effectiveness research, assessing their risk of bias (RoB) becomes an indispensable step in systematic reviews. Yet this task remains time-consuming and prone to reviewer subjectivity. While large language models may accelerate the process, they lack transparent, traceable judgments linked to trial reports.

Objective

To bridge methodological gaps and improve both efficiency and consistency, this study developed and externally validated TRoB-1, a fine-tuned open-weight large language model workflow for RoB assessment of RCTs.

Methods

TRoB-1 was developed specifically for the Cochrane risk of bias tool version 1 (RoB 1), which is the most widely adopted instrument for critical appraisal of RCTs. The workflow generates preliminary judgments and supporting quotations from reviewer-selected passages for the target RoB domains. The workflow was built on 2-stage supervised fine-tuning of Gemma 2-9B-Instruct using 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation. The training set comprised 4321 RoB records extracted from systematic reviews of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, and hypertension. The validation set consisted of 161 records from recently published RCTs covering a broader disease area. The reference standard was established by 2 independent reviewers. Two clinicians blinded to the reference standard verified TRoB-1-assisted assessments through a locally hosted web interface. Using the same reference standard, the performance of TRoB-1 raw outputs was compared with that of the Gemma 2 base workflow, and clinician-verified outputs were compared with raw TRoB-1 outputs.

Results

TRoB-1 successfully generated structured outputs for all 161 validation records. In independent clinician-assisted assessments using the same workflow, raw TRoB-1 accuracy ranged from 73.3% (n=118) to 73.9% (n=119), compared with 52.2% (n=84) to 60.2% (n=97) for the Gemma 2 base model. After verification, accuracy ranged from 82.0% (n=132) to 84.5% (n=136) and macro-F1 from 0.709 to 0.776. Accuracy remained higher for raw TRoB-1 after excluding invalid base-model outputs, and verification did not change any correct judgment to an incorrect one. Clinician 1 corrected 13 initially incorrect judgments and clinician 2 corrected 18. The F1-score for judgments of high-RoB increased from 0.600 to 0.784 for clinician 1 and from 0.571 to 0.821 for clinician 2.

Conclusions

TRoB-1 combined task-specific fine-tuning, evidence-linked outputs, and clinician verification in a transparent workflow for reviewer-supported RoB assessment. The TRoB-1 web interface provides a practical platform for integrating RoB into evidence synthesis, particularly for living systematic reviews where timely updates are critical.

title: Lipid-lowering therapy for secondary stroke prevention beyond statin monotherapy: a mechanism-informed approach across drug classes and stroke subtypes.
authorString: Hsieh CY, Sung SF.
abstractText:
Introduction

Intensive lipid lowering is crucial for secondary prevention of ischemic stroke, but achieving low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) targets and selecting additional agents beyond statins are challenging. Stroke mechanisms vary in their contribution to atherosclerosis, so the benefits, risks, and treatment burdens of aggressive LDL-C reduction may differ among phenotypes.

Areas covered

The authors searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar for studies published through September 2026 on lipid-lowering therapy after ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack. The authors prioritize randomized trials, subgroup analyses, stroke-specific observational studies, meta-analyses, and major guidelines or consensus documents and assess the evidence by study design, stroke phenotype, and whether outcomes were clinical events or surrogate measures, including LDL-C target attainment and plaque imaging.

Expert opinion

Future lipid management after ischemic stroke could improve by combining stroke phenotype and atherosclerotic burden with established cardiovascular risk and LDL-C targets. Early combination therapy may help plaque-driven stroke patients reach targets, but its effect on recurrence is unproven. Evidence is limited by few stroke-specific trials, reliance on surrogate endpoints, and barriers including advanced imaging and biologic reimbursement. Phenotype-stratified trials should test whether mechanism-informed care improves outcomes and cost-effectiveness beyond guidelines.

title: Association Between Revascularization Timing and Outcomes for Coronary Artery Disease in Patients Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation.
authorString: Yamaguchi M, Yamanaka F, Shishido K, Moriyama N, Ochiai T, Miyashita H, Sugiyama Y, Sato D, Koyama E, Shimizu K, Tobita K, Matsumoto T, Mizuno S, Tanaka Y, Murakami M, Saito S.
abstractText:
Background

Coronary artery disease (CAD) is common in patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS), yet the optimal timing of coronary revascularization in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) remains uncertain.

Methods

We retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients with severe AS and stable CAD, defined as fractional flow reserve ≤0.80, instantaneous wave-free ratio ≤ 0.89, or visual stenosis ≥90%, who underwent TAVI between October 2013 and July 2023. Patients were categorized into two groups: PCI-first and TAVI-first. The primary endpoint was 1-year incidence of major adverse cardiac events (MACE: all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, and unplanned revascularization). The secondary endpoint was 3-year MACE stratified by PCI after TAVI among the TAVI-first group.

Results

Of 1126 TAVI patients, 209 met criteria for concomitant CAD (PCI-first, n = 112; TAVI-first, n = 97). The TAVI-first group had lower frailty and fewer New York Heart Association functional class III/IV symptoms, whereas the PCI-first group had more blood transfusions. At 1 year, the crude incidence of MACE was higher in the PCI-first group, although this difference was not significant after propensity score adjustment (HR 1.62; 95% CI 0.60-5.2; p = 0.36). Among TAVI-first group, patients who underwent PCI after TAVI had a lower incidence of MACE (log-rank p = 0.007), but the 90-day landmark analysis showed no significant difference (0/24 vs. 5/62 events; log-rank p = 0.23).

Conclusions

In patients with severe AS and CAD, a PCI-first strategy was associated with a higher incidence of bleeding and transfusion without improvement in short-term outcomes. A TAVI-first strategy with selective PCI during follow-up may be a reasonable alternative, although the long-term benefit of post-TAVI PCI awaits confirmation in randomized trials.

title: Management of Spinal Surgery in Severe Hemophilia B under Marstacimab Prophylaxis.
authorString: Pfrepper C, Weise M, Kalus U, Siegemund A, Siegemund T, Klöter T.
abstractText:
Abstract

Marstacimab is an antibody directed against tissue factor pathway inhibitor aiming to rebalance hemostasis in patients with severe hemophilia. There are currently no reports on the management of patients under marstacimab prophylaxis undergoing major surgeries outside clinical trials. We report a patient with severe hemophilia B and a history of myocardial infarction who underwent major elective spinal surgery followed by urgent revision surgery while receiving marstacimab prophylaxis. For the first operation, the last dose of marstacimab was administered 12 days before surgery and plasma-derived factor (F) IX was administered to achieve a trough level of 50 IU/dL to maintain hemostasis. For the second operation, performed only seven days after the last marstacimab dose, the trough level was reduced to 30 IU/dL to limit the potential additive prothrombotic effect of both agents, as relevant residual marstacimab concentrations were expected. No relevant bleeding occurred. To prevent thrombotic complications, both surgeries were performed under thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin, and acetylsalicylic acid was continued. Thrombin generation was normalized under marstacimab and equal or higher than with 54 IU/dL FIX activity depending on the assay. This supports our strategy of providing sufficient FIX replacement while minimizing thrombotic risk. Due to the long half-life of marstacimab, low factor trough levels may be sufficient to provide adequate hemostasis in patients undergoing major surgeries.

title: Therapeutic Effects of Biochanin A in Diabetic Myocardial Injury: Evidence from an Experimental Model
authorString: Bechir MLE, Akin AT, Ceylan T, Kaymak E, Varinli Ş, Toluk A.
abstractText: Objective Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a diabetes-associated cardiovascular complication characterized by progressive myocardial structural remodeling and functional deterioration, representing a leading cause of diabetes-related morbidity and mortality. Biochanin A (BCA), a phytoestrogenic isoflavone derived from Trifolium pratense , exhibits pleiotropic biological activities including antidiabetic, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant effects. This study evaluated the therapeutic effects of BCA in a streptozotocin (STZ)-induced rat model of diabetic myocardial injury. Methods Forty male Wistar albino rats were randomized into four groups: Control, BCA (20 mg/kg/day), STZ (45 mg/kg), and STZ + BCA, with BCA administered i.p. for 30 days post-induction. Cardiac stress markers (ANP, NT-proBNP), endoplasmic reticulum stress (GRP78), and apoptosis (caspase-3) were assessed via immunohistochemistry, alongside serum myocardial injury markers (CK-MB, hs-cTnT, LDH), oxidative stress parameters (SOD, CAT, MDA), and pro-inflammatory mediators (TNF-α, IL-6, NF-κB). Results BCA treatment significantly reduced hyperglycemia, increased SOD and CAT levels, decreased MDA, reduced circulating TNF-α, IL-6, and NF-κB, and lowered serum myocardial injury markers. Immunohistochemistry showed reduced ANP, NT-proBNP, GRP78, and caspase-3 immunoreactivity, accompanied by improved myocardial architecture on histopathology. Conclusion These findings suggest that BCA exerts multitarget therapeutic effects on diabetic myocardial injury, through modulation of glycemic, oxidative, inflammatory, and ER stress-related apoptotic pathways, highlighting it as a promising candidate for the management of diabetic cardiac complications.

title: Community health worker-led hypertension management with independent prescribing in rural Lesotho: a cluster-randomised non-inferiority trial.
authorString: Gerber F, Sanchez-Samaniego G, Gupta R, Lejone TI, Tahirsylaj T, Raeber F, Esquivel-Valdés I, Saavedra EB, Mathulise M, Kabi T, Mokaeane M, Maphenchane M, Molulela M, Khomolishoele M, Mota M, Mofokeng M, Sematle MP, Sao L, Tlahali M, Litaba M, Basler DB, Kindler K, Ayakaka I, Grimm P, Burkard T, Chammartin F, Amstutz A, Labhardt ND.
abstractText:
Background

Hypertension is the leading global risk factor for premature mortality, yet treatment coverage and control remain poor, particularly in low-income and middle-income countries. Whether community health workers can manage hypertension, including independent prescribing and titrating of antihypertensive therapy, remains unknown. We aimed to assess whether hypertension care led by community health workers with independent prescribing was non-inferior to usual facility-based care for maintaining blood pressure control among adults with treated, controlled hypertension.

Methods

We conducted a pragmatic, cluster-randomised, open-label, non-inferiority trial in 103 villages in rural Lesotho. Adults with treated, controlled hypertension (<140/90 mm Hg) were eligible. Villages were randomly assigned 1:1, stratified by district and access to health facility, by an independent statistician using a computer-generated sequence to hypertension care led by community health workers, including independent prescribing and titrating of antihypertensive therapy (amlodipine/hydrochlorothiazide combination pills at doses of 5 mg amlodipine and 12·5 mg hydrochlorothiazide or 10 mg amlodipine and 25 mg hydrochlorothiazide) with clinical decision support, or to usual nurse-led, facility-based care. The primary endpoint was blood pressure control at 12 months among all randomised participants except individuals who became pregnant during follow-up, with a non-inferiority margin of -10 percentage points absolute risk difference. The study has been completed and is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05684055).

Findings

Between Sept 8, 2023, and May 31, 2024, we enrolled 807 participants (417 in 51 control villages, 390 in 50 intervention villages; two empty clusters; mean age 64·4 years [SD 14·3]; 82% female). At 12 months, blood pressure was controlled in 300 (78%) of 386 participants in the intervention group and 303 (74%) of 412 in the control group (adjusted odds ratio 1·29, 95% CI 0·93-1·80); non-inferiority was met. The adjusted absolute risk difference was 5·1% (95% CI -0·9 to 11·2). Serious adverse events (deaths and hospitalisations) were similar in the two groups, with no excess events attributed to the intervention.

Interpretation

These findings support community-based hypertension care with task-sharing to trained community health workers as a promising approach to maintaining blood pressure control, especially in settings with limited access to physician-led and nurse-led hypertension care.

Funding

Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, World Diabetes Foundation, and Swiss National Science Foundation.

title: Nonculprit Lesion Complexity and Timing of Complete Revascularization in Patients Presenting With Acute Coronary Syndrome and Multivessel Disease: Insights From the BIOVASC Trial.
authorString: Scherillo G, Elscot JJ, Bennett J, Sabaté M, Esposito G, Boersma E, den Dekker WK, Van Mieghem NM, Diletti R.
abstractText:
Background

The optimal timing of complete revascularization for patients with acute coronary syndrome, multivessel disease and complex nonculprit coronary lesions (NCL) remains unclear.

Methods

The BIOVASC trial randomized patients with acute coronary syndrome and multivessel disease to immediate complete revascularization and staged complete revascularization. The primary end point was a composite of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, unplanned ischemia-driven revascularization, or cerebrovascular events at 2-year follow-up. In this exploratory post hoc analysis, patients were classified as having complex NCL if at least 1 nonculprit lesion met the following criteria: true bifurcation; severe calcification; lesion length >20 mm; aorto-ostial lesion; left main lesion. We aimed to compare a strategy of immediate complete revascularization and staged complete revascularization in patients presenting with acute coronary syndrome and multivessel disease with complex NCL. Moreover, we sought to compare patients with complex and noncomplex NCLs in terms of clinical outcomes.

Results

Among the 1525 patients enrolled in the BIOVASC trial, 550 (36.1%) had a complex NCL. The presence of a complex NCL was associated with a significantly higher incidence of the primary end point compared with noncomplex NCL (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.49 [95% CI, 1.11-2.02]; P=0.01), including spontaneous myocardial infarction (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.86 [95% CI, 1.12-3.09]; P=0.02). In patients with complex NCL, the cumulative incidence of the primary end point was 15.7% in the immediate complete revascularization group and 17.5% in the staged complete revascularization group (hazard ratio, 0.86 [95% CI, 0.57-1.31]; P=0.49). No significant interaction was observed between the presence of a complex NCL and revascularization strategy for the primary end point (P for interaction=0.40).

Conclusions

In patients with acute coronary syndrome and multivessel disease, patients with complex NCL experienced worse clinical outcomes at 2-year follow-up, driven by higher rates of myocardial infarction. However, no statistically significant interaction was observed between NCL complexity and the effect of immediate complete revascularization versus staged complete revascularization.

Registration

title: Challenges for human oversight in detecting system malfunctions in AI-assisted medical diagnostics.
authorString: Schlicker N, Tepohl C, Kholmovaia A, Steffens N, van Berkel N, Mayr A, Grgic I, Hirsch MC, Langer M.
abstractText: Increasingly, physicians must oversee AI systems to detect system malfunctions. We studied 48 physicians in a randomized controlled study using an increasingly malfunctioning AI for cardiac auscultation. Diagnostic performance declined alongside AI reliability, even when physicians were cognitively forced to make an initial classification, and when human performance exceeded AI reliability. Physicians' confidence declined faster than their trust in AI. Results call for specification of oversight goals and processes ensuring patient safety.

title: Effectiveness of ultrasound-guided versus surgeon-delivered superficial parasternal intercostal plane (SPIP) block in adult cardiac surgery: a randomized controlled trial.
authorString: Mohammed AA, Abdelrady MM, Mohamed Sayed AA, Gad El Rabb N, Farouk M, Ali MA.

journal.title: Revista espanola de anestesiologia y reanimacion

abstractText:
Background

Superficial parasternal intercostal plane (SPIP) block is increasingly used to improve analgesia after cardiac surgery. This study compared the analgesic efficacy and clinical outcomes of ultrasound-guided versus surgeon-delivered SPIP block in adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery via median sternotomy.

Methods

This prospective, randomised controlled trial included 88 adult patients undergoing elective valve replacement surgery. Patients were randomly assigned to receive either ultrasound-guided SPIP performed by an anaesthesiologist (Group P, n = 44) or surgeon-delivered parasternal block under direct vision (Group S, n = 44). Both groups received 40 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine. The primary outcome was postoperative pain intensity assessed using the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) during the first 24 hours after extubation. Repeated pain measurements were analysed using a linear mixed-effects model. Secondary outcomes included time to first rescue analgesia, 24 -h fentanyl consumption, extubation time, ICU length of stay, chronic pain assessed using the Leeds Assessment of Neuropathic Symptoms and Signs (LANSS) questionnaire at 3 and 6 months, and patient satisfaction.

Results

Exploratory pairwise analyses suggested lower postoperative NRS scores in Group P at 6, 12, 16, 20, and 24 hours after extubation. However, the primary linear mixed-effects analysis demonstrated a significant effect of time (p < 0.001) but no significant overall treatment effect (p = 0.198) or group × time interaction (p = 0.408). Compared with Group S, Group P had a longer median time to first rescue analgesia (20 [16-24] vs 12 [9.5-12] h; p < 0.001), lower 24 -h fentanyl consumption (100 [0-125] vs 300 [200-300] µg; p < 0.001), and a shorter ICU stay (2 [2<-- -->-3] vs 3 [3<-- -->-4] days; p < 0.001). Group P also demonstrated lower LANSS scores at 3 months (2 [2<-- -->-3] vs 4 [3<-- -->-5]; p = 0.001) and 6 months (0.5 [0<-- -->-1] vs 2 [2<-- -->-3]; p = 0.001).

Conclusion

Although the predefined longitudinal mixed-effects analysis did not demonstrate a significant overall treatment effect on postoperative pain intensity, ultrasound-guided SPIP was associated with lower opioid requirements, prolonged time to first rescue analgesia, shorter ICU stay, and reduced long-term neuropathic pain compared with surgeon-delivered parasternal block. Although exploratory analyses showed lower pain scores at selected postoperative time points, the primary longitudinal mixed-effects model did not demonstrate a significant overall treatment effect. Ultrasound-guided SPIP may therefore be considered a valuable component of multimodal analgesia for adult cardiac surgery, particularly where ultrasound expertise and equipment are available.

title: Comparing learning outcomes in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) basic life support training using self-training video with learning feedback vs. traditional onsite training in a running population
authorString: Triganjananun C, Kitiyakara T, Saelee R, Atiksawedparit P, Chalermdamrichai P, Chumkliang P, Phattharapornjaroen P.
abstractText: Background: Sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) can occur during running events and immediate and effective cardiopulmonay resuscitation (CPR) significantly improves survival. Training race participants in basic life support (BLS) could potentially increase survival chances during these events. Online learning may improve access to BLS training by reducing instructor, travel and organizational costs. While online video training alone may not fully replicate in-person learning, this study explores a refined online training model with online platform feedback. The aim was to compare CPR performance, knowledge, and confidence scores in traditional onsite training vs. self-training video with learning feedback as an alternative method for teaching BLS. Methods: Runners were invited into the study and voluntarily participated in either 1) traditional BLS training or 2) online self-training videos with learning feedback. CPR training dummies were sent to public parks and running groups for the VDO group to use. Both groups were assessed for CPR performance by certified BLS instructors, and self-assessments for knowledge and confidence scores in BLS were collected through a questionnaire before and after the training. Result: Of the 738 included runners, 161 participants were in the VDO group, and 577 were in the onsite training group. BLS competency was achieved by 97.5% of the video group and 99.8% of the face-to-face groups (p value = 0.25). Knowledge and confidence scores increased statistically significantly in both groups. Although improvements were observed, the increase in knowledge scores in the VDO group was associated with an odds ratio of 0.5 (95% CI: 0.34, 0.74, p-value of 0.001), and the increase in confidence for assisting unconscious patients was with an odds ratio of 0.33 (95% CI: 0.22, 0.5, p-value of <0.001), compared with the F2F group. Conclusion: Self-training videos with learning feedback achieved competent BLS skills in runners and improved knowledge and confidence in performing basic life support, but to a lesser extent than onsite training. Such a method could potentially be used to increase BLS training in runners. Clinical trial number : not applicable.

title: Non-invasive and invasive imaging for guiding PCI of chronic total occlusions.
authorString: Rubio PM, Dijkstra T, Saboe A, Sanchez AA, Henriques JPS, Opolski MP, Nap A, Dan K, Sanz Sanchez J, Waksman R, Claessen BEPM, Garcia-Garcia HM.
abstractText:
Introduction

Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for chronic total occlusions (CTO) remains technically challenging, with lower technical success than non-CTO PCI. Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) may improve procedural and stent-related outcomes by supporting procedural planning, lesion crossing, and stent optimization.

Areas covered

A literature search of PubMed, Google scholar, identified randomized trials, registries, observational studies, meta-analyses, and consensus documents on CCTA and IVUS in CTO PCI. CCTA enables three-dimensional assessment of cap morphology, occlusion length, tortuosity, calcification, and distal vessel quality, refining complexity assessment and strategy selection. IVUS provides real-time guidance for proximal cap identification, guidewire position, reentry techniques, vessel sizing, and stent optimization. Artificial intelligence and image co-registration are also discussed.

Expert opinion

CCTA and IVUS provide complementary information across the stages of CTO PCI. Selective preprocedural CCTA may be most valuable in anatomically complex lesions, whereas IVUS supports lesion crossing and should be strongly considered for stent optimization. Wider adoption will depend on workflow integration, operator training, automated image analysis, and prospective validation of imaging-guided strategies.

title: Clinical and Venographic Distinctions Between Extrinsic and Intrinsic Dural Venous Sinus Stenosis: Implications for Venous Stenting.
authorString: Schartz D, Tanzillo D, Santos AN, Bender MT, Hauck EF.
abstractText:
Introduction

Dural venous sinus stenosis (VSS) is associated with intracranial hypertension and may be treated with venous sinus stenting. VSS can be either extrinsic (extramural compression related to elevated ICP) or intrinsic (narrowing typically due to arachnoid granulations), with potentially important clinical distinctions and implications for venous stenting.

Materials and methods

We performed a single-center retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients evaluated with catheter venography for suspected VSS and/or cerebral venous outflow disorders from October 2021 to March 2026. Patients were categorized as having intrinsic or extrinsic venous stenosis. Clinical distinctions between groups were investigated.

Results

Among 162 patients (mean age, 40.2 years; 96% female), 108 (67%) had extrinsic and 54 (33%) had intrinsic stenosis. Patients with extrinsic stenosis were younger (35.6 vs. 49.5 years; P<0.0001), had higher BMI (38.1 vs. 34.8 kg/m2; P=0.018), and higher opening pressure (36.0 vs. 29.3 cmH2O; P=0.006). Extrinsic stenosis was associated with higher torcula pressure (30.1 vs. 25.7 mmHg; P=0.03), higher trans-stenotic pressure gradient (15.8 vs. 11.9 mmHg; P=0.02), and more frequent occipital emissary venous drainage (62% vs. 44%; P=0.03). Ninety patients (56%) underwent stenting. Pulsatile tinnitus clinically resolved in 20/22 patients (91%) with intrinsic stenosis versus 29/43 (67%) with extrinsic stenosis (Fisher exact P=0.065, Pearson χ2 P=0.038). Symptomatic stent-adjacent stenosis occurred in 7/58 (12%) of stented extrinsic patients and 0/32 (0%) stented intrinsic patients and was significantly different (Fisher exact P=0.048, Pearson χ2=0.041). Other stenting outcomes did not differ significantly.

Conclusions

Extrinsic and intrinsic VSS have distinct clinical and venographic profiles and may have different outcomes following venous stenting, suggesting they could represent related but distinct venous outflow disorders. Further research may optimize venous stenting patient selection and inform clinical trial design.

title: Weight loss at a cost: Semaglutide and PYY3-36 aggravate pre-existing metabolic osteoporosis in female Wistar rats.
authorString: Kloock S, Zytner P, Geiger N, Sequeira V, Schmitt-Böhrer A, Felker J, Sarwar H, Weich A, Ignatius A, Fassnacht M, Haffner-Luntzer M, Dischinger U.
abstractText: Incretin mimetics like semaglutide and peptide YY3-36 (PYY3-36) reduce appetite and body weight, however their individual and combined effects on bone in the setting of metabolic disease and associated osteoporosis (MetOP) lack mechanistic insights. Here, female Wistar rats were randomized to: [1] Healthy control, [2] MetOP-Saline, [3] MetOP-Sema, [4] MetOP-PYY, [5] MetOP-Sema+PYY. Animals in group 2-5 received a "Western diet" in combination with nitric oxide synthase inhibitor L-NAME to induce MetOP as previously described. Randomization to treatments occurred in week 9. After 16 weeks, femora were collected for micro-computed-tomography, histological analysis, RNA-seq, and qPCR. Serum was analyzed for bone turnover markers and steroid profiles (LC-MS/MS). Semaglutide alone and in combination with PYY3-36 significantly reduced body weight. Semaglutide induced a modest reduction in trabecular bone volume fraction (BV/TV), whereas PYY3-36 alone and in combination with semaglutide caused more pronounced trabecular deterioration, with the combination group exhibiting increased trabecular separation. Cortical bone parameters were unaffected. Osteoclast numbers were increased in the semaglutide and PYY3-36 groups. Gene expression analysis demonstrated only mild changes in femora of semaglutide-treated rats, while PYY3-36 treatment significantly upregulated angiogenesis- and extracellular matrix-associated genes. Collectively, these findings suggest that semaglutide modestly impairs bone health. PYY3-36 treatment led to deteriorated bone markers and increased resorption, potentially limiting its clinical application. Semaglutide and PYY3-36 in combination further aggravate bone loss in MetOP. These findings highlight the need to evaluate gut hormone-based weight loss strategies for long-term skeletal safety, especially in the vulnerable setting of pre-existing osteoporosis.

title: Efficacy and safety of posterior wall isolation in persistent atrial fibrillation is modified by ablation energy source.
authorString: Zhang DT, Chadha S, Kaiteris A, Amancherla S, Almasry IO, Fan R, Rashba EJ, Singh A.
abstractText:
Background

Posterior wall isolation (PWI) is a common adjunct to pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) in catheter ablation of persistent atrial fibrillation (AF), yet randomized data have been discordant. Prior syntheses have pooled studies across ablation energy sources, which may obscure energy-specific effects. We examined whether the association of PWI with arrhythmia recurrence in persistent AF is modified by ablation energy source.

Methods

We searched Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science for studies comparing PWI plus PVI with PVI alone in persistent AF. The primary endpoint was recurrence of all atrial tachyarrhythmias; secondary endpoints were recurrence of AF alone, procedural time, and procedural complications. Studies were stratified a priori by energy source (cryoballoon, radiofrequency [RF], and pulsed field [PF]). Odds ratios (OR) and mean differences were pooled using random-effects models, with subgroup differences assessed by the test for interaction.

Results

Twenty-two studies with 4400 patients with persistent AF (2029 PWI and PVI, 2371 PVI alone) were included. Compared with PVI alone, PWI was associated with reduced recurrence of all atrial tachyarrhythmias overall (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.40-0.73), but the effect differed by energy source (test for subgroup differences p = 0.0006): cryoballoon OR 0.34 (95% CI 0.26-0.43), RF OR 0.67 (95% CI 0.43-1.04), and PF OR 0.96 (95% CI 0.55-1.70). A concordant pattern was observed for recurrence of AF alone (overall OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.25-0.51). PWI was associated with longer procedural times, with a graded effect across energies (cryoballoon mean difference 51.1 min; p = 0.007 for subgroup differences). Procedural complications did not differ between groups overall (OR 1.29, 95% CI 0.92-1.82) or by energy source (p = 0.49).

Conclusions

In persistent AF, the association of PWI with freedom from atrial arrhythmia was concentrated in cryoballoon-based ablation and was not evident with RF or PF, without an excess of complications. These findings suggest that the conflicting literature on PWI may be explained, in part, by differences in ablation energy source rather than by the anatomic target alone. Because energy source is partly confounded with study design and the cryoballoon evidence rests on few randomized trials, this association is hypothesis-generating and merits evaluation in energy-specific randomized trials. No benefit was observed in the pulsed field ablation stratum, the modality in which adjunctive PWI is now most commonly performed, so its routine use may not confer the benefit reported with earlier energy sources.

title: The Relationship Between Sleep Quality, Glycemic Control, and Maternal-Neonatal Outcomes Among Women with Gestational Diabetes Mellitus in Tanzania
authorString: Kaguti F, Stephano EE, Zeng Y, Sabuni PA, Mabrouk SJ, Sunny CE, Jia G.
abstractText: Background Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a common pregnancy complication associated with significant maternal and neonatal risks. In low- and middle-income countries such as Tanzania, the rising burden of GDM is compounded by limited healthcare resources. Poor sleep quality has emerged as a modifiable factor linked to worsened insulin resistance and adverse pregnancy outcomes. However, data on sleep quality among women with GDM in sub-Saharan Africa remain scarce. This study aimed to assess sleep quality and its associations with glycemic control and maternal and neonatal outcomes among Tanzanian women with GDM. Methods A prospective longitudinal study was conducted in seven regional referral hospitals in Tanzania from August to October 2025. Convenience sampling enrolled pregnant women (18–45 years) diagnosed with GDM in the second trimester. The Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) was administered at enrollment to evaluate participants’ sleep quality over the preceding month retrospectively. Demographic and glycemic data were collected at enrollment, while maternal-neonatal outcomes were extracted within 24 hours post-delivery. Data were analyzed using Stata 19.5 with descriptive statistics and linear and multivariate logistic regressions. Results A total of 360 women with GDM were enrolled in this study. The mean PSQI score was 10.8 ± 4.83, with poor sleep quality (PSQI > 5) highly prevalent at 91.4%. Higher education and being separated/widowed were associated with worse sleep. The overall glycemic control of participants was poor, with a mean fasting blood glucose of 13.6 ± 5.80 mmol/L. Poor sleep quality was independently associated with higher fasting blood glucose (β = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.20–0.36, P < 0.001). For maternal outcomes, each 1-point increase in PSQI score raised the risk of gestational hypertension (AOR = 1.11, 95% CI: 1.01–1.22, P =  0.036) and sepsis/infection (AOR = 1.14, 95% CI: 1.03–1.26, P  < 0.001); no significant association was found between sleep quality and postpartum hemorrhage. For neonatal outcomes, each 1-point increase in PSQI raised the odds of neonatal hypoglycemia by 16% (AOR 1.16, 95% CI 1.07–1.27, P  < 0.001). Conclusion Poor sleep quality is highly prevalent among Tanzanian women with GDM and is independently associated with poorer glycemic control, hypertensive disorders, maternal infection, and neonatal hypoglycemia. Integrating routine sleep screening and low-cost sleep interventions into antenatal GDM care may improve glycemic control and maternal-neonatal outcomes in resource-limited settings. Clinical Trial Number: Not applicable

title: Modified Posterior Wall Ablation in Persistent Atrial Fibrillation: the BOX-AF Randomized Clinical Trial.
authorString: Zhou G, Wu X, Zheng L, Li J, Xia Y, Lin Z, Cai H, Chen S, Ding Y, Wei Y, Lu X, Huang D, Jiang R, Zhou D, Yin X, Sun Y, Jiang C, Liu S.

journal.title: Europace : European pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac electrophysiology : journal of the working groups on cardiac pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac cellular electrophysiology of the European Society of Cardiology

abstractText:
Aims

The efficacy of left atrial posterior wall isolation (PWI) for persistent atrial fibrillation (AF) is controversial. We propose a modified left atrial posterior wall ablation strategy.

Objectives

To evaluate the efficacy and safety of modified posterior wall ablation in patients with persistent AF who underwent first-time radiofrequency catheter ablation.

Methods and results

In this multicenter, single-blind randomized trial, 276 patients with persistent AF were assigned 1:1 to pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) with (BOX+) or without modified posterior wall ablation (BOX-). Seven participants withdrew, leaving 269 (BOX+, n=139; BOX-, n=130) for primary endpoint analysis. The primary endpoint was freedom from any documented atrial arrhythmia lasting > 30 seconds without antiarrhythmic drugs after a 3 -month blanking period. At 12-month follow-up, the primary endpoint occurred in 120 of 139 patients (86.3%) in the BOX+ group and 113 of 130 (86.9%) in the BOX- group (hazard ratio 1.046, 95% CI, 0.54 - 2.01; P = 0.894). The BOX+ group exhibited longer procedure time and ablation time. Acute successful PWI was achieved in 91 (65.5%) patients assigned to BOX+. In a nonprespecified, post-randomization analysis, arrhythmia-free survival was 93.4% in patients with acute successful PWI, 72.9% in those with attempted but unsuccessful PWI, and 86.9% in controls without attempted PWI (overall log-rank P=0.002). Adverse events were similar between groups.

Conclusion

Routine addition of modified posterior wall ablation did not improve overall outcomes of first-time ablation in persistent AF. However, achieving successful PWI was associated with significantly lower recurrence.

title: Oxidized LDL pathophysiology and potential as a therapeutic target in atherosclerosis.
authorString: Nilsson J, Villines TC, Libby P, Hansson GK.
abstractText: Uptake of oxidized and other forms of modified low-density lipoprotein (LDL) drives formation of foam cells, a hallmark of atherosclerotic plaques. Experimental studies demonstrating the proinflammatory and cytotoxic properties of oxidized LDL have led to the concept of LDL oxidation as one key factor in both development and destabilization of atherosclerotic plaques. Such data positioned oxidized LDL as a promising target for prevention or mitigation of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Yet the failure of multiple antioxidants to reduce cardiovascular risk in large randomized clinical trials has hampered this prospect. Such null studies have stimulated interest in an alternative approach: the therapeutic potential of antibodies against oxidized LDL. High levels of IgM against oxidized LDL phospholipids are associated with lower cardiovascular risk and these antibodies function primarily through neutralization and stimulation of clearance of modified LDL. IgG antibodies against aldehyde-modified peptide sequences in apolipoprotein B-100, the signature protein component of LDL, are also associated with lower risk of cardiovascular disease but experimental studies have shown that these antibodies function by locally forming immune complexes with oxidized LDL that limit the inflammatory activity of certain plaque macrophages. A phase 2 pilot study showed that one such antibody, orticumab, reduces an imaging index of local coronary arterial inflammation in patients with psoriasis. Thus, emerging evidence supports the possibility of using oxidized LDL antibodies to limit atherothrombotic disease.

title: Economic Evaluations of Algorithm-Enabled Remote Monitoring of Cardiac Implantable Electronic Devices: Systematic Review.
authorString: Daghash H, Pandey R, P W Kenny R, Fernandez-Garcia C, Meinert E, S Sagoo G.
abstractText:
Background

Algorithm-enabled remote monitoring using cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) is increasingly used to support earlier detection of clinical deterioration in heart failure and in at-risk populations. However, the economic value of these technologies remains uncertain because intervention design, implementation, and evaluation methods vary.

Objective

This study aimed to systematically identify, appraise, and synthesize full economic evaluations of algorithm-enabled CIED remote monitoring in adults with established heart failure or at risk of heart failure.

Methods

A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines. Searches were performed in MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library, with supplementary searches of health technology assessment sources. Eligible studies reported full economic evaluations of algorithm-enabled remote monitoring linked to CIEDs. Data were extracted using a structured form and synthesized narratively due to heterogeneity. Methodological and reporting quality were assessed using the CHEQUE (Criteria for Health Economic Quality Evaluation) checklist and CHEERS (Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards) 2022 statement. One reviewer screened records and extracted the data. A second reviewer independently checked subsets of the screening decisions and extracted the data.

Results

Ten economic evaluations were included. They used models, trial data, or observational data; some were reported within health technology assessments. Substantial heterogeneity was observed in population definitions, intervention characteristics, algorithm types, monitored parameters, clinical response pathways, and economic methods. Cost-effectiveness and cost-utility analyses were most common, with time horizons ranging from short-term follow-up to lifetime modeling. Several studies reported economically favorable findings, including dominance (ie, less costly with better health outcomes) or cost-effectiveness. However, outcomes varied across studies, and favorable estimates often relied on assumptions about reduced hospitalization and length of stay, while quality-adjusted life year gains were generally modest. Reporting of key implementation factors, including alert burden and diagnostic performance, was limited.

Conclusions

There is economic evidence for algorithm-enabled CIED remote monitoring suggesting potential value in some settings, but the evidence remains methodologically heterogeneous and difficult to compare directly across studies. Findings are sensitive to differences in intervention design, modeling approaches, and clinical input data, which limit certainty and transferability. More robust and standardized evidence is needed before economic conclusions can be applied confidently across different devices, algorithms, and health care settings.

title: Results of Pulmonary Valve Replacement with The INSPIRIS RESILIA Prosthesis: A Systematic Review.
authorString: Pérez CJ, Portilla-Rodríguez G, Guarín-Muñoz L, Penagos-López D, Sánchez-Colmenares O, Rios W, Parra J, Núñez-Ricardo F.
abstractText:
Introduction

Pulmonary valve replacement is increasingly common in patients with congenital heart disease. The limited durability of conventional bioprostheses has led to the introduction of the INSPIRIS RESILIA valve, initially designed for the aortic position. However, evidence on its performance in the pulmonary position is limited and heterogeneous.

Methods

A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses statement in PubMed®, Excerpta Medica dataBASE, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials. Observational studies with patients undergoing pulmonary valve replacement with the INSPIRIS RESILIA bioprosthesis were included. Data on baseline characteristics, transvalvular gradients, mortality, complications, prosthetic insuficiency, and need for reintervention were extracted. This study was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420251117859).

Results

Three retrospective cohort studies and two retrospective case series were identified that included pediatric and adult populations, mainly with a diagnosis of tetralogy of Fallot. The findings were consistent in showing adequate perioperative safety. Smaller studies showed favorable results. In contrast, larger studies with longer follow-up reported more rapid progression to moderate/severe pulmonary insuficiency and shorter durability of the bioprosthesis.

Conclusion

INSPIRIS RESILIA may be associated with acceptable short-term outcomes in pulmonary valve replacement, but its medium- and long-term durability may be inferior to that of reference bioprostheses. Medium- and long-term safety remains inconclusive due to limited follow-up, modest sample sizes, heterogeneity in definitions, possible confounding by anatomical substrate, and study limitations.

title: Occupational health outcomes among migrant and non-migrant construction workers: A systematic review and narrative synthesis.
authorString: Prabhala J, Minhas S, Levine E, Park C, Caplan S, Mitchell R, Zimmerman C, Wang X, Rydberg J, Mak J, Banning S, Bhambhani V, Jayram D, Buller AM, Stoklosa H.
abstractText: Construction remains one of the world's most hazardous industries, with migrants comprising a substantial part of its workforce. Little evidence exists on occupational health disparities between migrant and non-migrant construction workers. This review compares occupational health outcomes between these two groups to inform equitable worker protection strategies. Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically searched fourteen electronic databases and gray literature for studies published from January 1990 to May 2025. Eligible studies reported quantitative occupational health outcomes for both groups. Study quality was appraised using adapted Joanna Briggs Institute criteria and results were narratively synthesized. Thirty-eight studies across fifteen high-, upper-middle, and lower-middle-income countries were included, totaling 55,615 adverse health outcomes among migrant construction workers and 566,643 among non-migrant construction workers. Most studies were of low to moderate quality and were primarily conducted in high-income settings. Migrant construction workers experienced higher rates of fatal and general occupational injury than non-migrants. While migrants had excess risk for fatal falls, traumatic brain injury, heat-related mortality, and ocular trauma, they experienced lower all-cause morbidity and mortality. Patterns of non-fatal injuries, musculoskeletal disorders, mental health problems, and cardiovascular and metabolic disease were mixed. Occupational and structural factors significantly associated with morbidity and/or mortality among migrants included fewer years of employment and work experience, type of work, limited safety training and briefing attendance, and lower educational attainment. Associated socio-demographic and cultural factors included poor language proficiency, ethnicity, gender, risk-taking attitudes, and low awareness of workplace hazards; the role of age varied across studies. Migrant status is a significant determinant of occupational health in the construction sector. Strengthening labor protections for migrant workers and providing multilingual safety training are likely to reduce harm. Disaggregating occupational safety and health surveillance data by migrant status will further strengthen the evidence needed to protect the most at-risk construction workers. Registration: PROSPERO CRD42014009154.

title: Impact of Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Following Cardiac Arrest on Organ Donation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authorString: Ferreira-Alves B, Reis-Pardal J, Cuboia N, Santos-Dias F, Azevedo L, Roncon-Albuquerque R.
abstractText: Organ donation following cardiac arrest (CA) increasingly contributes to the donor pool. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is used in situ for organ preservation in donation after circulatory death (DCD). ECMO is also used in refractory CA for cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR), and, in selected patients with unfavorable neurological outcomes and diagnosed brain death, it can lead to donation after brain death (DBD). In this study, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the impact of ECMO use following CA on organ donation. We searched three electronic databases (PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science) and included single-arm and comparative studies (ECMO versus other in situ organ preservation techniques). The organ use rate per donor was assessed. We included 69 primary observational studies (15 comparative). The most common clinical scenario was controlled DCD (n = 49), followed by uncontrolled DCD (n = 23), and DBD (n = 8). Multiorgan donation occurred in 88% of DBD cohorts, 46% of controlled DCD, and 22% of uncontrolled DCD. The overall meta-analytic effect measure from comparative studies showed that ECMO is associated with a higher organ use rate than other techniques (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.01-1.36, I2 = 82.4%). Subgroup analyses across clinical scenarios and comparator techniques showed that estimates favored ECMO in controlled and uncontrolled DCD, without statistical significance. In DBD post ECPR, no benefit of ECMO was observed. ECMO is likely superior to other techniques in controlled DCD. In uncontrolled DCD, underpowered evidence favored ECMO. In DBD following ECPR, no clear advantage of ECMO-based preservation is demonstrated.

title: Epidemiology, Etiology, and Outcomes of Cardioembolic Stroke in Young Adults 2014-2025: A Systematic Review.
authorString: Hassanien D, Frol S, Al-Hashmi AM, Imam Y.
abstractText:
Introduction

Cardioembolic (CE) stroke is an important and potentially preventable cause of young-onset ischemic stroke, yet its global prevalence, causes, diagnostic practices, and outcomes are incompletely defined. Better characterization of CE burden in adults aged 15-55 years is needed to guide investigation and secondary prevention.

Methods

We registered the review with PROSPERO CRD420251047443 and followed PRISMA 2020. We searched PubMed, Scopus, EMBASE, Web of Science and Cochrane for observational studies from January 2014 to May 2025 on cardioembolic stroke proportions in patients aged 15 to 55. Two reviewers screened and extracted data in Rayyan with a third reviewer resolving disagreements. Study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Analysis comprised descriptive and stratified synthesis of overall and regional CE proportions, subgroup analyses by age, sex, region and period, and tabulated summaries of CE sources and outcomes.

Results

Twenty-three studies (n = 16,301 patients) met inclusion (median NOS = 6). The pooled mean proportion of CE stroke was 18.0%, with regional means of Europe 19.9%, Asia 11.5%, the Americas 22.0%, and Middle East & Africa 24.8%. Younger patients (<40 years) more often had structural causes (e.g., PFO, cardiomyopathy), while older patients had higher AF-related proportions. Diagnostic intensity varied, limited use of TEE and prolonged rhythm monitoring in some regions likely underestimated CE detection. CE strokes were associated with higher initial severity, greater recurrence (5-14% across cohorts), and worse functional outcomes compared with many non-cardioembolic subtypes; mortality was comparable overall but higher when AF was present.

Conclusion

CE stroke accounts for 18% of ischemic stroke in young adults but shows wide geographic and diagnostic variability driven by regional cardiac disease patterns and access to advanced cardiac testing. Standardized, tiered cardiac evaluation (including TEE and prolonged rhythm monitoring) and consistent reporting are needed to improve etiologic attribution and reduce recurrence through timely anticoagulation and targeted interventions.

title: Single vs. Dual Antiplatelet Therapy after Fenestrated and Branched Endovascular Aortic Repair: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
authorString: Alanezi T, Alghofili H, Alhazmi K, Lindsay TF.

journal.title: European journal of vascular and endovascular surgery : the official journal of the European Society for Vascular Surgery

abstractText:
Objective

This study aimed to compare single vs. dual antiplatelet therapy after fenestrated or branched endovascular aortic repair (FBEVAR).

Data sources

PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global were searched from inception to 12 July 2026, with a supplementary targeted PubMed search on 5 September 2026.

Review methods

Comparative studies of post-operative antiplatelet therapy were included. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and certainty of evidence using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach. Outcomes were synthesised narratively when clinical and methodological differences precluded meaningful pooling; an additional quantitative summary of study defined bleeding outcomes was also reported.

Results

Six retrospective cohorts comprising 3 623 patients were included, with 3 197 patients in separately extractable single or dual antiplatelet therapy groups. Several studies reported associations favouring dual antiplatelet therapy for target vessel patency. However, differences in outcome definitions, analytical units, and treatment classification precluded a common pooled estimate, and one association was attenuated after accounting for treatment changes. Evidence regarding ischaemic events, mortality, re-intervention, and endoleak was insufficient for reliable pooled comparisons. Five cohorts reported peri-operative bleeding using heterogeneous definitions and observation periods, of which a four study summary yielded an odds ratio of 1.30 (95% confidence interval 0.87 - 1.94) for dual vs. single antiplatelet therapy. Given the differences in outcome definitions, this does not estimate a common clinical effect.

Conclusion

The current evidence comparing single and dual antiplatelet therapy after FBEVAR is based on heterogeneous cohort studies, focuses largely on surrogate outcomes such as target vessel patency, and shows no clear benefit for dual antiplatelet therapy. Comparative bleeding risk as well as clinical outcomes of single vs. dual antiplatelet therapy after FBEVAR remain uncertain. Future prospective studies are needed to better delineate superiority of one regimen over the other.

title: Optimizing Frontline Targeted Therapies in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia: An Italian Inter-Regional Delphi Consensus on Patient Risk Stratification, Cardiovascular Safety, and Endpoint Interpretation.
authorString: Molica S, Loseto G, Pennese E, Aji F, Fama A, Giordano A, Giordano G, Merchionne FI, Miccolis RM, Palumbo G, Pinto P, Plebani S, Scardino S, Schiattone L, Solimando AG, Specchia MR, Tonialini L, Fraticelli V, Scalzulli PR, D'Angela D, Oliva S, Maggi A.
abstractText:
Background

While landmark trial data have established targeted agents as the frontline standard of care in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), real-world clinical gaps remain regarding high-risk disease biology, patient frailty, cardiovascular comorbidities, healthcare accessibility, and the clinical interpretation of surrogate endpoints.

Methods

A modified two-round Delphi process engaged an expert panel of 19 Italian hematology specialists and a multidisciplinary scientific board to evaluate 16 evidence-based statements across four key clinical domains. Statements were formulated based on literature evidence-informed from a systematic review of the literature. When high-tier evidence was lacking, statements used lower-level data and expert consensus to address clinical gaps. Consensus was pre-defined as an aggregate agreement of ≥ 70% using a forced-choice 4-point Likert scale.

Results

Continuous monotherapy with second-generation covalent BTK inhibitors (cBTKis) was preferred over time-limited regimens for patients with TP53-disrupted disease (94.6%), individuals aged > 80 years or meeting frailty criteria (100%), and those with socio-logistic or caregiver constraints (95.0%). Conversely, time-limited regimens were universally favored for fit patients aged < 70 years without TP53 aberrations (100%), while remaining a viable option in young, fit patients with TP53 disruptions (78.9%). Baseline cardiovascular risk stratification using population-validated tools (SCORE2, SCORE2-OP, SCORE2-Diabetes) reached 85.0% agreement. Second-generation cBTKis were preferred over ibrutinib in patients with elevated cardiovascular risk (95.0%). Panelists agreed that undetectable measurable residual disease (uMRD) is not a universal surrogate for progression-free survival (70.0%). Time to next treatment (TTNT) was unanimously endorsed as an efficacy indicator for time-limited therapy (100%), but viewed primarily as a safety surrogate during continuous cBTKi therapy (79.0%). Upon relapse after time-limited cBTKi-venetoclax therapy, re-challenge with a covalent BTKi was established as the preferred option (89.5%).

Conclusion

This consensus bridges clinical guidelines and real-world practice, providing a structured framework that incorporates molecular risk, functional frailty, cardiovascular scoring, and healthcare accessibility to guide frontline CLL management.

title: Mitral Valve Repair Failure: Mechanisms, Re-repair Feasibility, and Outcomes of Reintervention. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authorString: Al-Tawil M, Kolashov A, Imperatore G, Wang W, Gowan K, Sicouri S, Ramlawi B, Haneya A.
abstractText:
Background

Mitral valve repair is the preferred treatment for degenerative mitral regurgitation whenever feasible and durable. Amid the increasing volume of mitral repairs, mitral valve repair failure has emerged as an increasingly recognized clinical entity in contemporary mitral surgery.

Methods

A systematic literature search was conducted to identify studies reporting intraoperative or interval/postoperatively detected mitral valve repair failure. Evidence synthesis included a systematic summary and analysis of incidence, failure modes, factors favoring re-repair, re-repair techniques and intervention-specific outcomes.

Results

Intraoperative mitral valve repair failure was reported across nine unique studies totaling 18,429 patients undergoing initial mitral valve repair, of whom 580 (3.1%) experienced intraoperative failure requiring re-cross-clamping. Re-repair was the primary management strategy in intraoperative failure, with a pooled re-repair rate of 82%. Interval mitral valve repair failure was analyzed from 12 studies including 1,363 patients, occurring at a mean of 6 years following the index repair. Disease progression was the most frequent mechanism of interval failure (44%), followed by technical failure (35%) and new disease (17%). In interval failure, valve replacement remained the most employed strategy, while re-repair was performed in 35% of patients. Re-repair was associated with significantly superior long-term survival (78.3% vs. 58.3%; HR 2.44, 95% CI [1.79-3.33], p < 0.001).

Conclusions

Mitral valve re-repair is a safe and feasible option in selected patients with degenerative mitral valve repair failure and is associated with improved long-term survival. Early technical failures and localized, non-calcified defects with preserved leaflet tissue are most likely to benefit from re-repair.

title: Gene-based map of cardiovascular diseases
authorString: Ozcelik T, Kayaalp B, Çil K.
abstractText:
Background:

Rare coding variants contribute to cardiovascular disease, but their effects across disease groups remain incompletely characterized. In particular, the influence of functionally and clinically informed variant classification and sex-specific genetic effects on gene-phenotype associations remains understudied.

Methods:

We analyzed whole-genome sequencing data from up to 483,311 UK Biobank participants across six genetic ancestry groups and eight cardiovascular phenotype groups. Gene-burden testing integrated state-of-the-art missense classification and predicted pathogenic germline variants. We performed combined-sex and sex-stratified analyses, followed by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We additionally adjusted for cardiometabolic traits in sensitivity analyses, estimated penetrance among qualifying-variant carriers, and assessed genetic prevalence across eight ancestry groups.

Results:

We identified 86 exome-wide significant gene-phenotype associations: 40 established and 46 novel. Novel associations included EHMT2 with atrial fibrillation, P2RX1 with arrhythmias, P2RY4 with complete atrioventricular block, and NOSTRIN with atherosclerotic heart disease in females. After cardiometabolic adjustment, 60 associations retained exome-wide significance and 18 additional associations emerged, including CDH11, PARVA, and ADAMDEC1 with atherosclerosis-related phenotypes.

Conclusions:

These findings identify novel cardiovascular gene-phenotype associations implicating purinergic signaling, endothelial nitric oxide regulation, and vascular wall biology. Variant selection shapes penetrance estimates and the interpretation of inherited susceptibility.

title: Evaluation of an inclusivity intervention to increase participation of under-represented groups in a pragmatic primary care heart failure randomised controlled trial: study protocol.

title: The Safety and Feasibility of Monitoring Cardiac Arrhythmic Events Before and After Conversion From Conventional Intermittent Hemodialysis to Home Nocturnal Hemodialysis: A Pilot Study.
authorString: Ye WWQ, Aravindanathan G, Chauhan VS, Noad R, McGrath-Chong M, Kaushal A, Gilbert C, Chan CT.

journal.title: Hemodialysis international. International Symposium on Home Hemodialysis

abstractText:
Introduction

Patients on hemodialysis have an increased risk of sudden cardiac death and an increased cardiac arrhythmia burden due to large fluid and electrolyte shifts, especially during the long inter-dialytic period. Arrhythmia burden may be decreased on home nocturnal hemodialysis due to prolonged fluid removal and clearance. This study examined the safety and feasibility of prolonged cardiac monitoring in patients who were converting from conventional hemodialysis (12 h) to home nocturnal hemodialysis (30+ h).

Methods

Patients from a single center in Toronto, Ontario, Canada with a low cardiac risk profile, who were eligible to perform hemodialysis at home, were enrolled. Participants underwent the insertion of an implantable loop recorder and cardiac arrhythmia were monitored during conventional hemodialysis, and for 1 year after conversion to home nocturnal hemodialysis.

Findings

Ten participants completed the study. The average ultrafiltration rate per session during conventional hemodialysis was 6.87 mL/h/kg, and the average cardiac ejection fraction was 52.6%. There were no adverse effects associated with implantable loop recorder implantation, usage, or removal. One participant recorded three sinus bradycardia and two sinus pause events during conventional hemodialysis that resolved after conversion to home nocturnal hemodialysis. All other participants did not experience any arrhythmic events before or after conversion to home nocturnal hemodialysis.

Discussion

Our pilot study demonstrated a safe and feasible protocol for prolonged monitoring of cardiac arrhythmia in a stable population undergoing conversion from conventional to home nocturnal hemodialysis. Due to the small sample size, future work is required to delineate the full effect of home nocturnal hemodialysis on cardiac arrhythmia burden in patients with increased cardiac comorbidities.

title: Twenty-Year Forecast of Thoracic Surgeon Demand in Chile: Simulated Scenarios Using Bayesian Methods and Publicly Available Data.
authorString: Perez-Castro P, Camhi E, Bustamante M, Berrios R, Mordojovich G, Valenzuela R, Santolaya R, Cavada G.
abstractText:
Introduction

Internationally, the thoracic surgery workforce is undergoing rapid changes due to increased training availability, particularly in Chile. There is currently no method for adequately forecasting the number of training spots needed to meet demand in future years.

Methods

A national registry of thoracic surgeons was constructed using publicly available data from the Chilean Superintendency of Health (as of October 2024). Surgeons practicing cardiac or vascular surgery, retirees, and those living abroad were excluded. A Bayesian projection model was developed that incorporates parameters such as retirement age, entry of new surgeons (including graduates and foreign-certified individuals), accidental mortality, population growth, and dynamic demand growth. Monte Carlo simulations (1000 iterations) were conducted across five scenarios (1 to 5 graduates/year, plus one certified surgeon/year). Absolute error analysis identified the optimal annual number of new graduates.

Results

Of the 107 thoracic surgeons listed in Chile, only 67 were actively practicing non-cardiac thoracic surgery. The majority were concentrated in the Metropolitan Region (capital). Sex distribution was predominantly male (83.5%), with a mean age of 50.2 years. The corrected model (using 67 active surgeons as the baseline) shows that a scenario with 1 graduate per year results in a projected shortage, while scenarios with 3-5 graduates per year lead to potential oversupply. The optimal scenario, minimizing supply-demand mismatch, was training approximately two to three surgeons per year (2.6 graduates/year).

Conclusions

Strategic workforce planning is essential to avoid future imbalances in thoracic surgeon availability. Bayesian modeling provides a robust framework for anticipating demand, guiding training capacity, and ensuring equitable distribution across regions, thereby avoiding both shortages and saturation of the specialty in Chile.

title: Multiorgan failure in a young patient with necrotizing fasciitis: a case report of septic shock progressing to mixed shock with fatal cardiac outcome.
authorString: Kraus RF, Kaufmann C, Alt V, Kees MG.
abstractText:
Background

Necrotizing soft tissue infections (NSTIs) are rare, life-threatening conditions requiring immediate and aggressive treatment. Despite advances in medical care, mortality remains high, largely due to septic shock and severe complications.

Case representation

We report the case of a young adult with necrotizing fasciitis (NF) of the left leg complicated by recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding and infective endocarditis, resulting in severe heart failure and ultimately leading to death. The fatal outcome was most likely attributable to prolonged sepsis with multiorgan involve- and impairment and a 1.5-cm paravalvular abscess caused by vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium.

Conclusion

The treatment of a septic patient with progressive heart failure highlights the value of an integrative, multidisciplinary approach to complex clinical decision-making and the real-world challenges that may require patient-tailored, nonstandard therapeutic strategies.
