This pilot biomonitoring study explored polymer mass in dissected versus non-dissected ascending aortic tissue. A total of 16 ascending aortic samples (8 acute type A aortic dissection [AD] and 8 acute type B dissection with arch involvement but a non-dissected ascending aorta [ND]) were examined using pyrolysis-gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (Py-GC/MS) to screen 11 polymers. Both groups had aortic disease. Polymer-related signals were reported in all samples, with total mass estimates ranging from 1.92 to 155.58 µg/g tissue. The predominant reported polymer was polyamide 66 (PA66; 50.7%), followed by polyvinyl chloride (PVC; 40.5%) and polyethylene terephthalate (PET; 8.8%). AD tissues showed a 3.9-fold higher estimated polymer burden than ND tissues (74.51 ± 42.81 vs. 19.25 ± 16.48 µg/g, p = 0.0077). PET estimates were also higher in AD tissues (7.36 ± 6.44 vs. 0.89 ± 1.49 µg/g, p = 0.025), but PET identification was tentative and polymer-specific tests were exploratory. Total polymer mass correlated with ascending aortic diameter (Spearman's rho = 0.865, p < 0.001). The age- and group-adjusted association (coefficient 0.079 mm per µg/g; p = 0.0098) was sensitive to omission of one observation (p = 0.140). These findings describe a difference in estimated polymer burden between two diseased-tissue groups. Incomplete analytical validation and possible perioperative contamination limit interpretation; particle identity, tissue localization, vascular toxicity and causality were not established. Further analytical and multicenter validation is needed.

title: The Impact of Lifestyle Interventions and Mental Health Management on Arrhythmias in Heart Failure.
authorString: Ariyaratnam JP, Elliott AD, Middeldorp ME, Sanders P.
abstractText:
Purpose of review

To summarise contemporary evidence on the impact of lifestyle interventions and mental health management on arrhythmias in patients with heart failure (HF), and to highlight emerging therapeutic opportunities.

Recent findings

Lifestyle modification targets shared risk factors in both arrhythmias and HF. In atrial fibrillation (AF), weight loss, exercise, alcohol reduction, and risk factor management reduce arrhythmia burden and improve arrhythmia-related symptoms and quality of life. Similarly, in both HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), exercise training improves functional capacity and quality of life, whilst dietary interventions and weight loss are particularly beneficial in HFpEF. Mental health disorders represent novel targets for intervention for arrhythmias in HF; these conditions are common in arrhythmia and HF patients and associated with poorer outcomes, but early data suggests that mental health interventions do not reduce arrhythmia burden or cardiovascular outcomes despite improving overall psychological well-being and quality of life. Lifestyle intervention to improve physical health is central to HF and arrhythmia care and established as a central pillar of management. Mental health represents an important but under-recognised target which requires urgent further investigation.

title: Robotic ultrasound-guided biopsy, ablation, and access: a bibliometric analysis and validation-evidence map : Original Article.
authorString: Song X, Song Z, Li Z, Wu J, Chen S, Fu Z.
abstractText: Robotic assistance is increasingly used in ultrasound-guided biopsy, ablation, and percutaneous access, but the extent of experimental and human evaluation varies across these procedures. We combined bibliometric analysis with a publication-level assessment of procedural application and the highest reported validation setting in studies published during 2000-2025. Searches of PubMed and the Web of Science Core Collection returned 1,198 records corresponding to 857 unique publications. The Technology corpus included 197 focused Master publications and 210 adjacent Edge publications (n = 407). Of the Master publications, 184 reported direct evaluation: V0 (bench, phantom, simulation, or in vitro; n = 55), V1 (ex vivo or cadaver; n = 32), V2 (live animal; n = 27), and V3 (human; n = 70). These concerned biopsy (n = 51), ablation (n = 57), access (n = 74), or other procedures (n = 2). Human-stage evaluation was reported in 40/51 biopsy publications (78.4%), 23/57 ablation publications (40.4%), and 7/74 access publications (9.5%). Among 70 V3 reports, 68 described interventions in patients and two described non-interventional evaluation. Fifty-four of the 57 ablation reports could be assigned to five predefined pathways. Human evaluation was most common in biopsy, whereas ablation and especially access included more preclinical work. These counts characterize the reported settings of evaluation and cannot establish clinical effectiveness, independent patient cohorts, or the maturity of individual technologies.

title: [Social inequality and health: what role do molecular genetics, gene-environment interactions, and epigenetics play?].
authorString: Schmidt B.
abstractText: Due to significant progress in molecular genetic research, the understanding of genetic and epigenetic influences on human health is growing. Recently, researchers in social epidemiology have demanded incorporating (epi)genetic factors for explaining social inequalities in health. But how can this be done in a meaningful way?Robust empirical evidence for a strong effect of disease-associated genetic factors in the sense of direct health selection is scarce. In addition, the latest large-scale genome-wide association studies do not support a strong impact of genetic factors on socioeconomic position itself. However, genetic associations with indicators of socioeconomic status may be helpful in investigating the causal direction of health inequalities. The first empirical studies have suggested that socioeconomic status exerts a social causal effect on, for example, cardiovascular diseases, high body mass index (BMI), and diabetes mellitus. Socioeconomic status can also exert its indirect influence on disease development by modifying the expression of genetic effects. These gene-environment interactions may also be mediated by epigenetic changes.The incorporation of molecular (epi)genetic factors into social epidemiological research takes greater account for the complex interplay of various causes and effects across the life course and across generations. In particular, it offers the potential to identify specific pathways through which social factors influence biological pathways underlying disease development.

title: Targeting the DNA damage response networks in disease: mechanistic insights and preclinical therapeutic potential of natural products.
authorString: Song LY, Wang YY, Fu YJ, Li WY, Li TG, Wang Y, Wu SJ, Li L, Qiu Y, Yang ZS.
abstractText: Natural products are increasingly described as modulators of the DNA damage response (DDR), but the field is limited by a recurring ambiguity: many reported effects reflect changes in DNA damage markers, oxidative stress, inflammation, or cell-cycle state rather than direct regulation of defined DDR targets. This distinction is critical because the same compound may damage DNA, enhance repair, suppress stress signaling, or alter cell fate depending on material type, dose, exposure context, and disease model. Here, we synthesize natural product-DDR research through an evidence-stratified framework that separates direct target or pathway modulation from indirect DDR-associated effects. We first outline the core DDR modules and then evaluate natural products across cancer, fibrosis, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disorders, reproductive dysfunction, and aging-related conditions. Rather than treating all studies equally, we use a four-tier evidence system: Tier 1 denotes direct target engagement supported by causal or pathway-specific functional validation; Tier 2 denotes target-linked or pathway-functional evidence without complete direct-target or causal validation; Tier 3 denotes in vivo or combined in vitro-in vivo evidence for repair-capacity preservation or defined DDR-associated signaling without direct target engagement; and Tier 4 denotes in vitro, ex vivo, or predominantly marker-level evidence. Mixed-evidence studies are assigned according to the most mechanistically specific component directly demonstrated, while complementary indirect or marker-level findings remain explicitly described. This framework identifies where natural products have credible mechanistic support, where claims remain marker-level or context-dependent, and which translational barriers-pharmacokinetics, bioavailability, formulation, target exposure, safety, and drug-drug interactions-must be addressed before DDR-focused applications can advance. The review therefore reframes natural products not as uniformly safe multitarget agents, but as context-dependent chemical probes and therapeutic leads whose DDR relevance must be judged by mechanism, evidence strength, and disease setting.

title: How high sensitivity cardiac Troponin Point of Care Testing can be integrated into existing or new pathways for chest pain assessment in the emergency department.
authorString: Velocci S, Baldetti M, Paganelli C, Belardi R, Dimasi P, Andreis G, Cunti P, Terrinoni A, Bernardini S, Legramante JM, Minieri M.

journal.title: Scandinavian journal of clinical and laboratory investigation

abstractText: Chest pain is a leading cause of Emergency Department (ED) admissions, accounting for about 10% of cases in Italy. Rapid detection of ischemic events using high-sensitivity cardiac Troponin I (hs-cTnI) enables faster rule-out and improved patient flow. However, turn-around time (TAT) may be delayed by sample transport and centralized lab processing. This study aims to assess the time and economic advantages of implementing Point-of-Care Testing (POCT) for hs-cTnI in the ED. Our observational study included 86 adults with atraumatic chest pain consecutively presenting to the ED (September-October 2024). Hs-cTnI was measured at triage using a POCT device and in the Central Laboratory. Time to result availability, ED length of stay, and operating costs were extracted from hospital systems. Data were analyzed with descriptive statistics, and POCT versus laboratory turnaround times were compared using the Mann-Whitney test. A statistically significant difference between central laboratory and POCT (median 80 vs 4.5) mean time between blood collection and visualization of hs-cTnI results by the ED physician was found. Even though the POCT cost per test is higher than the central laboratory, the use of POCT may help saving about €25 per patient by reducing ED length of stay (LOS). In conclusion, POCT hs-cTnI testing at triage significantly shortens time to clinical decision-making in chest pain patients, reducing ED length of stay and helping mitigate overcrowding. Despite higher analytical costs, the time saved yields an overall economic benefit, supporting POCT adoption for early risk stratification in the ED.

title: Influence of Systolic Blood Pressure and Pulse Pressure on Heart Failure Risk in Elderly Treated Hypertensive Patients.
authorString: Coccina F, Cuccurullo C, Anzoletti N, Porreca E, Pierdomenico SD.

journal.title: High blood pressure & cardiovascular prevention : the official journal of the Italian Society of Hypertension

abstractText:
Introduction

It is unclear whether systolic blood pressure (BP) and pulse pressure (PP), either clinic or ambulatory, differ in their ability to predict heart failure (HF) in elderly hypertensive patients.

Aim

To evaluate the influence of clinic and ambulatory systolic BP and PP on HF risk in elderly treated hypertensive subjects.

Methods

In this retrospective study, we assessed 1314 individuals (aged ≥ 65 years) undergoing clinic and ambulatory BP measurement. Association of BP parameters with HF was investigated by univariable and multivariable Cox regression analyses. Differences between competing models were assessed by receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC) analysis, Akaike's Information Criterion (AIC) and Schwarz Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC).

Results

During the follow-up (7.0 ± 4.0 years), 126 HF events occurred. After adjustment for covariates, clinic systolic BP and PP were not significantly associated with HF risk, whereas daytime systolic BP, daytime PP, nighttime systolic BP and nighttime PP were, showing a hazard ratio (95% confidence interval), for each standard deviation increase, of 1.45 (1.21-1.73), 1.19 (1.01-1.43), 1.54 (1.31-1.80) and 1.29 (1.08-1.55), respectively. ROC analysis showed that models including daytime or nighttime systolic BP better predicted HF than those involving daytime or nighttime PP and that nighttime BP parameters better predicted HF than daytime ones (all P < 0.05). Comparison of competing models using AIC and BIC gave the same results.

Conclusions

In elderly treated hypertensive patients, both ambulatory systolic BP and PP are predictors of HF, but systolic BP is superior to PP and nighttime parameters are superior to daytime ones.

title: Whole embryo barcoding reveals convergent origins of mesodermal cells during mammalian gastrulation
authorString: Secchi MA, Martin PJ, Cornwall-Scoones J, Van Egeren D, Dooley PJ, Liu EY, Liu N, Masaltseva A, King HD, Jokhai RT, Qiu X, Loh KM, Gottgens B, Camargo F, Bowling S.
abstractText: Classical fate-mapping and recent single-cell trajectory studies have suggested that mesoderm diversification during gastrulation proceeds through progressive fate bias and branching lineage segregation. Here, we combine inducible CRISPR-based lineage recording with single-cell RNA sequencing to reconstruct clonal relationships across mouse embryos barcoded at primitive streak onset and analyzed at early organogenesis. Mesodermal clones diverged after streak formation, but their developmental outputs remained extensively overlapping, revealing a clonal architecture that is not a simple branching lineage tree. Using sampling-aware statistical models, we quantify distinct clonal origins of paraxial mesoderm across the anterior-posterior axis, show that endothelial cells arise from multiple mesoderm origins but demonstrate transcriptional differences that correspond to anatomical position and clonal lineage, and identify clonal sharing between extra-embryonic mesoderm and embryonic derivatives, including cardiac lineages and a shared hindlimb-allantois progenitor. In the heart, progenitors corresponding to classical heart fields remain multipotent, contributing both myocardial and non-myocardial cell types. Together, our findings support a model in which mesodermal diversity is assembled through spatially distinct, fate-biased progenitor pools whose descendants converge on shared cell states. Our findings challenge simple branching models of mesoderm diversification and provide a clonal framework for understanding how tissue diversity emerges in the embryo.

title: Single-Session HRV Biofeedback Alters Neural Activity but Not Subjective Anxiety
authorString: Dao C, Man I, Healy K, Estel K, Nelli SM.
abstractText: Anxiety and stress are among the most prevalent mental health concerns worldwide, yet barriers to effective treatment remain high. Biofeedback-based approaches offer a promising, low-cost complement to traditional interventions. The present study examined whether real-time heart rate variability (HRV) biofeedback enhances the efficacy of paced breathing for reducing state anxiety, and whether self-reported and neural measures of anxiety relief converge. Healthy adults completed a speeded Stroop task for stress induction, followed by a ten-minute paced breathing exercise. Participants were randomly assigned to an HRV biofeedback condition, in which real-time cardiac variability was displayed, or a control condition with the same breathing cue and no physiological feedback. State anxiety was assessed using the Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-S), and neural activity was measured via EEG spectral power across delta, theta, alpha, and beta frequency bands. The Stroop task reliably elevated state anxiety, and paced breathing reduced STAI-S scores equivalently in both groups; HRV biofeedback did not confer additional subjective benefit. In contrast, EEG analyses revealed that the biofeedback group showed increases in delta and bilateral theta power relative to controls, and spatially widespread increases in alpha and beta power. Time-frequency analyses further showed more extensive and sustained spectral modulation in the biofeedback condition. These findings reveal a dissociation between self-reported and neural responses to a brief HRV biofeedback intervention: paced breathing alone was sufficient to reduce acute state anxiety, while HRV biofeedback produced distinct changes in neural oscillatory activity without enhancing self-reported anxiety relief. These results show that subjective anxiety recovery and neural recovery can diverge during acute HRV biofeedback, suggesting that physiological engagement with biofeedback emerges before conscious benefits.

title: Combining non-linear and spectral cardiac variability metrics differentiates rat alcohol drinking with and without challenge
authorString: De Oliveira Sergio T, Zareb AW, Frasier RM, Wean SE, Starski PA, Grippo A, Hopf F.
abstractText: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) remains a substantial global challenge, with notable individual and sex differences. Heart rate variability (HRV) offers a potential link into the autonomic system underlying alcohol drinking. While simpler, time-domain HRV metrics have been explored, non-linear indicators could provide unique insights into more complex states like compulsive drinking, intake that persists despite negative consequences. We examined heart rate traces from male and female rats during intake of alcohol-only and alcohol+10mg/L quinine, a putative compulsive drinking model. In particular, we re-analyzed previously published findings, but newly focused on several non-linear HRV metrics: the Poincare ratio (possibly reflecting sympathovagal balance) and MultiScale entropy (MSE, perhaps reflecting unpredictability in broader and narrower time windows), along with the previously unexamined spectral HRV metrics (the parasympathetic indictor high-frequency HRV, HF-HRV%). HRV was assessed for the first ~1100 heart beats (~2.5 minutes), to assess HRV correlates of greater alcohol front-loading while having approximately similar amount of data per session. Lower Poincare ratio and higher HF-HRV% were overall related to higher alcohol consumption. In contrast, compulsive drinking, but not alcohol-only, was associated with lower broader-window HRV entropy, which was more pronounced in males. Drinking- and sex-related patterns were further identified using Principle Component Analysis, Ordinary Least Squares, and Linear Mixed Models. Limitations included perhaps being underpowered to detect significant relationships, especially in females. Thus, our preliminary findings suggest that combining HRV metrics could represent useful biomarkers for consumption levels during front-loading, which distinguished general intake from compulsion.

title: Global mapping of VEGF-A driven changes in the RNA bound phospho-proteome reveals a molecular switch to coordinate angiogenesis in endothelial cells
authorString: Wardman R, Tikhonova A, Bennewitz K, Hermann L, Joshi S, Schwarz JJ, Stein F, Ola R, Dobreva G, Hammes A, Kroll J, Heineke J.
abstractText: RNA binding proteins (RBPs) serve as upstream master regulators of cellular fate transitions at the post-transcriptional level. RBP-RNA interactions are dynamically regulated by post-translational modifications to coordinate cellular responses. We hypothesised that changes in RBP phosphorylation will play a key role in coordinating angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, in endothelial cells (ECs). Therefore, we used phospho-proteomic analysis of the mRNA bound proteome to identify global phosphorylation changes in mouse cardiac ECs during acute and prolonged VEGF-A stimulation. Of the differentially phosphorylated RBPs, we found that the phosphorylation of serine 199 within mRNA bound Phf6 (PHD finger protein 6) was consistently increased following VEGF-A stimulation. Phf6 phosphorylation at this specific site was sufficient and required to induce a pro-angiogenic phenotype, facilitating a change in Phf6 conformation promoting interaction with distinct RNAs. We show here that Phf6 phosphorylation at serine 199, downstream of VEGF-A, acts as a molecular switch to differentially coordinate a decrease of anti-angiogenic RNAs (i.e. extracellular matrix genes) and an increase in pro-angiogenesis related RNAs, in part by differentially regulating their stability, to promote angiogenesis.

title: Biochemical reassessment of the activation of PANK1 by SGLT2 inhibitors
authorString: Guo Z, Zang J, Chen L.
abstractText: Although SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) show cardiovascular benefits in addition to glycemic control, their molecular target for cardiovascular effect remains unclear. A recent study reported that two SGLT2i, empagliflozin and dapagliflozin, directly activate pantothenate kinase 1 (PANK1), which mediate their cardioprotective effect. PANK1 phosphorylates pantothenate with ATP to yield 4′-phosphopantothenate and ADP, representing the rate-limiting enzyme of coenzyme A (CoA) biosynthesis. We therefore reassessed this claim using purified recombinant human PANK1. The malachite green assay detected free inorganic phosphate (Pi) but neither ADP nor 4′-phosphopantothenate and its signals do not reflect PANK1 activity. In the ADP-Glo assay, empagliflozin and dapagliflozin did not stimulate PANK1 under either basal conditions or acetyl-CoA feedback inhibition, while the activator PZ-2891 enhanced the activity of PANK1. These results show that SGLT2i do not directly activate PANK1, challenging the proposed PANK1-dependent cardioprotection mechanism.

title: High +Gz Exposure Alters Urinary Extracellular Vesicle miRNAs in Humans
authorString: Mizohata Y, Akiyama M, Takei F, Inuzuka E, Konishi T, Ohrui N.
abstractText: High +Gz exposure elicits complex cardiovascular, autonomic, and endocrine responses, but the associated molecular responses in humans remain poorly understood. We investigated whether microRNAs (miRNAs) encapsulated in urinary extracellular vesicles (uEVs) are altered following acute high +Gz exposure. Twenty-one healthy young men undergoing human centrifuge training provided urine samples before, immediately after, and on the morning after exposure. Candidate uEV-encapsulated miRNAs were identified by RNA sequencing and Gene Ontology analysis, and 16 miRNAs related to ischemia, hypoxia, blood pressure regulation, and mechanical stress were quantified by quantitative PCR. Salivary cortisol, urinary catecholamines, and heart rate were also assessed. Six uEV-encapsulated miRNAs increased significantly after high +Gz exposure. miR-20b-5p, miR-125b-5p, and miR-130a-3p increased immediately after exposure and returned to baseline by the following morning, whereas miR-335-5p, miR-17-5p, and miR-92a-3p remained elevated. Urinary adrenaline, noradrenaline, and dopamine increased immediately after exposure; adrenaline returned to baseline by the following morning, whereas noradrenaline and dopamine remained elevated. Salivary cortisol and heart rate also increased. These findings demonstrate distinct transient and sustained temporal responses of uEV-encapsulated miRNAs to high +Gz in humans, paralleling different catecholamine response patterns. Although their tissue origins and functional roles remain unresolved, these findings provide new molecular-level insights into the human physiological response to high +Gz.

title: A brief breathing challenge reveals a cardiac correlate of generalized anxiety beyond resting physiology and interoceptive measures
authorString: Zhang X, Ngo HQ, Shi K, Kvamme TL, Ip C, Silvanto J.
abstractText: Physiological markers measured at rest, such as heart rate variability, have proved relatively weak predictors of mental health symptoms. One potential reason is that resting measures are influenced by uncontrolled state factors, such as spontaneous breathing, whereas a standardized challenge holds these constant and may reveal regulatory differences not evident at rest. Here we asked whether respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) during slow paced breathing, a challenge that strongly increases RSA, carries information about symptoms beyond resting RSA and interoceptive measures. In 207 young adults (mean age 23.6 years, SD = 3.1), electrocardiogram (ECG) was recorded at rest and during slow (6 breaths/min) and fast (20 breaths/min) paced breathing. Lower RSA during slow breathing, relative to that predicted by resting RSA, was associated with more severe generalized anxiety symptoms (β = −0.21, BF₁₀ = 13), also when depressive symptoms were controlled, whereas resting RSA was not. The association was concentrated among participants with at least moderate anxiety symptoms, whose resting RSA was typical but whose rest-adjusted slow-breathing RSA was 0.62 SD lower, and who in exploratory analyses also showed weaker phase coupling between heart period and respiration. Interoceptive accuracy, measured with heartbeat counting or heart rate discrimination, was unrelated to symptoms, self-report and slow-breathing RSA, and interoceptive questionnaires tracked distress shared across anxiety and depressive symptoms rather than generalized anxiety symptoms. At the group level, slow-breathing RSA thus carries information about generalized anxiety symptoms beyond resting RSA and self-reported interoception. Brief paced-breathing challenges may therefore increase the sensitivity of autonomic markers in anxiety research and merit testing in clinical samples.

title: Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Incidence During and After COVID-19 Social Distancing in Korea: A Nationwide 16-Year Interrupted Time-Series Analysis
authorString: Choi IY, Jeon Y, Lee IK, Kim K.
abstractText:
Background:

Pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is a rare but devastating event. However, the extent to which large-scale public health interventions, such as COVID-19 social distancing policies, affected the incidence of pediatric OHCA remains unclear. Methods We conducted a nationwide interrupted time-series analysis using data from the Korea Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Registry (2008-2023). The primary outcome was the monthly incidence of OHCA among individuals aged 0-18 years. The study period was divided into three phases: pre-intervention (January 2008-February 2020), social distancing (March 2020-April 2022), and post-lifting (May 2022-December 2023). We used segmented Poisson regression, adjusted for population size and seasonal variation, to estimate changes in monthly incidence at each policy change and reported the results as incidence rate ratios (IRRs). To determine whether these changes differed by age, we compared children with adults (19-64 years) and elderly individuals (≥65 years). Results Of the 456,839 registry entries, 10,965 were pediatric OHCAs, of which 6,891 underwent resuscitation in the emergency department. The crude incidence was 7.04, 7.14, and 8.35 per 100,000 person-years in the three phases, respectively. Before the pandemic, incidence rose slightly (annual IRR 1.006 [95% CI 1.001-1.012]; P = 0.032). At the implementation of social distancing, incidence fell immediately (IRR 0.926 [95% CI 0.865-0.991]; P = 0.027), without a significant change in slope (P = 0.081). After restrictions were lifted, incidence rose immediately (IRR 1.138 [95% CI 1.048-1.235]; P = 0.002) and then declined gradually (monthly IRR 0.993 [95% CI 0.988-0.999]; P = 0.023). These changes were confined to children aged 1-11 years (implementation IRR 0.812 [95% CI 0.666-0.991]; post-lifting IRR 1.562 [95% CI 1.278-1.909]). The pattern of change differed significantly by age group (P < 0.001), mainly because incidence rose in children, but not in adults or elderly individuals, after restrictions were lifted. Conclusions Nationwide social distancing was associated with a transient decrease in pediatric OHCA incidence, which was concentrated among children aged 1-11 years and was followed by a rebound above the expected level after restrictions were lifted. Surveillance of pediatric OHCA should account for abrupt changes in children's daily environments, including the closure and reopening of schools and childcare facilities.

title: Design and Validation of a Compact Sensor for Peripheral Pulse Waveform Capture
authorString: Naim A, Ranaweera R, Nandadeva D, Divulwewa K, Ratnayake A, Wijayakulasooriya J.
abstractText: Peripheral pulse waveforms captured across different sites of the vascular tree provide valuable insights into cardiovascular health. This study presents a low-cost compact sensor designed to minimize intrusion at the measurement site while capturing the pulse waveform. The sensor performance was characterized and evaluated through both in-vitro benchtop experiments and a pilot in-vivo clinical study against invasive arterial pressure waveforms. The proposed sensor was able to capture pulse waveform morphology with reliable beat to beat tracking. Although offsets were present in the calculated features, fundamental temporal trends and cardiac cycle profiles were preserved. Thus, this work lays the foundation for a scalable hardware platform capable of multi-site pulse monitoring, enabling its integration with emerging computational frameworks for cardiovascular risk screening.

title: "Wow, this could be massive": Donor-Conceived Families Experience with Unexpected Recontact for Risk of Inherited Cardiac Conditions
authorString: Mitchell LA, Ruscigno A, Mulhern S, Yeates L, Macciocca I.
abstractText:
Introduction:

Recontacting families post-gamete donation, after a genetic diagnosis is made in the donor, can create complex challenges for healthcare providers and families. However, there is little literature that explores the family experience. This study aimed to explore the experiences of parents and donor-conceived young people navigating the recontact process and undergoing predictive genetic testing for an inherited cardiac condition.

Methods:

Semi-structured interviews were conducted to explore participants' experiences in unexpectedly being recontacted and undergoing predictive genetic testing for an inherited cardiac condition. Interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim. A reflexive thematic analysis was performed.

Results:

Thirteen participants agreed to be interviewed, nine were parents and four were donor conceived young people. Four overarching themes were identified: (1) Out of the Blue, (2) A ripple effect on the family, (3) Calm after the storm, (4) Beneath the Ripples: the psychological impact.

Discussion:

Interviews provided insights into fertility services recontact and the predictive genetic testing process. From the themes, we conceptualize a ripple effect model. Findings highlight how cardiac genetics and fertility services are evolving, and the critical role of genetic counselors. The recontact process affects the entire family. However, most participants adapted and moved forward from this event.

title: Cardiovascular and metabolic trajectories in men engaged in a multidimensional preventive care program: a prospective observational study
authorString: Bedin L, Lepoittevin M, Roujansky P, Benani A, Gounane R, Salomon J, Sorberts E, Steg GP, Bodard S.
abstractText:
Objectives:

To describe within-individual changes in cardiometabolic, functional and neuroendocrine markers between two standardized evaluations in men engaged in a structured preventive care program, and to examine transitions across clinical risk categories.

Design:

Prospective observational cohort study using routinely collected data; paired within-individual analyses.

Setting:

Single preventive health center in Paris, France, offering a standardized multidisciplinary assessment with individualized lifestyle, supplementation and, when indicated, pharmacological recommendations. Participants: 279 men aged 18 years or older with a first evaluation (CU1) between October 2022 and November 2025 and a second evaluation (CU2) by May 2026 (32.3% of 865 eligible men); median interval 13.3 months (IQR 12.0 - 15.6). No exclusion criteria were applied. Primary and secondary outcome measures: Within-individual change in continuous markers (Hodges-Lehmann estimate, 95% CI; Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment over 36 tests) and transitions across fixed clinical thresholds (paired odds ratios).

Results:

Median age was 51.2 years, BMI 24.5 kg/m2 and SCORE2 2.9%. Visceral adipose tissue mass decreased (delta -49 g, 95% CI -80.5 to -18.5; q=0.006), with small decreases in body mass and fat mass. Handgrip strength increased (right +2.35 kg, 1.70 to 3.00; left +1.70 kg, 1.05 to 2.30; q<0.001). HDL cholesterol increased (+3.5 mg/dL, 2.5 to 4.5; q<0.001), with decreases in the triglyceride/HDL and total/HDL ratios. Blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, fasting glucose (after adjustment), insulin, HOMA-IR, SCORE2 and salivary cortisol and DHEA did not change. The proportion of men below the grip strength reference value decreased from 60.1% to 47.6% (paired OR 0.34, 0.19 to 0.61) and with HDL cholesterol superior to 46 mg/dL from 26.7% to 16.5% (OR 0.25, 0.12 to 0.54).

Conclusions:

In this selected, health-engaged population of men who completed both evaluations, changes in a favorable direction were observed for handgrip strength, HDL cholesterol and visceral adiposity, whereas blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, glycemic markers and SCORE2 were stable. Without a comparison group, these changes cannot be distinguished from regression to the mean, test retest effects or secular trends.

title: Association between the triglyceride-glucose index and waist circumference with electrocardiogram ST-T changes: a cross-sectional study
authorString: Li X, Feng Y, Liu Y, Li T.
abstractText: Background Electrocardiogram (ECG) ST-T changes are early, important manifestations of myocardial ischemia and are closely associated with cardiovascular disease risk. The triglyceride-glucose-waist circumference index (TyG-WC), a composite marker of insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome, has an unclear relationship with ECG ST-T changes. This study aimed to investigate the association between TyG-WC and ECG ST-T changes in an older adult population. Methods This cross-sectional study included 15,966 older adults who underwent comprehensive health examinations. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) regression was used to fit the dose-response relationship between TyG-WC and ST-T changes. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to evaluate the strength of the association. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and decision curve analyses were used to assess model performance. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Nanchong Gaoping District People's Hospital and all participants provided written informed consent. Results The mean age of participants was 73.5 ± 7.0 years, and 46.5% (n = 7,426) were male. The prevalence of ST-T abnormalities was 25.1% (n = 4,012). After multivariable adjustment, each one-unit increase in TyG-WC was associated with a 0.5% increase in the odds of ST-T changes (adjusted OR = 1.005, 95% CI 1.004–1.006, P < 0.001). RCS analysis revealed a linear positive association between TyG-WC and ST-T changes (P overall = 0.001, P non-linearity = 0.318). TyG-WC showed a modest but statistically superior discriminative ability compared with TyG alone (AUC 0.576 vs. 0.569; DeLong P < 0.001). Conclusions TyG-WC was independently, linearly associated with ECG ST-T changes in older adults, showing superior discriminative ability compared with TyG alone. TyG-WC may serve as a simple screening tool for identifying individuals at high risk of subclinical myocardial ischemia. Trial registration Not applicable (observational study).

title: De novo duplication 4(q21-q28) in sibs, as a possible ovarian germinal mosaicism, more clinical analysis delineation
authorString: Arana IN, VILLA-PEREZ V, VEGA AV.
abstractText: Two additional cases are described with partial trisomy 4q, resulting from a de novo duplication of chromosome 4, involving segments q21-q28. This time a sibling is affected. The clinical manifestations are similar to other cases with de novo 4q duplication involving the same segments. Although a single distinctive phenotype has not been established, most reported cases of de novo duplication share a similar clinical spectrum depending on the specific duplicated segment of chromosome 4q. The major clinical manifestations are growth and psychomotor retardation, microcephaly, epicantic fold, antimongoloid slant of palpebral fissures, low-set and malformed auricles, high nasal bridge, long philtrum small mouth, micrognathia, short neck, additionally, one patient presented congenital heart disease, and both presented congenital pyloric hypertrophy stenosis, dorsal edema of the hands and feet, the hypertrichosis as the most important clinical manifestations. Diverse genes involved in neural, cardiovascular, acrorenal, and skeletal development—identified in molecular studies of the duplication—are reviewed; these genes are potentially responsible for the phenotypic anomalies reported in each chromosomal region. We reported the another family directly affected with the same de novo direct duplication in the literature of a rare chromosomal trisomy, as the second ovarian germline mosaicism case which was demonstrated through cytogenetic and molecular analysis, confirmed by fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) with a painting probe and microsatellites studies. Besides, deep in a clinical analysis of karyotype-phenotype correlation in each duplicated segment.

title: Modified robotic atrial septal defect repair on beating heart: a nine-year single-centre experience with learning-curve analysis and comparison with thoracoscopy
authorString: Feng H, Li M, Kong J, Dai Y, Wu Y, Tang Y.
abstractText: Objective To evaluate a modified robot-assisted technique for atrial septal defect (ASD) repair on beating heart and to compare perioperative outcomes with thoracoscopic repair. Methods 198 patients with ASD underwent modified ASD repair using the Da Vinci robotic surgical system on beating heart in the Department of Cardiovascular Surgery of the First Affiliated Hospital with Nanjing Medical University. Cumulative sum (CUSUM) analysis was used to build learning curves for operation time and cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) time. Patients operated after both curves had plateaued formed the robotic group (n = 117); 113 patients treated thoracoscopically during the same period served as the comparison group. Results The learning curves for operation time and CPB time were 81 cases and 66 cases respectively. ASD diameter and pulmonary artery systolic pressure were higher in the robotic group, which also contained seven patients with partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection (PAPVC) and one with anomalous drainage of the inferior vena cava. CPB time was shorter in the robotic group. Operation time, mechanical ventilation time, intensive care unit stay, postoperative hospital stay and 24-hour chest drainage did not differ. Echocardiography at 3, 30 and 90 days and at one year showed no residual shunt or tricuspid regurgitation in either group. Conclusions The modified robot-assisted technique for beating-heart ASD repair is safe and reproducible. Once the learning curve is complete, CPB time is shorter than with thoracoscopy despite greater anatomical complexity, and the technique offers a valid minimally invasive option for defects that are unsuitable for device closure.

title: Association Between Glycemic Variability and Pupillary Autonomic Function in Type 2 Diabetes: A Cross-Sectional Study
authorString: Ito M, Yamamoto Y, Fukuyama H, Ohigashi M, Inoue C, Ohsugi K, Inoue M, Tamai K, Kusunoki Y, Koyama H, Gomi F.
abstractText: Background Although glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) reflects average glycemia, it does not capture glucose fluctuations. Glycemic variability has been linked to cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy, but its association with pupillary autonomic function in type 2 diabetes remains unclear. We examined this association using continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and dynamic pupillometry. Methods We conducted a single-center, cross-sectional analysis of 53 patients with type 2 diabetes from a prospective cohort. All had a phakic study eye, at least 10 days of valid CGM data, and no use of medications known to affect the pupillary light reflex. Glycemic variability was quantified as the standard deviation (CGM SD) and coefficient of variation (%CV) of sensor glucose. Eye-tracking pupillometry assessed five indices, including the sympathetically influenced re-dilation ratio (D1%) and the predominantly parasympathetically mediated relative constriction amplitude (AMP%). We used Pearson correlations and further examined the D1%–glycemic variability associations using multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, diabetes duration, and HbA1c. Results The mean age was 64.5 ± 8.6 years, and mean HbA1c was 7.1 ± 0.6%. D1% correlated positively with CGM SD ( r  = 0.316, P  = 0.021) and %CV ( r  = 0.302, P  = 0.028), but not with mean glucose or time in range. Both associations remained after adjustment (CGM SD: β = 0.229, P  = 0.005; %CV: β = 0.303, P  = 0.024) and across post hoc adjustment sets accounting for constriction amplitude, cardiac autonomic function, peripheral neuropathy, and retinopathy stage. In unadjusted analyses, AMP% was not significantly correlated with any CGM metric, and HbA1c was not significantly correlated with any pupillary index. The unadjusted D1% associations did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. Conclusions Greater CGM-derived glycemic variability was associated with a higher pupillary re-dilation ratio after adjustment for HbA1c and other covariates, whereas no corresponding association was observed for constriction amplitude. These exploratory findings require confirmation in larger, longitudinal studies before their physiological and clinical significance can be established.

title: Lipoprotein(a) in Pediatric Type 1 Diabetes: The Role of Pubertal Maturation Beyond Glycemic Control – A retrospective cross-sectional study
authorString: Wołoszyn-Durkiewicz A, Rozwadowska-Kunecka P, Okonek M, Gawlak G, Banach M, Myśliwiec M.
abstractText: Background and Aims: Children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes (T1D) are at increased lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an inherited CVD risk factor, but data in pediatric T1D are limited. We assessed Lp(a) concentrations, the prevalence of elevated Lp(a), and their associations with clinical characteristics, lipid profile, and pubertal maturation. Methods This retrospective, cross-sectional study included 516 children and adolescents (0–18 years) with T1D. Serum Lp(a) was measured by particle-enhanced immunoturbidimetric assay. Elevated Lp(a) was defined as ≥ 50 mg/dL. Associations with clinical variables, lipid parameters, and Tanner stage were evaluated using non-parametric tests and multivariable analysis. Results Median Lp(a) concentration was 8.0 mg/dL, and elevated Lp(a) was found in 66 patients (12.8%). Lp(a) was not associated with diabetes duration, HbA1c, new-onset diabetes, or diabetic ketoacidosis. Weak positive correlations were observed with LDL-C ( r s =0.259, p  < 0.001) and non-HDL-C ( r s =0.264, p  < 0.001). Lp(a) increased across Tanner stages, and the prevalence of elevated Lp(a) rose from 7.0% in stage 1 to 19.8% in stage 5. Tanner stage remained independently associated with Lp(a) after adjustment for sex, HbA1c, and LDL-C. Conclusions Elevated Lp(a) was common in pediatric T1D and increased with pubertal maturation. These findings suggest that pubertal stage should be considered when interpreting Lp(a) concentrations. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine the clinical value of Lp(a) in cardiovascular risk assessment.

title: Subclinical Left Ventricular Myocardial Impairment and the Threshold Effect of Intact Parathyroid Hormone in Maintenance Hemodialysis Patients with Secondary Hyperparathyroidism: A Two-Dimensional Speckle-Tracking Echocardiographic Study
authorString: Zhang F, Duan Y, Yang Q, Shu L, Bai J, Sun H.
abstractText: Background To investigate the value of two-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography (2D-STE)-derived global longitudinal strain (GLS), 17-segment strain and peak strain dispersion (PSD) for detecting left ventricular myocardial impairment in maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT), and to define the cutoff of intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH) that signals myocardial impairment. Methods A total of 88 consecutive maintenance hemodialysis patients fulfilling the diagnostic criteria of SHPT (December 2023–December 2025) were retrospectively enrolled and divided by iPTH into a low-PTH group (n = 36) and a high-PTH group (n = 52); 43 healthy volunteers served as controls. All underwent 2D-STE. Myocardial impairment was defined as an absolute GLS < 16%. Logistic regression and ROC analysis assessed the predictive performance and optimal cutoff of iPTH. Patients were followed up until July 2026, and Cox regression was used exploratorily for cardiovascular events. Results GLS decreased stepwise across the three groups (17.6%, 16.5% and 12.2%; P < 0.001). Although EF was normal in all 88 dialysis patients, GLS was already < 16% in 71.6%. Segmental strain showed a basal-predominant, relatively apically preserved pattern (high- vs. low-PTH: basal 11.32% vs. 15.39%, apical 14.51% vs. 18.78%, both P < 0.001), and PSD was higher in the high- than in the low-PTH group (75.60 vs. 55.00 ms, P < 0.001). iPTH was an independent determinant of GLS (β = −0.0044, P < 0.001); each 100 pg/mL increase conferred a 3.8-fold higher odds of myocardial impairment (adjusted OR 4.531, 95% CI 1.978–10.380, P < 0.001), with an optimal cutoff of 190.8 pg/mL (AUC 0.859, sensitivity 82.5%, specificity 92.0%). In exploratory Cox regression (median follow-up 22.0 months), only age remained an independent predictor. Conclusions Patients with MHD complicated by SHPT have subclinical myocardial impairment preceding the decline in EF, characterized by reduced global GLS, a basal-predominant segmental pattern with relative apical preservation, and impaired mechanical synchrony. The iPTH–impairment association is threshold-like, and approximately 190.8 pg/mL may serve as a warning cutoff. Combining GLS with 17-segment strain and PSD may allow earlier detection of myocardial impairment.

title: Prevalence and Diagnostic Concordance of Metabolic Syndrome amongst University Students in Navrongo Upper East Region of Ghana: A Cross-Sectional study
authorString: Donzooya GN, Mohammed MY, Kunduzore AY, Nyaah KE, Sunwiale SS, Dang-i AY, Adu-Frimpong M.
abstractText: Background Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is a cluster of cardiometabolic abnormalities that significantly predisposes individuals to cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Although MetS has traditionally been associated with older adults, emerging evidence indicates an increasing burden amongst young adults, particularly university students. However, data on the prevalence and comparative diagnostic performance of MetS criteria amongst university populations in Ghana remain limited. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted amongst 219 undergraduate students aged 18–36 years at the University of Technology and Applied Sciences (UTAS), Navrongo, Ghana. Anthropometric measurements, blood pressure, and fasting blood samples were collected following standard protocols. MetS was defined using four criteria, namely World Health Organization (WHO), National Cholesterol Education Programmed Adult Treatment Panel III (NCEP ATP III), International Diabetes Federation (IDF), and Harmonized (H_MS) definitions. Logistic regression analysis was applied to identify risk factors associated with MetS. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and Cohen’s kappa statistics were used to evaluate diagnostic performance and agreement between criteria. Results The prevalence of MetS varied across diagnostic criteria, with the highest prevalence observed using IDF (10.1%), followed by H_MS (8.2%), NCEP ATP III (7.3%), and WHO (5.5%). Females exhibited higher prevalence of MetS under IDF, NCEP ATP III, and H_MS criteria, while males showed slightly higher prevalence under WHO criteria. Low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) was the most prevalent component (76.3%), followed by elevated fasting blood glucose (25.6–29.2%) and elevated blood pressure (18.7%). Logistic regression analysis identified fasting blood glucose as the strongest predictor of MetS across all definitions ( p <  0.001). ROC analysis showed that the H_MS definition demonstrated the highest discriminatory ability relative to the WHO definition (AUC = 0.677), followed by NCEP ATP III (AUC = 0.638), while IDF exhibited poor performance (AUC = 0.491). Kappa agreement analysis established fair concordance between WHO and NCEP ATP III (k = 0.238, p  < 0.001) and between WHO and H_MS (k = 0.286, p  < 0.001), but poor agreement between WHO and IDF (k=-0.013, p  = 1.00). Conclusion Although the overall prevalence of MetS amongst UTAS students was relatively low, a substantial proportion exhibited one or more metabolic abnormalities, indicating early cardiometabolic risk. The harmonized definition demonstrated better alignment with the WHO-based classification and may be a useful screening approach in this population. These findings highlight the need for early screening and targeted lifestyle interventions amongst university students.

title: Direct Effects of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Ligands on Myocardial Function in Isolated Hearts from Streptozotocin-Induced Diabetic Rats
authorString: Akcabag E, Aksoyalp ZS, Oner F, Bayram Z, Ozbey G, Nacitarhan C, Ozdem S, Tasatargil A, Ozdem SS.
abstractText: Purpose Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor ligands are widely used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity and have demonstrated cardioprotective effects beyond glycemic control. This study investigated the direct effects of GLP-1 receptor ligands and the dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor sitagliptin on myocardial function in isolated hearts from streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats. Methods Diabetes was induced in male Wistar rats by a single intraperitoneal injection of streptozotocin (50 mg/kg). Hearts from control and diabetic rats were retrogradely perfused for 30 min using a Langendorff system with GLP-1 (7–36), GLP-1 (9–36), exendin-4 (1–39), sitagliptin, glimepiride, pioglitazone, or metformin. Cardiac functional parameters, plasma total and active GLP-1 concentrations and serum total antioxidant status (TAS), total oxidant status (TOS), total sulfhydryl groups (TSG), advanced oxidation protein products (AOPP), and ischemia-modified albumin (IMA) were assessed. Results Diabetic hearts exhibited significantly lower heart rates and impaired left ventricular contractility and relaxation, indicated by reduced left ventricular + dP/dt max and -dP/dt min values, compared with controls. GLP-1 (7–36), GLP-1 (9–36), and exendin-4 (1–39) partially improved contractility and relaxation. Compared with controls, diabetic rats exhibited significantly higher plasma total and active GLP-1 concentrations, increased serum TOS and AOPP levels, and reduced TSG levels, whereas serum TAS and IMA levels remained unchanged. Conclusion These findings suggest that GLP-1 receptor ligands partially improve myocardial contractility and relaxation in isolated hearts from streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats, although the mechanisms underlying these effects remain to be elucidated.

title: Investigating reliability and internal consistency of the Spider, a multisystemic symptom screening tool for people with hypermobility related disorders
authorString: Ewer E, Potts HWW, De Pauw R, De Wandele I, Simmonds JVS.
abstractText:
Background: Hypermobility Spectrum Disorders (HSD) and hypermobile Ehlers Danlos Syndrome (hEDS) are often associated with symptoms affecting many bodily systems. The Spider questionnaire assesses eight common symptoms: pain, fatigue, neuromusculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, urogenital, cardiac dysautonomia, anxiety, and depression. This study evaluated the Spider’s reliability and internal consistency. Methodology: Ethical approval was obtained. Hypermobility support organisations aided recruitment through social media advertisements. Participants self-selected based on inclusion criteria and completed two online surveys, one-to-two weeks apart. Data collection included demographics, the Spider questionnaire and the SF-36/PEDS-QL. Relative reliability was assessed using Intraclass Correlation Coefficients (ICC). Absolute reliability was evaluated using the Standard Error of Measurement (SEM), Minimal Detectable Change (MDC), and Bland-Altman analysis. Pearson correlations with SF-36/PedsQL scores were compared across timepoints to monitor stability. Internal consistency was analysed using Cronbach’s alpha (α).

Results:

617 participants aged 13-65 with HSD/hEDS or symptomatic hypermobility completed both surveys. Test-retest reliability was good to excellent in individual domains and total score (ICC: 0.79 to 0.92). SEM ranged from 4.0 to 11.60 and MDC from 11.08 to 32.13. Seven domains and the total score demonstrated acceptable internal consistency (α=0.70 to 0.91). The pain domain had marginally lower internal consistency (α=0.69).

Conclusions:

The Spider questionnaire demonstrated good to excellent test-retest reliability. Seven of the eight domains and the total score demonstrated acceptable internal consistency. These findings support the reliability of Spider scores for repeated measurement over time.

title: Vericiguat attenuates high phosphate-induced vascular smooth muscle cell calcification through the PKG/VASP/NF-kB/NLRP3 pathway
authorString: Bu L, Hao X, Li S, Zhao Y, Li H, Ma M.
abstractText: Background Vascular calcification is a common pathological feature of chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and is closely associated with arterial stiffness and adverse cardiovascular outcomes. High extracellular phosphate is a major driver of vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) calcification, promoting osteogenic phenotypic switching, inflammatory activation, and mineral deposition. Vericiguat, an oral soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) stimulator approved for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, enhances cyclic guanosine monophosphate signaling and exerts anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects. However, its effect on high phosphate-induced vascular calcification remains unclear. Methods A7r5 cells were exposed to 10 mmol/L β-glycerophosphate (β-GP) to establish an in vitro calcification model. Vericiguat was administered at 100 µmol/L. The PKG inhibitor Rp-8-Br-PET-cGMPS was used at 10 µM to evaluate the involvement of PKG signaling. Calcification, phenotypic switching, and inflammatory signaling were assessed by Alizarin Red S staining, calcium content assay, Western blotting, and ELISA. Results High phosphate significantly increased mineral deposition and calcium content in A7r5 cells. It also decreased the contractile markers α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) and SM22α while increasing the osteogenic markers bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP2) and runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2). Vericiguat markedly attenuated these changes, indicating inhibition of calcification and phenotypic switching. Mechanistically, vericiguat increased the p-VASP (Ser239)/VASP ratio and reduced the p-IkBα/IkBα ratio, suggesting activation of PKG/VASP signaling and suppression of NF-kB activity. Pharmacological inhibition of PKG partially abolished the protective effects of vericiguat on calcification and osteogenic transdifferentiation. Vericiguat also suppressed high phosphate-induced activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, as shown by reduced expression of NLRP3, ASC, p-Caspase-1, and IL-1β, together with decreased IL-1β secretion. These anti-inflammatory effects were partially reversed by PKG inhibition. Conclusions Vericiguat attenuates high phosphate-induced VSMC calcification and inflammatory activation, at least in part through the PKG/VASP/NF-kB/NLRP3 signaling pathway. Vericiguat may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for phosphate-driven vascular calcification.

title: A Wearable Patch with Iontronic Linear Sensing and Mechanically Compliant Wireless Readout for Physiological Signals
authorString: Su Z, Guo C, Zhou L, Liu K, Wang X, Zhang R, Teng B, Xu H, Guo CF, Wang W, Bai N.
abstractText: Wearable wireless sensing patches enable continuous monitoring of physiological mechanical signals in clinical and daily settings. However, they often suffer from limited linearity and motion-induced drift due to deformation during body movement during daily activities. We report an integrated, flexible, and miniaturized wearable patch (FMWP) that couples an iontronic pressure sensor with a wireless readout circuit for skin-mounted monitoring. The sensor employs a CNT-doped ionic film with double-sided irregular microstructures that deform progressively, producing a nearly proportional increase in contact area and hybrid ion-electron transport, thereby enabling iontronic capacitive sensing with a high sensitivity (13.5 kPa -1 ) and wide linear range (2–450 kPa, R 2  ~ 0.999). A quadrant-grid spacer suppresses preload contact and stabilizes the baseline capacitance, achieving fast dynamic response (6 ms response, 9 ms relaxation) and durability over 5,000 loading cycles. The backend uses rigid electronic islands interconnected by serpentine copper traces to mechanically limit deformation around functional components and suppress deformation-induced electrical variations, while a patterned porous fiber layer provides breathability and reliable, removable skin adhesion. The FMWP enables real-time, smartphone-based multi-parameter physiological signal monitoring, including pulse, respiration, cardiac microvibrations, and swallowing, offering a practical platform for long-term health assessment.

title: SynForge-Cardio: A Unified Multimodal Synthetic Dataset Generation Framework for Privacy-Preserving Cardiovascular AI
authorString: Kumar SS, N K, M AT, G RS.
abstractText: Multimodal cardiovascular AI development is constrained by privacy regulation, institutional data silos and class imbalance, and open-source synthetic-data tools are largely modality-specific. We present SynForge-Cardio, an orchestration framework that coordinates established generators for chest X-ray (latent diffusion with optional LoRA adaptation), 12-lead ECG (parametric and bounded morphology-preserving augmentation, with an optional TimeGAN path) and tabular EHR data (size-aware routing among jitter augmentation, a Gaussian copula and CTGAN) behind a shared prompt interface, rule-based router and quality and privacy reporting layer. The modalities are generated independently from separate public datasets (NIH ChestX-ray14, PTB-XL, UCI Cleveland Heart Disease); no patient-level joint synthesis or cross-modality consistency is claimed. The router reached 94.6% modality-routing accuracy on a fixed prompt benchmark, and 1,105 automated tests passed with 3 skipped. In train-on-synthetic, test-on-real experiments with five seeds, augmenting a 25%-real training set changed held-out AUROC by − 0.041 to + 0.050 across three CXR tasks (none significant), by + 0.019 for ECG MI-versus-NORM (from bounded real-waveform augmentation, not an independently learned generator) and by + 0.017 for EHR heart-disease classification, which is not evidence of benefit given the 61-record hold-out. Privacy screening is empirical only; no formal privacy guarantee is established.

title: Insulin Resistance in Type 1 Diabetes: An Integrative Transcriptomic Analysis of Insulin Signaling, Immunometabolic Dysfunction, and Peripheral Insulin Exposure-Related Pathways
authorString: Andrade LJdO, de Oliveira GCM, Bittencourt AMV, Salles OJdM, de Oliveira LM.
abstractText: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is defined by autoimmune β-cell destruction and absolute insulin deficiency, yet a substantial proportion of patients develop clinically relevant insulin resistance (IR) that elevates exogenous insulin requirements, glycemic variability, and cardiovascular risk. The molecular architecture of this IR phenotype remains incompletely mapped and may involve coordinated dysregulation across insulin signaling, lipid metabolism, innate immune activation, mitochondrial function, and tissue-level energy homeostasis. Here we present a fully bioinformatic integrative framework that interrogates publicly available peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) transcriptomes from individuals with T1D (GSE9006, GSE55098, GSE72377, GSE156035) together with a subcutaneous adipose reference signature of insulin resistance (GSE245948). The analytic pipeline comprises differential expression modeling (limma), weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), gene-set variation and single-sample enrichment scoring (GSVA/ssGSEA), protein–protein interaction network construction (STRING/Cytoscape), functional enrichment (clusterProfiler/Enrichr), and supervised molecular feature selection (LASSO and random forest). Five a priori biological axes guide the investigation: (1) intracellular insulin signaling, (2) lipid metabolism and storage, (3) metabolic inflammation and innate immunity, (4) mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, and (5) transcriptional correlates of hepatic and skeletal-muscle insulin action detectable in circulating cells. Candidate genes within each axis (INSR, IRS1, IRS2, PIK3CA, AKT2, SLC2A4, FOXO1, GSK3B, PPARGC1A, CD36, SREBF1, FASN, TNF, IL6, NFKB1, NLRP3, TFAM, NDUFS1, SOD2, NFE2L2 and related molecules) serve as investigation targets rather than presupposed results. Findings are interpreted strictly as systemic molecular signatures compatible with IR mechanisms, not as direct functional evidence of muscle or hepatic insulin resistance. Independent cross-dataset validation and explicit separation of leukocyte inflammatory programs from classical metabolic-tissue IR programs are enforced throughout. This open-source roadmap generates prioritized candidate pathways for experimental validation and advances a systems-level view of immunometabolic dysfunction in T1D.

title: Comparative Real-World Safety Profiles of Pembrolizumab Plus Axitinib Versus Pembrolizumab Plus Lenvatinib in Advanced Renal Cell Carcinoma: A Pharmacovigilance Study
authorString: Guo z, Guo D, Tang B, Hang N, Gao C, Rong X, Han J, Luo P, Gao R, Shen Z, Li Q, Wang C, Li L, Xie Z, Zhang B, Wang L.
abstractText: Objective Pembrolizumab plus axitinib (P + A) and pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib (P + L) are already used as first-line standard treatments for advanced renal cell carcinoma (aRCC); however, their real-world safety and the toxicity patterns that each regimen tends to cause have not been clearly and systematically explained. This study aimed to compare the adverse event (AE) spectra of these two immune checkpoint inhibitor-tyrosine kinase inhibitor (ICI-TKI) combinations; the main focus was on toxicity features specific to each regimen, differences in immune-related adverse events (irAEs), and time-to-onset patterns. Methods This study collected individual case safety reports of aRCC patients who received P + A or P + L from two independent pharmacovigilance cohorts; it used three methods for imbalance analysis, namely the reporting odds ratio (ROR), the proportional reporting ratio (PRR), and the Bayesian confidence propagation neural network (BCPNN); the rules for finding signals were set as follows: the lower limit of the 95% confidence interval (CI) of ROR > 1, PRR ≥ 2 with χ² ≥ 4, and IC₀₂₅ > 0; the analysis looked at both the System Organ Class (SOC) level and the Preferred Term (PT) level, with special attention to ten clinically relevant irAEs; these were also divided by sex, age group, and time of onset. Results A total of 897 and 648 reports were included in the P + A and P + L groups, respectively; both regimens covered a wide range of SOCs, but their safety profiles showed clear differences; P + A had more obvious signals in hepatobiliary disorders and certain immune-related toxicities, especially stronger signals for Immune-mediated hepatic disorder and Immune-mediated myocarditis; in contrast, P + L was mainly linked to vascular, renal, metabolic, and endocrine toxicities, with higher signals for Hypertension, Proteinuria, Palmar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia syndrome, and Immune-mediated hypothyroidism; subgroup analyses showed that some immune toxicities changed with age, for example, P + A-related Immune-mediated hepatic disorder had stronger signals in younger patients, while the P + L-related Hypothyroidism signals was more obvious in older patients; analysis of temporal onset showed different paths for different irAEs, such as very early start, middle-stage peak, and late build-up patterns. Several potential novel signals, including Tumor necrosis and Immune-mediated hyperthyroidism, were identified. Conclusion Pembrolizumab plus axitinib and pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib exhibited markedly distinct safety profiles in the treatment of aRCC. The P + A regimen was primarily characterized by hepatobiliary and cardiac-specific immunotoxicities, whereas the P + L regimen was more closely associated with vascular, renal, metabolic, and endocrine toxicities. Age stratification and temporal profiling provided novel evidence to inform personalized monitoring strategies. Because spontaneous reporting databases have intrinsic constraints, our observations should be confirmed in prospective clinical investigations.

title: Transformer-Based Cardiovascular Risk Assessment via Retinal and ECG Signals Under a Leakage-Free Protocol
authorString: Jinkathoti S, Vani MS.
abstractText:
Background:

Deep learning on retinal fundus images and on the electrocardiogram (ECG) has each shown promise for cardiovascular risk assessment, and multimodal fusion is often claimed to reach near-perfect accuracy. Such claims are frequently confounded by data leakage and by evaluation on data that does not actually contain the stated modalities.

Methods:

We re-implemented a trans-former-based multimodal framework and evaluated it under a strict leakage-free protocol on two public datasets: PTB-XL (21,799 twelve-lead ECGs; myocardial-infarction vs. normal, 1513 held-out test ECGs on the official patient-respecting fold) and China-Fundus-CIMT (2,903 patients, carotid intima-media-thickness-defined risk; three-fold patient-level cross-validation). A spectro-temporal ECG transformer and a retinal vision transformer were trained independently and combined by decision-level fusion; all preprocessing, model selection and thresholds were confined to training folds. Each modality was compared with strong baselines.

Results:

The ECG transformer reached 90.75% accuracy and an AUC of 0.970 (sensitivity 88.91%, specificity 91.80%), exceeding lo-gistic-regression, random-forest and gradient-boosting baselines (AUC 0.835-0.869). The retinal transformer reached 71.34+/-4.57% accuracy and an AUC of 0.764+/-0.016; notably, an age-plus-sex logistic baseline (AUC 0.854) outperformed the image model, indicating limited added value of the fundus images for this label. Because the two cohorts share no patients, fusion could only be studied by simulation and did not constitute per-patient validation.

Conclusions:

Under rigorous evalua-tion, ECG-based MI detection is strong and reproducible, whereas retinal CIMT-risk prediction is modest and does not beat demographics, and genuine multimodal fusion will be investigated in future research.

title: Current Status of Senolytics and Senomorphics: Mechanistic Insights, Clinical Progress, and Future Directions
authorString: Ahmed F, Mishra P, Khanam R.
abstractText:
Background:

Cellular senescence contributes to aging, chronic inflammation, and age-related diseases. Senolytics eliminate senescent cells, whereas senomorphics modulate their pathological activities, including the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). This review examines their mechanisms, preclinical and clinical evidence, safety, and translational challenges.

Methods:

Published mechanistic, preclinical, and clinical literature on senolytic and senomorphic therapies was reviewed, focusing on therapeutic targets, disease-specific findings, safety, and clinical translation.

Results:

Senolytics, including dasatinib plus quercetin, navitoclax, and fisetin, target senescent-cell survival pathways, whereas senomorphics, including rapamycin, metformin, and Janus kinase inhibitors, modulate inflammatory signaling and SASP-associated pathways. Preclinical studies suggest benefits across metabolic, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, and neurodegenerative disease models. However, human evidence remains limited and heterogeneous. Early clinical studies demonstrate the feasibility of senescence targeting and changes in selected biomarkers, but consistent clinical benefit remains unestablished. Major challenges include senescent-cell heterogeneity, insufficiently validated biomarkers, treatment-related toxicity, and the physiological roles of senescence in tissue repair and tumor suppression.

Conclusions:

Senolytics and senomorphics are promising but investigational therapeutic strategies. Clinical translation requires validated biomarkers, disease-specific patient selection, improved therapeutic selectivity, adequately powered trials with clinically meaningful endpoints, and long-term safety assessment. Aligning therapeutic strategies with senescent-cell phenotypes, disease context, and treatment objectives may improve clinical relevance.

title: Central Chronotropic Incompetence After Rhombencephalitis.
authorString: Schmick A, Saguner AM, Nierobisch N, Ferdinand O, Tatsch L, Globas C, Stiefel M, Hermann M, Patriki D.
abstractText:
Background

Rhombencephalitis is a rare inflammatory brainstem condition. Central cardiovascular dysfunction, specifically chronotropic incompetence (CI), remains an underrecognized chronic sequela.

Case summary

A 50-year-old man was evaluated for progressive exertional dyspnea. Cardiopulmonary and structural cardiac assessments were unremarkable. One year earlier, he survived idiopathic biopsy-proven necrotizing rhombencephalitis, successfully managed with immunomodulatory therapy. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing unmasked profound CI. At the 2-year follow-up, peak oxygen uptake and workload normalized, but functional limitation persisted because of a rigidly blunted maximal heart rate.

Discussion

This unique case demonstrates a persistent decoupling of the heart-brain axis. The isolated CI may reflect focal structural destruction of medullary sympathetic premotor neurons, despite preserved intrinsic cardiac function.

Take-home messages

In otherwise unexplained exercise intolerance following brainstem injury, central autonomic dysfunction may be considered as a potential contributor. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing may help identify a disproportionate chronotropic limitation when routine cardiac investigations are unremarkable.

title: Atrial Flutter in Adolescence Due to Invasive Cardiac Lipoma: A Rare Presentation.
authorString: Damera MM, Chmaisse A, Qureshi Z, Turrentine M, Hussain S, Ayers MD.
abstractText:
Background

Primary cardiac tumors are rare, with lipomas comprising ∼10% of benign cases. Although typically asymptomatic, invasive variants may infiltrate myocardium and generate significant arrhythmogenic substrate.

Case summary

A 14-year-old previously healthy male patient presented with atrial flutter and was found to have a large, infiltrative lipomatous mass involving the right atrium, right ventricle, and tricuspid valve. Biopsy and partial debulking confirmed invasive cardiac lipoma, but complete excision was precluded by extensive myocardial infiltration. Despite antiarrhythmic therapy, he developed recurrent atrial flutter and ventricular dysfunction. Electrophysiology study identified a cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent flutter that was successfully ablated; however, a second tumor-associated circuit was not amenable to ablation because of anatomical barriers. Sinus rhythm was restored with cardioversion and amiodarone with subsequent recovery of ventricular function.

Discussion

Invasive cardiac lipomas present unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges, often requiring multimodal imaging, multidisciplinary management, aggressive rhythm control, and consideration of cardiac transplantation in select patients.

title: Concomitant Wire-Loop Repositioning and Transapical Valve Replacement for a Migrated Sutureless Aortic Valve.
authorString: Hamada Y, Kawamura T, Yoshioka D, Watanabe Y, Misumi Y, Kawamura A, Yajima S, Saito S, Shimamura K, Miyagawa S.
abstractText:
Background

Sutureless aortic prosthesis migration is rare but potentially catastrophic.

Case summary

A 78-year-old woman on hemodialysis underwent minimally invasive double valve replacement using a sutureless aortic bioprosthesis. Failure to wean from cardiopulmonary bypass prompted intraoperative angiography, which raised suspicion of cranial migration of the aortic prosthesis, with bilateral coronary hypoperfusion; subsequent computed tomography confirmed the diagnosis. Because repositioning after surgical excision of the native leaflets would cause severe aortic regurgitation, a transapical transcatheter valve was prepositioned before transfemoral wire-loop repositioning. Coronary flow was restored, the failed valve was replaced, and 5-month follow-up showed preserved ventricular function and stable frame position.

Discussion

Prepositioning a transapical transcatheter valve before wire-loop repositioning enabled immediate valve replacement while minimizing the empty-annulus interval.

Take-home message

Failed passage of a Perceval sizer should preclude sutureless implantation; prepositioned transapical valve replacement with wire-loop repositioning is a viable bailout.

title: Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement in an Incomplete Ring With LAMPOON Facilitated By Aortic Prosthesis.
authorString: Ozdemir D, Singh M, Bruckel J, Bajwa F, Hisamoto K, Melito E, Ling F.
abstractText:
Background

Transcatheter mitral valve replacement in large incomplete flexible mitral bands is high risk because limited anchoring and anterior leaflet displacement may cause embolization or left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction.

Case summary

A 54-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy, prior coronary artery bypass grafting, aortic valve-in-valve transcatheter aortic valve replacement, mitral repair with a 31-mm Duran AnCore band, and tricuspid annuloplasty presented with NYHA functional class IV heart failure from severe recurrent mitral regurgitation. Computed tomography excluded SAPIEN M3 (predicted neo-LVOT 0 mm2) and showed a long anterior mitral leaflet, raising concern for dynamic obstruction despite a predicted neo-LVOT of 347.6 mm2 for a 29-mm balloon-expandable valve. He underwent antegrade base-to-tip laceration of the anterior mitral leaflet to prevent outflow obstruction, followed by valve-in-ring transcatheter mitral valve replacement, with no paravalvular leak or significant LVOT gradient.

Discussion

Anterior aortic prosthetic anatomy facilitated valve anchoring despite the incomplete flexible band, which would have been prohibitive in the absence of anterior bioprosthesis.

Take-home message

Adjacent prosthetic anatomy may be leveraged in selected complex valve-in-ring procedures after meticulous multimodality planning and procedural expertise.

title: Surgical Resection of a Large Right Ventricular Metastasis From Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
authorString: Ingason AB, Grosser RA, Gregg AC, Chow OS, Lee BE, Hyun J, Gulkarov I.
abstractText:
Background

Intracavitary right ventricular metastasis is a rare presentation of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), often associated with dismal prognosis given associated complications such as tumor embolism, valve dysfunction, and right ventricular outflow tract obstruction.

Case summary

A 59-year-old man presenting with palpitations and tachycardia was found to have concomitant intracavitary right ventricular mass and lung mass. Ventricular mass was resected on cardiopulmonary bypass along with wedge resection of lung lesion, providing symptomatic relief and tissue diagnosis of pleomorphic NSCLC. The patient went on to receive systemic therapy (first immunotherapy, then targeted therapy) achieving 14-month overall survival.

Discussion

This case highlights a rare presentation of NSCLC with intracavitary cardiac metastasis and options for multimodal surgical and medical management.

Take-home messages

Intracavitary right ventricular metastasis from NSCLC is rare and associated with poor prognosis. Surgical resection may be necessary to prevent fatal complications, such as right ventricular outflow tract obstruction.

title: Endoaortic Balloon Occlusion for Minimally Invasive Mitral Valve Replacement After Previous Balloon-Expandable TAVI.
authorString: Agostini G, Barbero C, Galanti GA, La Montagna L, Ciancamerla F, La Torre MW, Salizzoni S, Rinaldi M.
abstractText:
Background

Prior transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) may complicate minimally invasive mitral valve surgery when endoaortic balloon occlusion (EABO) is considered. Guidance for EABO after TAVI remains limited.

Case summary

A 56-year-old woman with radiation-induced multivalvular disease underwent staged transfemoral balloon-expandable TAVI and coronary revascularization, followed by minimally invasive mitral valve replacement using EABO. Pre-TAVI computed tomography identified a potential ascending-aortic landing zone, and continuous TEE confirmed balloon positioning above the TAVI frame. EABO achieved complete aortic occlusion without migration, frame contact, or evidence of cerebral malperfusion.

Discussion

Prior balloon-expandable TAVI may not preclude EABO in carefully selected patients with favorable ascending-aortic anatomy. Imaging-based selection, continuous TEE surveillance, and controlled inflation are central to safety.

Take-home message

Prior balloon-expandable TAVI does not preclude EABO in selected patients with a suitable ascending-aortic landing zone.

title: Mitochondrial DNA-cGAS-STING induces macrophage pyroptosis via phospho-IRF3-mediated NLRP3 expression in ionising radiation-induced atherosclerosis progression.
authorString: Pang S, Chen Y, Zhu X, Guan X, Ding S, Yu D, Luan T, Liu M, Shi M, Jiang S, Cao Y, Liu J, Sun D, Liu J, Liu Z, Luo X, Jie Y, Gu A, Lin Q, E M.
abstractText:
Background and purpose

Ionising radiation (IR) is a major cancer-treatment modality, yet the mechanisms driving IR-triggered cardiovascular injury are poorly defined. This work aimed to uncover how IR accelerates atherosclerosis (AS) and the underlying molecular mechanisms.

Experimental approach
