In adjusted models, each 10 mL/min/1.73 m² increase in eGFR difference, indicating higher eGFRcys relative to eGFRcr, was associated with lower risks of mortality (Hazard Ratio [HR] 0.88, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.80-0.96) and kidney function decline (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.71-0.91), with a similar trend for MACE (HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.83-1.00). In patients hospitalised with ACS, eGFR discordance reflecting lower cystatin C-based eGFR than creatinine-based eGFR is associated with adverse long-term cardiorenal outcomes, even among patients with preserved creatinine-based kidney function.

title: Frequency of Antibody-Mediated Positive Interference in a Healthy Danish Cohort Using Combined Immunodepletion and Ultracentrifugation with a High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin I Assay.
authorString: Khachatryan M, Strandkjaer N, Banerjee A, Hansen MB, Hasselbalch RB, Knudsen SS, Kristensen JH, Hilsted L, Dahl M, Overgaard M, Ladefoged SA, Bundgaard H, Iversen KK, Hammarsten O.

journal.title: The journal of applied laboratory medicine

abstractText: Diagnosis of myocardial infarction relies in part on cardiac troponin (cTn) concentrations exceeding the 99th percentile upper reference limit. Positive antibody-mediated interference (PAI) occurs when anti-cTn antibodies form macrotroponin complexes with slow clearance or when heterophilic antibodies generate cTn-independent signals. PAI may inflate the upper reference limit and may increase the risk of missed myocardial infarction. We determined the frequency of PAI using the Abbott Alinity High-Sensitivity cTnI Assay and assessed its impact on the 99th percentile in a healthy Danish reference population. In a cross-sectional cohort of 1053 healthy individuals used to establish Danish 99th percentiles, PAI was assessed in samples within the sex-specific highest 10% of cTn concentrations. Ultracentrifugation and immunodepletion were used to evaluate molecular weight and the effect of IgG removal on measured cTnI. Concordant results from both methods were considered confirmatory for PAI. Sex-specific 99th percentiles were recalculated after excluding individuals with confirmed PAI. A low-dilution combined ultracentrifugation and immunodepletion protocol enabled detection of PAI at cTnI concentrations as low as 3.5 ng/L. Among the 86 highest samples, 48 (56%) were classified as PAI, corresponding to an overall frequency of 4.6%. Exclusion of PAI reduced the 99th percentile from 45 ng/L to 10 ng/L overall, from 66 ng/L to 11 ng/L among men, and from 21 to 8 ng/L among women. PAI detected with our method that combines immunodepletion and ultracentrifugation is common and substantially inflates the 99th percentile for the Abbott Alinity High-Sensitivity cTnI Assay.

title: FGF13 attenuates myocardial infarction-induced cardiac injury by modulating oxidative stress and NF-κB signaling.
authorString: Zhang Y, Wang Y, Yang X, Li C, Pan J.
abstractText: Myocardial infarction (MI) is a major cause of heart failure characterized by cardiomyocyte loss, adverse remodeling, and oxidative stress, with limited effective therapeutic targets. Fibroblast growth factor 13 (FGF13), an intracellular FGF family member, has not been fully explored in MI. Integrated transcriptomic analyses, including single-cell and bulk RNA sequencing datasets, revealed that FGF13 is predominantly expressed in cardiomyocytes and is downregulated following MI. In an MI model with AAV-mediated FGF13 overexpression, FGF13 improved cardiac function, as evidenced by increased ejection fraction and fractional shortening, reduced ventricular dilation, and attenuated fibrosis and apoptosis in vivo. In vitro, hypoxia decreased FGF13 expression in a time-dependent manner, accompanied by increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and activation of NF-κB signaling. FGF13 overexpression reduced ROS accumulation, suppressed p65 phosphorylation, and restored SOD2 expression. Moreover, TNF-α-induced NF-κB activation promoted oxidative stress, whereas FGF13 partially reversed these effects. Collectively, FGF13 alleviates MI-induced cardiac injury and adverse remodeling, accompanied by reduced oxidative stress and NF-κB activation, highlighting its potential role in the response to ischemic cardiac injury.

title: Management of blood pressure in patients with frailty: update and perspectives-a 2026 mini-review.
authorString: Ishikawa J.

journal.title: Hypertension research : official journal of the Japanese Society of Hypertension

abstractText: Intensive blood pressure lowering reduces primary outcomes regardless of frailty status. Consideration of blood pressure targets is necessary in individuals with disabilities and reduced activities of daily living, because blood pressure tended to decline at the end of life in observational studies. Among older nursing home residents with frailty who were receiving treatment with antihypertensive agents and had a systolic blood pressure below 130 mm Hg, an antihypertensive treatment step-down strategy did not lead to statistically lower all-cause mortality than usual care. The benefit of intensive blood pressure lowering in individuals with autonomic dysfunction has not been clarified, and blood pressure management is often challenging. Blood pressure measurements may be affected by frailty. Optimal blood pressure, rather than a fixed target blood pressure level, should be considered by balancing the reduction in cardiovascular events with the maintenance of quality of life in patients with disabilities and those near the end of life.

title: Pulse wave analysis detected by a computerized method using the cardio-ankle vascular index in aortic stenosis.
authorString: Suzuki N, Suzuki Y, Ogata Y, Kabutoya T, Yoneyama T, Nakagawa Y, Fukatani K, Hoshide S, Kario K.

journal.title: Hypertension research : official journal of the Japanese Society of Hypertension

abstractText: Although pulsus parvus et tardus is a classical physical finding in aortic stenosis (AS), objective quantitative assessment of pulse waveform morphology has been limited. We developed a novel computerized pulse waveform parameter, initial upstroke time (iUT), derived from cardio-ankle vascular index (CAVI) pulse waveforms to quantify the delay in the initial systolic upstroke. We analyzed 158 patients with mild or greater AS who underwent CAVI measurement and echocardiography. Associations of conventional upstroke time (UT) and iUT with echocardiographic measures of AS severity, including aortic valve area (AVA), peak aortic jet velocity (Vmax), and mean pressure gradient (MPG), were evaluated using multivariable regression analyses. Diagnostic performance was assessed by receiver operating characteristic analysis. Both UT and iUT were significantly correlated with AVA and Vmax; however, iUT showed stronger correlations. In multivariable analyses including both parameters, iUT remained independently associated with AVA (standardized β = -0.488, P < 0.001) and Vmax (standardized β = 0.573, P < 0.001), whereas UT was not associated with Vmax and showed only a borderline association with AVA. Compared with UT, iUT also demonstrated superior diagnostic performance for identifying severe AS defined by Vmax ≥4.0 m/s (area under the curve [AUC], 0.843 vs. 0.678; P = 0.005) and MPG ≥ 40 mmHg (AUC, 0.795 vs. 0.637; P = 0.003), but not for AVA ≤ 1.0 cm². A novel computerized pulse waveform parameter reflecting the initial systolic upstroke was more strongly associated with echocardiographic measures of AS severity than conventional UT. Automated analysis of CAVI pulse waveforms may provide an objective adjunct for assessing AS without additional testing.

title: Outcomes of heart transplantation with or without pre-transplant mechanical circulatory support: a single-center cohort study in Korea.
authorString: Kim CE, Hong JH, Lee JY, Jung SW.
abstractText:
Background

Heart transplantation is considered the definitive treatment for patients with end-stage heart failure (HF). Many patients with end-stage HF progress to cardiogenic shock or severe low cardiac output states while on the waiting list and require mechanical circulatory support (MCS) as a bridge to transplantation. The primary endpoint of this study was to assess overall survival after heart transplantation according to pre-transplant MCS use. The secondary outcomes included postoperative complications, intensive care utilization, and perioperative transfusion requirements.

Methods

This retrospective single-center study included recipients of heart transplantation. A total of 100 consecutive patients were categorized into three groups according to pre-transplant MCS use (ECMO, LVAD, and non-MCS groups). Follow-up was censored on February 28, 2026.

Results

The mortality was significantly higher and the overall survival was significantly lower in the ECMO group than in the non-MCS group. Overall survival significantly differed among the three groups (log-rank P = 0.001), driven mainly by worse survival in the ECMO group than in the non-MCS group, whereas survival did not significantly differ between the ECMO and LVAD groups.

Conclusions

The ECMO group showed a significantly worse survival than the non-MCS group, whereas survival did not significantly differ between the ECMO and LVAD groups, which was likely attributed to the small sample size of the LVAD group. Postoperative continuous renal replacement therapy and other markers of organ dysfunction were more frequent in the ECMO group and likely reflected the greater severity of illness in these patients rather than the independent risk factors.

title: ENPP1 deficiency in siblings with apparently discordant phenotypes: case report and a review of the literature.
authorString: Wada T, Miyahara Y, Hasegawa Y, Hirata K, Matsuoka K, Ishii Y, Mochizuki N, Okamoto N, Etani Y, Kawai M.

journal.title: Journal of pediatric endocrinology & metabolism : JPEM

abstractText:
Objectives

ENPP1 deficiency encompasses a phenotypic spectrum from generalized arterial calcification of infancy (GACI) to autosomal recessive hypophosphatemic rickets type 2 (ARHR2), and phenotypic variability has been reported even among individuals carrying the same variants; however, the extent of intrafamilial phenotypic concordance remains unclear.

Case presentation

Case 1, a 20-month-old boy, presented with genu varum and fibroblast growth factor 23-mediated hypophosphatemic rickets. Genetic testing identified compound heterozygous ENPP1 variants, c.937_938insT (p.Gln313LeufsTer18), and a deletion involving exons 8-13. Ultrasonography revealed valvular calcifications, carotid intimal irregularity, and nephrocalcinosis. Case 2, his younger brother, developed fetal hydrops, diffuse cardiovascular calcification, and severe cardiac dysfunction in late gestation and died shortly after preterm birth. Postmortem examination demonstrated extensive vascular calcification consistent with GACI; genetic testing identified the same variants. A sibling-based literature review of genetically confirmed cases with shared biallelic ENPP1 variants identified 21 publications describing 26 unrelated families. Including the present family, 27 families comprising 61 affected individuals were analyzed; 24 families (88.9 %) had concordant phenotypes, whereas three (11.1 %) had discordant phenotypes. Among 19 individuals who presented with hypophosphatemia or ARHR2 without a documented history of GACI and underwent cardiovascular, calcification, and/or hearing assessment, 14 had abnormal findings.

Conclusions

Documented GACI status was generally concordant among affected siblings. Frequent cardiovascular, calcification-related, and/or hearing abnormalities in patients presenting with hypophosphatemia or ARHR2 without a documented history of GACI highlight the importance of multisystem assessment and support GACI and ARHR2 as overlapping manifestations within the ENPP1 deficiency spectrum.

title: An effective approach for the management of men's sexual dysfunction via local administration of Sildenafil/cyclodextrin-loaded hydrogels.
authorString: Osman SK, Yassin AM, Mohammed AM, Yassin TM, Abdelsalam AM, Marzouk AA, Ahmed F, Taha EA, Alshora DH, Ibrahim MA.
abstractText: This study aimed to enhance the bioavailability of Sildenafil via cyclodextrin inclusion complexation and to formulate various hydrogel systems containing modified Sildenafil as an alternative, safe treatment for erectile dysfunction. Oral administration of Sildenafil is accompanied by severe hypotension, making this drug contraindicated for patients with cardiac dysfunction, which may lead to fatal acute and severe hypotension. Therefore, topical and local administration is considered an option to avoid side effects accompanying oral administration. The current work was divided into three distinct segments. First, we enhanced the solubility of sildenafil by forming and characterizing inclusion complexes with hydroxypropyl-β-CD. Secondly, hydrogels were prepared and characterized using different gelling agents, including Carbopol 940, HPMC, and Gelatin. Lastly, the selected hydrogel system was utilized for the in vivo application in participants (n = 60). The gel formulation was applied locally on the penis 0.5 h before intercourse, and both intravaginal latency time (IVLT) and International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-5) were monitored before and after drug application. Besides, irritation studies were conducted on rat models. The drug solubility and dissolution rate were markedly improved via inclusion complexation with cyclodextrin. Also, the medicated hydrogel formulations exhibited good consistency, spreadability, and homogeneity. Notably, the gel composed of HPMC, loaded with modified Sildenafil, demonstrated the fastest release rate compared to the other gelling agents. The in vivo results revealed a remarkable improvement in both erectile dysfunction and premature ejaculation parameters (IVLT and IIEF-5). Also, the results showed that there is no sign of irritation upon application. The modified Sildenafil hydrogel is an alternative and safe therapy for patients suffering from erectile dysfunction and premature ejaculation since this route of administration avoids severe risks accompanying oral administration.

title: Low-Dose Versus High-Dose Drug-Coated Balloon After Jetstream Atherectomy for Severely Calcified Femoropopliteal Lesions: The JUPITER Multicenter Study.
authorString: Ogata K, Nishihira K, Nakai M, Tokuda T, Yoshioka N, Tanaka A, Kojima S, Yamaguchi K, Yanagiuchi T, Takei T, Nakama T, Shibata Y, Tsujita K, LEADers PAD investigators.

journal.title: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions

abstractText: Second-generation low-dose drug-coated balloons (LD-DCBs) have shown clinical efficacy comparable to high-dose DCBs (HD-DCBs) for femoropopliteal artery (FPA) lesions. Whether paclitaxel dose density remains clinically relevant after aggressive vessel preparation with atherectomy in severely calcified FPA lesions remains uncertain. This study aimed to compare 1-year clinical outcomes of second-generation LD-DCB and HD-DCB following Jetstream atherectomy in patients with severely calcified FPA lesions. This study aimed to compare 1-year clinical outcomes of second-generation LD-DCB and HD-DCB following Jetstream atherectomy in patients with severely calcified FPA lesions. This multicenter retrospective study included 262 patients with severely calcified FPA lesions who underwent endovascular therapy with Jetstream atherectomy followed by second-generation LD-DCB (n = 175) or HD-DCB (n = 87). Propensity-score matching yielded 79 well-balanced pairs. The primary outcome was 1-year primary patency; secondary outcomes included freedom from clinically driven target-lesion revascularization (TLR), limb salvage, and overall survival. In the overall cohort before matching, 1-year primary patency was similar between second-generation LD-DCB and HD-DCB (86.8% vs. 83.1%, log-rank p = 0.578), with comparable freedom from TLR, limb salvage, and overall survival. After propensity score matching, primary patency remained similar between groups (88.5% vs. 84.9%, log-rank p = 0.588), as did freedom from TLR, limb salvage, and overall survival. Findings were consistent across calcification-related subgroups. In an exploratory Cox analysis, second-generation LD-DCB was not associated with an increased risk of restenosis compared with HD-DCB. After Jetstream atherectomy for severely calcified FPA lesions, second-generation LD-DCB and HD-DCB were associated with comparable 1-year clinical outcomes, suggesting that either strategy may be a reasonable treatment option.

title: Inverse association between serum osteocalcin and pericardial adipose tissue in Koreans: cross-sectional study.
authorString: Shin M, Choi BH, Joo NS.
abstractText:
Background

Osteocalcin (OC), a bone matrix protein of osteoblastic origin, is thought to play a role in systemic metabolic function. However, the relationship between serum OC levels and pericardial adipose tissue (PAT) volume remains unclear.

Methods

Using a cross-sectional design, 438 participants (88 females, 350 males) who underwent cardiac CT imaging were enrolled. Simple and partial correlation analyses were performed. OC levels were divided into tertile groups to assess their relationship with PAT, adjusting for age, sex, smoking, hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Linear and logistic regression models were also applied.

Results

The mean participant age was 55.7 years. The average serum OC level was 15.9 ng/mL, and the mean PAT volume was 127.6 cm3. OC level and PAT volume showed an inverse correlation that was significant in both unadjusted (r=-0.158, P=0.001) and covariate-adjusted (r=-0.106, P=0.032) analyses. Inter-tertile PAT differences remained significant after stratification (P<0.05). In multivariate regression analysis, the inverse association remained statistically significant after adjustment for age, sex and smoking (P=0.019), but not after additional adjustment for body mass index (P=0.656). After adjustment, relative to the highest OC tertile, the odds ratios for being classified into the highest PAT tertile were 2.73 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.43-5.21) for the lowest and 2.99 (95% CI, 1.59-5.66) for the middle OC tertile.

Conclusion

Serum OC level was inversely associated with PAT volume; however, this association was attenuated after adjusting for adiposity-related variables, suggesting that shared metabolic or body composition factors may partly account for the observed relationship.

title: CT-based Epicardial Adipose Tissue Change as a Promising Biomarker of Obstructive Coronary Artery Disease Progression: A Longitudinal Observational Study.
authorString: Zhang W, Zhang L, Chen M, Fu J, Jin D, Xiong X, Chen X, Zhang F, Guan X, Zhou Q, Xu X.
abstractText: To evaluate the association between CT-based longitudinal changes in epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) volume and obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD) progression. We included 583 suspected CAD patients (median age, 60 years; 348 men) who underwent coronary CT angiography (CCTA) between June 2010 and June 2017, and received follow-up CCTA at an interval of ≥ 2 years (median interval, 3.33 years; IQR, 2.67 to 4.33 years). 107 patients progressed to obstructive CAD. EAT volume and coronary artery calcium score (CACS) were measured on non-contrast CCTA. Annualised EAT volume change was calculated as the difference between follow-up and baseline scans divided by the follow-up duration. Obstructive CAD progression was defined as new-onset ≥50% stenosis in initially non-obstructive patients. The association of EAT with obstructive CAD progression was evaluated by univariate and multivariate logistic regression. Annualised EAT volume change was 3.47 cm³ in the obstructive progression group and 2.07 cm³ in the no obstructive progression group (P = 0.006). In univariate analysis, only age, CACS, baseline largest luminal diameter stenosis and annualised EAT volume change were significantly associated with obstructive CAD progression. Annualised EAT volume change remained independently associated with obstructive CAD progression (adjusted OR = 1.06, P = 0.007) after adjustment for variables significant in univariate analysis. Annualised EAT volume change was independently associated with obstructive CAD progression. Annualised EAT volume change may represent a CT-based imaging marker of obstructive CAD progression.

title: A Topology-Feature Disentangled Deep Clustering Method for scRNA-seq Based on Graph-to-MLP Distillation.
authorString: Gao X, Liu H, Zhao Y, Lv X, Zhao X, Chen C.
abstractText: Graph neural networks (GNNs), owing to their ability to model topological relationships between cells, have gradually emerged as a mainstream approach in the clustering analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. However, their practical application still faces the following challenges: (1) excessive smoothing undermines cellular heterogeneity; (2) pre-constructed graphs introduce end-to-end dependencies; (3) large-scale cellular graph computations are computationally intensive. To fully utilise the expression profiles and topological information contained within scRNA-seq data and overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a Graph-to-MLP (G2M) knowledge distillation method incorporating AdaBoost principles, and builds upon this to develop a graph-disentangled single-cell clustering framework-scAdaG2M. This framework utilises a GNN teacher model to learn higher-order topological relationships and local neighbourhood structures between cells on a cellular graph, whilst multiple lightweight MLP student models perform feature learning in an ungraphed setting. By combining this with an AdaBoost-style dynamic reweighting strategy, the framework enhances the model's ability to characterise cells that are difficult to distinguish, cells with blurred boundaries, and potentially rare cell populations, thereby mitigating the dilution of cellular heterogeneity caused by over-smoothing. At the same time, this framework effectively decouples graph-based modelling from graph-free reasoning, reduces the end-to-end reliance on pre-constructed graphs, and significantly reduces the computational overhead associated with large-scale cellular graphs. All datasets used in this study are publicly available. Detailed information about all the single-cell datasets analyzed in this paper is provided in Supplementary Table 1. The source code is available at https://github.com/gxl1110/scAdaG2M and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21512950. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Liver radiomics on routine cardiac CT identifies hepatic stress states that predict heart failure.
authorString: Modanwal G, Dhamdhere R, Singh A, Lebowitz M, Sirasapalli SK, Alkhaleefah M, Bose B, Nasir K, Rajagopalan S, Al-Kindi S, Madabhushi A.
abstractText:
Aims

Heart failure (HF) prevention remains limited because early multisystem cardiometabolic dysfunction is not captured by conventional risk tools. We evaluated whether liver radiomic phenotypes derived opportunistically from coronary artery calcium computed tomography (CAC-CT) identify imaging-defined hepatic stress states associated with incident HF.

Methods and results

We analysed 59 237 individuals undergoing CAC-CT (CLARIFY: 46 028; Houston Methodist: 13 209). Liver regions were segmented and radiomic features extracted to derive a Liver Radiomics Score (LRS). The model was trained in a CLARIFY derivation cohort (Dtr, n = 9205), validated in a hold-out cohort (Dts, n = 36 823), and externally evaluated in Houston Methodist (Dext, n = 13 209). The mean follow-up was 1411 days (SD 760.1) in the pooled Dtr and Dts cohorts (1144 HF events) and 470 days (SD 596) in Dext (212 HF events). Continuous LRS was associated with incident HF [Dts: hazard ratio (HR) 1.63, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.52-1.74; P < 0.001; Dext: HR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.07; P = 0.004] and remained significant after multivariable adjustment in Dts. Increasing LRS quartiles showed progressively adverse hepatic, haemodynamic, and cardiometabolic profiles and higher HF risk. Among 17 806 Dts participants with PREVENT data, adding LRS modestly improved discrimination across CAC- and PREVENT-based models (P < 0.001) and improved reclassification metrics (7-year net reclassification improvement up to 0.25; including integrated discrimination improvement up to 0.015). High LRS identified elevated risk in low-risk groups: among participants with CAC=0, high LRS conferred ∼2.5-fold higher 5-year HF incidence, and ∼2.9-fold in PREVENT-low individuals.

Conclusion

In this large multicentre cohort, liver radiomics from CAC-CT captured hepatic stress states linked to HF risk and modestly improved risk stratification beyond CAC and PREVENT scores.

title: Pericarditis in COVID-19: a focus on the paediatric population.
authorString: Bou Jaoude CR, Yassine F, Sleem B, Awada A, Bitar FF, Arabi M.
abstractText:
Background

COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2, is primarily a respiratory illness but may cause cardiovascular complications, including pericarditis. Pediatric SARS-CoV-2-associated pericarditis remains uncommon and likely underreported. This review summarizes the epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, management, and outcomes of pericarditis associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection in children.

Methods

We narratively reviewed the available literature on SARS-CoV-2-associated pericarditis in the pediatric population, including isolated acute pericarditis, myopericarditis, pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, and pericardial involvement in multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C).

Results

The true incidence of pediatric SARS-CoV-2-associated pericarditis remains unclear. Reported cases suggest that older children and adolescents are more commonly affected, typically presenting with chest pain, fever, dyspnea, or tachycardia, whereas younger children may exhibit nonspecific symptoms. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria supported by electrocardiography, echocardiography, inflammatory markers, and cardiac biomarkers, with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging useful when myocardial involvement is suspected. Available evidence suggests a predominantly immune-mediated pathophysiology involving cytokine dysregulation and systemic inflammation, with limited evidence of direct viral invasion. Management is largely extrapolated from established pediatric pericarditis principles and adult data. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and colchicine are first-line therapies, while corticosteroids or intravenous immunoglobulin may be considered in selected inflammatory or MIS-C-associated cases, and interleukin-1 blockade in refractory or recurrent disease. Most affected children recover, although severe pericardial effusion, tamponade, and recurrence have been reported.

Conclusion

Pediatric SARS-CoV-2-associated pericarditis encompasses a spectrum of clinical presentations and generally carries a favorable prognosis. Nevertheless, potentially serious complications emphasize the importance of early recognition, differentiation from myocarditis and MIS-C, and structured follow-up.

title: The cath lab readiness gap: a national survey of technology-driven role shifts and training needs among nurses and radiographers in France.
authorString: Mette C, Begue F, Pausé JB, Piot O, Maujean J, Sambourg J, Desroche LM.
abstractText: Rapid technological change in cath labs is redistributing operational responsibilities towards nurses and radiographers. We aimed to quantify this redistribution, and to assess whether training, regulatory framing, and professional recognition have kept pace. A national cross-sectional online survey was conducted in 2025 among 371 professionals in French catheterisation or electrophysiology laboratories (207 nurses, 60 radiographers, 78 cardiologists, 26 nurse managers). The primary outcome - perceived change in responsibilities - was analysed as binary (moderate or strong increase vs other responses) by logistic regression adjusted for profession, age, sex, and seniority. A strong increase in responsibilities of nurses and radiographers was reported by 54.6% of nurses and 48.3% of radiographers, versus 25.6% of cardiologists and 38.5% of nurse managers. Nurse/radiographer status was the strongest predictor (adjusted OR 6.11 [95% CI 2.86-13.66] vs cardiologists and nurse managers; p < 0.001). Training was predominantly apprenticeship-based (on-the-job mentoring, 66.3%); the perceived adequacy of nurses' and radiographers' initial training was rated 20/100 by nurses and 31.5/100 by radiographers, versus 40/100 by cardiologists (p < 0.001). About half of nurses and radiographers considered that procedures are often performed outside the formal regulatory scope (52% and 45%, respectively); 93% of nurses and 90% of radiographers demanded regulatory clarification. Technology is redistributing responsibilities towards nurses and radiographers faster than training, regulatory framing, or recognition - a readiness gap perceived far more acutely by paramedical than medical professionals. Every technology deployment should integrate team readiness, regulatory clarification, and recognition commensurate with current practice.

title: Circulating miR-10b-5p drives Kawasaki vasculitis via endothelial reprogramming and nominates CXCL8 as an early diagnostic biomarker.
authorString: Park S, Kang G, Kim M, Kim MH, Yang H, Lim B, Jung S, Cho YK, Kim YK, Park WJ, Yoon S, Eom GH.
abstractText: Kawasaki disease (KD) is an acute systemic vasculitis and the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children, yet no specific biomarker enables early diagnosis at emergency department presentation. We aimed to define the molecular mechanisms driving KD vasculitis and to identify a clinically actionable early diagnostic marker. Whole microRNA sequencing of buffy coat specimens from patients with KD and febrile controls identified 68 upregulated microRNAs, of which 13 were prioritized. Candidates were validated in two KD-like vasculitis mouse models, and miR-10b-5p was consistently elevated. Inhibition of miR-10b-5p by a miRCURY locked nucleic acid inhibitor attenuated aortic root inflammation in vivo. In human coronary artery endothelial cells from adult donors, miR-10b-5p directly suppressed marker of proliferation Ki-67 (MKI67) and chromobox 5 (CBX5), driving a transition from proliferative and metabolic programs toward a proinflammatory phenotype, as confirmed by single-cell and bulk RNA sequencing. Chromatin accessibility profiling revealed increased accessibility at the C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 8 (CXCL8) promoter, and motif analysis identified CCAAT enhancer binding protein alpha (CEBPA) as the key transcriptional activator; CEBPA knockdown abrogated miR-10b-5p-induced CXCL8 upregulation, and direct binding was confirmed by binding assays and chromatin immunoprecipitation. Serum CXCL8 was markedly elevated in patients with KD relative to febrile controls at first presentation before definitive diagnosis and declined significantly at the 8-week follow-up. Receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated diagnostic utility, with sensitivity and specificity of 83.3% at an optimal cut-off of 20.91 pg/ml. In conclusion, we define a miR-10b-5p-MKI67/CBX5-CEBPA-CXCL8 axis driving endothelial reprogramming and neutrophil-recruiting inflammation in KD and identify serum CXCL8 as a candidate biomarker for timely KD recognition.

title: Mental Health Diagnoses Among Children With and Without Complex and Chronic Conditions.
authorString: Newmaster M, Hall M, DePorre A, Krager M, Nadler C, Plencner L, Berry JG, Puls HT.
abstractText: Mental health (MH) diagnoses can complicate outcomes of underlying medical conditions. However, prevalence of MH diagnoses across the spectrum of complex and/or chronic conditions is poorly understood. We aimed to (1) compare prevalence of MH diagnoses across categories of complex and chronic conditions and (2) identify factors associated with MH diagnoses among children with noncomplex chronic conditions (NCCCs) and complex chronic conditions (CCCs). Retrospective cross-sectional study of 2.9 million children aged 5 to 17 years from MarketScan Medicaid Database representing 12 US states in 2022. The primary exposure was mutually exclusive categories of complex and chronic conditions: noncomplex nonchronic (NCNC) conditions, NCCCs, and CCCs. The outcome was presence of a mood or anxiety MH diagnosis (anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorders, trauma-related disorders, and suicide/self-injury) coded at 1 inpatient/emergency department or 2 outpatient encounters. Prevalence of MH diagnoses increased with increasing medical complexity and chronicity: 7.6% in NCNC, 16.0% in NCCCs, and 20.0% in CCCs (P < .001). Among children with a CCC, categories with the greatest adjusted odds of MH diagnoses were cardiac (odds ratio [OR] 1.49; 95% CI, 1.44-1.54), neurologic (OR 1.18; 95% CI, 1.14-1.23), and renal (OR 1.13; 95% CI, 1.06-1.21). Among youth with NCCCs or CCCs, Black and Hispanic children had lower odds of MH diagnoses compared to non-Hispanic white children. MH prevalence increased significantly with increasing medical complexity and chronicity. Differences in MH diagnoses were identified across individual NCCC and CCC categories and sociodemographic characteristics. These results may inform future screening, intervention, and health equity efforts among medically vulnerable populations.

title: Evo2VED: a database of DNA large language model-derived scores for variant interpretation.
authorString: Zhu R, Zhou X, Liang I, Mendes M, Engchuan W, Safarian N, Zhou H, Cheng H, Trost B, Breetvelt E, Vorstman J, Tang H, O'Brien SJ, Scherer SW, Ohno-Machado L.
abstractText: The Evo2 Variant Effect Database (Evo2VED; https://dnallmved.org/) is a publicly accessible resource cataloging precomputed Evo2-derived variant effect scores, defined as allelic score differences, for 6.48 million human variants common in the gnomAD non-Finnish European population. Evo2VED includes scores from the 7B and 40B models under three scoring schemes, alongside annotations of variant function, evolutionary constraint, allele age, and disease associations. It integrates genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from UK Biobank, FinnGen, and the Million Veteran Program. Three complementary modules support variant-level interpretation, regional and region-set exploration, and trait-level analysis through flexible queries, interactive visualizations, and downloadable results. Evo2VED also catalogs associations between Evo2 annotations and per-SNP heritability across thousands of traits from these biobanks. A guided workflow connects GWAS with associated regions and individual variant evidence. Case studies of hypertension and depression illustrate how regional comparisons of Evo2 scores and GWAS signals can guide candidate variant prioritization. Evaluations using massively parallel reporter assays, molecular QTLs, fine-mapping probabilities, and clinical annotations assess associations with Evo2 scores alone and their added value beyond conservation and regulatory annotations. By providing accessible scores, contextual annotations, and comparative analyses, Evo2VED facilitates exploration and application of genomic language model predictions in human genetics research.

title: The mini-heart: a step toward non-invasive cardiac pump models.
authorString: Sawhney AS, Nayyer A, Wu SM.

title: Renal Artery Revascularization via Upper-Extremity Approach after Unintentional Extensive Stent-Graft Coverage during Endovascular Aneurysm Repair.

title: Left Atrial Appendage Closure or Anticoagulation for Atrial Fibrillation: Navigating Heterogeneity in Clinical Evidence: JACC Evidence Review.
authorString: Bikdeli B, Arun AS, Pawar S, Dhruva SS, Butala NM, Yong C, Spatz ES, Cohen DJ, Bittl JA, Albert CM, Leon MB, Makkar RR, Nazarian S, Krumholz HM, Gupta A.

journal.title: Journal of the American College of Cardiology

abstractText: Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has emerged as an alternative to long-term anticoagulation for preventing stroke or systemic embolism in selected patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) based on several randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that collectively enrolled >7,000 participants. In this JACC Evidence Review, we interpret the major RCTs as distinct experiments, clarify what each can and cannot establish, and offer a phenotype-based framework for interpreting the evidence. The most recent RCTs, OPTION, CLOSURE-AF, and CHAMPION-AF, have prompted efforts to pool the evidence into a single summary estimate. However, these trials are not one coherent evidence base; they are distinct clinical experiments that asked different questions. They differ in patient phenotype, comparator, device generation, postprocedure antithrombotic regimen, endpoint construction, and follow-up duration. Study-level meta-analysis of published reports remains methodologically valid for estimating the broad direction of effect of a device class, but when the component trials differ materially in patient phenotype, comparator, and outcome construction, the pooled estimate does not map to a common patient group or treatment decision. Patient eligibility as well as thromboembolic and bleeding risk varied markedly across trials. In addition, device technology has progressed, and comparators have evolved from warfarin to direct oral anticoagulants. Heterogeneity and insufficient details also exist about the antithrombotic therapy regimen in LAAC arms and adjunct antiplatelet therapy in control arms. Methodological issues further complicate interpretation, including the use of bleeding events (ie, the putative ancillary benefit of LAAC compared with anticoagulation) within composite endpoints tested for noninferiority, varying noninferiority margins, analytical approaches that may undermine the interpretation of noninferiority, and exclusion of periprocedural bleeding from primary safety endpoints in some trials. Finally, the standard of care for anticoagulation in AF has evolved, obviating concomitant aspirin use in stable individuals on therapeutic anticoagulation, thereby reducing bleeding risk compared with that of the control arm of LAAC RCTs. For most anticoagulation-eligible patients, anticoagulation remains the preferred first-line strategy. LAAC is a reasonable option when long-term anticoagulation is unsafe or unsustainable provided that procedural risk, adjunct antithrombotic feasibility, surveillance needs, and competing mortality are carefully considered. RCT evidence in this latter population is limited, and RCTs in other populations have features that limit their support for LAAC as an alternative to anticoagulation. Because LAAC and anticoagulation offer different types of risk, aligning the most applicable evidence with patient values through shared decision-making is central to care.

title: Representation of women and sex-disaggregated outcomes of trials in ANCA-associated vasculitis.
authorString: Ivković V, Bruchfeld A, Floyd L, Lees JS, Nelveg-Kristensen KE, Oh SS, Park PG, Shin JI, Weiner M, Kronbichler A, Stevens KI.
abstractText:
Importance

Women are generally underrepresented in randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Data on the representation of women, and on potential differences in outcomes between women and men, are lacking for RCTs in anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV).

Objective

We sought to evaluate representation of women and reporting of sex-disaggregated outcomes in RCTs of AAV.

Data sources

A PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL search was carried out for RCTs on AAV published from the beginning of indexation to 1st May 2025.

Study selection

We included trials enrolling patients with AAV. Studies which were not RCTs or did not explore AAV; were not main reports of RCTs; enrolled only a minority of patients with AAV; or in which only a part of the study was an RCT were excluded.

Data extraction and synthesis

Two authors screened publications, one extracted the data, and another verified a random sample for accuracy. The review was registered prospectively in PROSPERO (CRD420251000135).

Main outcomes and measures

Representation of women was expressed as a percentage of enrollment and as the participation-to-prevalence ratio (PPR), defined as the ratio between enrollment of women and prevalence of AAV in women, calculated using a random-effects meta-analysis.

Results

Fifty-six RCTs were included, of which 54 (96%) trials enrolling 5284 patients provided data on sex. A total of 2418 (45.8%) patients were women (weighted PPR of 0.95; 0.90-1.00). Using time- and location-specific prevalence estimates (38 trials), the weighted PPR was 0.86 (0.74-0.99). Women were underrepresented (PPR < 0.8) in 13 (24%) and overrepresented (PPR ≥1.2) in seven (13%) RCTs. Women were more frequently recruited in RCTs based in Asia and Australia (56.9%) compared to European (41.9%) and global (two or more continents) RCTs (48.3%) (p < 0.001). Enrollment of women increased across five-year time periods (p for trend = 0.02) but was not associated with RCT size or quality. No trial compared baseline characteristics across sex. Only three studies (5%) reported sex-disaggregated outcomes, one of them in the main text. Including follow-up publications, sex-disaggregated outcomes were available for only 20 of 56 trials (36%).

Conclusions and relevance

Overall, women are not underrepresented in RCTs performed in AAV, although representation varied considerably between trials. More importantly, trials almost never report sex-disaggregated outcomes and very rarely report whether differences may exist between women and men. To prevent disparity of care, these gaps need to be addressed, and reporting of sex-disaggregated outcomes should become a standard in RCTs.

title: Rationale and Design of a Multicenter, Randomized Controlled Trial: LEAP-Block.
authorString: Zhu K, Li X, Zhu H, Li W, Wang Y, Ellenbogen KA, Gold MR, Yao Y, Fan X.

journal.title: Journal of the American Heart Association

abstractText:
Background

Atrioventricular block with normal cardiac function is common with right ventricular pacing, which raises risks of pacing-induced cardiomyopathy and symptomatic heart failure in some patients with high pacing burden. Left bundle-branch area pacing demonstrates protective potential to reduce the risk of heart failure on the basis of observational studies. Evidence from a large multicenter randomized controlled trial remains limited.

Methods

The LEAP-Block (Impact of Left Bundle Branch Area Pacing Versus Right Ventricular Pacing in Atrioventricular Block) study is a prospective multicenter, investigator-initiated randomized controlled trial aiming to verify the hypothesis that left bundle-branch area pacing might have superior impact to right ventricular pacing in reducing the risk of cardiovascular events in patients with atrioventricular block requiring high burden of ventricular pacing and left ventricular ejection fraction ≥50%. A total of 484 patients will be randomized to either left bundle-branch area pacing or right ventricular pacing (1:1). The primary end point is the composite events of all-cause death, heart failure events, and upgrade to biventricular pacing-delivered cardiac resynchronization therapy during at least 24 months of follow-up. Secondary end points include changes in echocardiographic, electrocardiographic, and pacing parameters and device-related complications.

Conclusions

The LEAP-Block study aims to compare the impact of left bundle-branch area pacing versus conventional right ventricular pacing in patients with atrioventricular block and preserved cardiac function with respect to midterm clinical outcomes. This trial will provide high-quality evidence for the selection of optimal pacing strategies in clinical practice.

Registration information

clinicaltrials.gov. Identifier: NCT04730921.

title: Underweight and obesity as outcome predictors after transcatheter aortic valve implantation: insights from the DOUBLE-CHOICE trial.
authorString: Buske M, Abdel-Wahab M, Ender J, Desch S, Lankisch N, Schrader H, von der Emde S, Lauten P, Rudolph TK, Geisler T, Massberg S, Adam M, Baldus S, Sossalla S, Joner M, Möllmann H, Wolf A, Kim WK, Borger MA, Noack T, Boening A, Bleiziffer S, Hohenstein S, Thiele H, Feistritzer HJ.

journal.title: Clinical research in cardiology : official journal of the German Cardiac Society

abstractText:
Background

An "obesity paradox" has been described after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), suggesting lower mortality in patients with higher body mass index (BMI) despite greater comorbidity. In contrast, underweight consistently predicts adverse outcomes. Whether these associations reflect a true biological effect or are primarily driven by residual confounding, frailty, and patient selection remains uncertain.

Methods

This prespecified subgroup analysis included eligible patients from the randomized DOUBLE-CHOICE trial comparing two transcatheter heart valves and two anesthesia strategies (minimalist approach with local anesthesia only vs. standard care with conscious sedation). The primary endpoint was a 30-day composite of all-cause mortality, vascular and bleeding complications, infections requiring antibiotic therapy, and neurologic events. Associations were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, frailty, diabetes, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and anesthesia strategy.

Results

Among 752 patients (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2, n = 192; BMI < 30 kg/m2, n = 560), obese patients had lower rates of the 30-day primary endpoint (15.2% vs. 27.6%; p < 0.001). After multivariable adjustment, obesity remained independently associated with lower risk (adjusted OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.30-0.75; p = 0.002). In contrast, underweight (BMI < 20 kg/m2; n = 23) was associated with a higher incidence of the primary endpoint (55.0% vs. 23.4%; p = 0.003) and remained an independent predictor after adjustment (adjusted OR 3.74, 95% CI 1.30-9.52; p = 0.005).

Conclusion

In this randomized TAVI population, obesity was independently associated with favorable 30-day outcomes, whereas underweight identified a small but high-risk subgroup with substantially increased procedural risk. These findings identify underweight as a potential high-risk phenotype requiring further investigation in future studies incorporating more detailed measures of frailty and body composition.

title: Effects of Sacred Dances versus Conventional Physical Training on Functional Capacity and Quality of Life in Women with Heart Failure: Protocol for a Randomized Active-Controlled Crossover Non-Inferiority Trial (RED-WHF)
authorString: VON FLACH MT, Fernandes ES, Almeida MCBdA, Suarez HC, Correia MvF, Junquilho AAL, Abreu AMFdN, Dias CMCC, Ritt LEF.
abstractText: This protocol describes the RED-WHF trial, a randomized, active-controlled, two-period crossover clinical trial designed to evaluate whether Sacred Dances (SD)—as a mind-body intervention—are non-inferior to conventional physical training (PT) regarding functional capacity and quality of life in women with heart failure (HF). Sedentary behavior and emotional stress significantly worsen HF prognosis, yet conventional exercise programs face barriers in patient adherence and variable motivation. Sacred Dances, a form of low-to-moderate-intensity moving meditation, may enhance physical fitness while promoting emotional well-being and spiritual connection (flourishing). We will recruit 30 sedentary women aged 18 to 70 with stable HF (NYHA class I-III) and a documented left ventricular ejection fraction. Participants will be randomized 1:1 to one of two treatment sequences: SD followed by PT, or vice versa. Each 12-week intervention phase consists of two weekly sessions, lasting 90 minutes for SD (with 60 minutes of active dancing to allow choreography instruction) and 60 minutes for PT, separated by a 3-week washout period. Primary outcomes are functional capacity (6-minute walk test [6MWT]) and health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L Index and VAS). Secondary outcomes include adherence rates, spiritual attitudes (ARES scale), symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress (DASS-21), and perceived subjective impact (EUPI-12). Statistical planning incorporates linear mixed models (LMM) with treatment, period, and sequence fixed effects, and an intention-to-treat approach with multiple imputation for missing data. To establish non-inferiority, a 30-meter margin for the 6MWT difference will be applied. The study was approved by the local Ethics Committee (CEP/EBMSP opinion 7.443.180, CAAE: 86133125.0.0000.5544) and prospectively registered in the Brazilian Registry of Clinical Trials (ReBEC ID: RBR-85tkdz5).

title: Generative AI Versus Primary Care Physicians from Plan Initiation to Long-Term Maintenance of Chronic Disease Self-Management: A Vignette-Based Validation Study
authorString: Zhao Z, Yang H, Wang Q, Wang Y, Cheng W, Ma X.
abstractText:
Background:

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may provide personalised and dynamically adjustable support for chronic disease self-management. However, previous studies have largely focused on isolated questions and a limited range of evaluation dimensions. Objective To compare the quality of self-management advice generated by GenAI and primary care physicians (PCPs) across multiple stages of chronic disease management and evaluation dimensions. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional, source-blinded comparative evaluation using 15 standardised vignettes of diabetes and hypertension derived from authentic primary care follow-up records. Each vignette comprised three sequential management stages, with medical accuracy, readability, and behaviour-change potential assessed across the three simulated stages; individualisation and multidisciplinary integration at plan initiation; contextual adaptability during acute adjustment; and empathy during long-term maintenance. The GenAI system and 22 PCPs independently generated advice which was independently rated by three clinicians，one each from general practice, endocrinology, and cardiology. across seven dimensions. Linear mixed-effects models were used for the primary comparisons, and case-level paired and physician-distribution analyses were conducted as robustness analyses. Results The GenAI system achieved estimated marginal means above 4.0 in all dimensions except readability. It scored significantly higher than PCPs in six of the seven dimensions, with adjusted mean differences ranging from 1.16 to 1.56 points (P<.001). Readability was the only exception, with no significant difference between GenAI and PCPs (−0.22, 95% CI −0.54 to 0.11; P=.19). The GenAI mean exceeded the individual means of all recruited PCPs in the six dimensions but ranked at approximately the 23rd percentile for readability. Conclusions Our findings indicated the GenAI system may generate more highly rated self-management advice than PCPs across most evaluated dimensions but offered no advantage in readability. These findings provide pre-implementation evidence for GenAI as a potential source of structured and adaptive chronic disease self-management support. Patient-level pilot studies and subsequent randomised trials are needed to determine its acceptability and effects on behaviour and clinical outcomes.

title: Lower Preoperative Serum Magnesium Is Associated With Postoperative Atrial Fibrillation After Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study
authorString: Zhang Y, Wang S, Zhang H, Lu Y, Wang Z, Wei J.
abstractText: Background Postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) is the most common arrhythmic complication after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). We evaluated whether pleural drainage tube placement influences POAF and identified clinical factors associated with POAF, particularly serum magnesium. Methods In this single-center retrospective cohort study, we screened 602 consecutive adults who underwent CABG between September 2020 and June 2026. The exposure was intraoperative pleural drainage tube placement, and the outcome was POAF. Associations were assessed by multivariable logistic regression, propensity score matching (PSM), inverse probability of treatment weighting, and overlap weighting. Results A total of 520 patients were included (mean age 64.8 ± 7.9 years; 372 men, 71.5%). Pleural drainage tubes were placed in 166 patients (31.9%), and POAF occurred in 135 patients (26.0%). Lower serum magnesium was independently associated with POAF in a dose-dependent manner: adjusted OR per 0.05 mmol/L increment 0.78 (95% CI 0.67–0.91, P < 0.001); magnesium tertiles showed a significant trend (P for trend = 0.011); and magnesium below the internally derived cutoff of 0.815 mmol/L was associated with increased risk (adjusted OR 1.94, 95% CI 1.19–3.15, P = 0.008; AUC 0.612). The E-value for this association was 2.13. Pleural drainage tube placement was not independently associated with POAF: crude OR 1.32 (95% CI 0.87–2.00), adjusted OR 1.36 (95% CI 0.85–2.15), and PSM OR 1.37 (95% CI 0.81–2.33). The study was underpowered to detect an OR below 1.78 for the drainage association. Conclusions Lower preoperative serum magnesium was independently associated with POAF in a dose-dependent manner, whereas pleural drainage tube placement was not. Because perioperative magnesium supplementation was not recorded, these findings cannot establish whether magnesium optimization would reduce POAF risk; this hypothesis requires prospective randomized trials. Clinical trial number: not applicable.

title: Predictors of Clinically Meaningful 1-Year Health Status Improvements Following Endovascular or Surgical Revascularization: Insights From the BEST-CLI Trial.
authorString: Smolderen KG, Menard M, Farber A, Rahman MM, Rosenfield K, Strong M, Doros G, Goodney P, Shah SK, Powell RR, Suckow B, Houland K, Siracuse J, Romain G, Cleman J, Scierka L, Mena-Hurtado C.

journal.title: Journal of the American Heart Association

abstractText:
Background

Despite efforts to promote limb salvage in chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), the factors associated with meaningful health status improvement after revascularization remain poorly understood. We examined predictors of meaningful 1-year health status improvement following revascularization for CLTI.

Methods

We pooled endovascular and surgical arms from the BEST-CLI (Best Endovascular Versus Best Surgical Therapy in Patients With CLTI) randomized controlled trial, including patients with CLTI (150 international sites, 2014-2019). Health status was assessed at baseline and 1 year using the peripheral artery disease-specific Vascular Quality of Life questionnaire, the generic European Quality-of-Life 5 Dimensions, and the Short Form-12 Physical and Mental Component Summary. Distribution-based minimal clinically important difference thresholds were defined as 0.5 SD of baseline health status scores. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of no meaningful 1-year improvement (same/worsened versus improved).

Results

Among 1017 patients (72.0% men, mean age 66.8±9.7 years), clinically meaningful improvements were reported by 76.5% for Vascular Quality of Life, 52.8% European Quality-of-Life 5 Dimensions, 56.7% for Short Form-12 Physical Component Summary, and 42.1% for Short Form-12 Mental Component Summary, regardless of revascularization type (surgical versus endovascular). Cardiometabolic risk factors and higher preprocedural health status increased the odds of no meaningful improvement. Revascularization type was not associated with Vascular Quality of Life improvement (odds ratio, 1.059 [95% CI, 0.91-1.23]; P=0.445; C statistic=0.77).

Conclusions

One-year postrevascularization, over three-fourths of individuals with CLTI perceived meaningful improvements in peripheral artery disease-specific health, and over half improved overall physical health, regardless of procedure type. Cardiometabolic risk factors and higher preprocedural health status predicted 1-year health status response. REGISTRATION: URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT02060630.

title: Effect of intensive blood pressure control on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes: prespecified analysis of secondary outcomes of BPROAD randomised controlled trial.
authorString: Wang W, Xu Y, Xu F, Pan H, Geng X, Li Y, He Y, Xing G, Lu J, Wang T, Liu Y, Li T, Duan P, Zhang Q, Wang J, Zhao Y, Lu P, Zheng R, Chen Y, Fu S, Wu S, Chen W, Zheng H, Deng J, Chen S, Liu J, Li B, Hu W, Wu S, Niu J, Wang J, Zhou Q, Liu L, Wang X, Zhou Y, Liu D, Li Q, Shang D, Zheng A, Zhang C, Xu Y, Wang J, He X, Wang S, Wang Z, Yuan G, Peng J, Cui P, Wang S, Dang H, Yan F, He N, Wan Q, Yang J, Liu Y, Ning G, Li M, Bi Y, BPROAD Research Group.
abstractText:
Objective

To evaluate the effect of intensive compared with standard treatment of systolic blood pressure (SBP) on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes.

Design

Multicentre, open label, outcome assessor masked, randomised controlled trial.

Setting

145 clinical centres across seven geographical regions in China.

Participants

12 821 adults aged ≥50 years with type 2 diabetes, raised SBP, and increased cardiovascular risk, of whom 12 434 without probable dementia at baseline were included in this cognitive ancillary study. Further assessments were performed annually and at the end of study.

Interventions

Participants were randomly assigned to receive intensive treatment targeting SBP <120 mm Hg or standard treatment targeting SBP <140 mm Hg for up to five years.

Main outcome measures

The primary cognitive outcome was a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment. Secondary cognitive outcomes included all cause dementia, mild cognitive impairment, changes in cognitive functions, and changes in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics. A subset of participants underwent brain MRI at baseline (n=862) and at the end of study (n=605) to assess changes in white matter lesion volume and total brain volume.

Results

6219 participants were assigned to receive intensive treatment and 6215 to receive standard treatment. Baseline mean age was 63.7 years, and 5567 (44.8%) participants were women. After one year, mean SBP was 121.6 mm Hg in the intensive treatment group and 133.2 mm Hg in the standard treatment group. During a median follow-up of 3.8 years, the primary cognitive outcome of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment occurred in 747 participants (3.69 events per 100 person years) in the intensive treatment group and 783 participants (3.89 events per 100 person years) in the standard treatment group (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.86 to 1.06; P=0.38). In the MRI substudy (428 intensive treatment v 434 standard treatment), the intensive treatment group had a smaller increase in white matter lesion volume compared with the standard treatment group (between group difference -0.09 inverse hyperbolic sine (asinh) transformed cm3, 95% CI -0.15 to -0.02; P=0.01).

Conclusions

Over a median of about four years, no statistically significant difference in incidence of a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment was observed among adults with type 2 diabetes receiving standard treatment of SBP (target <140 mm Hg) and intensive treatment (target <120 mm Hg). Intensive treatment was, however, associated with a reduction in the accrual of cerebral white matter lesion volume.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03808311.

title: Assessing the inclusion of frailty scores in either the methodology or results of clinical intervention trials of heart failure: A scoping review.
authorString: Al-Shalabi M, Nazar NA, Patel M.
abstractText: Chronic heart failure is highly prevalent in older adults, in whom frailty is common and associated with poorer outcomes. Despite advances in guideline-directed medical therapy, concerns regarding tolerability and polypharmacy contribute to under-utilization in frail patients. This scoping review aimed to map the existing evidence on how clinical interventional trials of heart failure management have incorporated frailty, specifically, whether trials have (i) stratified outcomes according to frailty status and/or (ii) adjusted treatment strategies based on frailty. We searched MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL and ClinicalTrials.gov for interventional trials of heart failure published up to August 2025 that incorporated frailty using validated assessment tools. Eligible studies stratified outcomes by frailty status and/or adjusted interventions based on frailty. Data were extracted and a narrative synthesis was conducted. Ten studies met the inclusion criteria. Seven were post-hoc analyses of randomized controlled trials, two were prespecified analyses, and one was a randomized controlled trial. Two studies evaluated exercise-based interventions, one on implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, and the remainder on pharmacological-based therapies. Nine studies used the Rockwood cumulative deficit approach to measure frailty, although the parameters used varied between studies. Available secondary analyses suggest preserved efficacy across frailty groups for most pharmacological interventions, whereas other modalities did not show convincing improvements in heart failure-specific outcomes among frail patients. Primary evidence of heart failure interventions incorporating frailty remains limited, with a large bulk of the evidence available being retrospective. Although several reported pharmacological interventions appear to have preserved efficacy across frailty levels, some of these therapies were not recommended in current guidelines, and heterogeneity in frailty measurement reduced the confidence of conclusions drawn. The gaps identified in this review highlight the need for further primary evidence that incorporates frailty, plus a standardized holistic method of measuring frailty in heart failure patients.

title: Optimal Kidney Protection by Moderate Aggressive Treatment of Hypertension.
authorString: Kjeldsen SE, Burnier M, Zoccali C, Mancia G.
abstractText:
Purpose of commentary

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) has almost never been counted as an important incident endpoint in randomized clinical trials (RCTs) in the prevention of complications and outcomes in essential hypertension but rather included in broader safety assessments. Although target systolic blood pressure (SBP) < 130 and even < 120 mmHg is recommended by some guidelines, it is unclear whether such aggressive treatment has a favorable effect on hypertension-related decline of CKD.

New observations

During the past two decades several RCTs have been performed with patients randomized to more aggressive SBP target vs. SBP target closer to standard treatment. Several large RCTs have targeted and/or otherwise achieved SBP as low as 120 mmHg or maybe even lower in fractions of middle-aged and older high risk essential hypertensive people with major worsening of kidney function. However, other RCTs showed neutral effects or even reduction in kidney endpoints with achieved SBP below 130 mmHg and possible benefit in preventing cardiovascular outcomes though inclusion of soft endpoints in some trials diluted the cardiovascular message. Intensive BP lowering is associated with greater declines in kidney function in all major RCTs investigating target SBP < 120 mmHg. The long-term clinical significance of these changes must be interpreted alongside possible cardiovascular risks. Hence, one should aim at a SBP target < 130 mmHg in middle-aged and older hypertensive patients if the treatment is otherwise well tolerated. The benefits of low SBP targets in patients who develop CKD should be reassessed in the context of new available treatments providing kidney protection such as SGLT2-inhibitors, aldosterone antagonists and GLP1-agonists.

title: Cardiovascular risk, evaluation and management in patients with hypertriglyceridaemia: a Consensus Statement from the International Atherosclerosis Society.
authorString: Aggarwal R, Bursill C, Figtree GA, Hocking SL, Mason RP, Michos ED, Miller M, Nelson AJ, Nicholls SJ, Rye KA, Steg PG, Watts GF, Zoungas S, Libby P.
abstractText: The prevalence of hypertriglyceridaemia is increasing globally owing to high rates of obesity and diabetes mellitus. Hypertriglyceridaemia is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, mediated through the cholesterol content of triglyceride-rich lipoprotein remnant particles rather than through triglycerides per se. Although plasma levels of triglycerides can be measured with a simple blood test, hypertriglyceridaemia remains underdiagnosed and undertreated. Hypertriglyceridaemia can result from various primary or secondary aetiologies, the identification and management of which is an important first step. Hypertriglyceridaemia can be managed with lifestyle measures, lipid-lowering therapy with statins in indicated patients to reduce cholesterol levels and, in refractory situations, with the addition of triglyceride-specific pharmacological therapies. Emerging therapies with considerable promise for the management of hypertriglyceridaemia include those targeting apolipoprotein C-III, angiopoietin-related protein 3 or fibroblast growth factor 21. However, so far, there is no evidence from randomized clinical trials that pharmacotherapies targeting triglycerides can reduce the occurrence of cardiovascular events, suggesting that elevated levels of triglycerides serve as a marker of atherosclerotic risk that should prompt optimization of modifiable cardiovascular risk factors. In this Consensus Statement, we provide clinical context and evidence for the evaluation, diagnosis and management of hypertriglyceridaemia.

title: Respiratory-compensated non-contrast vs breath-hold contrast-enhanced MR angiography in pediatric Fontan patients.
authorString: Zeilinger MG, Giese D, Schmidt M, Rick M, Rompel O, Akers MF, Schmidt M, Kopp M, May MS, Csesnjevar R, Dittrich S, Uder M, Treutlein C.
abstractText:
Objectives

To compare a highly accelerated ECG-triggered and navigator-gated, non-contrast respiratory-compensated 3D magnetic resonance angiography with Dixon water-fat separation (NC-MRA) to respiratory-suspended non-ECG-triggered multiphase contrast-enhanced MRA (CE-MRA) in pediatric patients with partial or total cavopulmonary connection (PCPC/TCPC).

Materials and methods

In this prospective single-center study, between 02/2021 and 09/2023, 30 consecutive pediatric patients (mean age 3.6 ± 0.8 years) with PCPC or TCPC underwent 1.5 T cardiovascular MRI under deep sedation and mechanical ventilation. NC-MRA was acquired before contrast administration alongside standard CE-MRA. Two blinded readers independently evaluated image quality using a 5-point Likert scale and measured vascular diameters of predefined aortic segments, the Glenn anastomosis, Fontan conduit, and pulmonary arteries in consensus. Datasets were presented in randomized order. We used paired statistical testing for method comparison and Cohen's kappa to assess inter-rater agreement.

Results

Mean NC-MRA acquisition time (5:55 ± 2:19 min) was comparable to that of multiphase CE-MRA (5:48 ± 3:03 min), including pre-contrast acquisition p = 0.54). Overall image quality was generally comparable between techniques for most vascular segments (NC-MRA median 5, IQR 5-5, CE-MRA median 5, IQR 4-5, p = 0.06-0.52). No significant differences were found in vascular diameter measurements across all segments (p = 0.06-0.59). Inter-reader agreement was at least substantial (κ > 0.65).

Conclusion

Respiratory-compensated NC-MRA at 1.5 T provides image quality and vascular diameter measurements comparable to CE-MRA in pediatric PCPC/TCPC patients. Eliminating breath-holds and contrast administration, the technique simplifies workflow, avoids mechanical ventilation, and improves patient safety in this vulnerable population.

Key points

Question Is a non-contrast, ECG-triggered, and navigator-gated 3D MRA sequence diagnostically equivalent to conventional breath-hold CE-MRA for vascular assessment in pediatric Fontan patients? Findings There were no significant differences in vascular diameters, and image quality was comparable between both sequences in most segments, showing substantial inter-rater agreement and diagnostic reliability. Clinical relevance Non-contrast, ECG-triggered, and navigator-gated MRA enables reliable vascular assessment in pediatric Fontan patients without gadolinium or breath-holds, reducing anesthesia requirements, improving safety, and simplifying workflow in this vulnerable population.

title: Coronary Perfusion Pressure During Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation is Associated with Outcomes from Pediatric In-hospital Cardiac Arrest.
authorString: Kienzle MF, Gardner MM, Zuckerberg J, Patterson E, Alvey J, Reeder RW, Cooper K, Graham K, Nadkarni V, Berg RA, Sutton RM, Morgan RW, ICU-Resuscitation Project (ICU-RESUS) Investigators and the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Collaborative Pediatric Critical Care Research Network Investigators.
abstractText:
Background

Multiple animal studies and one adult study establish that coronary perfusion pressure (CoPP) during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is associated with survival outcomes, such as return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Yet, CoPP during pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (pIHCA) has not been investigated. We hypothesized that an average CoPP ≥20mmHg during the first 10 minutes of CPR for pIHCA would be associated with higher rates of ROSC.

Methods

We performed a secondary analysis of the ICU-RESUScitation trial, a cluster randomized, step-wedged trial of a physiology-focused quality improvement bundle in pIHCA. Index CPR events among patients ≥37 weeks corrected gestational age and <18 years with invasive arterial blood pressure (BP) and central venous pressure (CVP) monitoring were eligible for inclusion. The primary exposure was event-level average CoPP (≥20mmHg vs <20mmHg) during the first 10 minutes of CPR; secondary exposure was CoPP <10 mmHg. The primary outcome was sustained ROSC ≥20 minutes. Multivariable modified Poisson regression with adjustment for confounders evaluated the relationship between CoPP and outcomes.

Results

Among 111 included patients, median age was 0.2 years [0.0, 0.6]. Seventy-one (64%) achieved ROSC. Thirty (27%) had CoPP ≥20mmHg. Patients with CoPP ≥20mmHg were more frequently ≥1 year of age and less frequently had congenital heart disease. In adjusted models, average CoPP ≥20mmHg was associated with higher rates of ROSC (aRR 1.48 [95%CI 1.12, 1.95]; p=0.005). CoPP <10 mmHg was associated with lower rates of ROSC.

Conclusions

In this first investigation of CoPP during CPR for pIHCA, CoPP ≥20mmHg was associated with ROSC.

title: Standards Defining Echocardiography Core Laboratory (ECL) in Clinical Practice and Research.
authorString: Saeed S, Muraru D, Popescu BA, Donal E, Delgado V, Edvardsen T.
abstractText: Echocardiography is extensively utilized in both clinical practice and research due to its accessibility. Echocardiography core laboratories (ECLs) adhering to societal guidelines offer superior readings and interpretations compared with the on-site assessments by reducing measurement variability and enhancing study precision. In the present work, we aim to define minimum standards for clinical echocardiography laboratories and research ECLs based on recommendations from the American Society of Echocardiography and the European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging, as well as on expert opinion and our experience in European countries. Accurate acquisition of high-quality images is crucial for ensuring reproducibility, repeatability and reliability of the echocardiographic measurements. In addition to the commonly used workstations, an academic ECL must also possess the necessary capacities and skilled personnel to conduct sophisticated research projects. Personnel should hold advanced certification in echocardiography, indicating postgraduate training and experience beyond the basic cardiovascular ultrasound education. They should be capable of designing, performing, and interpreting complex echocardiography studies. Reproducibility of the ECL should be validated using a small, randomly selected sample, preferably in the early analytic phase. ECL readings and interpretations are superior to site-reported measurements and serve as the gold standard in observational studies and clinical trials. To ensure internal validity, an academic ECL should continuously evaluate/report reproducibility, repeatability and reliability. ECL should be formally acknowledged and accredited by an international scientific imaging society.

title: Global Prevalence of Obstetric Causes of Critical Illness in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authorString: Kuppusamy P, Kale DP, Manjrekar MR, Hardwaria P.
abstractText:
Objectives

To determine the prevalence, risks, and outcomes of obstetric causes of critically ill pregnant women admitted to the ICU.

Data sources

We searched the PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Ovid, and ScienceDirect databases up to May 15, 2026.

Study selection

We included studies reporting primary data on critically ill pregnant and postpartum women (up to 48 d post-delivery) admitted to an ICU, with relevant obstetric risk factors and maternal outcomes.

Data extraction

Two reviewers independently performed data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment using the adapted Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. The pooled prevalence was estimated using a random-effects model with 95% CIs.

Data synthesis

Of the 3,735 total records, 50 studies met the eligibility criteria, encompassing 7,756,232 women receiving obstetric care in tertiary hospitals across 20 countries, with 49,299 ICU admissions. Globally, 1.0% (95% CI, 0.8-1.3%) of pregnant and postpartum women experience critical illness and require admission to an ICU. The frequency varies according to the country's income levels, with the highest in low-income countries (4.1%) and the lowest in high-income countries (0.5%). Notably, 72.3% of ICU admissions were attributed to known obstetric causes, primarily obstetric hemorrhage (23.3%) and hypertension in pregnancy (26.9%). Nearly 33.3% of ICU patients required either respiratory or transfusion support, and the maternal mortality rate among ICU-admitted obstetric women was 8.5%.

Conclusions

Nearly one in 100 pregnancies require admission to intensive care due to critical illness, and nearly three-quarters of these admissions were due to direct obstetric causes, with high maternal morbidity and mortality. Obstetric hemorrhage and hypertensive disorders account for the majority of ICU admissions. Strengthening obstetric care in resource-limited settings through the expansion and optimization of intensive care services is essential for improving maternal and neonatal outcomes and reducing preventable morbidity and mortality.

title: High on the Heart? Cannabis Use and Cardiovascular Disease: A Systematic Review.
authorString: Chehade MJ, Haas MJ, Mooradian AD.

journal.title: Journal of the American Heart Association

abstractText: Cannabis use has increased substantially over the past 2 decades following shifts in public perception, legalization, and medical usage. Although neurological and psychiatric effects are well known, the cardiovascular effects of cannabis exposure are largely understudied. This review evaluates the cardiovascular effects of cannabis use by examining clinical evidence, epidemiological data, and underlying biochemical mechanisms. This review examines cannabis-related cardiovascular conditions, including atherosclerosis, arrhythmias, heart failure, and stroke. The analysis focused on cannabinoid composition, route of administration, frequency of use, and cardiovascular outcomes. Evidence indicates that acute and high Δ<sup>9</sup>-tetrahydrocannabinol/cannabidiol ratio cannabis use is associated with increased risks of various cardiovascular outcomes, especially among younger individuals without cardiovascular risk factors. Given rising use and increasing Δ<sup>9</sup>-tetrahydrocannabinol potency, clinicians must routinely assess cannabis exposure when evaluating cardiovascular disease, especially in younger patients. Future research must prioritize the development of standardized exposure metrics in cannabis-related cardiovascular disease research, thus allowing clinicians and patients to better understand the cardiovascular risks of cannabis use and initiate effective cessation strategies.

title: Proteomics and Risk of Incident Ischemic Stroke: Meta-Analysis of the ARIC Study and CHS.
authorString: Wang W, Wu Y, Kalani R, Ye T, Bartz TM, Zhang MJ, Pankow JS, Lakshminarayan K, Alonso A, Lutsey PL, Ballantyne CM, Matsushita K, Johansen MC, Gottesman RF, Coresh J, Pan W, Walker KA, Heckbert SR, Psaty BM, Sitlani CM, Brody JA, Finkel N, Gudmundsdottir V, Gudnason V, Longstreth WT, Chen LY, Floyd JS.
abstractText:
Background

Ischemic stroke preventive therapies have been slow to emerge due to a limited understanding of the underlying molecular mechanisms. We aimed to discover new protein risk factors that are potential etiologic factors and may be candidates for therapeutic intervention.

Methods

We included ARIC study (Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities) and CHS (Cardiovascular Health Study) participants without prevalent stroke at the time of proteomic profiling (1990-1992 in ARIC and 1992-1993 in CHS). Relative concentrations of proteins in blood were assessed with aptamers (n=4954). Ischemic stroke events were adjudicated through 2019 in ARIC and 2015 in CHS. Study-specific Cox regression adjusting for ischemic stroke risk factors was used to estimate associations between proteins and incident ischemic stroke. Study-specific estimates were combined using fixed-effects meta-analysis. Replication was conducted in 2 independent cohorts (AGES-Reykjavik, UK Biobank). Proteins with a false discovery rate q value <0.05 were considered replicated. Mendelian randomization analyses assessed for potential causal associations between proteins and ischemic stroke.

Results

Median follow-up was 25 and 12 years in ARIC and CHS. 1397 out of 14 139 (10%) participants experienced an ischemic stroke. 44 proteins were significantly associated with ischemic stroke risk (P<1.0×10-5), of which 26 are novel. In 2 independent cohorts, 37 (84%) associations were directionally concordant, and 26 (59%) met criteria for replication. Mendelian randomization analyses suggested MMP12 (matrix metallopeptidase-12) and CNTN1 (contactin-1) may be causally related to ischemic stroke risk. In multivariable Mendelian randomization analyses, higher MMP12 levels had a direct protective effect on ischemic stroke risk, while CNTN1 had a direct harmful effect.

Conclusions

This proteomic and genomic investigation of ischemic stroke identified novel risk biomarkers and 2 potential etiologic CNTN1 factors that are regulated in response to atherosclerosis and obesity.
