Whether these disturbances are reflected in coronary plaque composition remains incompletely understood. We evaluated the association of metabolic and renal dysfunction with intraplaque lipid burden using near-infrared spectroscopy intravascular ultrasound.

Methods

Intraplaque lipid burden was assessed by the maximum lipid core burden index (LCBI) within a 4-mm segment (maxLCBI4mm), and lipid-rich plaque (LRP) was defined as maxLCBI4mm≥324.7. Multivariable linear regression models were constructed with maxLCBI4mm as the dependent variable, and multivariable logistic regression models were used to evaluate associations with LRP.

Results

Among 483 patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention with pre-intervention near-infrared spectroscopy intravascular ultrasound imaging, lower estimated glomerular filtration rate and higher hemoglobin A1c were independently associated with greater intraplaque lipid burden and higher odds of LRP. In analyses standardized per 1 SD, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol showed the strongest association with maxLCBI4mm (β=52.51; 95% CI, 27.49-77.53), followed by estimated glomerular filtration rate (β=33.38; 95% CI, 9.97-56.80) and hemoglobin A1c (β=24.71; 95% CI, 3.71-45.71). Similarly, lower estimated glomerular filtration rate (odds tatio [OR], 1.36; 95% CI, 1.06-1.75) and higher hemoglobin A1c (OR, 1.37; 95% CI, 1.05-1.77) were independently associated with LRP. No significant interaction between estimated glomerular filtration rate and hemoglobin A1c was observed.

Conclusions

Metabolic and renal dysfunction are independently associated with intraplaque lipid burden assessed by near-infrared spectroscopy intravascular ultrasound. These findings provide intracoronary imaging evidence linking the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic framework to plaque-level lipid accumulation.

title: Eight Novel Sonographic Signs
authorString: Ji X.
abstractText: Ultrasound is a widely used imaging modality in clinical practice, and sonographic signs serve as valuable teaching tools that aid in pattern recognition and diagnosis. This review consolidates five novel sonographic signs previously proposed by the author, including the Cracked Earth Sign for subcutaneous edema, the Mushroom Cap Sign for localized gallbladder adenomyomatosis, the LTS Sign for dilated cardiomyopathy, the LTI Sign for endocardial fibroelastosis, and the Three Pipes Sign for the suprasternal long-axis view of the aortic arch. The SFH Sign for advanced cervical insufficiency, the Gentle Upslope Sign for the parvus–tardus waveform, and the Fenestrated Ring Sign for diffuse gallbladder adenomyomatosis are proposed for the first time in this paper. Collectively, these eight signs span the fields of superficial ultrasound, abdominal ultrasound, echocardiography, and obstetric ultrasound. For each sign, its naming logic, definition, clinical implications, and teaching value are described. This review aims to facilitate a better understanding of these signs and to promote their use as teaching aids in ultrasound education.

title: Preclinical testing of a novel tandem endo-Wheat delivery system.
authorString: Pedroza AJ, Vallee A, Ghostine S, Julien M, Fleurot S, Kratzberg J, Fabre D, Guihaire J, Haulon S.
abstractText:
Background

Endovascular repair of pathology affecting the proximal aorta is an area of active innovation. Physician-modified composite valve-graft devices have successfully been implemented to repair the aortic root, but several technical challenges remain. While treatment of aortic root pathology requires complete seal at the level of the sinuses of Valsalva and bridging stents into the coronary arteries ("endo-Bentall"), aortic dissection originating above the sinotubular junction can be addressed in principle via a procedure analogous to surgical aortic valve replacement and separate graft replacement of the ascending aorta ("endo-Wheat"). Here, we report the technical description and preclinical assessment of a novel fenestrated endograft, and delivery system intended for tandem use with a balloon-expandable aortic valve prosthesis.

Methods

A novel endo-Wheat device and sheath system were fabricated following iterative design refinements. Laboratory-based testing was performed using a 3D-printed phantom of a thoracoabdominal aorta with an acute type A aortic dissection.

Results

This endo-Wheat system is designed to enable coronary artery perfusion through via aortic root fenestrations while establishing a seal at the sinotubular junction. We demonstrated techinical feasibility with tandem delivery of the fenestrated endograft and balloon-expandable TEVAR in rapid succession. We identify technical challenges with the implementation of this system and subsequent design modifications.

Conclusions

We conclude that this device may provide a reliable, off-the-shelf solution for treatment of acute type A aortic dissection in poor operative candidates.

title: Longitudinal Endoleak Behaviour Following Complex Aortic Repair With Branched Devices.
authorString: Vuthivanich C, Konstantinou N, Stana J, Hasemaki N, Elkady M, Becker D, Tsilimparis N.

journal.title: Journal of endovascular therapy : an official journal of the International Society of Endovascular Specialists

abstractText:
Objective

This study aimed to determine the incidence, natural history, outcomes and risk factors of endoleak following branched endovascular aortic repair (BEVAR) for complex abdominal aortic aneurysm (cAAA) and thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysms (TAAAs).

Methods

This retrospective, single-centre study enrolled patients with cAAA and TAAA treated with BEVAR. Patients with at least 1 target vessel incorporated using directional branches were included. End points were spontaneous resolution of endoleak detected on completion angiography, 3-year freedom from persistent type I/III endoleak and endoleak-related reintervention. Multivariable Cox regression analyses were performed to identify independent risk factors for type II endoleak (T2EL) and branch-related endoleak (BREL).

Results

In a 6-year period, 298 patients underwent fenestrated/branched endovascular aortic repair (F/BEVAR) of which 129 patients (mean age 72 ± 9 years; 62% male) underwent F/BEVAR for 36 cAAA (27.9%) and 93 TAAA (72.1%) with at least 1 directional branch. In all, 458 reno-mesenteric arteries were incorporated using directional branches. Completion intra-operative angiography detected endoleak in 81 patients (64.8%), of which 43.2% demonstrated spontaneous resolution on postoperative computed tomographic angiography. During a mean follow-up of 20.2 ± 19.9 months, 14 branches (3.0%) in 14 patients (10.9%) developed BREL, predominantly type Ic. Freedom from persistent type I/III endoleak and endoleak-related reintervention were 70.6% and 68.5% at 3 years, respectively. Aneurysm diameter ≥80 mm (hazard ratio [HR] 2.76, 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.54-4.95; P < .001), post-dissection aetiology (HR 1.84, 95% CI, 1.02-3.33; P = .043) and accessory renal artery (ARA) ≥3 mm in diameter that was not incorporated or pre-emptively embolised (HR 2.03, 95% CI, 1.11-3.74; P = .022) were identified as independent risk factors for T2EL.

Conclusion

Immediate endoleak following BEVAR was common, but a substantial proportion were self-limiting. Type Ic endoleak was the most common type of BREL and the most frequent indication for endoleak-related reintervention. Large aneurysm diameter, post-dissection aetiology and ARA increased risk for T2EL.Clinical ImpactEndoleak following branched endovascular aortic repair (BEVAR) was commonly detected on completion angiography; however, immediate intervention was not required after ensuring adequate sealing zones and optimised bridging stent configuration, as 43% demonstrated spontaneous resolution on early postoperative imaging. Type Ic endoleak was the predominant form of branch-related endoleak, highlighting the importance of meticulous attention to target vessel landing zones. When anatomically feasible, incorporation of accessory renal artery ≥3 mm in the repair is recommended; alternatively, pre-emptive embolisation may reduce type II endoleak incidence.

title: Comparison of Prosthetic Valve Deformation and Hemodynamic Performance Between Bicuspid and Tricuspid Aortic Valve Anatomy After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement.
authorString: Feng D, Zhou Z, Ma H, Niu G, Zhang H, Zhao Z, Zhang E, Zhang B, Ye Y, Li Z, Wang M, Zhao J, Wu Y.

journal.title: Journal of the American Heart Association

abstractText:
Background

This study compared prosthetic valve deformation and postprocedural hemodynamic performance between bicuspid and tricuspid aortic valve anatomy after transcatheter aortic valve replacement with the Venus-A prosthesis.

Methods

We retrospectively evaluated patients who underwent transcatheter aortic valve replacement between 2012 and 2022 and underwent postoperative computed tomography within 1 year. Predischarge echocardiographic assessments included the mean transvalvular gradient and paravalvular leak. Computed tomography measurements included expansion ratio, ellipticity, implantation depth, asymmetric leaflet expansion, and hypoattenuated leaflet thickening. The leaflet inflow and valve waist were collectively defined as the functional valve portion.

Results

Among 212 patients (106 bicuspid and 106 tricuspid), the mean age was 74.2±7.6 years, and 43.9% were women. Patients with bicuspid anatomy had a significantly lower oversizing ratio and underwent balloon predilation and postdilation more frequently than those with tricuspid anatomy. Residual transvalvular gradients were higher with bicuspid than tricuspid anatomy (12.0 [interquartile range, 8.2-17.0] versus 10.0 [7.2-14.0] mm Hg; P=0.014), whereas moderate to severe paravalvular leak did not differ significantly. Prosthetic ellipticity was greater in bicuspid anatomy, but expansion ratios, including those within the functional valve portion, did not differ significantly. Implantation depth, asymmetric leaflet expansion, and hypoattenuated leaflet thickening incidence also did not differ significantly.

Conclusions

Following Venus-A implantation, bicuspid anatomy was associated with greater prosthetic ellipticity and higher residual gradients, despite no significant difference in prosthetic expansion.

title: NNMT Safeguards Vascular Aging by Modulating an Endothelial LMNA-HSP Stress-Response Axis.
authorString: Guo J, Tu H, Yin J, Gao S, Liu D, Wang M, Lin Y, Zhang X, Meng L, Sun J, Wang D, Li Y, Wang M, Li J.
abstractText:
Background

NNMT (nicotinamide N-methyltransferase) is a pivotal metabolic-epigenetic integrator that regulates cellular methylation balance. Although its expression and function exhibit profound, context-dependent heterogeneity in metabolic diseases and cancer, its role within the vascular system, particularly in aging endothelial cells, remains elusive.

Methods

We examined NNMT expression in a small, pathological, male-only cohort of older versus younger plaque-adjacent human carotid intimal donors, primary mouse aortic endothelial cells, and senescent human umbilical vein endothelial cells. Using endothelial-targeted adeno-associated virus-Tie systems, we assessed the effects of NNMT restoration and knockdown on vasodilation and arterial stiffness in aged mice. Mechanistic insights were obtained through exploratory multiomics integration.

Results

We established that NNMT expression exhibits an exploratory inverse association in a small, pathological, male-only cohort of older versus younger plaque-adjacent human carotid intimal donors, a pattern mirrored by declines observed in primary mouse aortic endothelial cells and senescent human umbilical vein endothelial cells. Functional assays demonstrated that NNMT restoration improves vasodilation and arterial stiffness in aged mice, whereas knockdown exacerbates these deficits. Mechanistically, exploratory multiomics integration, including Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation and transcriptomic analyses, suggests that NNMT-associated reduction in histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation occupancy at the LMNA (lamin A/C) promoter correlates with its transcriptional maintenance, a process influenced by S-adenosylmethionine supplementation. Downstream, we identified that NNMT-induced LMNA stabilization operates in concert with HSF1 (heat shock transcription factor 1) activation and nuclear translocation, a process accompanied by enhanced binding to HSP90 and HSP70 promoters to drive their transcription. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the vascular protective effects of the natural compound Heterophyllin B are mediated, at least in part, by NNMT, as these benefits were partially attenuated after endothelial NNMT knockdown in vivo.

Conclusions

We identify a protective, age-dependent role for NNMT in vascular endothelium. Our findings reveal that NNMT maintains endothelial homeostasis through coordinated regulation of nuclear LMNA and the downstream HSP (heat shock protein) stress response, highlighting the therapeutic potential of this pathway for addressing age-related endothelial dysfunction.

title: Partial reprogramming reveals lineage-specific uncoupling of rejuvenation, function, and recoverability in human cells
authorString: Washizu K, Wang X, Draper JM, Yamanaka S, Kunitomi A.
abstractText: Partial reprogramming is therapeutically useful only if cells keep its benefits while recovering their lineage identity and function after the reprogramming factors are withdrawn. Whether the relationship between reprogramming depth and recovery differs between lineages is unknown. Using reversible, traceable Sendai-OSKM, we prospectively isolated intermediate reprogramming states from primary human fibroblasts, cytotoxic T cells, and aortic endothelial cells and followed their recovery. Outcomes diverged: fibroblasts kept a reduced DNA methylation age but retained stromal remodeling and incomplete proliferative recovery; T cells recovered only from shallow reprogramming, with enhanced effector function; endothelial cells rapidly recovered identity, kept a reduced methylation age, and markedly improved vascular function. None of this tracked iPSC derivation efficiency. Multiome and knockdown analyses identified TOX as a shared progression dependency, whereas its candidate downstream programs were predominantly lineage-specific. Partial reprogramming involves a lineage-specific tradeoff between rejuvenation and recovery that must be optimized one lineage at a time.

title: Transbaffle Transcatheter Valve-in-Valve Implantation for Systemic Atrioventricular Bioprosthetic Stenosis in a Patient With Fontan Circulation.
authorString: Quennelle S, Torras O, Aldebert P.
abstractText:
Background

We report the case of a 29-year-old woman with an atrioventricular canal defect with left ventricular hypoplasia and mitral atresia in the setting of situs inversus and dextrocardia, palliated with Fontan circulation.

Case summary

At 21 years of age, she underwent systemic atrioventricular valve replacement with a 33-mm Hancock II bioprosthesis (Medtronic). Eight years later, she developed progressive bioprosthetic stenosis: mean transvalvular gradient of 11 mm Hg with restricted leaflet motion. Given prohibitive surgical risk, transcatheter valve-in-valve (ViV) implantation using a 29-mm Sapien 3 (Edwards Lifesciences) prosthesis was performed via transbaffle access. The procedure resulted in immediate hemodynamic improvement with reduction of the mean gradient.

Discussion

Only a few cases of transbaffle ViV implantation in the systemic atrioventricular position in patients with a Fontan circulation have been reported.

Take-home message

This case illustrates the feasibility of transbaffle ViV implantation in complex Fontan anatomy and highlights transcatheter therapy as a valuable alternative in high-risk adult congenital heart disease.

title: A novel mouse model recapitulates features of the neurodevelopmental disorder 3p25.3 microdeletion syndrome
authorString: Morgan ST, Kueh A, Keniry A, Eccles S, Blewitt ME, Vanyai HK.
abstractText: Neurodevelopmental disorders globally affect approximately 15% of children and adolescents, but many disorders do not have mouse models, thus limiting our ability to further understand them and ultimately develop treatments. In our study, we developed a novel mouse line to model 3p25.3 microdeletion syndrome (  6qE3  del/+ ) that reliably recapitulates key features of the syndrome.  6qE3  del/+ mice display congenital heart defects, craniofacial defects, skeletal anomalies and brain changes. We also generated another neurodevelopmental disorder model for a gene often included in the deleted region,  Brpf1 , and found that congenital heart defects and craniofacial defects may be partly attributable to the heterozygous loss of  Brpf1 in  6qE3  del/+ mice. Together our work offers new neurodevelopment models, and provides evidence that treatments developed for  Brpf1 haploinsufficiency may also benefit 3p25.3 microdeletion syndrome.

title: Placental angiogenic biomarkers for triage of suspected preeclampsia and prediction of maternal and neonatal morbidity in a high-risk population.
authorString: Lodewijks EJ, Hendrix MLE, Suiters MJM, Scheepers HCJ, Bons JAP, Al-Nasiry S.
abstractText:
Objective

Placental angiogenic biomarkers, including soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) and placental growth factor (PlGF), are used to predict preeclampsia (PE) and related adverse outcomes . This study aimed to assess differences in sFlt-1/PlGF ratios among high-risk women according to PE, maternal and neonatal morbidity, and to evaluate the predictive performance of thresholds > 38 and > 85, including time to delivery.

Methods

In this retrospective cohort study, 289 high-risk singleton pregnant women (2015-2019) were included. sFlt-1/PlGF ratios were measured after 24 weeks of gestation and compared across outcome groups.

Results

sFlt-1/PlGF ratios were significantly lower in the reference group compared to the confirmed and the suspected PE group. Ratios > 38 were associated with PE (OR 12.2 (95% CI 4.9-30.7; p < 0.001)), maternal morbidity (OR 22.5 (95% CI 8.9-56.7; p < 0.001)), neonatal morbidity (OR 4.0 (95% CI 2.0-8.0; p < 0.001)) and delivery within one, two, and three weeks (OR 20.0, 9.2, and 14.6; all p < 0.001).

Conclusion

The sFlt-1/PlGF ratio supports individualized management in high-risk pregnancies.

title: Engineering a Solid Dispersion-Integrated Fast-Dissolving Oral Film of Nicardipine Hydrochloride for Rapid Delivery in Hypertensive Urgency.
authorString: Gadade RS, Karmakar A, Kumar L.
abstractText: Nicardipine hydrochloride (NCH) is considered an ideal treatment for hypertensive crises, particularly for the management of hypertensive urgency. NCH is a BCS class II drug with limited solubility and exhibits significant first-pass metabolism upon oral administration, which increases the daily dosing frequency. Therefore, the study focuses on developing and evaluating an NCH-solid dispersion (NCHSD) loaded oral fast-dissolving film (OSD-ODF) for the treatment of hypertensive urgency. The NCHSD was prepared by the solvent-casting method using PVP K90 as the carrier at a 1:3 drug-to-carrier ratio. The solubility of NCH was increased by a factor of 23. The NCHSD released 86.0 ± 12.6% of the drug within 6 min. A central composite design was employed to optimize OSD-ODF, with HPMC E6 and PEG 400 concentrations as variables and disintegration time, drug content, weight variation, and tensile strength as responses. A fast disintegration and rapid-release profile were achieved for the optimized ODF with a disintegration time of 88 ± 3.14 s and 104.73 ± 2.00% drug release within 1 min. The in vitro cellular study demonstrated cytocompatibility of optimized ODF in Caco-2 and NIH 3T3 cells. The findings of the cellular permeability study in Caco-2 cells revealed a significant enhancement of the permeability coefficient (p ≤ 0.05) for optimized ODF, about 9 times greater permeability than pure NCH dispersion. This suggests successful development of NCHSD-loaded optimized ODF with better solubility, fast disintegration, rapid release profile, adequate mucoadhesion and biocompatibility. The findings of this work conclude that the prepared OSD-ODF holds excellent potential and is safe for the treatment of hypertensive urgency.

title: Assessment of eligibility for evidence-based pharmacological therapies in acute heart failure across heart failure with reduced and non-reduced ejection fraction.
authorString: Hui M, Salimian S, Turgeon RD, Greene SJ, Mentz RJ, Virani SA, Hawkins NM, Moghaddam N.
abstractText:
Background

Initiation of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) after stabilization of an acute heart failure (AHF) episode is well-tolerated and improves outcomes. In this study, we evaluated GDMT eligibility across the spectrum of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) in a contemporary AHF population.

Methods

Data from VancOuver CoastAL Acute Heart Failure Audit (VOCAL-AHF) of patients discharged with AHF were retrospectively analyzed. Eligibility for GDMT was determined based on major society guidelines. Heart failure phenotypes were defined as HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%), HFmrEF (41-49%), and HFpEF (≥50%).

Results

Among 1587 patients in VOCAL-AHF, there were 782 (49.3%) HFrEF, 132 (8.3%) HFmrEF, and 673 (42.4%) HFpEF. Mean age was 73±15 years and 58% were men. In HFrEF, eligibility for angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNI) was 64.4%, β-blockers 89.6%, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRA) 73.8%, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) 82.2%. Overall, 64.5% were eligible for quadruple therapy. In HFmrEF, 60.6% were eligible for steroidal MRA, 66.7% for SGLT2i, and 56.8% for ARNI with 56% candidate for initiation of all three agents. Eligibility for finerenone was 62.1% based on clinical criteria and 34.1% based on strict trial criteria. Corresponding values in HFpEF were 67.4%, and 37.1%. Overall, 66.6% of patients with non-reduced EF were eligible for dual-therapy with finerenone and SGLT2i.

Conclusion

Most patients with AHF, across LVEF categories, are eligible for in-hospital GDMT initiation, with a substantial proportion of those with non-reduced EF also meeting criteria for contemporary disease-modifying therapies, highlighting an important and previously underrecognized therapeutic opportunity in this population.

title: Individualized Glucocorticoid Replacement with Prednisone in Central Adrenal Insufficiency Using a Clinical Dose-Finding Algorithm.
authorString: Santos-Neto PF, Bottino AM, Correa-Silva SR, Abucham J.

journal.title: Endocrine practice : official journal of the American College of Endocrinology and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists

abstractText:
Objective

For over 30 years, we have treated patients with central adrenal insufficiency (CAI) using an in-house clinical algorithm (based exclusively on signs/symptoms) to individualize prednisone replacement within a predefined low dose range. The aim of this study is to describe prednisone dose distribution produced by this algorithm, determine associations between doses and patient characteristics, and compare long-term outcomes across dose groups.

Methods

Retrospective study. Seventy-seven patients with CAI (63 years; 64% men) on long-term prednisone use were selected in their last visit (2021-2022). Long-term outcomes were extracted from records; quality of life (QoL SF-36), health events, and patient education/self-management were assessed by recent in-person questionnaires.

Results

Algorithm dose distribution was 2.5mg in 70%, 3.75mg in 14%, and 5.0mg in 16% (P=0.001). Allocation to 2.5 mg was associated with older age and lower body weight/surface area (P<0.0001). No significant differences were observed, respectively, between 2.5mg and 5.0mg doses for: incidence of diabetes (P=0.74), hypertension (P=0.24), dyslipidemia (P=0.78); bone mineral density in lumbar spine (1.013 vs 0.911 g/cm2, P=0.19), total femur(0.930 vs. 0.952 g/cm2, P=0.70), and femoral neck(0.808 vs. 0.816 g/cm2, P=0.88); prevalence of weight gain (51% vs. 33%, P=0.25), weight gained [5.5(2.25-9.75) vs. 5.0(3.0-14.5)kg], health events(0.450.99), and QoL(0.13ConclusionsIndividualizing low-range prednisone replacement with a structured algorithm produced a dose distribution tied to patient age and body size, with comparable long-term outcomes. These findings support the use of tailored low-dose prednisone through a clinical algorithm as a safe method to avoid glucocorticoid over-and under replacement in CAI.

title: Sympathetic neuroeffector remodeling and cardiomyocyte ferroptosis in heart failure: A stage- and compartment-specific framework for β-adrenergic/cAMP signaling.
authorString: Zhang Z, Yang Z, Jia Z, Xing Y, Wang H, Niu H, Bi X, Zhu A.
abstractText: Heart failure is characterized by sympathetic remodeling, altered myocardial adrenergic responsiveness, and cardiomyocyte injury, with ferroptosis emerging as a potential contributor to adverse cardiac remodeling. This review proposes a dynamic "sympathetic-ferroptosis continuum" within a "nerve terminal-cardiomyocyte" dual-compartment framework linking cardiac sympathetic dysfunction, β1-adrenergic receptor (β1-AR)/cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling, and cardiomyocyte ferroptosis susceptibility. Sustained sympathetic drive can coexist with altered norepinephrine (NE) homeostasis at cardiac nerve terminals and myocardial β1-AR desensitization, creating a functional mismatch between sympathetic activity and myocardial signaling responsiveness. At sympathetic nerve terminals, altered β1-AR/cAMP signaling may influence tyrosine hydroxylase-dependent NE synthesis and synapsin 1/RIM1α-associated vesicle mobilization and release, alongside changes in NE transporter-mediated reuptake. In cardiomyocytes, dysregulated compartment-specific cAMP signaling may affect YAP-associated iron homeostasis, LPCAT3-mediated phospholipid remodeling, SLC7A11/GSH/GPX4-dependent antioxidant defenses, and NOX4-related oxidative stress, thereby modifying ferroptosis susceptibility. Together, these pathways provide an integrated mechanistic framework linking neurocardiac signaling imbalance with cardiomyocyte ferroptosis susceptibility. This framework identifies potential targets for preserving adaptive cAMP signaling, improving sympathetic neurotransmitter homeostasis, and limiting ferroptosis-related injury, providing new directions for compartment-specific cardioprotective strategies in heart failure.

title: Step change in glaucoma polygenic risk score performance enables clinical utility.
authorString: MacGregor S, Ni G, Seviiri M, Kolovos A, Le NQ, Hassall MM, Schmidt J, Gharahkhani P, Tang V, Souzeau E, Qassim A, Nandakumar P, Shringarpure S, Granka JM, Cooke Bailey JN, Aung T, Landers J, Graham SL, Healey PR, Khawaja AP, Pasquale LR, Wiggs JL, O'Brien J, Weinreb RN, Willoughby CE, Lotery A, Mitchell P, Mackey DA, Hewitt AW, Haan N, Siggs OM, Craig JE.
abstractText:
Purpose

Open-angle glaucoma (OAG) is the leading cause of irreversible blindness and is highly heritable. Despite effective treatments, approximately 50% of cases remain undiagnosed. We aimed to develop and validate a clinically applicable, genetics-based risk prediction tool for OAG across diverse ancestries.

Design

Genetic association study and risk prediction analysis.

Participants

More than 6 million individuals contributing genome-wide association study data from multiple ancestry groups.

Methods

We constructed a comprehensive polygenic risk score (PRS) for OAG using a multitrait modeling framework that integrated glaucoma-related traits, including intraocular pressure, optic disc parameters, and ocular hypertension. PRS performance was evaluated for OAG risk across major ancestry groups and assessed for associations with age at diagnosis, treatment escalation, surgical outcomes, and familial risk.

Main outcome measures

Odds ratios (ORs) for OAG by PRS percentile, age at disease onset, absolute risk estimates, treatment escalation, glaucoma surgery, and OAG risk in first-degree relatives.

Results

In Australian individuals of European ancestry, those in the top 10% of the PRS distribution had a 10-fold increased risk of OAG compared with the remainder (OR 10.04, 95% CI 7.43-13.59), substantially outperforming our previously published PRS (OR 4.2). Similar performance was observed in U.S. European ancestry data (OR 9.09, 95% CI 5.09-16.26). In UK Biobank Europeans the OR for the top 10% versus the remainder was 4.91 (95% CI 4.25-5.69). Although performance was attenuated in other ancestry groups (OR top 10% vs. remainder: 4.01 in South Asian, 3.39 in East Asian, and ranging from 2.26 to 3.81 in African ancestry populations depending on cohort), high PRS percentiles corresponded to elevated absolute risk across all groups. On average, individuals in the highest-risk decile developed glaucoma approximately 25 years earlier than those in the lowest decile and had ∼100-fold (OR 96.83, 95% CI 52.61-178.21) higher risk. The PRS also predicted treatment escalation in early disease, prevalent and incident glaucoma surgery, and OAG risk among first-degree relatives.

Conclusions

This enhanced PRS, available for clinical use through an accredited genotyping workflow, enables effective risk stratification for OAG across diverse ancestries, facilitating earlier identification and treatment of high-risk individuals while supporting resource rationalisation for those at low risk. Performance is strongest in European ancestry populations, and further work is needed to improve equity of performance across ancestries.

title: Targeted inhibition of Bcl6 effectively suppresses alloactivation of CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells with potential for T cell-directed immunosuppression.
authorString: Myriam B, Rens K, Henrik J, Carolina R, Peter J S, Antonia S, Kerstin A, Christoph D, Fulvia F, Nora F, Christian H, Lorenz J, Yige H, Johannes S, Dennis A H, Bernhard B, Carla C B, Louisa S.

journal.title: American journal of transplantation : official journal of the American Society of Transplantation and the American Society of Transplant Surgeons

abstractText: Bcl6 is a key transcriptional repressor regulating T cell fate; however, its role in T cell alloimmune responses is largely unknown. We investigated Bcl6 expression in T cells within allografts and the potential of targeting Bcl6 to modulate CD4<sup>+</sup> T cell alloactivation. Using mIFISH, we found that Bcl6<sup>+</sup>CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells were highly prevalent in kidney transplant biopsies during rejection. In mixed lymphocyte reactions, pharmacological Bcl6 inhibition (Bcl6i) potently suppressed proliferation and effector cytokine production of human CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells in a dose-dependent manner. Acting in PBMC and isolated T cell subsets alike, Bcl6i effects were direct, T cell-specific and irrespective of T cell differentiation state. Gene expression and flow cytometry showed Bcl6i reshaped T cell fate by altering key transcriptional programs. Bcl6i suppressed Th1, Th2 and Th17 transcription factors and upregulated TCF1. In addition, T cell inhibitory receptor TIGIT was up- and costimulatory receptor ICOS downregulated. Importantly, we validated the response to Bcl6i in donor-reactive CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells from kidney transplant patients, highlighting the translational potential of Bcl6 as a target for T cell-directed immunosuppression in transplantation.

title: Pooled cohort analysis of renin-angiotensin system inhibition and the risk of kidney outcomes in APOL1-mediated chronic kidney disease in the CRIC and SPRINT studies.
authorString: Fischman CJ, Zee J, Xu Y, Zhao Y, Bress A, Ofori-Atta B, Shulman R, Crump J, Rader DJ, Cohen JB, CRIC Study Investigators.
abstractText:
Introduction

Apolipoprotein L1 (APOL1) variants are common in individuals of African descent and increase risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (RASis) are a mainstay of therapy for hypertension and proteinuric CKD but were not historically recommended as first-line anti-hypertensive therapy in Black individuals. Here, we evaluated RASis versus other antihypertensive therapy on kidney outcomes in Black individuals by APOL1 genotype.

Methods

We included Black participants with APOL1 genotyping on first-line anti-hypertensive therapy from the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) and Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial (SPRINT). We evaluated whether the impact of RASi-prescription on kidney outcomes was modified by APOL1 risk allele number or baseline albuminuria, using Cox models with inverse probability of treatment weighting and marginal structural models.

Results

A total of 3418 participants (62% from SPRINT), 40%, 44% and 16% carrying zero, one and two APOL1 risk alleles, respectively, were included. RASi-use compared to other first-line antihypertensive therapy was associated with a comparably lower risk of the kidney outcome in individuals with zero (hazard ratio (HR) 0.62 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.44-0.87]), one (HR 0.68 [95% CI 0.49-0.94]) or two risk alleles (HR 0.59 [95% CI 0.40-0.86]). This benefit was driven by albuminuric participants, but estimates were similarly low for RASi-use compared to other antihypertensive therapy in albuminuric (HR 0.62, 95% CI [0.41-0.93]) and non-albuminuric (HR 0.37, 95% CI [0.13-1.08]) participants with two APOL1 risk alleles, although the estimate was imprecise in non-albuminuric participants.

Conclusions

RASi-based therapy, addressed as a time-updated pooled treatment, provided similar benefit across APOL1 genotypes, driven by albuminuric participants. Among individuals with two APOL1 risk alleles, outcomes were similar regardless of baseline albuminuria. However, further studies are needed due to small sample sizes and the inability of statistical methods to capture clinical variables that may have affected prescription changes.

title: Atrial fibrillation begets atrial fibrillation revisited: Early entrenchment of AF episodes.
authorString: Spitaler P, Bilgeri V, Feuchtner G, Tugrul B, Barbieri F, Adukauskaite A, Stühlinger M, Pfeifer BE, Gasser S, Bauer A, Linz D, Dichtl W.
abstractText:
Background

The 7-day threshold defining persistent atrial fibrillation (AF) is clinically entrenched but biologically arbitrary. Whether episode termination follows scale-free dynamics or time-dependent entrenchment remains uncertain.

Objective

To quantify the probability of spontaneous termination and assess its dependence on episode duration using large-scale pacemaker monitoring.

Methods

Continuous pacemaker monitoring data from the ACaSA study were analyzed. Device-detected AF episodes were reconstructed from daily burden using predefined continuity rules. Termination was modelled as the conditional probability that an ongoing episode would terminate within the subsequent 24 hours. Duration dependence was assessed using a shared frailty Weibull survival model, and episode duration distributions were compared using the Vuong likelihood-ratio test.

Results

After excluding patients with single-chamber devices or 100% baseline AF burden, 251 of 281 pacemaker recipients contributed 204,775 patient-days. Device-detected AF occurred in 154 patients, who contributed 7002 reconstructed episodes. Termination probability declined from 91.1% at 1 hour to 72.1% at 12 hours, 33.3% at 24 hours, and 4.3% at 7 days. Episode durations were better described by a lognormal distribution than by a scale-free power-law model.

Conclusion

Device-detected AF episodes show marked early entrenchment, with spontaneous termination becoming progressively less likely as episode duration increases. These findings support the concept that "AF begets AF" even at short timescales and suggest that persistence beyond 24 hours identifies a state with a substantially reduced likelihood of near-term spontaneous termination.

Trial registration number

NCT05127720.

Clinicaltrials

Gov id

NCT05127720.

title: Balancing mechanical stability and biological performance through a dual-setting approach in granular silicate-CPCs.
authorString: Steinacker VC, Wutz S, Renner T, Konrad JK, Higuchi T, Huber C, Müller-Richter U, Hartmann S, Kübler AC, Gbureck U.
abstractText: Granular bone substitute systems are widely used to treat complex and irregular defects due to their adaptability and prefabricated nature, which eliminates in situ setting-related instability. However, their limited mechanical stability makes their performance highly dependent on intraoperative handling and increases the risk of impaired tissue ingrowth. In this study, granular brushite- and monetite-based calcium phosphate cements (CPCs) were developed and systematically investigated to improve mechanical performance and cytocompatibility through a dual-setting approach. Silicate-based precursors, specifically tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) and 1,8-bis(triethoxysilyl)octane (BTESO), were incorporated into the CPC formulation prior to granulation to establish a reinforcing secondary network within the cement matrix. Structural and mechanical properties were assessed, including compression-induced changes, which were analysed using micro-computed tomography (μCT). The biocompatibility of the CPCs was further investigated using WST assays, cell counting, DNA quantification, and scanning electron microscope with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX). The incorporation of TEOS significantly increased mechanical stability and cytocompatibility compared to conventional formulations. TEOS-modified granules exhibited less than one-third of the compression-induced deformation observed for the control, which showed a height reduction of more than 5 mm. μCT analysis further revealed a shift in the intergranular pore-size peak from approximately 350 to 250 μm after compression in the control, whereas no apparent shift was observed for TEOS-modified granules. Granule size itself affected intergranular pore geometry, with larger granules showing higher metabolic activity. TEOS-modified granules showed the most favourable overall biological response, whereas the addition of BTESO provided no further mechanical or biological benefit. Furthermore, a cryosectioning approach enabled fluorescence imaging of osteoblast-like cells on CPCs with high autofluorescence, allowing visualisation of cell morphology on the material surface. Overall, the dual-setting approach, particularly using TEOS, improved resistance to compression while preserving intergranular pore architecture and maintaining favourable cytocompatibility, thereby addressing a key limitation of granular CPC-based bone substitute systems. In parallel, cryosectioning enables reliable fluorescence-based visualisation of cells on highly autofluorescent materials, offering a practical approach for the biological assessment of such systems.

title: Relaxin-2 reverses diastolic dysfunction and suppresses sustained arrhythmias in a rat model of Heart Failure with preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF).
authorString: Palma JB, Gabris-Weber B, McMahon B, Mauro AJ, St Hilaire C, Cuevas RA, Dschietzig TB, Romero G, Salama G.
abstractText:
Aims

Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) afflicts millions annually and current treatments provide symptomatic relief. The goal is to test the effects of synthetic human Relaxin-2 (RLX) on diastolic dysfunction (DD) and arrhythmia vulnerability.

Methods and results

Male ZSF1 rats were placed on a normal diet (ND, N = 8 controls) or a high-fat diet (HFD, N = 11), resulting in the development of DD in 11-weeks, based on serial echocardiograms (enlarged left atrium (LA), wall thickness, doppler flow: E/e'). Once HFpEF was confirmed, ND and HFpEF rats were randomly treated with Relaxin (400 µg/kg/day RLX, N = 6) or the vehicle (N = 5) for 2-weeks using implanted minipumps. Echocardiograms were repeated for 2 more weeks, then hearts were isolated, optically mapped, subjected to programmed electrical stimulation (PES) and tissues dissected for immuno-fluorescence (IF), and qPCR analysis. Circulating levels of glucose, RLX and NT-pro-ANP were measured, pre- and post-treatment. Echocardiograms indicated that RLX reversed DD by reducing LA dimensions and E/e'. Optical mapping showed that vehicle-treated, ND rats (N = 3) had non-sustained atrial (1/3), and ventricular (3/3) arrhythmias and RLX-treatment reduced them to 0/3 and 1/3, respectively. Vehicle-treated, HFD rats had non-sustained (2/5) and sustained (2/5) atrial and ventricular arrhythmias (N = 5). RLX-treatment (N = 6) suppressed sustained atrial and ventricular arrhythmias (0/6) but not non-sustained atrial (2/6) and ventricular (3/6) arrhythmias. RLX tended to increase conduction velocity (CV), particularly at short cycle lengths consistent with increased Nav1.5, Connexin-43, β-catenin and Wnt1 expression, based on IF. There were no significant changes in fibrosis in this HFpEF model. NT-pro-ANP was elevated in HFpEF and reduced towards control values by RLX. qPCR analysis showed that RLX decreased Dickkopf (DKK1) and Matrix Metallopeptidase 1a (MMP1A) genes and increased SCN5A expression compared to vehicle (N = 6 and 5, respectively).

Conclusions

The ZSF1 model showed indications of HFpEF, including DD, enlargement of the LA, hemodynamic stress, increased vulnerability to sustained AF and VF, and elevated glucose and blood pressure. RLX treatment largely reversed DD, hemodynamic stress, and suppressed sustained arrhythmias. RLX elicited cardiac genomic changes, most likely through Wnt/canonical signaling, demonstrating RLX's potential as a therapy for HFpEF.

title: Computed Tomography-Derived Left Atrial Intramyocardial Fat and Low-Voltage Zones in Atrial Fibrillation.
authorString: Keresteci AH, Çöteli C, Düzgün SA, Sezer C, Hazırolan T, Yorgun H, Aytemir K.
abstractText:
Introduction

Left atrial low-voltage zones (LVZs) are associated with atrial fibrosis and arrhythmia recurrence after atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation and are thought to underlie many recurrences despite durable pulmonary vein isolation. However, noninvasive markers of the arrhythmogenic atrial substrate remain poorly characterized. We sought to investigate the association between computed tomography (CT)-derived left atrial intramyocardial fat (inFAT) and electroanatomically defined LVZs.

Methods and results

In this single-center retrospective study, 145 consecutive patients undergoing first-time radiofrequency AF ablation underwent preprocedural dual-source CT and high-density left atrial voltage mapping in sinus rhythm. LVZs were defined as contiguous regions with bipolar voltage < 0.5 mV. ADAS 3D post-processing was used to quantify total inFAT, dense inFAT, and fat-myocardial admixture. LVZs were identified in 51 patients (35.2%). Compared with patients without LVZs, those with LVZs had a higher prevalence of persistent AF (58.8% vs. 17.0%; p < 0.001) and a greater left atrial volume index (LAVi) (74.41 [64.87-99.50] vs. 62.99 [52.78-74.73] mL/m2; p < 0.001). Patients with LVZs also demonstrated larger volumes of total inFAT, dense inFAT, and fat-myocardial admixture, accompanied by lower radiodensity values of total and dense inFAT. In multivariable logistic regression analysis, persistent AF (adjusted odds ratio [OR]: 5.389; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.162-13.433; p < 0.001) and dense inFAT volume (adjusted OR: 3.439; 95% CI: 1.107-10.677; p = 0.033) remained independently associated with the presence of LVZs, whereas LAVi did not. Among the CT-derived fat metrics, only dense inFAT retained an independent association with LVZs after adjustment for clinical covariates.

Conclusion

CT-derived dense inFAT was independently associated with left atrial LVZs and may represent a novel noninvasive marker of the arrhythmogenic atrial substrate in AF. Prospective studies are warranted to determine its role in substrate-guided ablation strategies and risk stratification.

title: C/EBP-β-mediated upregulation of CaV1.2 calcium channel increases arterial constriction in mice with ibrutinib-associated hypertension.
authorString: Zhang L, Yin S, Hou W, Yang D, Jia Y, Liu Y, Wang Y, Zhao S, Gao X, Sun X, Lu X, Li J, Chu M, Xiong X, Zhu H, Wang J.
abstractText: Ibrutinib, a Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is indicated for treating chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), but hypertension is a common cardiovascular adverse event. Previous studies have linked ibrutinib to cardiac events through dysregulated intracellular calcium handling, but the mechanisms underlying ibrutinib-associated hypertension remain largely unknown. Here, we followed up 225 CLL patients receiving ibrutinib or managed with watch-and-wait strategy, and identified ibrutinib as an independent risk factor for hypertension. In mice, ibrutinib elevated arterial blood pressure (BP) without structural remodeling of small arteries, and it potentiated K+-induced vasoconstriction. In vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), ibrutinib upregulated CaV1.2 channel expression and function, as evidenced by enhanced CaV1.2 currents and K+-triggered-[Ca2+]i elevation. Mechanistically, ibrutinib suppressed casein kinase 2 (CK2)-mediated HSP90β phosphorylation, and stabilized C/EBP-β, which bound to the promoter of Cacna1c gene and drove CaV1.2 transcription. Significantly, C/EBP-β knockdown attenuated ibrutinib-induced CaV1.2 hyperactivity and vasoconstriction. Collectively, these findings reveal a CK2-HSP90β-C/EBP-β-CaV1.2 signaling cascade through which ibrutinib enhances vascular Ca2+ influx and vasoconstriction, thereby elevating arterial BP. Thus, this study nominates C/EBP-β as a therapeutic target for ibrutinib-associated hypertension.

title: Transcriptional regulation of NK cell state by ELF4 links innate immune licensing to kidney fibrosis.
authorString: Li S, Hu H, Lanzar ZR, Gu X, Cruz-Morales E, Bochi-Layec AC, Sanchez-Navarro A, Park J, Shrestha R, Liu H, Donner AJ, Lin MH, Bell TA, Miner JH, Ruella M, Vivier E, Lucas CL, Hunter CA, Susztak K.
abstractText: Fibrosis is a common outcome of chronic tissue injury, yet immune regulators that are conserved across species and translatable to human disease remain poorly defined. By integrating human kidney transcriptomes with multiple murine models of kidney fibrosis, we identified the ETS transcription factor ELF4 as a conserved, immune-enriched regulator associated with disease severity. ELF4 expression was highest in natural killer (NK) cells. Genetic deletion of Elf4, including NK cell-specific ablation, attenuated experimental kidney injury, with reduced inflammation, fibrosis, and loss of renal function. Single-cell and functional analyses showed that ELF4 deficiency disrupts late-stage NK cell maturation and broadly suppresses cytotoxic and interferon-γ (IFNγ) effector programs. Mechanistically, ELF4 directly sustains STAT1 transcription, maintaining a STAT1-TBX21 program required for NK cell maturation and effector competence. Consistent with this framework, NK cell depletion, IFNγ neutralization, or antisense-mediated suppression of Elf4 phenocopied renal protection. Together, these findings identify ELF4 as a transcriptional licensing factor that links NK cell state to kidney injury and highlight innate immune programming as a potential therapeutic entry point in chronic kidney disease.

title: Endothelin Receptor Antagonists in CKD-Associated Resistant Hypertension: Trial Lessons, Safety Boundaries, and Conditions for Future Clinical Testing.
authorString: Corrêa LMA, Brandão LKV, Delmiro Silva YR, Zanella J, Pinheiro IM.

journal.title: American journal of cardiovascular drugs : drugs, devices, and other interventions

abstractText: Resistant hypertension in chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains a common and difficult-to-treat phenotype after confirmation of true resistance, exclusion of pseudoresistance, and optimization of standard multidrug therapy. Endothelin receptor antagonists (ERAs) have re-entered this space largely through aprocitentan, a dual ETA/ETB receptor antagonist that provides modest but significant blood-pressure lowering in resistant hypertension. However, the clinical interpretation of this class remains constrained by edema/fluid retention, absence of direct comparison with spironolactone, and lack of established hard renal or cardiovascular outcome benefit in CKD-associated resistant hypertension. This Current Opinion reframes the ERA evidence as a set of trial-design lessons rather than as broad class rehabilitation. ASCEND showed that albuminuria reduction is insufficient when exposure and congestion risk are poorly controlled. SONAR demonstrated the value of response and tolerability enrichment. PRECISION clarified the incremental blood-pressure effect of aprocitentan on standardized background therapy, while confirming clinically relevant edema risk. ZENITH-CKD suggests that low-dose ERA strategies combined with SGLT2 inhibition may improve tolerability and testability. The practical implication is a narrow and monitored phenotype: rigorously confirmed resistant hypertension, CKD with residual cardiorenal risk, absence of unstable heart failure or marked natriuretic-peptide elevation, and capacity for close surveillance of weight, edema, renal function, hemoglobin, and albuminuria. At present, aprocitentan should be viewed as a selective add-on option rather than a routine fourth-line default, while future trials should test ERA strategies against contemporary guideline-based comparators and prespecified congestion-risk algorithms.

title: Association between methylmalonic acid and vascular calcification in patients with chronic kidney disease: an observational study.
authorString: Yang X, Jin J, Cheng M, Kang Y, Zhang S, Bai Y, Xu J.
abstractText:
Background

Methylmalonic acid (MMA) has been regarded as a risk factor for cardiovascular diseases. However, the association between MMA and vascular calcification (VC) in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains unclear.

Methods

Patients with CKD stage 5 were included and classified into either non-VC, mild VC, or severe VC groups. Restricted cubic splines (RCS) analysis and ordinal logistic regression were performed to examine the relationship between MMA and VC. Moreover, independent external validation was performed based on the NHANES dataset.

Results

A total of 144 patients with CKD were involved, among whom 82.6% had VC. Compared with individuals without VC, serum MMA levels were elevated among those with VC, especially in the severe VC group (P=0.012). RCS analysis revealed an approximately positive linear relationship between MMA and VC (P-nonlinear=0.11). After adjusting for all covariates, each 1 ng/mL increase in serum MMA was associated with 13% higher odds of being in a more severe VC category (OR=1.13, 95%: 1.05-1.22, P=0.001). Additionally, subgroup analyses indicated that the direction of association between MMA and VC was consistent across different age, gender, hypertension, and diabetes groups (P for interaction was 0.77, 0.65, 0.83, and 0.34, respectively). Finally, results were confirmed in the NHANES cohort (n=326).

Conclusion

High levels of MMA have a positive association with the risk of VC, particularly severe VC. This study may provide a novel risk marker for VC in patients with CKD.

title: Assessment of atrioventricular interaction and response to balloon pulmonary angioplasty in chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension using cardiac MRI.
authorString: Chen H, Cheng C, Lei Y, Yu J, Ghanbari F, Lin Q, Chen X, Hong C, Deng Y.
abstractText:
Objectives

This study aimed to evaluate atrioventricular interaction in patients with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) and to determine the effects of balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA) on reversible cardiac remodeling assessed by cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging.

Materials and methods

In this prospective single-center study, 52 patients with CTEPH (mean age: 58 ± 11 years; 34 females) and 35 healthy controls underwent CMR imaging. Twenty-five patients (mean age: 60 ± 12 years; 19 females) who underwent BPA received follow-up CMR at a mean interval of 7 ± 5 months. Cardiac structure, function, myocardial deformation, and epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) were assessed based on cine images.

Results

Compared with controls, patients with CTEPH demonstrated predominant right-sided cardiac involvement, characterized by reduced right ventricular ejection fraction (p < 0.001), marked enlargement of right atrial (RA) and ventricular (RV) volumes, and severely impaired right heart strain (all p < 0.001). Left ventricular systolic function was relatively preserved, with mildly impaired global circumferential strain (p = 0.011) and a trend toward attenuated longitudinal strain (p = 0.055), whereas all left atrial (LA) strain components were markedly impaired (all p < 0.05), indicating altered atrioventricular interaction. Following BPA, the right heart structure, RV function and deformation, and LA conduit strain improved. EAT was comparable between groups and remained unchanged after BPA.

Conclusion

CTEPH involves marked right heart systolic dysfunction and early biventricular diastolic abnormalities associated with impaired atrioventricular interaction. BPA could reverse cardiac remodeling by improving right heart structure, function, and partially recovering atrial deformation after pressure relief.

Key points

Questions Atrioventricular interaction abnormalities and reversible cardiac remodeling in chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) after balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA) remain insufficiently characterized. Findings CTEPH is associated with impaired right heart strain and altered atrioventricular interaction; BPA improves right heart structure and function and partially recovers atrial deformation. Critical relevance statement Cardiac MRI-derived myocardial deformation and atrial phasic function may reflect alterations in atrioventricular interaction in CTEPH and complement conventional metrics in assessing cardiac remodeling and recovery after BPA.

title: Integrated transcriptomic and cistromic analyses reveal associations between mechanotransduction-associated transcription and clock-gene expression in pulmonary arterial hypertension and TEAD-sensitive CRY1/CLOCK responses.
authorString: Wu R, Zhang Y, Xiong Y, Sun Y, Fu M, Cao S, Wang J.
abstractText: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) involves vascular remodeling in an abnormal mechanical environment, but the relationship between mechanotransduction-associated transcription and clock-gene expression remains unclear. We integrated three PAH lung transcriptomic cohorts, donor-level endothelial analyses, vascular cell-state and spatial transcriptomic data, endothelial perturbation transcriptomics, and chromatin-binding data, with validation in human pulmonary artery endothelial cells (HPAECs). In 83 PAH lung samples, restricted maximum likelihood (REML) random-effects pooling showed a positive association between mechanotransduction and clock-related scores (Spearman ρ = 0.393, 95% confidence interval 0.185-0.567; Hartung-Knapp sensitivity P = 0.0279), which weakened when restricted to genes detectable across cohorts. Endothelial pseudobulk data from GSE169471 supported a positive donor-level association (n = 8, ρ = 0.738); the six-donor GSE210248 analysis used different score pairs. Associations varied in direction across vascular cell states, while molecular programs in 217 spatial regions differed by donor and lesion context. In HUVECs, activated YAP/TAZ increased CRY1 and CLOCK expression, with partial attenuation by TEAD-binding-deficient mutants. ChIP-seq identified candidate binding sites near both genes. In HPAECs, a stiffer substrate was associated with higher nuclear YAP/TAZ and CRY1/CLOCK protein levels; construct comparisons and independent TEAD1 knockdown supported TEAD-sensitive expression induction. Beyond prior CRY1 findings, this study provides evidence for CLOCK responses in pulmonary artery endothelium and cell-state heterogeneity. The findings support a candidate regulatory link, not altered circadian function or a causal mechanism of PAH vascular remodeling.

title: Exploring the pathogenic mechanisms of bisphenol A-induced postmenopausal osteoporosis using network toxicology and molecular docking.
authorString: Wang Y, Wang H, Tang X, Ma L.

journal.title: The Journal of international medical research

abstractText: ObjectiveBisphenol A, a widely used endocrine-disrupting chemical commonly found in plastics and food packaging materials, has shown to exhibit bone toxicity and increase the risk of osteoporosis. In postmenopausal women, whose endogenous estrogen levels are substantially reduced, the osteotoxic effects of bisphenol A may be amplified, potentially further increasing the risk of postmenopausal osteoporosis. However, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood.MethodsFour publicly available databases were used: SwissTargetPrediction and ChEMBL to identify bisphenol A targets and GeneCards and Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man to identify genes associated with postmenopausal osteoporosis. Overlapping targets between bisphenol A and postmenopausal osteoporosis were identified, followed by protein-protein interaction network construction using STRING and Cytoscape to identify hub genes. Functional enrichment analyses, including Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes analyses, were performed using clusterProfiler. Molecular docking was conducted using AutoDockTools to predict binding affinities. External validation of hub gene expression was performed using the GSE56815 transcriptomic dataset, with differential expression analysis conducted using limma and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction.ResultsA total of 86 overlapping targets between bisphenol A and postmenopausal osteoporosis were identified, and five hub genes (estrogen receptor 1, insulin, tumor protein p53, tumor necrosis factor, and matrix metallopeptidase 9) were identified. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment analysis showed predominant enrichment in lipid and atherosclerosis, phosphoinositide 3-kinase-Akt, advanced glycation end product-receptor for advanced glycation end product, and mitogen-activated protein kinase pathways. Molecular docking predicted the strongest binding affinity between bisphenol A and estrogen receptor 1 (-7.26 kcal/mol). External validation using GSE56815 revealed no significant differential expression of the hub genes in peripheral blood monocytes after false discovery rate correction.ConclusionThis study provides a hypothesis-generating framework that identifies estrogen receptor 1, insulin, tumor protein p53, tumor necrosis factor, and matrix metallopeptidase 9 as candidate mediators of bisphenol A-induced postmenopausal osteoporosis through interconnected endocrine, inflammatory, and metabolic pathways. These findings highlight the need for experimental validation in bone-relevant tissues.

title: Lutein Targets TLR4 as a Potential Immunotherapeutic Strategy for Treatment of Doxorubicin-Induced Cardiomyopathy.
authorString: Khedr EG, Badr NH, El-Feky OA.
abstractText: Toll-like receptor 4 is an immune receptor associated with inflammatory diseases, including cardiac conditions. Lutein, a natural carotenoid with potent anti-inflammatory effects, protects against coronary heart disease and other cardiovascular issues. We aimed to explore its potential cardioprotective effects against doxorubicin-induced cardiomyopathy (DIC), focusing on the TLR4/NF-κB and JAK/STAT pathways. We compared its effects with olmesartan, commonly used to manage DIC. This study was performed on five groups of rats: control, doxorubicin (Dox)-treated, lutein-treated, olmesartan-treated, and combination-treated groups. Induction of DIC was performed using Dox (4.5 mg/kg every other day) for ten days. In treatment groups, lutein (50 mg/kg/day) or olmesartan (10 mg/kg/day) was administered for 10 days alongside Dox, while the combination treatment group co-administered lutein (50 mg/kg/day) and olmesartan (10 mg/kg/day) for the same duration alongside Dox. The results indicated that lutein protected cardiomyocytes from Dox-induced histopathological changes, including myocardial fiber disorganization, vascular congestion, and perivascular edema. It decreased the levels of TLR4, NF-κB, p-JAK2, and p-STAT1/3 relative to the Dox group, exhibiting an anti-inflammatory effect through suppression of the TLR4/NF-κB and JAK/STAT pathways. It also had regulatory effects on Akt/mTOR signaling, another pathway linked to TLR4 activation. In comparison to olmesartan, lutein had superior effects on IL-6/JAK2/STAT1/NF-κB and Akt/mTOR levels. Combination treatment also demonstrated cardioprotective effect at histopathological, biochemical, and molecular levels, being more effective than olmesartan on IL-6/NF-κB and Akt/mTOR levels. Moreover, Lutein administration alongside Dox showed anti-inflammatory and cardioprotective effects against DIC, suggesting it as a promising adjunct therapy, either alone or with olmesartan.

title: Partial loss of NONO function disrupts paraspeckle-like assembly and expands the MRXS34 phenotypic spectrum to a suspected renal medullary tubular disorder.
authorString: He J, Zhang X, Shi Y, Liang Y, Dai C, Wang C, Xu Y.
abstractText:
Background

Pathogenic variants in NONO cause X-linked syndromic intellectual developmental disorder 34 (MRXS34; MIM #300967), characterized by neurodevelopmental delay, cardiac defects, and brain malformations. Renal involvement, particularly renal medullary tubular abnormalities, is poorly described in this disorder.

Methods

Clinical evaluations included echocardiography, cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), renal ultrasonography, and trio-based whole-exome sequencing (WES). We performed functional studies in HEK293T cells transiently transfected with wild-type or mutant NONO expression constructs. We quantified NONO mRNA expression by reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), protein expression by western blotting, the NONO-SFPQ interaction by co-immunoprecipitation, and subcellular localization by confocal immunofluorescence microscopy.

Results

A 1-month-17-day-old male infant presented with multiple muscular ventricular septal defects, biventricular left ventricular noncompaction cardiomyopathy, corpus callosum dysgenesis, hyperkalemia with markedly elevated aldosterone, and renal ultrasound abnormalities suggestive of a medullary tubular disorder. Trio-WES identified a novel hemizygous frameshift variant, c.671_672del p.(Val224Glyfs*8), in NONO (NM_007363.5). This variant resulted in a 92.6% reduction in NONO mRNA expression relative to wild-type (P < 0.001), consistent with enhanced transcript degradation/NMD, and expression of a truncated protein of approximately 27 kDa at reduced levels (P < 0.01). Co-immunoprecipitation showed that the interaction between mutant NONO and SFPQ was reduced but not completely abolished. Confocal immunofluorescence revealed altered paraspeckle-like foci and reduced SFPQ signal.

Conclusions

We report a possible association of MRXS34 with a suspected renal medullary tubular disorder, with MSK not excluded, expanding the phenotypic spectrum of NONO-related disorders to include renal medullary/tubular abnormalities. The c.671_672del variant causes partial loss of function through reduced transcript and protein expression, altered subcellular localization, and impaired paraspeckle-like assembly, possibly secondary to impaired NONO-SFPQ heterodimerization. These findings suggest that NONO-related disease should be considered in patients with unexplained renal medullary/tubular anomalies.

title: Epigenetic regulation of the complement system in age-related chronic inflammation: mechanisms and therapeutic prospects.
authorString: Wang Y, Zhao H, Kong M, Qin K, Teng Y, Zhu Z, Li Y, Liu D, Cui L, Sun Y.
abstractText: Aging is accompanied by progressive changes in epigenetic regulation, immune function, and tissue homeostasis, which may contribute to chronic low-grade inflammation and age-related disease. The complement system is an important component of innate immunity and participates in immune surveillance, tissue homeostasis, and inflammatory regulation. Increasing evidence suggests that DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNAs can influence the expression of complement components and regulatory proteins, while complement-associated inflammatory signaling may reciprocally affect cellular epigenetic states. In this review, we summarize current evidence linking epigenetic regulation with complement biology during aging and discuss how this relationship varies across tissues and disease contexts. Particular attention is given to the central nervous system, where complement-dependent synaptic remodeling can support physiological circuit refinement but may become excessive or dysregulated under pathological conditions. We further examine the epigenetic-complement relationship in Alzheimer's disease, age-related macular degeneration, and atherosclerosis, and consider age-associated clonal hematopoiesis as a potential modifier of myeloid and inflammatory states. Rather than proposing a uniform linear pathway from epigenetic aging to complement activation and disease, we propose a context-dependent framework in which age-associated epigenetic remodeling may coexist with physiological adaptation or, under specific genetic, metabolic, environmental, cellular, and tissue contexts, contribute to reduced regulatory reserve and persistent complement-associated inflammation. This framework highlights the potential of cell-, tissue-, and disease-stage-specific strategies targeting the epigenetic-complement axis while preserving physiological complement functions.

title: EXPRESS: The Medin-Aorta-Brain Axis: Linking Vascular Aging to Alzheimer's Disease.
authorString: Triposkiadis F, Xanthopoulos A.

journal.title: Journal of cerebral blood flow and metabolism : official journal of the International Society of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism

abstractText: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by the accumulation of cerebral amyloid-β (Aβ). Medin amyloid is present in the aging aorta and has been linked to cerebrovascular dysfunction. We hypothesize that medin contributes to AD pathogenesis through a systemic aorta-brain axis. Aortic medin may promote aortic stiffening, thereby increasing cerebral pulsatile load and impairing perivascular clearance. Furthermore, cerebral medin co-localizes with Aβ, exacerbating neurovascular injury. This hypothesis requires validation. We outline falsifiable predictions, a staged biomarker framework, and the interpretation of circulating medin levels. Medin targeting may be a strategy to maintain vascular compliance and reduce Aβ aggregation, pending safety studies.

title: Contribution of angiotensin receptor type II to dermal extravasation caused by bradykinin in mice: Implications for sartan-induced angioedema.
authorString: Dao VT, Fahimi E, Bisha M, Kurz T, Hansen FK, Aközbek C, Suvorava T, Kojda G.
abstractText:
Background

While non-allergic angioedema induced by ACE inhibitors and sacubitril are caused by reduced bradykinin degradation and over-activation of bradykinin receptor type 2 (B2), the pathophysiology of sartan-induced angioedema is not fully understood. As angiotensin II receptor (AT) type 1 blockers (sartans) increase circulating angiotensin II, enhanced activation of AT2 by angiotensin II likely occurs. The aim of this study was to investigate whether the AT2 agonist compound 21 (C21) inhibits ACE activity and increases bradykinin-induced dermal extravasation.

Methods

Increased plasma angiotensin II by telmisartan was measured at a dose that reduced systolic blood pressure by 20 mmHg. C21 was synthesized and its biological activity assessed by vasorelaxation of aortic rings of control mice which was absent in rings of AT2-/y mice. As for Miles Assays AT2-/y mice were backcrossed to C57BL/6 J (AT2-/y-C57). Blood pressure remained unchanged by C21.

Results

In Miles assays in C57BL/6 J, but not in AT2-/y-C57, C21 potentiated dermal extravasation induced by bradykinin that was inhibited by the AT2 antagonist PD123319, while extravasation by the ACE resistant B2 agonist labradimil remained. Pre-treatment of human endothelial cells with C21 strongly reduced ACE activity in cell homogenates in an AT2 dependent manner suggesting a cellular loss of ACE and indicating reduced tissue ACE activity. Correspondingly, increased ACE activity in plasma occurred following treatment with C21.

Conclusion

These data suggest an increase of bradykinin-induced skin extravasation due to direct AT2 activation which may contribute to explaining the molecular mechanism underlying the occurrence of sartan-induced non-allergic angioedema.

title: Deconstructing coronary microvascular resistance: From reperfusion injury to adaptive Haemodynamics.
authorString: Tas A, Alan Y, Ozcan A, Boerhout CKM, Tekelioglu B, Kara Tas I, Kavak İ, Kahraman S, van de Hoef TP, Perera D, Erturk M, Umman S, Parker KH, Piek JJ, Sezer M.
abstractText: The prognostic meaning of elevated coronary microvascular resistance (MR) differs between acute and chronic coronary syndromes (ACS and CCS). After reperfusion in ACS, high MR, measured invasively as the index of microcirculatory resistance (IMR) or hyperaemic microvascular resistance (hMR), is an established marker of microvascular injury, microvascular obstruction and adverse outcomes. In CCS, elevated hMR or IMR alone has not consistently been associated with adverse cardiovascular events, whereas a reduced coronary flow reserve (CFR) has. We examine the physiological basis of MR and the assumption that high resistance is uniformly pathological. Using adenosine-derived haemodynamic endotypes defined by CFR and hMR, we describe an endotype without coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) in which a preserved CFR coexists with high hMR and a higher resting resistance. In this endotype, wave-intensity and reservoir-pressure analyses show preserved hyperaemic augmentation of accelerating wave energy, favourable aortic reservoir function and low excess pressure. We discuss the hypothesis that the higher resting microvascular tone reflects a compensatory myogenic response to pulsatile load, and the evidence still needed to distinguish adaptation from association. The absence of excess events does not exclude clinically relevant disease, because angina and quality of life are separate outcomes. Since microvascular resistance dynamically sets resting flow and its augmentation, a high MR may reflect pathology that limits flow or autoregulation that adjusts it. Its interpretation should therefore consider mechanism and vasodilator capacity rather than a single threshold, and endotyping by CFR, MR and, where indicated, acetylcholine testing may improve patient selection for targeted therapies.

title: [French translation of the TRANS-Q questionnaire for assessing quality-of-life improvement after chest masculinization surgery: Validation and clinical application].
authorString: Maze E, Guerreschi P, Martinot-Duquennoy V, Medjkane F, Leroy C, Ngo B.

journal.title: Annales de chirurgie plastique et esthetique

abstractText:
Objectives

The primary objective of this study was to propose the first French version of the TRANS-Q questionnaire and to evaluate its internal validity. The secondary objective is to assess the improvement in quality of life following gender-affirming mastectomy in the FTM transition pathway at our center.

Methods

This retrospective single-center study included 69 patients operated on between 2018 and 2023 at Lille University Hospital. The TRANS-Q questionnaire underwent translation and linguistic adaptation into French prior to use. Patients were contacted by telephone to complete the French-translated TRANS-Q. Two techniques were compared: double-incision mastectomy with nipple graft (n=47) and periareolar mastectomy (n=22).

Results

Our French version of the TRANS-Q demonstrated good internal consistency (α1=0.859; α2=0.902) and high reproducibility (ICC-1=0.919; ICC-2=0.952). A significant improvement in quality of life after surgery was observed (P<0.001). No statistically significant difference in satisfaction was found between the two techniques (p>0.05).

Conclusion

The French version of the TRANS-Q demonstrates good internal validity and constitutes a relevant tool for assessing satisfaction among transgender patients in French-speaking countries. Chest masculinization surgery by mastectomy significantly improves quality of life, with no difference in patient-reported satisfaction between techniques when the surgical indication is appropriately established.

title: Early Correlates of High-Risk Lymphatic Subtype on T2-Weighted Pre-fontan Cardiac MRI and Associated Clinical Outcomes.
authorString: Rastogi R, Zweben B, Joyce J, Shustak RJ, Vaiyani D, Schreier M, Pinto E, Smith C, Dori Y, Dewitt A, Ravishankar C, Biko DM, Goldberg DJ, Gupta M.
abstractText: Lymphatic dysfunction is a severe complication of the Fontan circulation. Type 3 and 4 lymphatic subtypes identified on T2-weighted cardiac MRI (CMR) are associated with worse Fontan outcomes. Correlates of lymphatic subtype are incompletely described. Of the 171 patients with single ventricle physiology who underwent pre-Fontan CMR with T2-weighting to define lymphatic subtype between 2017 and 2021, 148 had standard-risk lymphatics (subtypes 1, 2, and 3 without pre-Fontan chylous effusions), and 23 had high-risk lymphatics (subtypes 3 with a history of pre-Fontan chylous effusions and 4). The two groups did not differ by demographic, anatomic, or pre-Fontan surgical features. High-risk subtype patients had more pre-fontan hospital days (84 vs. 44, p < 0.001), worse atrioventricular valve regurgitation (AVVR) by echocardiogram, higher aortopulmonary collateral (APC) burden (38% vs. 30%, p = 0.004) and Qp: Qs (1.2 vs. 1.05, p = 0.01) by CMR, and higher left pulmonary artery pressure (11mmHg vs. 10mmHg, p = 0.04) and higher systemic ventricular end diastolic pressure (8mmHg vs. 7mmHg, p = 0.02) by cardiac catheterization. High-risk patients were more frequently deemed to be unsuitable for Fontan palliation (22% vs. 4%, p = < 0.001) while those who did undergo palliation had longer post-Fontan length of stay (14 days vs. 9 days, p = 0.01) and more post-fontan chest tube days (10.5 vs. 7, p = 0.002). This study demonstrates a link between pre-Fontan clinical factors and lymphatic subtype. Further work is needed to understand whether modification of these risk factors might impact lymphatic anatomy.

title: Self-Expandable Harmony Valve Implantation in Supravalvular Pulmonary Position After Senning Procedure: A Case Report.
authorString: Crauciuc A, Georgiev S, Eicken A, Ewert P, Gendera K.
abstractText: Transcatheter pulmonary valve implantation has emerged as a minimally invasive therapeutic strategy for the management of right ventricular outflow tract dysfunction, particularly in patients considered unsuitable for repeat surgical intervention. Implantation of the self-expandable Harmony valve represents a therapeutic option for patients with large right ventricular outflow tracts that are unsuitable for balloon-expandable devices. However, significant anatomical variability, particularly in patients following the atrial switch procedure, poses procedural challenges and underscores the importance of meticulous pre-procedural planning. A 44-year-old male with Transposition of the Great Arteries underwent a Senning-Brom procedure in infancy, followed by surgical correction of a baffle leak and pulmonary valve reconstruction at the age of 22. Over time, he developed progressive severe pulmonary regurgitation, confirmed by serial MRI, showing worsening regurgitant fraction (44%) and significant left ventricular (subpulmonic) dilation. The pre-procedural CT screening report for the Harmony valve (TPV25) revealed complex LVOT anatomy, with adequate proximal anchoring but suboptimal distal oversizing. Despite complex anatomy and suboptimal distal oversizing, the procedure was undertaken based on the anatomical dimensions of the main pulmonary artery, favorable proximal anatomy, and a safe distance from the coronary arteries. The procedure was performed via femoral access, and the valve was advanced into the pulmonary artery and deployed in a controlled, stepwise manner at a high level of the bifurcation. Final angiography confirmed stable positioning, optimal anchoring, and complete resolution of pulmonary regurgitation, with preserved coronary flow and no evidence of compression, indicating a successful outcome. This case demonstrates that Harmony valve implantation in a supravalvular pulmonary position is feasible in patients with Transposition of the Great Arteries following atrial switch repair, despite complex anatomy and suboptimal distal oversizing, when the procedure is guided by comprehensive multimodality imaging and adapted implantation strategies.

title: Delayed Intramyocardial Transplantation of Autologous Cardiac Atrial Stem Cells Attenuates Adverse Remodeling in Chronic Ischemic Cardiomyopathy
authorString: Hendrikx M, Daniels A, Fanton Y, De Bouver C, Jamaer L, Rummens J, Hensen K.
abstractText:
Background:

Cell therapy for chronic ischaemic cardiomyopathy remains limited by poor myocardial retention and uncertain regenerative efficacy. We evaluated the effects of delayed intramyocardial transplantation of autologous cardiac atrial stem cells in a large-animal model of established chronic myocardial infarction.

Methods:

Myocardial infarction was induced in Göttingen minipigs by two-hour left anterior descending coronary artery occlusion. After two months of post-infarction remodeling, animals were randomly allocated to intramyocardial transplantation of autologous cardiac atrial stem cells or control treatment. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and three-dimensional electromechanical mapping were performed before treatment and two months thereafter. Histological and immunofluorescence analyses assessed persistence and phenotype of transplanted cells.

Results:

At follow-up, left ventricular ejection fraction was preserved in treated animals but declined in controls (55 ± 9% versus 41 ± 7%; p = 0.0002). Treatment attenuated adverse ventricular remodeling, with preservation of end-systolic volume and regional wall thickening. Late gadolinium enhancement-defined infarct mass decreased from 6.2 ± 2.0 g to 4.0 ± 1.0 g in treated animals and was significantly lower than in controls at follow-up (p = 0.04). Electromechanical mapping demonstrated improved myocardial electrical viability and regional mechanical function. Transplanted cells persisted within the injured myocardium and exhibited cardiomyocyte-associated structural features.

Conclusions:

Delayed intramyocardial transplantation of autologous cardiac atrial stem cells attenuated adverse remodeling and was associated with improved regional myocardial structure and function in established chronic ischaemic cardiomyopathy.

title: The Burden of Occult Cerebrovascular Disease in CKD: A Scoping Review.
authorString: Vasaghi-Gharamaleki M, Jazayeri SB, Pillai A, Johansen KL, Murray AM, Sedaghat S, Sabayan B.
